Before the exam — a 3-pass plan

Pass 1 (understand): read each lecture's explanation and diagram. If the diagram makes sense, the formulas will follow.

Pass 2 (recall): close the notes and answer each lecture's recall questions from memory. Anything you cannot say out loud is what you revise next.

Pass 3 (do): work the practice problems listed in each lecture. The plan says these are for practice only — no guarantee they appear in exams — but they are the shapes the exam draws from.

Lecture 0 — Recap: 3-Space, Vectors, Planes and Quadric Surfaces (Anton 11.1–11.8)

This lecture is the toolbox for the whole course: how to describe points, arrows, lines, flat surfaces and curved surfaces in three-dimensional space.

Welcome — before we do any calculus, we need to be able to talk about space itself. Think of ordinary 3D space as a big empty room. To say where anything is, we use three numbers, (x, y, z): how far along the floor one way, how far along the floor the other way, and how high up. That is all a "coordinate system" is — three rulers at right angles to each other. The distance between two points is just Pythagoras' theorem stretched into three dimensions: square each difference, add them, and take the square root.

Now, a vector is simply an arrow: it has a length and a direction. We write it as three numbers, like ⟨1, 2, 3⟩, which tell us how far the arrow goes in the x, y and z directions. Its length, called its magnitude, is √(1² + 2² + 3²). If you divide a vector by its own length you get a unit vector — the same arrow, shrunk to length 1, pointing the same way. Unit vectors are handy because they carry pure direction and nothing else.

There are two ways to multiply vectors, and they answer two different questions. The dot product asks "how much do these two arrows agree?" — you multiply matching components and add: u·v = u₁v₁ + u₂v₂ + u₃v₃. It also equals ‖u‖‖v‖cos θ, where θ is the angle between the arrows, so you can use it to find angles. If the dot product is zero, the arrows are perpendicular — they do not agree at all. The cross product, u×v, is a new arrow that sticks straight out of both of them (right-hand rule: curl your fingers from u to v and your thumb points along u×v). Its length is ‖u‖‖v‖sin θ, which is exactly the area of the parallelogram the two arrows make. If the cross product is zero, the arrows are parallel.

A line in space is just a starting point plus a direction arrow, stretched out: r = r₀ + t v. As the number t grows, you walk along the line; if you only let t run between two values, you get a line segment. A plane is a flat sheet, and it is described by the arrow that sticks out of it at right angles — its normal. If n = ⟨a, b, c⟩ is the normal and P₀ is a point on the plane, every point P on the plane satisfies a(x − x₀) + b(y − y₀) + c(z − z₀) = 0. You can find a normal by taking the cross product of two arrows that lie in the plane.

Finally, quadric surfaces are the curved shapes you get from second-degree equations — ellipsoids (like a rugby ball), cones, paraboloids (like a satellite dish), hyperboloids (like a cooling tower) and the saddle, the hyperbolic paraboloid. You tell them apart by looking at their traces: slice the surface with a coordinate plane and see what curve comes out — an ellipse, a hyperbola, a parabola. The sign pattern in the equation is the giveaway: a hyperboloid of one sheet has two plus signs and one minus, while one of two sheets has one plus and two minus. And when rectangular coordinates get awkward, we switch to cylindrical coordinates (r, θ, z — like polar coordinates with height) or spherical coordinates (ρ, θ, φ — distance from the origin, angle round the equator, and angle down from the top). Watch out: in Anton's convention φ is measured from the positive z-axis, so φ = 0 is straight up and φ = π/2 is the flat xy-plane.

Why do we need all of this? Single-variable calculus lives on a number line: one input, one output. But real things move in space — a thrown ball, a satellite, a drone delivering a parcel. To say where anything is, and how it moves, you need three numbers, and vectors are the language for it. Think of giving directions in a city: "walk 3 blocks east, 2 blocks north, then go up 1 floor" is a vector. The address of the building is a point. The whole course is built on keeping those two ideas straight and letting them work together.

The most common confusion in this lecture is exactly that: a point is a place, a vector is an instruction. The same three numbers ⟨1, 2, 3⟩ can mean the place (1, 2, 3) or the instruction "go 1 east, 2 north, 3 up". A position vector is the instruction that takes you from the origin to the point — that is why the same numbers do both jobs, and why we write a point and its position vector with the same coordinates. Whenever you get stuck, ask yourself: am I looking at a place, or at a set of directions?

The second stuck point is the dot product versus the cross product. Students mix up which one gives a number and which one gives a vector. Hold onto this: the dot product measures agreement — one single number saying how much two arrows point the same way. In physics it is work: force · displacement. The cross product measures perpendicularity — it builds a brand-new arrow sticking straight out of both of them. In physics it is torque. And the order matters for the cross product (u × v = −(v × u)) but not for the dot product. If you remember "dot = a number about agreement, cross = an arrow sticking out", you will rarely mix them up.

A close cousin of that confusion is projection versus component. The scalar projection (the "component") is a number — how far along the other arrow you get. The vector projection is an arrow — the shadow that one vector casts onto the other. Same idea, different kind of answer, and the exam will ask for both, so check which one the question wants before you start.

Why is a plane described by its normal? Because "flat" means "every direction inside the sheet is perpendicular to one fixed arrow". Picture a tabletop: the normal is the direction a nail driven straight through the table would point. That is why you can find a normal by taking the cross product of any two arrows lying in the plane — the cross product is built to be perpendicular to both of them, so it is perpendicular to the whole sheet.

Finally, quadric surfaces look frightening until you realise the trick: a trace is just a slice. Slice a loaf of bread and the cross-section tells you the shape of the loaf; slice a quadric with a coordinate plane and the curve you get — ellipse, hyperbola or parabola — tells you the shape of the surface. The sign pattern in the equation is a shortcut for the same thing: two plus signs and one minus is a hyperboloid of one sheet, one plus and two minus is a hyperboloid of two sheets. But if the equation is not in standard form, complete the square first — the sign pattern only speaks clearly once the squares are completed.

A small worked check — spherical to rectangular. Take the spherical point (ρ, θ, φ) = (2, π/3, π/4). The formulas are x = ρ sin φ cos θ, y = ρ sin φ sin θ, z = ρ cos φ. First, sin φ = sin(π/4) = √2/2 and cos φ = √2/2; cos θ = cos(π/3) = 1/2 and sin θ = √3/2. Then x = 2 · (√2/2) · (1/2) = √2/2; y = 2 · (√2/2) · (√3/2) = √6/2; z = 2 · (√2/2) = √2. So the point is (√2/2, √6/2, √2). As a sanity check, x2 + y2 + z2 = 1/2 + 6/4 + 2 = 4, which is ρ2 — exactly as it should be, since ρ is the distance from the origin.

Distance: d = √[(x2 − x1)2 + (y2 − y1)2 + (z2 − z1)2]

Sphere, centre (h, k, l), radius r: (x − h)2 + (y − k)2 + (z − l)2 = r2

Magnitude: ‖v‖ = √(a12 + a22 + a32), unit vector = v / ‖v‖

Dot product: u·v = u1v1 + u2v2 + u3v3 = ‖u‖‖v‖cos θ, so cos θ = (u·v) / (‖u‖‖v‖)

Scalar projection: compv u = (u·v) / ‖v‖; vector projection: projv u = [(u·v) / ‖v‖2] v

Cross product: ‖u × v‖ = ‖u‖‖v‖ sin θ = area of the parallelogram; u × v = −(v × u)

Line: r = r0 + t v, i.e. x = x0 + at, y = y0 + bt, z = z0 + ct

Plane: a(x − x0) + b(y − y0) + c(z − z0) = 0, i.e. ax + by + cz = d

Distance from P1 to a plane: D = |ax1 + by1 + cz1 − d| / √(a2 + b2 + c2)

Cylindrical: x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ, z = z; Spherical: x = ρ sin φ cos θ, y = ρ sin φ sin θ, z = ρ cos φ

Ellipsoid: x2/a2 + y2/b2 + z2/c2 = 1; saddle (hyperbolic paraboloid): z/c = x2/a2 − y2/b2

Worked example — the angle between two vectors. Problem: u = ⟨1, 2, 3⟩, v = ⟨2, 0, 1⟩. Find the angle θ between them.

Step 1 — Find the dot product: u·v = (1)(2) + (2)(0) + (3)(1) = 2 + 0 + 3 = 5. This number alone tells us the arrows partly agree (it is positive, not zero).

Step 2 — Find the two lengths: ‖u‖ = √(1 + 4 + 9) = √14, and ‖v‖ = √(4 + 0 + 1) = √5.

Step 3 — Use cos θ = (u·v) / (‖u‖‖v‖): cos θ = 5 / (√14 · √5) = 5/√70.

Step 4 — Take the inverse cosine: θ = cos−1(5/√70) ≈ 53.3°. Answer: θ ≈ 53.3°. The arrows are neither perpendicular (that would need a dot product of 0) nor parallel — they meet at a bit more than a half-right-angle.

Watch out: φ in spherical coordinates is measured from the positive z-axis, not from the xy-plane — φ = 0 is straight up and φ = π/2 is the flat xy-plane, so swapping them turns every conversion upside down.

  • What does the dot product tell you about two vectors, and what value means they are perpendicular?
  • How is the cross product different from the dot product — what kind of answer does each one give?
  • How do you write the equation of a plane if you know one point on it and its normal vector?
  • How do you tell a hyperboloid of one sheet from a hyperboloid of two sheets just by looking at the equation?

Lecture 0 — Recap (Anton 11.1–11.8)

No exercises are assigned for Lecture 0 in the plan (recap, self-study). The three worked checks below use the section formulas.

Check 1 — Dot product and the angle between two vectors

Find the angle between u = ⟨1, 2, 3⟩ and v = ⟨2, 0, 1⟩.

Step 1. u · v = (1)(2) + (2)(0) + (3)(1) = 5.

Step 2. ‖u‖ = √(1 + 4 + 9) = √14, ‖v‖ = √(4 + 0 + 1) = √5.

Step 3. cos θ = (u · v)/(‖u‖‖v‖) = 5/√70, so θ = cos−1(5/√70) ≈ 53.3°.

Answer: θ ≈ 53.3°.

Check 2 — Cross product and area

Find u × v and ‖u × v‖ for u = ⟨1, 0, 0⟩, v = ⟨0, 1, 0⟩.

Step 1. u × v = |i j k; 1 0 0; 0 1 0| = k.

Step 2. ‖u × v‖ = 1, which is the area of the unit square in the xy-plane — consistent with ‖u × v‖ = ‖u‖‖v‖ sin 90° = 1.

Answer: u × v = k, ‖u × v‖ = 1.

Check 3 — Spherical to rectangular coordinates

Convert the spherical point (ρ, θ, φ) = (2, π/3, π/4) to rectangular coordinates (Anton's convention: φ is measured from the positive z-axis).

Step 1. x = ρ sin φ cos θ = 2 · (√2/2) · (1/2) = √2/2.

Step 2. y = ρ sin φ sin θ = 2 · (√2/2) · (√3/2) = √6/2.

Step 3. z = ρ cos φ = 2 · (√2/2) = √2.

Answer: (√2/2, √6/2, √2).

Lecture 1 — Vector-Valued Functions (Anton 12.1, pp. 841–847)

A vector-valued function is a journey: one number, t (think "time"), tells you where a moving point is at every moment, and the tip of its position arrow traces out a curve.

So far a function has taken in one number and given back one number, like f(x) = x². Now we upgrade: a vector-valued function takes in one number, t, and gives back a whole arrow — a vector. We write it as r(t) = x(t)i + y(t)j + z(t)k. Don't let the notation scare you: it is just three ordinary functions glued together, one for each coordinate. At each moment t, the arrow r(t) points from the origin to where our traveller is. If you follow the tip of that arrow as t changes, the tip draws a curve in space. That curve is the graph of the function.

Here is the first thing that trips students up, and it is the most-tested idea in this lecture: the domain of r(t). Each component function has its own domain — the set of t-values it accepts. The whole function only works where all of its components work, so the domain is the intersection of the component domains, not the union. Think of it like a road trip with three passengers: the trip can only go where every passenger is allowed to go. For example, if one component has ln t (needs t > 0) and another has √(t − 2) (needs t ≥ 2), then together they need t ≥ 2 — the stricter rule wins.

The same curve can be described in two languages. The parametric form writes the coordinates separately, x = x(t), y = y(t), z = z(t); the vector form packs them into one arrow, r(t). Switching between them is just repackaging, and the exercises ask you to do it both ways. Some curves you should recognise on sight. A straight line is r(t) = r₀ + t v — a starting point plus a direction, from last lecture. A circle in the plane is r(t) = a cos t i + a sin t j. And the beautiful one is the circular helix, r(t) = a cos t i + a sin t j + c t k: the point goes round in a circle while steadily climbing, like a spiral staircase or a corkscrew. The distance it climbs in one full turn is called the pitch, and it is 2πc — one turn takes t through 2π, and the height is c times that.

Two more useful constructions. A line segment joining two points r₀ and r₁ is r(t) = (1 − t)r₀ + t r₁ for 0 ≤ t ≤ 1: at t = 0 you are at r₀, at t = 1 you are at r₁, and in between you slide smoothly from one to the other. And a curve can be born as the intersection of two surfaces: if a point lies on both surfaces, its coordinates must satisfy both equations, so you set one variable equal to t and solve for the others. Finally, remember that the direction of increasing t is part of the picture — the same curve walked backwards is a different journey, and the sketches in the exercises always ask you to mark which way t grows.

Why does this idea exist? A function like f(x) = x2 tells you a quantity — a temperature, a price. But a planet's orbit, a roller-coaster track, the flight of a thrown ball are not quantities: they are places changing in time. One number, the time t, has to produce a whole position. That is what a vector-valued function is for. Think of a GPS log: you feed in the time on the clock, and out comes where you are. The curve it traces is the trail you left behind — like a snail's trail, or a jet's contrail in the sky.

Keep this picture in your head: the arrow r(t) always starts at the origin, and its tip is the traveller. As t grows, the tip moves and draws the curve. The curve is not the arrow — the curve is the path the tip has walked. That is why the same curve can be drawn by different functions (walk the same road at a different speed, or backwards), and why the direction of increasing t is part of the description, not decoration.

Here is a subtle trap that the exercises are built around: two curves can visit the same point at different times. Imagine two cars crossing the same crossroads, one at noon and one at 3 pm — the crossroads is shared, but the journeys are different. So if you solve r1(t) = r2(t) and find no t that works, the curves might still cross: they may reach the shared point at different parameter values. To find intersections properly, solve r1(t) = r2(s) with two different parameters, or check whether a point on one curve also lies on the other.

Another thing students stumble on: parametric form and vector form are the same curve in two costumes. Writing x = cos t, y = sin t is the same information as r(t) = cos t i + sin t j, just unpacked. The exercises ask you to switch between them because later lectures will hand you one form and expect the other. And a curve born as the intersection of two surfaces is just a point that has to satisfy two equations at once — set one variable equal to t and solve for the others, and the curve falls out.

A small worked check — a curve where two surfaces meet. Take the paraboloid z = x2 + y2 and the plane x − y = 0 (Exercise 12.1-35). A point on both must satisfy both equations. Set x = t. Then the plane says y = x, so y = t. Then the paraboloid says z = x2 + y2 = t2 + t2 = 2t2. So the intersection curve is r(t) = t i + t j + 2t2 k. Read it as a journey: the traveller walks along the line y = x on the floor while climbing the paraboloid, and the height grows like 2t2 — a parabola standing in the vertical plane y = x. That is the whole method: one variable becomes t, the other equations do the rest.

Vector-valued function: r(t) = x(t)i + y(t)j + z(t)k

Domain of r(t) = intersection of the domains of x(t), y(t), z(t)

Circular helix: r(t) = a cos t i + a sin t j + c t k; pitch (rise per turn) = 2πc

Line segment from r0 to r1: r(t) = (1 − t)r0 + t r1, 0 ≤ t ≤ 1

Line: r(t) = r0 + t v

Worked example — domain and value. Problem (Ex. 12.1-3): r(t) = cos πt i − ln t j + √(t − 2) k. Find the domain of r, and find r(3).

Step 1 — Look at each component separately. cos πt is happy for every t. ln t needs t > 0. √(t − 2) needs t − 2 ≥ 0, i.e. t ≥ 2.

Step 2 — The domain is the intersection: t must satisfy all the conditions at once, so t > 0 and t ≥ 2. The stricter one wins: the domain is [2, ∞).

Step 3 — Evaluate at t = 3 (which is allowed, since 3 ≥ 2). First component: cos 3π = −1. Second: −ln 3. Third: √(3 − 2) = √1 = 1.

Step 4 — Put it together: r(3) = −i − (ln 3)j + k. Answer: domain [2, ∞), r(3) = −i − (ln 3)j + k.

Watch out: the domain of a vector-valued function is the intersection of the component domains, not the union — a t-value is allowed only if every component accepts it, so the strictest component decides.

  • In your own words, what is a vector-valued function, and what does its graph look like?
  • Why is the domain the intersection of the component domains? Give an example where one component restricts it.
  • What curve does r(t) = a cos t i + a sin t j + c t k trace, and how far does it climb in one full turn?
  • How do you write the line segment joining two points r₀ and r₁ as a vector function?

Lecture 1 — Vector-Valued Functions (Anton 12.1)

Ex. 12.1: 1

Find the domain of r(t) = cos t i − 3t j and the value of r(t0) for t0 = π.

Step 1. Both components, cos t and −3t, are defined for every real t, so the domain is (−∞, +∞).

Step 2. r(π) = cos π i − 3π j = −i − 3π j.

Answer: domain (−∞, +∞); r(π) = −i − 3πj.

Ex. 12.1: 2

Find the domain of r(t) = ⟨3t + 1, t2⟩ and the value of r(t0) for t0 = 1.

Step 1. Both components are polynomials, defined for all real t, so the domain is (−∞, +∞).

Step 2. r(1) = ⟨3(1) + 1, 12⟩ = ⟨4, 1⟩.

Answer: domain (−∞, +∞); r(1) = ⟨4, 1⟩.

Ex. 12.1: 3

Find the domain of r(t) = cos πt i − ln t j + √(t − 2) k and the value of r(t0) for t0 = 3.

Step 1. The domain is the intersection of the component domains: ln t needs t > 0, √(t − 2) needs t ≥ 2, and cos πt needs nothing. Hence the domain is [2, +∞).

Step 2. r(3) = cos 3π i − ln 3 j + √(3 − 2) k = −i − (ln 3) j + k.

Answer: domain [2, +∞); r(3) = −i − (ln 3)j + k.

Ex. 12.1: 4

Find the domain of r(t) = ⟨2e−t, sin−1 t, ln(1 − t)⟩ and the value of r(t0) for t0 = 0.

Step 1. Component domains: 2e−t is defined for all t; sin−1 t needs −1 ≤ t ≤ 1; ln(1 − t) needs 1 − t > 0, i.e. t < 1. The intersection is [−1, 1).

Step 2. r(0) = ⟨2e0, sin−1 0, ln 1⟩ = ⟨2, 0, 0⟩.

Answer: domain [−1, 1); r(0) = ⟨2, 0, 0⟩.

Ex. 12.1: 5

Express the parametric equations x = 3 cos t, y = t + sin t as a single vector equation r = x(t)i + y(t)j.

Read off the components directly: r(t) = 3 cos t i + (t + sin t) j.

Answer: r(t) = 3 cos t i + (t + sin t)j.

Ex. 12.1: 6

Express the parametric equations x = 2t, y = 2 sin 3t, z = 5 cos 3t as a single vector equation r = x(t)i + y(t)j + z(t)k.

Read off the components directly: r(t) = 2t i + 2 sin 3t j + 5 cos 3t k.

Answer: r(t) = 2t i + 2 sin 3t j + 5 cos 3t k.

Ex. 12.1: 7

Find the parametric equations that correspond to the vector equation r = 3t i − 2 j.

The i-component is x and the j-component is y: x = 3t, y = −2.

Answer: x = 3t, y = −2.

Ex. 12.1: 8

Find the parametric equations that correspond to the vector equation r = (2t − 1)i − 3√t j + sin 3t k.

Read off the three components: x = 2t − 1, y = −3√t, z = sin 3t.

Answer: x = 2t − 1, y = −3√t, z = sin 3t.

Ex. 12.1: 9

Describe the graph of r = (3 − 2t)i + 5t j.

Step 1. The parametric equations are x = 3 − 2t, y = 5t.

Step 2. Eliminate t: t = y/5, so x = 3 − 2y/5, a straight line. It passes through (3, 0) (at t = 0) with direction vector −2i + 5j.

Answer: the line in 2-space through (3, 0) with direction vector −2i + 5j.

Ex. 12.1: 10

Describe the graph of r = 2 sin 3t i − 2 cos 3t j.

Step 1. x = 2 sin 3t, y = −2 cos 3t, so x2 + y2 = 4(sin2 3t + cos2 3t) = 4.

Step 2. The graph is a circle of radius 2 centred at the origin, traced as t increases (starting at (0, −2) when t = 0).

Answer: the circle x2 + y2 = 4 (radius 2, centre the origin).

Ex. 12.1: 11

Describe the graph of r = 2t i − 3 j + (1 + 3t)k.

Step 1. The parametric equations are x = 2t, y = −3, z = 1 + 3t, i.e. a line: r = (0i − 3j + 1k) + t(2i + 3k).

Step 2. It passes through (0, −3, 1) and is parallel to the vector 2i + 3k.

Answer: the line in 3-space through (0, −3, 1) parallel to 2i + 3k.

Ex. 12.1: 12

Describe the graph of r = 3i + 2 cos t j + 2 sin t k.

Step 1. x = 3 is constant, while y = 2 cos t, z = 2 sin t satisfy y2 + z2 = 4.

Step 2. The graph is a circle of radius 2 in the plane x = 3, centred at (3, 0, 0).

Answer: the circle of radius 2 in the plane x = 3, centred at (3, 0, 0).

Ex. 12.1: 13

Describe the graph of r = 2 cos t i − 3 sin t j + k.

Step 1. z = 1 is constant, while x = 2 cos t, y = −3 sin t satisfy x2/4 + y2/9 = 1.

Step 2. The graph is an ellipse in the plane z = 1, centred at (0, 0, 1), with semi-axes 2 and 3.

Answer: an ellipse centred at (0, 0, 1) in the plane z = 1.

Ex. 12.1: 14

Describe the graph of r = −3i + (1 − t)j + t k.

Step 1. The parametric equations are x = −3, y = 1 − t, z = t, i.e. r = (−3i + j) + t(−j + k).

Step 2. It is a line in the plane x = −3, passing through (−3, 1, 0) with direction vector −j + k; note y + z = 1 on the line.

Answer: the line in the plane x = −3 through (−3, 1, 0) with direction −j + k.

Ex. 12.1: 15

(a) Find the slope of the line in 2-space represented by r = (1 − 2t)i − (2 − 3t)j. (b) Find the coordinates of the point where the line r = (2 + t)i + (1 − 2t)j + 3t k intersects the xz-plane.

Step 1 (a). x = 1 − 2t, y = −2 + 3t. Eliminate t: t = (1 − x)/2, so y = −2 + 3(1 − x)/2 = −(1/2) − (3/2)x. The slope is −3/2. (Equivalently, direction vector ⟨−2, 3⟩ has slope 3/(−2).)

Step 2 (b). The xz-plane is y = 0, so 1 − 2t = 0, giving t = 1/2. Then x = 2 + 1/2 = 5/2 and z = 3(1/2) = 3/2.

Answer: (a) slope −3/2; (b) (5/2, 0, 3/2).

Ex. 12.1: 16

(a) Find the y-intercept of the line in 2-space represented by r = (3 + 2t)i + 5t j. (b) Find the coordinates of the point where the line r = t i + (1 + 2t)j − 3t k intersects the plane 3x − y − z = 2.

Step 1 (a). The y-intercept is where x = 0: 3 + 2t = 0 gives t = −3/2, and then y = 5(−3/2) = −15/2. The intercept point is (0, −15/2).

Step 2 (b). Substitute x = t, y = 1 + 2t, z = −3t into 3x − y − z = 2: 3t − (1 + 2t) − (−3t) = 2, i.e. 4t − 1 = 2, so t = 3/4. Then x = 3/4, y = 1 + 3/2 = 5/2, z = −9/4.

Answer: (a) (0, −15/2); (b) (3/4, 5/2, −9/4).

Ex. 12.1: 17

Sketch the line segment represented by each vector equation. (a) r = (1 − t)i + t j; 0 ≤ t ≤ 1. (b) r = (1 − t)(i + j) + t(i − j); 0 ≤ t ≤ 1.

Step 1 (a). At t = 0, r = i (the point (1, 0)); at t = 1, r = j (the point (0, 1)). The graph is the straight segment joining (1, 0) to (0, 1) in the xy-plane.

Step 2 (b). Expand: r = i + (1 − 2t)j. At t = 0 the point is (1, 1); at t = 1 it is (1, −1). The graph is the vertical segment x = 1 from y = 1 to y = −1.

Answer: (a) segment from (1, 0) to (0, 1); (b) segment from (1, 1) to (1, −1).

Ex. 12.1: 18

Sketch the line segment represented by each vector equation. (a) r = (1 − t)(i + j) + t k; 0 ≤ t ≤ 1. (b) r = (1 − t)(i + j + k) + t(i + j); 0 ≤ t ≤ 1.

Step 1 (a). At t = 0, r = i + j (the point (1, 1, 0)); at t = 1, r = k (the point (0, 0, 1)). The graph is the straight segment joining (1, 1, 0) to (0, 0, 1).

Step 2 (b). At t = 0, r = i + j + k (the point (1, 1, 1)); at t = 1, r = i + j (the point (1, 1, 0)). The graph is the vertical segment from (1, 1, 1) down to (1, 1, 0).

Answer: (a) segment from (1, 1, 0) to (0, 0, 1); (b) segment from (1, 1, 1) to (1, 1, 0).

Ex. 12.1: 19

Write a vector equation for the line segment from P to Q, where the figure shows P = (3, 4) and Q = (0, 0) in the xy-plane.

Step 1. The segment from r0 = 3i + 4j to r1 = 0 is r = (1 − t)r0 + t r1, 0 ≤ t ≤ 1.

Step 2. Substituting: r = (1 − t)(3i + 4j), 0 ≤ t ≤ 1.

Answer: r = (1 − t)(3i + 4j), 0 ≤ t ≤ 1.

Ex. 12.1: 20

Write a vector equation for the line segment from P to Q, where the figure shows a box of dimensions 2 (x) by 3 (y) by 4 (z) with P = (0, 0, 4) at the top corner on the z-axis and Q = (2, 3, 0) at the opposite bottom corner.

Step 1. r0 = 4k and r1 = 2i + 3j. The segment is r = (1 − t)r0 + t r1, 0 ≤ t ≤ 1.

Step 2. Substituting: r = (1 − t)(4k) + t(2i + 3j) = 2t i + 3t j + (4 − 4t)k, 0 ≤ t ≤ 1.

Answer: r = 2t i + 3t j + (4 − 4t)k, 0 ≤ t ≤ 1.

Ex. 12.1: 21

Sketch the graph of r(t) = 2i + t j and show the direction of increasing t.

Step 1. x = 2 is constant and y = t varies, so the graph is the vertical line x = 2 in the xy-plane.

Step 2. As t increases, y increases, so the direction of increasing t is upward.

Answer: the vertical line x = 2, traced upward as t increases.

Ex. 12.1: 22

Sketch the graph of r(t) = ⟨3t − 4, 6t + 2⟩ and show the direction of increasing t.

Step 1. x = 3t − 4, y = 6t + 2. Eliminate t: t = (x + 4)/3, so y = 6(x + 4)/3 + 2 = 2x + 10, a line of slope 2 through (−4, 2) (at t = 0).

Step 2. As t increases, both x and y increase, so the line is traced up and to the right.

Answer: the line y = 2x + 10, traced up-right as t increases.

Ex. 12.1: 23

Sketch the graph of r(t) = (1 + cos t)i + (3 − sin t)j, 0 ≤ t ≤ 2π, and show the direction of increasing t.

Step 1. (x − 1)2 + (y − 3)2 = cos2 t + sin2 t = 1: a circle of radius 1 centred at (1, 3).

Step 2. At t = 0 the point is (2, 3); as t increases, y = 3 − sin t decreases first, so the circle is traced clockwise.

Answer: the circle (x − 1)2 + (y − 3)2 = 1, traced clockwise as t increases.

Ex. 12.1: 24

Sketch the graph of r(t) = ⟨2 cos t, 5 sin t⟩, 0 ≤ t ≤ 2π, and show the direction of increasing t.

Step 1. x2/4 + y2/25 = cos2 t + sin2 t = 1: an ellipse centred at the origin with semi-axes 2 (x) and 5 (y).

Step 2. At t = 0 the point is (2, 0); as t increases, y increases first, so the ellipse is traced counterclockwise.

Answer: the ellipse x2/4 + y2/25 = 1, traced counterclockwise as t increases.

Ex. 12.1: 25

Sketch the graph of r(t) = cosh t i + sinh t j and show the direction of increasing t.

Step 1. x = cosh t, y = sinh t, so x2 − y2 = cosh2 t − sinh2 t = 1, with x = cosh t ≥ 1: the right branch of the hyperbola x2 − y2 = 1.

Step 2. As t increases, y = sinh t increases, so the branch is traced upward, starting at (1, 0) when t = 0.

Answer: the right branch of the hyperbola x2 − y2 = 1, traced upward as t increases.

Ex. 12.1: 26

Sketch the graph of r(t) = √t i + (2t + 4)j and show the direction of increasing t.

Step 1. x = √t ≥ 0, y = 2t + 4. Eliminate t: t = x2, so y = 2x2 + 4 with x ≥ 0: the right half of the parabola y = 2x2 + 4, starting at (0, 4) when t = 0.

Step 2. As t increases, both x and y increase, so the curve is traced up and to the right.

Answer: the half-parabola y = 2x2 + 4, x ≥ 0, traced up-right as t increases.

Ex. 12.1: 27

Sketch the graph of r(t) = 2 cos t i + 2 sin t j + t k and show the direction of increasing t.

Step 1. x2 + y2 = 4 and z = t: a circular helix of radius 2 around the z-axis, rising steadily.

Step 2. Looking down the z-axis, the (x, y) point moves counterclockwise as t increases, and z increases, so the helix winds upward counterclockwise.

Answer: a circular helix of radius 2 about the z-axis, rising counterclockwise as t increases.

Ex. 12.1: 28

Sketch the graph of r(t) = 9 cos t i + 4 sin t j + t k and show the direction of increasing t.

Step 1. x2/81 + y2/16 = 1 and z = t: an elliptical helix — the (x, y) point moves on the ellipse with semi-axes 9 and 4 while z rises steadily.

Step 2. As t increases the ellipse is traced counterclockwise (from (9, 0, 0)) and z increases.

Answer: an elliptical helix (ellipse x2/81 + y2/16 = 1 in the xy-plane, rising in z), traced counterclockwise as t increases.

Ex. 12.1: 29

Sketch the graph of r(t) = t i + t2 j + 2k and show the direction of increasing t.

Step 1. z = 2 is constant and y = x2: the parabola y = x2 in the plane z = 2.

Step 2. As t increases, x increases, so the parabola is traced from left to right (through its vertex (0, 0, 2) at t = 0).

Answer: the parabola y = x2 in the plane z = 2, traced left to right as t increases.

Ex. 12.1: 30

Sketch the graph of r(t) = t i + t j + sin t k, 0 ≤ t ≤ 2π, and show the direction of increasing t.

Step 1. x = y = t, so the curve lies above the line y = x in the xy-plane, with height z = sin t.

Step 2. As t goes from 0 to 2π the curve moves from (0, 0, 0) up to height z = 1 at t = π/2, back to z = 0 at t = π, down to z = −1 at t = 3π/2, and back to z = 0 at t = 2π — a single sine wave riding along the line y = x.

Answer: a sine wave of amplitude 1 along the line y = x (0 ≤ t ≤ 2π), from (0, 0, 0) to (2π, 2π, 0).

Ex. 12.1: 35

Sketch the curve of intersection of the surfaces z = x2 + y2 and x − y = 0, and find parametric equations for the intersection in terms of the parameter x = t.

Step 1. From x − y = 0, y = x = t.

Step 2. Substitute into the paraboloid: z = t2 + t2 = 2t2. The intersection is the parabola z = 2x2 in the plane y = x.

Answer: x = t, y = t, z = 2t2; i.e. r(t) = t i + t j + 2t2 k.

Ex. 12.1: 36

Sketch the curve of intersection of the surfaces y + x = 0 and z = √(2 − x2 − y2), and find parametric equations for the intersection in terms of the parameter x = t.

Step 1. From y + x = 0, y = −x = −t.

Step 2. Substitute: z = √(2 − t2 − t2) = √(2 − 2t2), which needs |t| ≤ 1. The intersection is the upper half of an ellipse in the plane y = −x.

Answer: x = t, y = −t, z = √(2 − 2t2), |t| ≤ 1; i.e. r(t) = t i − t j + √(2 − 2t2) k.

Ex. 12.1: 37

Sketch the curve of intersection of the surfaces 9x2 + y2 + 9z2 = 81 and y = x2 (z > 0), and find a vector equation for the curve in terms of the parameter x = t.

Step 1. Put x = t, y = t2 into the ellipsoid: 9t2 + t4 + 9z2 = 81, so z2 = (81 − 9t2 − t4)/9.

Step 2. Since z > 0, z = (1/3)√(81 − 9t2 − t4).

Answer: r(t) = t i + t2 j + (1/3)√(81 − 9t2 − t4) k.

Ex. 12.1: 38

Sketch the curve of intersection of the surfaces y = x and x + y + z = 1, and find a vector equation for the curve in terms of the parameter x = t.

Step 1. Put x = t, y = t into the plane: t + t + z = 1, so z = 1 − 2t.

Step 2. The intersection is the straight line through (0, 0, 1) with direction i + j − 2k.

Answer: r(t) = t i + t j + (1 − 2t)k.

Ex. 12.1: 39

Show that the graph of r = t sin t i + t cos t j + t2 k lies on the paraboloid z = x2 + y2.

Step 1. x = t sin t, y = t cos t, so x2 + y2 = t2 sin2 t + t2 cos2 t = t2.

Step 2. The z-component is t2, which equals x2 + y2, so every point of the curve satisfies z = x2 + y2.

Answer: x2 + y2 = t2 = z, so the curve lies on the paraboloid.

Ex. 12.1: 40

Show that the graph of r = t i + ((1 + t)/t) j + ((1 − t2)/t) k, t > 0, lies in the plane x − y + z + 1 = 0.

Step 1. x = t, y = (1 + t)/t = 1/t + 1, z = (1 − t2)/t = 1/t − t.

Step 2. Compute x − y + z + 1 = t − (1/t + 1) + (1/t − t) + 1 = 0. Every point of the curve satisfies the plane equation.

Answer: x − y + z + 1 = 0 for all t > 0, so the curve lies in the plane.

Lecture 2 — Calculus of Vector-Valued Functions; Arc Length (Anton 12.2–12.3, pp. 848–867)

Everything you know about differentiating and integrating works on vector functions too — you just do it one component at a time — and the length of a curve is found by adding up the speeds along it.

Here is the good news: you already know how to do calculus, and this lecture barely adds anything new. A vector-valued function is three ordinary functions wearing one coat, so its limit, its continuity and its derivative are all done component by component. The limit of r(t) is just the vector of the three component limits; r is continuous at t₀ exactly when each component is; and the derivative is r′(t) = x′(t)i + y′(t)j + z′(t)k. Integration works the same way — integrate each component, and remember the constant of integration is now a vector constant, not a single number. That is a classic lost mark, so write it as a vector, C = C₁i + C₂j + C₃k.

What does the derivative mean? Imagine the curve as a road and t as the time on your watch. Then r′(t) is your velocity arrow at that moment: it points along the road in the direction you are travelling, and its length is your speed. That is why r′(t) is called the tangent vector — it touches the curve and points along it. The tangent line at the point r(t₀) is just r(t₀) + s r′(t₀): start at the point and walk along the tangent arrow. The product rules also carry over, with one warning for the cross product: d/dt [r₁ × r₂] = r₁′ × r₂ + r₁ × r₂′, and the order matters, because swapping a cross product flips its sign.

There is one subtle trap: a curve can be continuous without being differentiable. Continuity just means the road has no gaps; differentiability means it has no sharp corners either. A curve is called smooth when r′ is continuous and never zero — never a corner, and never a moment where the traveller stops dead (r′ = 0) and could turn around. A corner like y = |x| at the origin looks innocent on a graph but is not smooth, because the direction changes abruptly there.

Now the second half of the lecture: arc length, the length of a winding road. You cannot measure a curve with a straight ruler, so you chop it into many tiny pieces, measure each piece as if it were straight, and add them up. In the limit, that sum becomes an integral: the length from t = a to t = b is L = ∫ab ‖r′(t)‖ dt. Read it in words: at each moment, your speed is ‖r′(t)‖; add up speed × tiny time over the whole journey, and you get the distance travelled. The quantity ds/dt = ‖r′(t)‖ is the rate at which arc length grows.

That idea leads to a beautiful trick: reparametrisation by arc length. Instead of measuring the journey by time t, measure it by distance travelled, s. The arc length function s(t) = ∫ ‖r′(u)‖ du tells you how far you have gone by time t; turn it around to get t as a function of s, and plug that back in. The new description r(s) has a magical property: ‖dr/ds‖ = 1, unit speed — one unit of parameter always means one unit of distance, like a car whose speedometer is locked at exactly 1. For a line r₀ + t v, the speed is ‖v‖, so s = ‖v‖t and r(s) = r₀ + (s/‖v‖)v. For the circular helix, s = t√(a² + c²). Fair warning: for most curves you cannot write the arc-length parametrisation in closed form — the point is that it exists and has unit speed, not that you can always compute it by hand.

Why does this lecture exist? Describing a journey is only half the job. Once you can write down where something is at every moment, you want to know how fast it is going, which way it is heading, and how far it has travelled. That is calculus on curves — and it is exactly the dashboard of a car. The speedometer reading is ‖r′(t)‖, the direction the car is pointing is the direction of r′(t), and the odometer reading is the arc length. Everything in this lecture is one of those three dashboard instruments.

The reassuring part: you already know how to differentiate and integrate. A vector-valued function is three ordinary functions wearing one coat, so its derivative is just three ordinary derivatives standing side by side. Each coordinate has its own speedometer, and r′(t) bundles the three readings into one arrow. The only genuinely new idea is what that arrow means: it is the velocity, tangent to the road, pointing the way you are travelling.

The stuck point students hit here is displacement versus distance travelled, and it is worth slowing down for. Walk 10 km out from home and 10 km straight back: your displacement is zero — you ended where you started — but the distance you travelled is 20 km. The integral ∫r′ = r(b) − r(a) is the displacement, the straight arrow from start to finish. The arc length L = ∫‖r′‖ is the odometer reading, the distance actually walked. They are equal only if you never turn and never backtrack. In an exam, if the question says "distance travelled", you want the arc length; if it says "displacement", you want r(b) − r(a).

A second subtlety: continuous is not the same as smooth. A road can be unbroken and still have a sharp corner — think of y = |x| at the origin, where the direction changes abruptly. And a traveller can stop dead in the middle of a smooth-looking road (r′ = 0) and turn around, which also breaks smoothness. Smoothness demands both: no corners, and never a full stop. That is why the definition insists r′ is continuous and never zero.

One beautiful fact from this lecture is worth carrying with you: if a point moves so that its distance from the origin never changes — if ‖r(t)‖ is constant — then its velocity is always perpendicular to its position, r(t)·r′(t) = 0. Picture a clock hand: the hand keeps its length, so its tip can only move sideways, at right angles to the hand. A satellite in a circular orbit is the same story — its velocity is always perpendicular to the line joining it to the centre of the Earth.

A small worked check — measuring a journey by distance instead of time. Take the line x = t, y = t (Exercise 12.3-21). Its velocity is r′(t) = i + j, so the speed is ‖r′‖ = √(1 + 1) = √2 — constant, as it should be for a straight road. The distance travelled by time t is s = √2 t, so t = s/√2. Putting that back in gives the arc-length parametrisation r(s) = (s/√2)i + (s/√2)j. Check the magic property: dr/ds = (1/√2)i + (1/√2)j, and ‖dr/ds‖ = √(1/2 + 1/2) = 1 — unit speed, one unit of parameter always means one unit of distance. The same idea answers a question that now makes sense: "where are you 25 units along the line x = 1 + t, y = 3 − 2t, z = 4 + 2t?" (Exercise 12.3-23). The speed there is √(1 + 4 + 4) = 3, so s = 3t, and at s = 25 the point is (28/3, −41/3, 62/3). Once the parameter is distance, "25 units along" is a real instruction.

Derivative (componentwise): r′(t) = x′(t)i + y′(t)j + z′(t)k

Tangent line at t0: r(t0) + s r′(t0)

Dot product rule: d/dt [r1·r2] = r1′·r2 + r1·r2′

Cross product rule: d/dt [r1 × r2] = r1′ × r2 + r1 × r2′ (order matters!)

Integral (componentwise): ∫ r(t) dt = (∫x) i + (∫y) j + (∫z) k + C, where C is a vector constant

Arc length: L = ∫ab ‖r′(t)‖ dt, and ds/dt = ‖r′(t)‖

Arc length function: s(t) = ∫t₀t ‖r′(u)‖ du

Arc-length parametrisation: ‖dr/ds‖ = 1 (unit speed)

Line: s = ‖v‖t; helix: s = t√(a2 + c2)

Smooth: r′ is continuous and r′(t) ≠ 0 for all t in the interval

Worked example — arc length. Problem (Ex. 12.3-11): find the arc length of r(t) = 3 cos t i + 3 sin t j + t k, for 0 ≤ t ≤ 2π.

Step 1 — Differentiate component by component: r′(t) = −3 sin t i + 3 cos t j + k. (The derivative of 3 cos t is −3 sin t, of 3 sin t is 3 cos t, and of t is 1.)

Step 2 — Find the speed, ‖r′(t)‖: ‖r′(t)‖ = √[(−3 sin t)2 + (3 cos t)2 + 12] = √[9 sin2 t + 9 cos2 t + 1]. Factor out the 9: 9(sin2 t + cos2 t) = 9, so this is √(9 + 1) = √10. The speed is constant — this helix is travelled at a steady pace.

Step 3 — Integrate the speed from 0 to 2π: L = ∫02π √10 dt = √10 · (2π − 0) = 2π√10.

Answer: L = 2π√10. Notice how the trig identity sin2 + cos2 = 1 did all the work — that is the signature of a circular helix.

Watch out: displacement ∫r′ = r(b) − r(a) is the straight-line arrow from start to finish, not the distance travelled — the distance travelled is the arc length L = ∫‖r′‖, which is always at least as big, and usually bigger.

  • Why is the derivative of a vector-valued function just the derivative of each component, and what does r′(t) mean physically?
  • What is the difference between a curve being continuous and being smooth?
  • In words, why is the arc length L = ∫ ‖r′(t)‖ dt? What does ‖r′(t)‖ represent at each moment?
  • What is special about an arc-length parametrisation, and what is ‖dr/ds‖ for it?

Lecture 2 — Calculus of Vector-Valued Functions; Arc Length (Anton 12.2–12.3)

Ex. 12.2: 4

Find the limit limt→1 ⟨3 ln t / t2, 3/(t2 − 1), sin 2t⟩.

Step 1. Limits are computed componentwise. First component: limt→1 3 ln t / t2 = 3 · 0 / 1 = 0.

Step 2. Third component: limt→1 sin 2t = sin 2.

Step 3. Second component: 3/(t2 − 1) → −∞ as t → 1− and → +∞ as t → 1+, so it has no (two-sided) limit. Since one component fails, the vector limit fails.

Answer: the limit does not exist (the middle component is unbounded near t = 1).

Ex. 12.2: 6

Determine whether r(t) is continuous at t = 0. (a) r(t) = et i + j + csc t k. (b) r(t) = 5i − √(3t + 1) j + e2t k.

Step 1 (a). A vector-valued function is continuous at t = 0 iff each component is. The component csc t = 1/sin t is undefined at t = 0, so r is discontinuous at 0.

Step 2 (b). The components 5, −√(3t + 1) and e2t are all continuous at t = 0 (note 3(0) + 1 = 1 > 0), so r is continuous at 0.

Answer: (a) discontinuous at 0; (b) continuous at 0.

Ex. 12.2: 16

Find r′(t0) for r(t) = cos t i + sin t j + t k, t0 = π/4; sketch the graph and draw the tangent vector.

Step 1. Differentiate componentwise: r′(t) = −sin t i + cos t j + k.

Step 2. At t = π/4: r′(π/4) = −(√2/2)i + (√2/2)j + k.

Step 3. The graph is the circular helix of radius 1 about the z-axis; r′(π/4) is the tangent vector at the point (√2/2, √2/2, π/4), pointing in the direction of increasing t.

Answer: r′(π/4) = −(√2/2)i + (√2/2)j + k.

Ex. 12.2: 22

Find parametric equations of the line tangent to the graph of r(t) = ln t i + e−t j + t3 k at the point where t = t0 = 2.

Step 1. r(2) = ln 2 i + e−2 j + 8k.

Step 2. r′(t) = (1/t)i − e−t j + 3t2 k, so r′(2) = (1/2)i − e−2 j + 12k.

Step 3. The tangent line is r(2) + s r′(2): x = ln 2 + s/2, y = e−2 − s e−2, z = 8 + 12s.

Answer: x = ln 2 + s/2, y = e−2 − s·e−2, z = 8 + 12s.

Ex. 12.2: 26

Find a vector equation of the line tangent to the graph of r(t) = sin t i + cosh t j + (tan−1 t)k at the point P0(0, 1, 0).

Step 1. P0 corresponds to t = 0, since r(0) = 0i + 1j + 0k.

Step 2. r′(t) = cos t i + sinh t j + (1/(1 + t2))k, so r′(0) = i + 0j + k = i + k.

Step 3. The tangent line is r = r(0) + s r′(0) = j + s(i + k).

Answer: r = j + s(i + k), i.e. r = s i + j + s k.

Ex. 12.2: 30

Calculate d/dt [r1(t) × r2(t)] first by differentiating the product directly and then by applying the product formula, where r1(t) = cos t i + sin t j + t k and r2(t) = i + t k.

Step 1 (direct). r1 × r2 = |i j k; cos t sin t t; 1 0 t| = (t sin t)i + (t − t cos t)j − (sin t)k. Differentiating: d/dt = (sin t + t cos t)i + (1 − cos t + t sin t)j − (cos t)k.

Step 2 (product formula). d/dt [r1 × r2] = r1′ × r2 + r1 × r2′. Here r1′ = −sin t i + cos t j + k and r2′ = k. Computing both cross products and adding gives the same vector: (sin t + t cos t)i + (1 − cos t + t sin t)j − (cos t)k. ✓

Answer: d/dt [r1 × r2] = ⟨sin t + t cos t, 1 − cos t + t sin t, −cos t⟩.

Ex. 12.2: 40

Evaluate ∫01 (e2t i + e−t j + t k) dt.

Step 1. Integrate componentwise: ∫01 e2t dt = (e2 − 1)/2; ∫01 e−t dt = 1 − e−1; ∫01 t dt = 1/2.

Answer: ((e2 − 1)/2)i + (1 − e−1)j + (1/2)k.

Ex. 12.2: 48

Solve the vector initial-value problem for y(t): y′′(t) = 12t2 i − 2t j, y(0) = 2i − 4j, y′(0) = 0.

Step 1. Integrate once: y′(t) = 4t3 i − t2 j + C1. The condition y′(0) = 0 gives C1 = 0.

Step 2. Integrate again: y(t) = t4 i − (1/3)t3 j + C2. The condition y(0) = 2i − 4j gives C2 = 2i − 4j.

Answer: y(t) = (t4 + 2)i − ((1/3)t3 + 4)j.

Ex. 12.3: 9

Find the arc length of the graph of r(t) = t3 i + t j + (√6/2) t2 k, 1 ≤ t ≤ 3.

Step 1. r′(t) = 3t2 i + j + √6 t k, so ‖r′(t)‖ = √(9t4 + 1 + 6t2) = √(3t2 + 1)2 = 3t2 + 1.

Step 2. L = ∫13 (3t2 + 1) dt = [t3 + t]13 = 30 − 2 = 28.

Note: the book's printed z-component is easily misread in the PDF text; the reading z = (√6/2)t2 is the one that makes ‖r′‖ = 3t2 + 1 and gives the book's answer L = 28.

Answer: L = 28.

Ex. 12.3: 11

Find the arc length of the graph of r(t) = 3 cos t i + 3 sin t j + t k, 0 ≤ t ≤ 2π.

Step 1. r′(t) = −3 sin t i + 3 cos t j + k, so ‖r′(t)‖ = √(9 sin2 t + 9 cos2 t + 1) = √10.

Step 2. L = ∫02π √10 dt = 2π√10.

Answer: L = 2π√10.

Ex. 12.3: 21

(a) Find the arc length parametrization of the line x = t, y = t that has the same orientation as the given line and has reference point (0, 0). (b) Find the arc length parametrization of the line x = t, y = t, z = t that has the same orientation as the given line and has reference point (0, 0, 0).

Step 1 (a). r(t) = t i + t j, r′(t) = i + j, speed ‖r′‖ = √2, so s = √2 t and t = s/√2. Hence x = s/√2, y = s/√2.

Step 2 (b). r(t) = t i + t j + t k, speed ‖r′‖ = √3, so s = √3 t and t = s/√3. Hence x = y = z = s/√3.

Answer: (a) x = s/√2, y = s/√2; (b) x = y = z = s/√3.

Ex. 12.3: 23

(a) Find the arc length parametrization of the line x = 1 + t, y = 3 − 2t, z = 4 + 2t that has the same direction as the given line and has reference point (1, 3, 4). (b) Use the parametric equations in (a) to find the point on the line that is 25 units from the reference point in the direction of increasing parameter.

Step 1 (a). Direction vector ⟨1, −2, 2⟩ has speed √(1 + 4 + 4) = 3, so s = 3t and t = s/3. Substituting: x = 1 + s/3, y = 3 − 2s/3, z = 4 + 2s/3.

Step 2 (b). Put s = 25: x = 1 + 25/3 = 28/3, y = 3 − 50/3 = −41/3, z = 4 + 50/3 = 62/3.

Answer: (a) x = 1 + s/3, y = 3 − 2s/3, z = 4 + 2s/3; (b) (28/3, −41/3, 62/3).

Ex. 12.3: 30

Find an arc length parametrization of the curve r(t) = sin(et) i + cos(et) j + √3 et k, t ≥ 0, that has the same orientation as the given curve and for which the reference point corresponds to t = 0.

Step 1. r′(t) = et cos(et) i − et sin(et) j + √3 et k, so ‖r′(t)‖ = √(e2t + 3e2t) = 2et.

Step 2. s = ∫0t 2eu du = 2(et − 1), so et = s/2 + 1 (s ≥ 0).

Step 3. Substitute et = s/2 + 1 into r(t).

Answer: r(s) = sin(s/2 + 1)i + cos(s/2 + 1)j + √3(s/2 + 1)k, s ≥ 0.

Ex. 12.3: 31

Show that the arc length of the circular helix x = a cos t, y = a sin t, z = ct for 0 ≤ t ≤ t0 is t0√(a2 + c2).

Step 1. r(t) = a cos t i + a sin t j + ct k, so r′(t) = −a sin t i + a cos t j + c k.

Step 2. ‖r′(t)‖ = √(a2 sin2 t + a2 cos2 t + c2) = √(a2 + c2), a constant.

Step 3. L = ∫0t0 √(a2 + c2) dt = t0√(a2 + c2).

Answer: L = t0√(a2 + c2).

Ex. 12.3: 35

Use the cylindrical-coordinate arc length formula L = ∫ √[(dr/dt)2 + r2(dθ/dt)2 + (dz/dt)2] dt to find the arc length of the curve. (a) r = e2t, θ = t, z = e2t, 0 ≤ t ≤ ln 2. (b) r = t2, θ = ln t, z = (1/3)t3, 1 ≤ t ≤ 2.

Step 1 (a). dr/dt = 2e2t, dθ/dt = 1, dz/dt = 2e2t. The integrand is √[(2e2t)2 + e4t + (2e2t)2] = √(9e4t) = 3e2t. So L = ∫0ln 2 3e2t dt = (3/2)(e2 ln 2 − 1) = (3/2)(4 − 1) = 9/2.

Step 2 (b). dr/dt = 2t, dθ/dt = 1/t, dz/dt = t2. The integrand is √[(2t)2 + t4(1/t)2 + t4] = √(t4 + 5t2) = t√(t2 + 5). So L = ∫12 t√(t2 + 5) dt = [(1/3)(t2 + 5)3/2]12 = (1/3)(27 − 6√6) = 9 − 2√6.

Answer: (a) 9/2; (b) 9 − 2√6.

Lecture 3 — Unit Tangent, Normal, Binormal Vectors; Curvature (Anton 12.4–12.5, pp. 868–882)

At every point of a curve there is a little three-arrow compass — forward, inward, and out — and curvature measures how sharply the road bends, like the tightness of a bend on a mountain road.

Imagine you are driving along a winding road. At any moment you can ask three questions: which way am I heading, which way is the road bending, and which way is "up" out of the plane of the bend? This lecture builds exactly those three arrows, and together they are called the TNB frame (or Frenet frame) — a little moving compass that travels with you along the curve.

The first arrow is the unit tangent, T. You already met the tangent vector r′(t) last lecture; T is simply that arrow shrunk to length 1: T(t) = r′(t) / ‖r′(t)‖. It points in the direction of increasing t — the direction of travel. The second arrow is the unit normal, N. Here is the clever bit: T always has length 1, and when a vector keeps a constant length while changing direction, its change must be perpendicular to it — think of a clock hand: the tip moves at right angles to the hand. So T′(t) is always perpendicular to T, and N is just T′ shrunk to length 1: N(t) = T′(t) / ‖T′(t)‖. In the plane, N points toward the inside of the bend — toward the concave side, where the road is curving. The third arrow is the binormal, B = T × N. Since T and N are perpendicular unit arrows, their cross product is a third unit arrow at right angles to both, and the three together form a right-handed set of axes at every point of the curve. There is also a shortcut: B = (r′ × r′′) / ‖r′ × r′′‖.

Those three arrows define three planes at each point, and the exam loves asking for them. The osculating plane is the TN-plane — the plane the curve is bending in, the plane of the road surface — and its normal is B. The normal plane is the NB-plane, the plane at right angles to the direction of travel, with normal T. The rectifying plane is the TB-plane, with normal N. A good way to remember: each plane is named by the arrow that is missing from it being its normal — the osculating plane contains T and N, so its normal is B.

Now, curvature, κ (the Greek letter kappa). Curvature answers one question: how fast is my direction changing? If you drive along a straight road, your direction never changes, so κ = 0. If you drive round a tight roundabout, your direction spins round quickly, so κ is large. Formally, κ is the rate at which T turns as you travel along the curve: κ(s) = ‖dT/ds‖, where s is distance along the curve. For an ordinary parameter t the working formula is κ(t) = ‖r′(t) × r′′(t)‖ / ‖r′(t)‖³. For a circle of radius a, the curvature is constant, κ = 1/a — a small circle bends sharply (large κ), a huge circle barely bends at all (small κ). A helix has constant curvature too: κ = a/(a² + c²). For a graph y = f(x), the formula is κ(x) = |y″| / [1 + (y′)²]3/2. Note the absolute value: κ is never negative.

Two friends of curvature help you picture it. The radius of curvature is ρ = 1/κ: a sharp bend has a small radius, a gentle bend a large one. The osculating circle is the circle of radius ρ that sits in the osculating plane, hugs the curve at that point, and shares the same T and N — it is the circle that best fits the bend right there, like a coin pressed against the inside of the curve. Finally, torsion, τ, measures something curvature cannot: how much the curve twists out of its osculating plane, like a corkscrew leaving the flat road. A plane curve never twists out, so its torsion is 0. The three Frenet–Serret formulas tie it all together: dT/ds = κN, dN/ds = −κT + τB, dB/ds = −τN.

Why does this lecture exist? The unit tangent T tells you where you are heading — but a road designer needs two more numbers. How sharply does the road bend? That decides the speed limit on the bend, the banking of the track, and the g-force a roller-coaster rider feels. And does the track twist out of its plane, like a corkscrew? Curvature answers the first question, torsion the second. This lecture is the geometry of bends and twists, and it exists because "which way am I going" is not enough — you also need "how fast is my direction changing".

The key intuition for the whole lecture is one sentence: a unit vector can only change by turning, never by growing. T always has length 1, so when it changes, the change has to be sideways — perpendicular to T itself. Think of a clock hand again: the hand stays the same length, so its tip moves at right angles to the hand. That is why T′(t) is always perpendicular to T, and why the unit normal N — which is just T′ shrunk to length 1 — points into the bend, toward the concave side, where the road is curving.

The stuck point in this lecture is the normal vector, and it deserves a slow walk-through. The tempting shortcut is N = r′′/‖r′′‖ — but that is wrong in general, and it is the most common error in this lecture. Here is why: the second derivative r′′ mixes two different things. Part of it is the traveller speeding up or slowing down, which points along the direction of travel; part of it is the traveller turning, which points into the bend. Only the turning part belongs in N. Going through T first — N = T′/‖T′‖ — strips out the speeding-up part, because T has already thrown away all information about speed. The shortcut r′′/‖r′′‖ only works when the curve is parametrised by arc length, because then the speed is locked at 1 and there is no speeding up left to confuse things.

A second thing to understand, not just memorise, is the curvature formula κ(t) = ‖r′ × r′′‖ / ‖r′‖3. That ‖r′‖3 in the denominator looks alarming, but it has a job: it strips out the speed. The same geometric bend, driven twice as fast, would make r′ and r′′ bigger and make the direction change faster per unit time — but the bend itself has not changed. The denominator cancels out exactly how fast you are traversing the curve, so that κ depends only on the shape of the road, not on how fast you drive it. That is also why κ is defined with respect to arc length, κ(s) = ‖dT/ds‖: distance along the road is the honest clock for measuring how fast direction changes.

A small worked check — curvature of a spiral. Take r(t) = et cos t i + et sin t j + et k at t = 0 (Exercises 12.4-11 and 12.5-15). First the velocity: r′(t) = et(cos t − sin t) i + et(sin t + cos t) j + et k, so at t = 0, r′(0) = i + j + k. The unit tangent is T = (i + j + k)/√3. Now the acceleration: differentiating once more gives r′′(t) = −2et sin t i + 2et cos t j + et k, so at t = 0, r′′(0) = 2j + k. The cross product is r′ × r′′ = (1, 1, 1) × (0, 2, 1) = (−1, −1, 2), whose length is √6. The speed is ‖r′‖ = √3, so ‖r′‖3 = 3√3, and κ = √6 / (3√3) = √2/3. The radius of curvature is ρ = 1/κ = 3/√2 ≈ 2.12 — a fairly gentle bend, so the osculating circle hugging the spiral at that point is a circle of radius about 2.12. And the unit normal there is N = (−i + j)/√2: notice it has no k-component, because at t = 0 the spiral is bending sideways, in the xy-plane.

One last picture to carry away: at the top of a cosine wave, y = cos x, the curvature at x = 0 is κ = 1 and the radius of curvature is ρ = 1 (Exercise 12.5-33) — the osculating circle there is a unit circle, the same size as the wave's own hump. And a plane curve never twists out of its plane, so its torsion is 0: torsion is the measure of "leaving the flat road", and a flat road cannot leave itself.

Unit tangent: T(t) = r′(t) / ‖r′(t)‖

Unit normal: N(t) = T′(t) / ‖T′(t)‖ (T′ ⊥ T because T has constant length 1)

Binormal: B(t) = T(t) × N(t), also B = (r′ × r′′) / ‖r′ × r′′‖

Planes: osculating = TN-plane (normal B); normal = NB-plane (normal T); rectifying = TB-plane (normal N)

Curvature: κ(s) = ‖dT/ds‖ = ‖r′′(s)‖ (arc-length parameter); κ(t) = ‖r′(t) × r′′(t)‖ / ‖r′(t)‖3

Circle of radius a: κ = 1/a; line: κ = 0; helix: κ = a / (a2 + c2)

Plane curve y = f(x): κ(x) = |y″| / [1 + (y′)2]3/2

Radius of curvature: ρ = 1/κ

Frenet–Serret: dT/ds = κN, dN/ds = −κT + τB, dB/ds = −τN (τ = torsion, 0 for a plane curve)

Worked example — curvature of a graph. Problem (Ex. 12.5-26): find the curvature of y = tan x at x = π/4.

Step 1 — Use the plane-curve formula κ(x) = |y″| / [1 + (y′)2]3/2, so we need the first and second derivatives. y′ = sec2 x, and y″ = 2 sec2 x tan x.

Step 2 — Evaluate at x = π/4. We know tan(π/4) = 1 and sec2(π/4) = 2. So y′ = 2 and y″ = 2 · 2 · 1 = 4.

Step 3 — Plug into the formula: κ = |4| / (1 + 22)3/2 = 4 / 53/2 = 4 / (5√5).

Answer: κ = 4/(5√5). The radius of curvature there would be ρ = 1/κ = (5√5)/4 — the osculating circle at that point has that radius.

Watch out: N is not r′′/‖r′′‖ in general — that shortcut works only when the curve is parametrised by arc length; for an ordinary parameter t you must use N = T′/‖T′‖, and forgetting this is the most common error in this lecture.

  • What are the three arrows of the TNB frame, and how is each one built from the one before it?
  • Why is T′ always perpendicular to T? (Hint: what is the length of T?)
  • In words, what does curvature measure, and why is the curvature of a circle 1/a?
  • What is the osculating circle, and how is its radius related to the curvature?
