Lecture 3 — Unit Tangent, Normal, Binormal Vectors; Curvature (Anton 12.4–12.5)

Ex. 12.4: 11

Find T(t) and N(t) at the given point: x = et cos t, y = et sin t, z = et; t = 0.

Step 1. r′(t) = et(cos t − sin t)i + et(sin t + cos t)j + etk. At t = 0: r′(0) = i + j + k, ‖r′(0)‖ = √3, so T(0) = (i + j + k)/√3.

Step 2. T(t) = [(cos t − sin t)i + (sin t + cos t)j + k]/√3, so T′(0) = (−i + j)/√3, ‖T′(0)‖ = √(2/3), and N(0) = T′(0)/‖T′(0)‖ = (−i + j)/√2.

Answer: T = (i + j + k)/√3, N = (−i + j)/√2.

Ex. 12.4: 14

Find T(t) and N(t) at the given point: r(t) = t i + t j + √(9 − t2) k; t0 = 1.

Step 1. r′(t) = i + j − (t/√(9 − t2))k. At t = 1: r′(1) = i + j − (1/√8)k = i + j − (1/(2√2))k, with ‖r′(1)‖ = √(1 + 1 + 1/8) = √(17/8) = √17/(2√2).

Step 2. T(1) = r′(1)/‖r′(1)‖ = (2√2 i + 2√2 j − k)/√17. (N(1) follows from T′(1)/‖T′(1)‖; it points in the direction of T′(1).)

Answer: T = (2√2 i + 2√2 j − k)/√17.

Ex. 12.4: 18

Use B(t) = T(t) × N(t) to find B(t) for the helix r(t) = a cos t i + a sin t j + ct k (a ≠ 0, c ≠ 0), and check with the direct formula B = (r′ × r′′)/‖r′ × r′′‖.

Step 1. r′(t) = −a sin t i + a cos t j + c k, ‖r′‖ = √(a2 + c2), so T = (−a sin t i + a cos t j + c k)/√(a2 + c2).

Step 2. T′(t) = (−a cos t i − a sin t j)/√(a2 + c2), ‖T′‖ = a/√(a2 + c2), so N = −cos t i − sin t j.

Step 3. B = T × N = (c sin t i − c cos t j + a k)/√(a2 + c2). Check: r′′ = −a cos t i − a sin t j, and r′ × r′′ = ⟨ac sin t, −ac cos t, a2⟩, whose norm is a√(a2 + c2); dividing gives the same B. ✓

Answer: T = (−a sin t i + a cos t j + c k)/√(a2 + c2), N = −cos t i − sin t j, B = (c sin t i − c cos t j + a k)/√(a2 + c2).

Ex. 12.4: 19

Find T(t), N(t), and B(t) for r(t) = cos t i + sin t j + k at t = π/4. Then find equations for the osculating, normal, and rectifying planes at the corresponding point.

Step 1. r′(t) = −sin t i + cos t j, ‖r′‖ = 1, so T = −sin t i + cos t j; at t = π/4, T = −(√2/2)i + (√2/2)j.

Step 2. T′(t) = −cos t i − sin t j, ‖T′‖ = 1, so N = −cos t i − sin t j; at t = π/4, N = −(√2/2)i − (√2/2)j. Then B = T × N = k.

Step 3. The point is (√2/2, √2/2, 1). Osculating plane (normal B = k): z = 1. Normal plane (normal T): −(x − √2/2) + (y − √2/2) = 0, i.e. y = x. Rectifying plane (normal N): −(x − √2/2) − (y − √2/2) = 0, i.e. x + y = √2.

Answer: T = −(√2/2)i + (√2/2)j, N = −(√2/2)i − (√2/2)j, B = k; osculating plane z = 1, normal plane y = x, rectifying plane x + y = √2.

Ex. 12.4: 20

Find T(t), N(t), and B(t) for r(t) = et i + et cos t j + et sin t k at t = 0. Then find equations for the osculating, normal, and rectifying planes at the corresponding point.

Step 1. r′(t) = eti + et(cos t − sin t)j + et(sin t + cos t)k. At t = 0: r′(0) = i + j + k, ‖r′(0)‖ = √3, so T = (i + j + k)/√3.

Step 2. T′(0) = (0i − (√3/3)j + (√3/3)k) (after differentiating T and evaluating), with ‖T′(0)‖ = √(2/3), so N = (−j + k)/√2. Then B = T × N = (2i − j − k)/√6.

Step 3. The point is (1, 1, 0). Osculating plane (normal B): 2(x − 1) − (y − 1) − z = 0, i.e. 2x − y − z = 1. Normal plane (normal T): (x − 1) + (y − 1) + z = 0, i.e. x + y + z = 2. Rectifying plane (normal N): −(y − 1) + z = 0, i.e. z = y − 1.

Answer: T = (i + j + k)/√3, N = (−j + k)/√2, B = (2i − j − k)/√6; osculating plane 2x − y − z = 1, normal plane x + y + z = 2, rectifying plane z = y − 1.

Ex. 12.5: 11

Use κ(t) = ‖r′(t) × r′′(t)‖ / ‖r′(t)‖3 to find the curvature: x = cosh t, y = sinh t, z = t.

Step 1. r′ = ⟨sinh t, cosh t, 1⟩, r′′ = ⟨cosh t, sinh t, 0⟩.

Step 2. r′ × r′′ = ⟨−sinh t, cosh t, −1⟩, so ‖r′ × r′′‖ = √(sinh2 t + cosh2 t + 1) = √2 cosh t.

Step 3. ‖r′‖ = √(sinh2 t + cosh2 t + 1) = √2 cosh t, so κ = (√2 cosh t)/(√2 cosh t)3 = 1/(2 cosh2 t).

Answer: κ(t) = 1/(2 cosh2 t).

Ex. 12.5: 15

Find the curvature and the radius of curvature at the stated point: x = et cos t, y = et sin t, z = et; t = 0.

Step 1. At t = 0: r′ = ⟨1, 1, 1⟩, r′′ = ⟨0, 2, 1⟩.

Step 2. r′ × r′′ = ⟨−1, −1, 2⟩, ‖r′ × r′′‖ = √6, ‖r′‖ = √3, so κ = √6/(√3)3 = √6/(3√3) = √2/3.

Step 3. Radius of curvature ρ = 1/κ = 3/√2.

Answer: κ = √2/3, ρ = 3/√2.

Ex. 12.5: 17

Confirm that s is an arc length parameter by showing that ‖dr/ds‖ = 1, and then apply κ(s) = ‖r′′(s)‖ to find κ(s): r(s) = sin(1 + s/2)i + cos(1 + s/2)j + (√3/2)(1 + s/2)k.

Step 1. dr/ds = (1/2)cos(1 + s/2)i − (1/2)sin(1 + s/2)j + (√3/2)k. Its norm is √[(1/4) + (3/4)] = 1, so s is an arc length parameter.

Step 2. r′′(s) = −(1/4)sin(1 + s/2)i − (1/4)cos(1 + s/2)j, so κ(s) = ‖r′′(s)‖ = 1/4 (constant).

Answer: ‖dr/ds‖ = 1; κ = 1/4.

Ex. 12.5: 26

Use κ(x) = |y′′| / [1 + (y′)2]3/2 to find the curvature: y = tan x at x = π/4.

Step 1. y′ = sec2 x, y′′ = 2 sec2 x tan x.

Step 2. At x = π/4: y′ = 2, y′′ = 4, so κ = 4/(1 + 4)3/2 = 4/(5√5).

Answer: κ = 4/(5√5).

Ex. 12.5: 33

In each part, use the formulas in Exercise 23 to find the radius of curvature at the stated points. Then sketch the graph together with the osculating circles at those points. (a) y = cos x at x = 0 and x = π. (b) x = 2 cos t, y = sin t (0 ≤ t ≤ 2π) at t = 0 and t = π/2.

Step 1 (a). κ(x) = |−cos x|/(1 + sin2 x)3/2. At x = 0: κ = 1, so ρ = 1. At x = π: κ = |−(−1)|/(1 + 0)3/2 = 1, so ρ = 1. The osculating circles both have radius 1: at (0, 1) the circle is centred at (0, 0) (below the peak); at (π, −1) it is centred at (π, 0) (above the trough).

Step 2 (b). κ(t) = |x′y′′ − y′x′′|/(x′2 + y′2)3/2 with x′ = −2 sin t, y′ = cos t, x′′ = −2 cos t, y′′ = −sin t. At t = 0: |0 − (1)(−2)| = 2, denominator 1, so κ = 2 and ρ = 1/2 (osculating circle at (2, 0), radius 1/2, centred at (3/2, 0)). At t = π/2: |(−2)(−1) − 0| = 2, denominator (4)3/2 = 8, so κ = 1/4 and ρ = 4 (osculating circle at (0, 1), radius 4, centred at (0, −3)).

Answer: (a) ρ = 1 at both x = 0 and x = π; (b) ρ = 1/2 at t = 0 and ρ = 4 at t = π/2.

Ex. 12.5: 43

Use the polar curvature formula to find κ at the indicated point: r = sin 3θ; θ = 0.

Step 1. The polar formula is κ = |r2 + 2(r′)2 − r r′′| / (r2 + (r′)2)3/2, where primes are d/dθ. Here r = sin 3θ, r′ = 3 cos 3θ, r′′ = −9 sin 3θ.

Step 2. At θ = 0: r = 0, r′ = 3, r′′ = 0, so κ = |0 + 2·9 − 0|/(0 + 9)3/2 = 18/27 = 2/3.

Answer: κ = 2/3.

Lecture 4 — Functions of Two or More Variables (Anton §13.1)

A function of two variables takes a pair of numbers (x, y) and gives back one height z, so its graph is a landscape you can walk on.

Until now, every function you met took one number in and gave one number back — you put in x, you got out y, and the graph was a curve on a flat page. Now we take two numbers in. Think of a hillside: at every spot on the ground, which we name by its two coordinates (x, y), there is a height. That height is the value of the function, f(x, y). So instead of a curve, the graph is a whole surface — a landscape with hills, valleys and flat plains.

Before you can even draw that landscape, you must ask: where is the function allowed to live? That is called the domain — simply, the set of points (x, y) for which the formula actually gives a real number. Two rules cause almost every domain question in this chapter. First, you cannot take the square root of a negative number, so whatever sits under a square root must be zero or positive. Second, you cannot take the logarithm of zero or a negative number, so whatever sits inside a ln must be strictly positive. And of course you cannot divide by zero. When you sketch a domain, draw its boundary with a solid line if the boundary points are included, and a dashed line if they are left out.

Now, how do you read a landscape without drawing the whole 3D hill? You use level curves — the same idea as the contour lines on a hiking map. A level curve is the set of points where the height is exactly the same, f(x, y) = k, for some fixed number k. On a map, one contour line joins all the places that are 100 metres high, another joins all the places that are 200 metres high, and so on. Where the contour lines crowd close together, the hill is steep; where they are far apart, the ground is gentle. A paraboloid, z = x² + y², is a bowl, and its level curves are circles that grow as the height grows. A saddle, z = x² − y², is a mountain pass — it goes up in one direction and down in the other — and its level curves are hyperbolas.

One more step, and you have the whole picture. A function of three variables, w = f(x, y, z), needs three inputs, so its "level" sets are not curves but surfaces — for example, f(x, y, z) = k can be a sphere, a plane or a cylinder. And a small warning that catches many students: the domain of a three-variable function is a solid lump of space, not a flat region. The function √(1 − x² − y² − z²) is defined inside the unit ball, the solid sphere, not just on the flat unit disk.

Before we go any further, ask the question that makes this whole chapter necessary: why do we need functions of two variables at all? In single-variable calculus, one input decided everything — the height of a thrown ball depended only on time, the area of a square only on its side. But most things in the real world refuse to behave like that. The temperature in a room depends on where you are standing and on the time of day. A farmer's crop yield depends on rainfall and on fertiliser. The pressure of a gas depends on its volume and its temperature. One input is simply not enough information to pin the answer down, so we let the function take two inputs at once. That is the whole jump: the input is no longer a single number on a line, it is a point on the ground, and the output is the height above that point.

Keep the hiking-map analogy, because it carries you through the entire chapter. Imagine a weather map of a country where, at every town, someone has written down the temperature. The map is flat, but the numbers on it tell you about a surface floating above it — high numbers where it is hot, low numbers where it is cold. A function of two variables is exactly that: a flat map (the xy-plane, your domain) with one number attached to every point on it. The graph is the surface you get when you lift every number up to its height. And just as a weather map only covers the country and not the sea beyond it, a function only lives on its domain — the set of points where the formula makes sense. A depth map of a swimming pool, for instance, only exists inside the pool; outside the walls there is no water and no depth to measure.

Here is the place students most often get stuck, so let us walk through it slowly: the difference between the graph and a level curve. The graph is the whole 3D surface — the actual hillside. A level curve is a flat line drawn on the ground that joins all the places with the same height — exactly one contour line on a hiking map. When you look at a contour map, you are not looking at the hill; you are looking at the hill's shadow, sliced into rings. Two mistakes follow from mixing them up. First, students try to "draw the graph" when the question asked for level curves, and end up sketching a 3D bowl instead of flat circles. Second, they forget that a level curve lives in the xy-plane, so it has no z in it — it is an equation in x and y only, f(x, y) = k. The worked example below does this correctly: it finds the height k first, then writes the level curve as f(x, y) = k.

Let us do one more short example together, this time about the domain, because domain questions are where the easy marks are. Take f(x, y) = ln(1 − x² − y²) (Ex. 13.1-23). The logarithm refuses zero and negative numbers, so we need 1 − x² − y² > 0, which is the same as x² + y² < 1. That is the inside of the unit circle — the open unit disk. The boundary circle x² + y² = 1 is not included, because on it the logarithm would be ln 0, which does not exist — so you draw it dashed. Notice how the whole problem was just two steps: ask what the formula forbids, then draw the region that remains. Almost every domain question in this lecture is solved the same way, with the square-root rule and the logarithm rule doing all the work.

And one quick level-curve example with three variables, so you see the pattern stretch. Take f(x, y) = yex (Ex. 13.1-66) and the point (ln 2, 1). The height there is f(ln 2, 1) = 1 · eln 2 = 1 · 2 = 2, so the level curve through that point is yex = 2. Same method as before — find the height, set the function equal to it — and it works whether the answer is a curve on the ground or, for a function of three variables, a whole surface in space.

So, to sum up before we move on: two inputs, one height; the domain is where the formula makes sense; the graph is a surface; and level curves are contour lines that let you read the surface from a flat page. Keep the hiking-map picture in your head, and every exercise in this lecture is just a different way of asking you to draw the map or read it.

f(x, y) — one height z for each point (x, y) in the domain D

Level curve: f(x, y) = k  (k is a fixed height)

Level surface (three variables): f(x, y, z) = k

Paraboloid: z = x2 + y2  ·  Saddle: z = x2 − y2  ·  Upper hemisphere: z = √(9 − x2 − y2)

Worked example — Ex. 13.1-65(a). Find the level curve of f(x, y) = x² − 2x³ + 3xy through the point (−1, 1).

Step 1 — Remember what "level curve through a point" means. We need the height k of the surface at that point, then the level curve is simply all the points (x, y) where the function equals that same height.

Step 2 — Plug the point into the function. f(−1, 1) = (−1)² − 2(−1)³ + 3(−1)(1) = 1 − 2(−1) − 3 = 1 + 2 − 3 = 0.

Step 3 — Write the level curve. The height at the point is k = 0, so the level curve is f(x, y) = 0, that is, x² − 2x³ + 3xy = 0.

Answer: k = 0, and the level curve is x² − 2x³ + 3xy = 0. (The same method gives k = 0 at (0, 0) and k = −18 at (2, −1).)

Watch out: a level curve is not the graph. The graph is the 3D surface; a level curve is a flat curve drawn on the ground (the xy-plane) joining points of equal height — and for a function of three variables, the domain is a solid in space, not a flat region.

  • What is the domain of a function of two variables, and which two rules (square root and logarithm) decide it?
  • How do you read steepness from a contour plot, and what shape are the level curves of z = x² + y²?
  • What is the difference between the graph of f(x, y) and one of its level curves?
  • How do you find the level curve of a function through a given point?

Ex. 13.1 — sketch the domain: 23. f = ln(1 − x² − y²); 24. f = √(x² + y² − 4); 25. f = 1/(x − y²); 26. f = ln xy.

Sketch the graph: 33. z = 3; 34. z = √(9 − x² − y²); 35. z = x² + y²; 36. z = x + y²; 37. z = x² − y²; 38. z = 4 − x² − y²; 39. z = x² + y² + 1; 40. z = x² + y² − 1; 41. z = y + 1; 42. z = x².

Sketch level curves: 51. z = x² + y², k = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4; 52. z = y/x, k = −2, …, 2; 53. z = x² + y, k = −2, …, 2; 54. z = x² + 9y², k = 0, …, 4; 55. z = x² − y², k = −2, …, 2; 56. z = y csc x, k = −2, …, 2.

Level curve/surface through a point: 65. f = x² − 2x³ + 3xy; 66. f = yex; 67. f = x² + y² − z; 68. f = xyz + 3.

Calculus 3 Lecture 13.1: Intro to Multivariable Functions (Domain, Sketching, Level Curves)

Functions of Several Variables (domain & range)

Why Does Calculus Need More Than One Derivative? Partial Derivatives, Visually (MathCraft8)

Lecture 4 — Functions of Two or More Variables (Anton §13.1)

Exercise Set 13.1, problems 23–28, 33–42, 51–56, 65–68. Two rules do almost all the domain work: a square root needs a non-negative argument, and a logarithm needs a strictly positive argument; a denominator must never be zero. A solid boundary line means the boundary is included in the domain, a dashed line means it is excluded.

Ex. 13.1: 23

Sketch the domain of f(x, y) = ln(1 − x2 − y2). Use solid lines for portions of the boundary included in the domain and dashed lines for portions not included.

The logarithm is defined only for a strictly positive argument, so we need 1 − x2 − y2 > 0, i.e. x2 + y2 < 1. That is the set of points strictly inside the circle of radius 1 centred at the origin. The boundary circle x2 + y2 = 1 is not included (there ln 0 is undefined), so it is drawn dashed.

Answer: The open unit disk x2 + y2 < 1, with the boundary circle dashed.

Ex. 13.1: 24

Sketch the domain of f(x, y) = √( x2 + y2 − 4 ). Use solid lines for portions of the boundary included in the domain and dashed lines for portions not included.

A square root needs a non-negative argument, so x2 + y2 − 4 ≥ 0, i.e. x2 + y2 ≥ 4. That is the set of points on or outside the circle of radius 2 centred at the origin. The boundary circle is included (√0 = 0 there), so it is drawn solid.

Answer: The region on and outside the circle x2 + y2 = 4, i.e. x2 + y2 ≥ 4, with the boundary circle solid.

Ex. 13.1: 25

Sketch the domain of f(x, y) = 1 / (x − y2). Use solid lines for portions of the boundary included in the domain and dashed lines for portions not included.

The only restriction is that the denominator must not be zero: x − y2 ≠ 0, i.e. x ≠ y2. The curve x = y2 is a parabola opening to the right with vertex at the origin, passing through (1, ±1) and (4, ±2). Every other point of the plane is in the domain, so the parabola is drawn dashed (excluded).

Answer: The whole plane except the parabola x = y2 (drawn dashed).

Ex. 13.1: 26

Sketch the domain of f(x, y) = ln xy. Use solid lines for portions of the boundary included in the domain and dashed lines for portions not included.

The logarithm needs xy > 0. A product is positive when both factors have the same sign: x > 0 and y > 0 (the first quadrant), or x < 0 and y < 0 (the third quadrant). On either axis xy = 0, so the axes are excluded and drawn dashed.

Answer: xy > 0 — the (open) first and third quadrants, axes excluded (dashed).

Ex. 13.1: 27

Describe the domain of f in words. (a) f(x, y) = xe√(2 − y)   (b) f(x, y, z) = √(25 − x2 − y2 − z2)   (c) f(x, y, z) = exyz

(a) The exponential is defined for every real exponent, so the only restriction comes from the square root: 2 − y ≥ 0, i.e. y ≤ 2. There is no restriction on x.

(b) The square root needs 25 − x2 − y2 − z2 ≥ 0, i.e. x2 + y2 + z2 ≤ 25. That is the solid ball of radius 5 centred at the origin, including its spherical boundary.

(c) The exponential exyz is defined for every real exponent, and xyz is defined for all (x, y, z), so there is no restriction at all.

Answer: (a) All points (x, y) with y ≤ 2 — the half-plane on and below the line y = 2. (b) The closed ball x2 + y2 + z2 ≤ 25 (radius 5, centre the origin). (c) All of space, ℝ3.

Ex. 13.1: 28

Describe the domain of f in words. (a) f(x, y) = √(4 − x2) / (y + 3)   (b) f(x, y) = ln(y − 2x)   (c) f(x, y, z) = xyz / (x + y + z)

(a) Two conditions: the square root needs 4 − x2 ≥ 0, i.e. −2 ≤ x ≤ 2, and the denominator needs y + 3 ≠ 0, i.e. y ≠ −3.

(b) The logarithm needs y − 2x > 0, i.e. y > 2x — the open half-plane strictly above the line y = 2x (the line itself is excluded).

(c) Only the denominator matters: x + y + z ≠ 0.

Answer: (a) The vertical strip −2 ≤ x ≤ 2 with the horizontal line y = −3 removed. (b) All points with y > 2x. (c) All of space except the plane x + y + z = 0.

Ex. 13.1: 33

Sketch the graph of f(x, y) = 3.

The graph is the surface z = 3. The height is 3 no matter what x and y are, so every point of the surface has z-coordinate 3: it is the horizontal plane 3 units above the xy-plane, parallel to it. Every trace is a horizontal line at height 3.

Answer: The horizontal plane z = 3.

Ex. 13.1: 34

Sketch the graph of f(x, y) = √(9 − x2 − y2).

Put z = √(9 − x2 − y2). Then z ≥ 0 and squaring gives x2 + y2 + z2 = 9, the sphere of radius 3 centred at the origin. The condition z ≥ 0 keeps only the upper half. The domain is the disk x2 + y2 ≤ 9, where z = 0 on the rim circle and z = 3 at the top point (0, 0, 3).

Answer: The upper hemisphere of radius 3 centred at the origin (top point (0, 0, 3), rim the circle x2 + y2 = 9 in the plane z = 0).

Ex. 13.1: 35

Sketch the graph of f(x, y) = x2 + y2.

The surface is z = x2 + y2 ≥ 0. In the plane y = 0 it is the parabola z = x2, and the same in the plane x = 0; rotating that parabola about the z-axis gives the surface. Horizontal slices z = k > 0 are circles of radius √k. The lowest point is the vertex (0, 0, 0), and the surface rises in every direction from it.

Answer: A circular paraboloid with vertex at the origin, opening upward along the z-axis.

Ex. 13.1: 36

Sketch the graph of f(x, y) = x + y2.

The surface is z = x + y2. For fixed x it is the parabola z = y2 + (constant) in the yz-direction, opening upward; for fixed y it is the straight line z = x + (constant) of slope 1. So the parabola z = y2 in the plane x = 0 is carried along the line z = x, y = 0. It passes through the origin, rises as |y| grows, and rises steadily as x increases.

Answer: A parabolic cylinder (parabola z = y2 shifted along the line z = x, y = 0); vertex line z = x in the plane y = 0.

Ex. 13.1: 37

Sketch the graph of f(x, y) = x2 − y2.

The surface is z = x2 − y2. In the plane y = 0 it is the upward parabola z = x2; in the plane x = 0 it is the downward parabola z = −y2. So the surface rises in the x-direction and falls in the y-direction from the origin, which is a saddle point: (0, 0, 0) is a minimum along the x-axis but a maximum along the y-axis. Horizontal slices z = k ≠ 0 are hyperbolas.

Answer: A hyperbolic paraboloid (saddle) with saddle point at the origin, rising toward ±x and falling toward ±y.

Ex. 13.1: 38

Sketch the graph of f(x, y) = 4 − x2 − y2.

This is the paraboloid z = x2 + y2 of Ex. 35 turned upside down and lifted by 4. Its highest point is the vertex (0, 0, 4); it falls away in every direction, and horizontal slices z = k < 4 are circles of radius √(4 − k). It meets the xy-plane (z = 0) in the circle x2 + y2 = 4 of radius 2.

Answer: A circular paraboloid with vertex (0, 0, 4), opening downward, meeting the xy-plane in the circle of radius 2.

Ex. 13.1: 39

Sketch the graph of f(x, y) = x2 + y2 + 1.

This is the paraboloid z = x2 + y2 of Ex. 35 shifted up by 1 unit. The vertex moves from (0, 0, 0) to (0, 0, 1), the lowest point of the surface; horizontal slices z = k > 1 are circles of radius √(k − 1). The surface never meets the xy-plane.

Answer: A circular paraboloid with vertex (0, 0, 1), opening upward.

Ex. 13.1: 40

Sketch the graph of f(x, y) = x2 + y2 − 1.

This is the paraboloid z = x2 + y2 of Ex. 35 shifted down by 1 unit. The vertex is (0, 0, −1), the lowest point; horizontal slices z = k > −1 are circles of radius √(k + 1). It meets the xy-plane (z = 0) in the unit circle x2 + y2 = 1.

Answer: A circular paraboloid with vertex (0, 0, −1), opening upward, meeting the xy-plane in the unit circle.

Ex. 13.1: 41

Sketch the graph of f(x, y) = y + 1.

The surface is the plane z = y + 1. It does not depend on x, so it is constant along every line parallel to the x-axis. In the yz-plane it is the line z = y + 1 of slope 1, crossing the z-axis at (0, 0, 1) and the y-axis at (0, −1, 0); the plane is that line swept parallel to the x-axis. It rises as y increases and is flat in the x-direction.

Answer: The plane z = y + 1, sloping upward in the y-direction with z-intercept 1.

Ex. 13.1: 42

Sketch the graph of f(x, y) = x2.

The surface is z = x2, independent of y. In the xz-plane it is the parabola z = x2 with vertex at the origin, and that parabola is repeated unchanged for every y — the surface is the parabola extruded parallel to the y-axis. Its lowest points form the whole y-axis (x = 0, z = 0), and it rises as |x| grows.

Answer: A parabolic cylinder: the parabola z = x2 extruded parallel to the y-axis, with vertex line the y-axis.

Ex. 13.1: 51

Sketch the level curve z = k for the specified values of k. z = x2 + y2; k = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4.

Set x2 + y2 = k. For k = 0 this is the single point (0, 0). For k > 0 it is a circle centred at the origin of radius √k: radii 1, √2 ≈ 1.41, √3 ≈ 1.73 and 2 for k = 1, 2, 3, 4. The circles are concentric, equally spaced in k but getting closer together in radius as k grows — as expected, since the paraboloid gets steeper further out.

Answer: k = 0: the point (0, 0); k = 1, 2, 3, 4: concentric circles of radii 1, √2, √3, 2.

Ex. 13.1: 52

Sketch the level curve z = k for the specified values of k. z = y / x; k = −2, −1, 0, 1, 2.

Set y/x = k, with x ≠ 0 (the function is undefined on the y-axis). Then y = kx: a straight line through the origin of slope k, with the origin itself removed (since x = 0 is excluded). For k = 0 this is the x-axis minus the origin; for k = ±1 the diagonals y = ±x (minus the origin); for k = ±2 the steeper lines y = ±2x (minus the origin). The five lines fan out from the origin like a pencil.

Answer: Lines y = kx through the origin (origin excluded) for k = −2, −1, 0, 1, 2.

Ex. 13.1: 53

Sketch the level curve z = k for the specified values of k. z = x2 + y; k = −2, −1, 0, 1, 2.

Set x2 + y = k, so y = −x2 + k. Each level curve is a parabola opening downward with vertex (0, k) on the y-axis. The five parabolas are congruent, shifted vertically by 1 unit from one another: vertices (0, −2), (0, −1), (0, 0), (0, 1), (0, 2). Each passes through (±1, k − 1) and (±2, k − 4).

Answer: Downward parabolas y = −x2 + k, vertices (0, k), for k = −2, −1, 0, 1, 2.

Ex. 13.1: 54

Sketch the level curve z = k for the specified values of k. z = x2 + 9y2; k = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4.

Set x2 + 9y2 = k, i.e. x2/k + y2/(k/9) = 1 for k > 0. For k = 0 this is the single point (0, 0). For k > 0 it is an ellipse centred at the origin with semi-axis √k along x and √k/3 along y (three times wider than tall): k = 1 gives axes 1 and 1/3; k = 2 gives √2 ≈ 1.41 and √2/3 ≈ 0.47; k = 3 gives √3 ≈ 1.73 and 1/√3 ≈ 0.58; k = 4 gives 2 and 2/3.

Answer: k = 0: the point (0, 0); k = 1, 2, 3, 4: concentric ellipses x2 + 9y2 = k with x-semi-axis √k and y-semi-axis √k/3.

Ex. 13.1: 55

Sketch the level curve z = k for the specified values of k. z = x2 − y2; k = −2, −1, 0, 1, 2.

Set x2 − y2 = k. For k = 0, x2 = y2, i.e. the two diagonal lines y = x and y = −x. For k > 0 the curve is a hyperbola opening left–right (along the x-axis) with vertices (±√k, 0): (±1, 0) for k = 1 and (±√2, 0) for k = 2. For k < 0 it is a hyperbola opening up–down (along the y-axis) with vertices (0, ±√|k|): (0, ±1) for k = −1 and (0, ±√2) for k = −2. All five curves share the same asymptotes y = ±x.

Answer: k = 0: the lines y = ±x; k = 1, 2: hyperbolas opening along x, vertices (±√k, 0); k = −1, −2: hyperbolas opening along y, vertices (0, ±√|k|).

Ex. 13.1: 56

Sketch the level curve z = k for the specified values of k. z = y csc x; k = −2, −1, 0, 1, 2.

Since csc x = 1/sin x, the function is undefined where sin x = 0, i.e. at x = nπ for integer n. Set y csc x = k, so y = k sin x (for x ≠ nπ). Each level curve is therefore a sine wave of amplitude |k|, broken at every vertical line x = nπ: it passes through (0, 0) — except that point is excluded — rises to (π/2, k), returns to zero at x = π, and repeats with alternating sign. For k = 0 the curve is the x-axis with the points x = nπ removed; for k = ±1 the amplitude is 1, for k = ±2 it is 2, and the k = −1, −2 waves are the upside-down versions of the k = 1, 2 waves.

Answer: Sine waves y = k sin x (amplitude |k|), with gaps at x = nπ; k = 0 is the x-axis minus the points (nπ, 0).

Ex. 13.1: 65

Let f(x, y) = x2 − 2x3 + 3xy. Find an equation of the level curve that passes through the point (a) (−1, 1)   (b) (0, 0)   (c) (2, −1).

The level curve through a point is f(x, y) = k where k = f at that point. (a) f(−1, 1) = (−1)2 − 2(−1)3 + 3(−1)(1) = 1 + 2 − 3 = 0. (b) f(0, 0) = 0 − 0 + 0 = 0. (c) f(2, −1) = 4 − 2(8) + 3(2)(−1) = 4 − 16 − 6 = −18.

Answer: (a) x2 − 2x3 + 3xy = 0. (b) x2 − 2x3 + 3xy = 0. (c) x2 − 2x3 + 3xy = −18.

Ex. 13.1: 66

Let f(x, y) = yex. Find an equation of the level curve that passes through the point (a) (ln 2, 1)   (b) (0, 3)   (c) (1, −2).

Again k = f at the point. (a) f(ln 2, 1) = 1 · eln 2 = 2. (b) f(0, 3) = 3e0 = 3. (c) f(1, −2) = −2e1 = −2e.

Answer: (a) yex = 2. (b) yex = 3. (c) yex = −2e.

Ex. 13.1: 67

Let f(x, y, z) = x2 + y2 − z. Find an equation of the level surface that passes through the point (a) (1, −2, 0)   (b) (1, 0, 3)   (c) (0, 0, 0).

The level surface is f(x, y, z) = k with k = f at the point. (a) f(1, −2, 0) = 1 + 4 − 0 = 5, so the surface is x2 + y2 − z = 5, i.e. the paraboloid z = x2 + y2 − 5. (b) f(1, 0, 3) = 1 + 0 − 3 = −2, i.e. the paraboloid z = x2 + y2 + 2. (c) f(0, 0, 0) = 0, i.e. the paraboloid z = x2 + y2.

Answer: (a) x2 + y2 − z = 5. (b) x2 + y2 − z = −2. (c) x2 + y2 − z = 0.

Ex. 13.1: 68

Let f(x, y, z) = xyz + 3. Find an equation of the level surface that passes through the point (a) (1, 0, 2)   (b) (−2, 4, 1)   (c) (0, 0, 0).

The level surface is f(x, y, z) = k with k = f at the point. (a) f(1, 0, 2) = 0 + 3 = 3. (b) f(−2, 4, 1) = (−2)(4)(1) + 3 = −8 + 3 = −5. (c) f(0, 0, 0) = 0 + 3 = 3.

Answer: (a) xyz + 3 = 3, i.e. xyz = 0. (b) xyz + 3 = −5, i.e. xyz = −8. (c) xyz + 3 = 3, i.e. xyz = 0.

Lecture 5 — Limit Along a Curve, General Limit and Continuity (Anton §13.2)

A limit in two variables only exists if you get the same answer no matter which road you take to the point — one road that disagrees is enough to kill it.

In single-variable calculus, you could only approach a point from two sides: from the left and from the right. If both sides agreed, the limit existed. Now imagine you are standing on the hillside from Lecture 4, and you want to walk to one particular spot, say the origin (0, 0). How many ways can you get there? Infinitely many. You can come along the x-axis, along the y-axis, along a straight road y = mx, along a curving path y = x², or along any winding track you like. The limit of f(x, y) as (x, y) approaches (x₀, y₀) is the height you are heading towards — but it only exists if every single road leads you to the same height.

That gives us the most useful idea in this whole lecture, and the one the exam loves to test. To prove a limit does NOT exist, you only need two roads that give different answers. Find one path where the limit is, say, 0, and another path where it is 1/2, and you are done — the limit cannot exist, because the function cannot be heading towards two different heights at once. This is why the book's exercises are built the way they are: a function like f(x, y) = x²y / (x⁴ + y²) gives 0 along every straight line y = mx through the origin, so a careless student stops there and declares the limit is 0. But walk in along the parabola y = x² and the value is 1/2 all the way. Two roads, two answers — no limit. Some functions are even sneakier: f(x, y) = x³y / (2x⁶ + y²) gives 0 along every line and every parabola, and only the cubic path y = x³ exposes it, giving 1/3.

But be careful — the logic only works in one direction. If ten roads all agree, that proves nothing. Agreement along many paths is not a proof; disagreement along two paths is. To prove a limit DOES exist, you need a method that covers all roads at once. The usual tools are the squeeze theorem (trap the function between two things that both go to the same place), polar coordinates (write x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ, and show the result goes to 0 as r → 0 no matter what θ is — the bound must not depend on θ), or a clever substitution like z = x² + y². For example, sin(x² + y²) / (x² + y²) becomes sin z / z as z → 0, which you already know is 1.

Finally, continuity is the same idea as in one variable, just in two dimensions: a function is continuous at a point if the limit there equals the value there, lim f = f(x₀, y₀). And the good news is that sums, products, quotients (as long as the denominator is not zero) and compositions of continuous functions are continuous. That means polynomials, exponentials, and sines and cosines of polynomials are continuous everywhere — so most of the limits in the first exercises are just direct substitution: plug the point in and you are done. The only interesting case is when the limit exists but does not equal the function's value (or the function is not defined there at all); that is called a removable discontinuity.

Now, why is a two-variable limit so much harder than a one-variable limit — and why does the exam keep asking about it? Go back to first-year calculus. There, to approach a point a on the number line, you had exactly two ways in: from the left and from the right. Two directions, two checks, done. The limit was a promise: "no matter which of the two sides you come from, the function settles on the same value." In two variables that promise becomes enormously stronger, because "which way you come from" is no longer a choice between two sides — it is a choice among infinitely many roads. Think of a village sitting on a hillside. You can reach it by the road from the east, the road from the west, a straight road from the south-east, a winding track that spirals in, or any path you can draw with your finger. If the village has one definite height, then every road must end at that height. But a function of two variables is allowed to be badly behaved: it can sit at height 0 along one road and height 1/2 along another, and then the question "what height is the function heading towards?" simply has no single answer. That is what "the limit does not exist" means — not that the function is broken or infinite, but that the roads disagree.

The ε–δ definition is the same idea you already know, just drawn in two dimensions. In one variable, "close to the point" meant "inside a little interval around a". In two variables it means "inside a little disk around (x₀, y₀)" — the distance is the straight-line distance √[(x − x₀)² + (y − y₀)²], and the definition demands that the function value be within ε of L for every point in that disk (except the centre itself, which is excluded — what happens exactly at the point never matters for a limit). The disk is the key image: it contains points from every direction at once, which is exactly why the limit has to work along every path.

Here is the place students most often get stuck, so let us walk through it slowly: the logic only works in one direction, and the exam is built to punish anyone who gets the direction backwards. Two roads disagreeing proves the limit does not exist — that is a finished proof, and you can stop. But ten roads agreeing proves nothing, because the eleventh road might be the one that disagrees. The book's exercises are deliberately designed as a ladder of traps. First, a function whose limit is 0 along both axes but not along the line y = x — the axes agree, a diagonal road disagrees. Then a function like the one in the worked example, which gives 0 along every straight line y = mx and is only caught by the parabola y = x², giving 1/2. Then worse: a function that gives 0 along every line and every parabola, and is only exposed by the cubic path y = x³, giving 1/3 (Ex. 13.2-34). Each time, the student who checks one more family of paths and stops gets it wrong. The moral is not "check more paths" — you can never check them all. The moral is that path-checking is only a weapon for destroying a limit, never for proving one.

Let us do one more short example together, the simplest kind of disagreement, so the pattern is automatic. In Ex. 13.2-15 the limit is 0 along the x-axis (y = 0) but 1/5 along the diagonal line y = x. Two roads, two answers — 0 and 1/5 — so the general limit does not exist, and you are done in two lines. Notice you did not need anything clever: the axes and one diagonal were enough. In practice, always try the axes first, then the lines y = mx, then the parabolas y = kx², then a cubic if you suspect a trap — and the moment any two disagree, stop and write "does not exist".

To prove a limit does exist, you need a method that covers all roads at once, and the most useful one is polar coordinates. Here is the intuition: write x = r cos θ and y = r sin θ. Then r is simply "how far you are from the point" and θ is "which direction you came from". Letting r → 0 means "walk into the point from any direction at once". If the function, rewritten in r and θ, goes to the same value as r → 0 no matter what θ is, you have proved the limit — because θ was never fixed, it covered every road simultaneously. The one thing you must check is that your bound does not secretly depend on θ: if the answer still contains a sin θ or cos θ that does not shrink away, you have proved nothing. A famous failure is xy/(x² + y²), which becomes ½ sin 2θ in polar coordinates — as r → 0 it stays ½ sin 2θ, a different number for every direction, so the limit does not exist. And the squeeze theorem works the same way as in one variable: trap the function between two things that both go to the same place, and it has nowhere else to go.

Finally, continuity is the same idea as in one variable, just in two dimensions: the limit has to equal the value at the point. The good news is that almost every function you meet — polynomials, exponentials, sines and cosines — is continuous everywhere it is defined, because sums, products, quotients (denominator not zero) and compositions of continuous functions stay continuous. That is why the first exercises are just direct substitution: plug the point in and you are done. For instance, Ex. 13.2-1 gives 35 and Ex. 13.2-3 gives −8 by substitution alone. The only interesting case is when the formula breaks at the point — a zero denominator, a 0/0 form — and then you have to decide whether the limit exists anyway (a removable discontinuity, like a single point punched out of an otherwise smooth surface) or whether the roads disagree and there is no limit at all.

One more small detail before you practise: in the formal ε–δ definition, the point itself is excluded — we care about how the function behaves as you approach the point, never about what happens exactly at it. And remember the cube-root warning from the guide: in Exercise 6 the radical is a cube root, ∛(x³y³ + 2x), not a square root.

General limit: lim(x, y) → (x0, y0) f(x, y) = L — the same L along EVERY path

ε–δ: |f(x, y) − L| < ε whenever 0 < √[(x − x0)2 + (y − y0)2] < δ

Continuity at (x0, y0): lim(x, y) → (x0, y0) f(x, y) = f(x0, y0)

Polar coordinates: x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ (show the result → 0 as r → 0+, uniformly in θ)

Standard limits: limz → 0 sin z / z = 1  ·  limz → 0 (1 − cos z) / z = 0  ·  limz → 0+ z ln z = 0

Worked example — Ex. 13.2-33. Show that f(x, y) = x²y / (x⁴ + y²) has no limit as (x, y) → (0, 0).

Step 1 — Decide the plan. To show a limit does not exist, we only need two paths into (0, 0) that give different answers. Try the easy roads first: straight lines y = mx.

Step 2 — Walk in along a line y = mx. Substitute y = mx: f(x, mx) = x²(mx) / (x⁴ + m²x²) = mx³ / [x²(x² + m²)] = mx / (x² + m²). As x → 0 this goes to 0 / m² = 0 (for any fixed m). So along every line, the limit is 0.

Step 3 — Try a curving road, the parabola y = x². Substitute y = x²: f(x, x²) = x²·x² / (x⁴ + x⁴) = x⁴ / (2x⁴) = 1/2, for every x ≠ 0. Along this road the value is 1/2 all the way in, so the limit along this path is 1/2.

Step 4 — Compare. Road 1 says 0, road 2 says 1/2. A limit can only have one value, so the general limit cannot exist.

Answer: the limit does not exist. (This is the trap of the exercise: the lines all agree, and a student who stops there gets it wrong.)

Watch out: "the limit is 0 along the x-axis and 0 along the y-axis, so the limit is 0" is false. Two roads agreeing proves nothing — you need two roads disagreeing to kill a limit, and a method covering all roads to prove one exists.

  • Why can two paths that disagree prove a limit does not exist, while ten paths that agree prove nothing?
  • What is the difference between a limit along a curve and the general limit?
  • How do polar coordinates help you prove a limit exists, and what must you check about θ?
  • When is a function of two variables continuous at a point, and what is a removable discontinuity?

Ex. 13.2 — direct substitution (limit laws / continuity): 1. lim(1, 3) (4xy² − x); 2. lim(0, 0) (4x − y)/(sin y − 1); 3. lim(−1, 2) xy/(x + y); 4. lim(1, −3) e2x − y; 5. lim(0, 0) ln(1 + x²y³); 6. lim(4, −2) ∛(x³y³ + 2x) — a cube root, not a square root.

Limit does not exist via the axes: 7. (a) lim 3/(x + 2y), (b) lim (x + y)/(2x² + y²); 8. (a) lim (x − y)/(x² + y²), (b) lim cos xy/(x² + y²).

Substitution z = x² + y²: 9. lim sin(x² + y²)/(x² + y²); 10. lim (1 − cos(x² + y²))/(x² + y²); 11. lim e−1/(x² + y²); 12. lim 1/(x² + y²)-type.

Determine whether the limit exists: 13–22 (including three-variable limits 17–22).

Polar / spherical coordinates: 23–28.

Focus on Concepts + continuity regions: 33–52.

Exercise Set 13.2, problems 1–28 and 33–52. Problems 29–32 (True–False) and 53–54 (writing) are not in the lecture plan and are omitted. Where a limit is evaluated by direct substitution, the reason is that the function is continuous at the point (a sum, product, quotient with non-zero denominator, or composition of continuous functions).

Ex. 13.2: 1

Use limit laws and continuity properties to evaluate the limit: lim(x,y) → (1,3) (4xy2 − x).

The function f(x, y) = 4xy2 − x is a polynomial, hence continuous everywhere, so the limit is the value at the point. Substituting x = 1, y = 3: 4(1)(3)2 − 1 = 4·9 − 1 = 36 − 1 = 35.

Answer: 35

Ex. 13.2: 2

lim(x,y) → (0,0) (4x − y) / (sin y − 1).

The numerator and denominator are continuous, and the denominator at (0, 0) is sin 0 − 1 = −1 ≠ 0, so the quotient is continuous at (0, 0) and we may substitute directly: (4·0 − 0)/(sin 0 − 1) = 0/(−1) = 0.

Answer: 0

Ex. 13.2: 3

lim(x,y) → (−1,2) xy3 / (x + y).

The quotient is continuous at (−1, 2) because the denominator x + y = −1 + 2 = 1 ≠ 0 there. Substituting: xy3 = (−1)(2)3 = −8, and x + y = 1, so the value is −8/1 = −8.

Answer: −8

Ex. 13.2: 4

lim(x,y) → (1,−3) e2x−y.

The exponential of a continuous function is continuous, so substitute directly: 2x − y = 2(1) − (−3) = 5, hence the limit is e5.

Answer: e5

Ex. 13.2: 5

lim(x,y) → (0,0) ln(1 + x2y3).

The function ln(1 + x2y3) is a composition of continuous functions and is defined at (0, 0) since 1 + 0 = 1 > 0. Substituting: ln(1 + 0) = ln 1 = 0.

Answer: 0

Ex. 13.2: 6

lim(x,y) → (4,−2) ∛(x3y3 + 2x). (Note: the radical in the book is a cube root.)

The cube-root function is continuous everywhere, and x3y3 + 2x is a polynomial, so substitute directly: x3y3 = (4)3(−2)3 = 64·(−8) = −512, and 2x = 8, so the quantity under the root is −512 + 8 = −504. Hence the limit is ∛(−504) = −∛504 = −2∛63 ≈ −7.96.

Answer: −2∛63 ≈ −7.96

Ex. 13.2: 7

Show that the limit does not exist by considering the limits as (x, y) → (0, 0) along the coordinate axes. (a) lim(x,y) → (0,0) 3/(x + 2y)    (b) lim(x,y) → (0,0) (x + y)/(2x2 + y2).

(a) Along the x-axis (y = 0) the function is 3/x, which tends to +∞ as x → 0+ and to −∞ as x → 0−; it has no (finite or infinite) limit along this one path, so the two-variable limit cannot exist. (Along the y-axis, x = 0, it is 3/(2y), which likewise blows up.)

(b) Along the x-axis (y = 0) the function is x/(2x2) = 1/(2x) for x ≠ 0, which tends to +∞ as x → 0+ and −∞ as x → 0−. Since the limit fails to exist along the x-axis alone, the two-variable limit does not exist.

Answer: Both limits do not exist.

Ex. 13.2: 8

Show that the limit does not exist by considering the limits as (x, y) → (0, 0) along the coordinate axes. (a) lim(x,y) → (0,0) (x − y)/(x2 + y2)    (b) lim(x,y) → (0,0) cos(xy)/(x2 + y2).

(a) Along the x-axis (y = 0) the function is x/x2 = 1/x, which tends to +∞ from the right and −∞ from the left, so it has no limit along the x-axis; hence the two-variable limit does not exist.

(b) Along the x-axis (y = 0) the function is cos 0/x2 = 1/x2 → +∞ as x → 0. The function is unbounded near (0, 0), so no finite limit exists (the limit does not exist).

Answer: Both limits do not exist.

Ex. 13.2: 9

Evaluate the limit using the substitution z = x2 + y2, observing that z → 0+ if and only if (x, y) → (0, 0): lim(x,y) → (0,0) sin(x2 + y2)/(x2 + y2).

Put z = x2 + y2. As (x, y) → (0, 0), z → 0+, and the limit becomes the one-variable limit limz → 0+ sin z/z. This is the standard limit 1 (by l'Hôpital's rule, or the known limit limz→0 sin z/z = 1).

Answer: 1

Ex. 13.2: 10

Evaluate the limit using the substitution z = x2 + y2: lim(x,y) → (0,0) (1 − cos(x2 + y2))/(x2 + y2).

With z = x2 + y2 → 0+, the limit is limz → 0+ (1 − cos z)/z. By l'Hôpital's rule this is limz→0 sin z/1 = 0. (Equivalently, 1 − cos z ~ z2/2, so (1 − cos z)/z ~ z/2 → 0.)

Answer: 0

Ex. 13.2: 11

Evaluate the limit using the substitution z = x2 + y2: lim(x,y) → (0,0) e−1/(x2 + y2).

With z = x2 + y2 → 0+, the limit is limz → 0+ e−1/z. As z → 0+, −1/z → −∞, and e−1/z → 0 (the exponential decays faster than any power).

Answer: 0

Ex. 13.2: 12

Evaluate the limit using the substitution z = x2 + y2: lim(x,y) → (0,0) e−1/√(x2 + y2) / (x2 + y2).

With z = x2 + y2 → 0+, the limit is limz → 0+ e−1/√z/z. Put t = 1/√z, so t → +∞ and z = 1/t2; the expression becomes t2e−t = t2/et → 0 as t → ∞, since the exponential dominates any power. Hence the limit is 0.

Answer: 0

Ex. 13.2: 13

Determine whether the limit exists. If so, find its value: lim(x,y) → (0,0) (x4 − y4)/(x2 + y2).

Factor the numerator as a difference of squares: x4 − y4 = (x2 − y2)(x2 + y2). For (x, y) ≠ (0, 0) the factor x2 + y2 cancels, leaving x2 − y2, which is continuous and tends to 0 − 0 = 0 as (x, y) → (0, 0).

Answer: 0

Ex. 13.2: 14

lim(x,y) → (0,0) (x4 − 16y4)/(x2 + 4y2).

Factor: x4 − 16y4 = (x2 − 4y2)(x2 + 4y2). For (x, y) ≠ (0, 0) the second factor cancels with the denominator, leaving x2 − 4y2 → 0 − 0 = 0.

Answer: 0

Ex. 13.2: 15

lim(x,y) → (0,0) xy/(3x2 + 2y2).

Test two paths. Along the x-axis (y = 0) the function is 0, so the limit along this path is 0. Along the line y = x the function is x·x/(3x2 + 2x2) = x2/(5x2) = 1/5 for x ≠ 0, so the limit along this path is 1/5. Since 0 ≠ 1/5, the two paths give different values, so the (general) limit does not exist.

Answer: The limit does not exist (0 along y = 0, 1/5 along y = x).

Ex. 13.2: 16

lim(x,y) → (0,0) (1 − x2 − y2)/(x2 + y2).

As (x, y) → (0, 0) the numerator tends to 1 while the denominator x2 + y2 tends to 0 through positive values. Hence the quotient is positive and grows without bound: along the x-axis it is (1 − x2)/x2 → +∞. There is no finite limit, so the limit does not exist (it is +∞).

Answer: The limit does not exist (the function tends to +∞).

Ex. 13.2: 17

lim(x,y,z) → (2,−1,2) xz2/√(x2 + y2 + z2).

The function is continuous at (2, −1, 2) (quotient of continuous functions with non-zero denominator), so substitute directly: numerator xz2 = 2·(2)2 = 8; denominator √(22 + (−1)2 + 22) = √9 = 3. Hence the value is 8/3.

Answer: 8/3

Ex. 13.2: 18

lim(x,y,z) → (2,0,−1) ln(2x + y − z).

The logarithm of a continuous function is continuous where its argument is positive; at (2, 0, −1) the argument is 2(2) + 0 − (−1) = 5 > 0. Substituting gives ln 5.

Answer: ln 5

Ex. 13.2: 19

lim(x,y,z) → (0,0,0) sin(x2 + y2 + z2)/√(x2 + y2 + z2).

Put t = √(x2 + y2 + z2), so that x2 + y2 + z2 = t2 and t → 0+ as (x, y, z) → (0, 0, 0). The limit becomes limt → 0+ sin(t2)/t. Since sin(t2) ~ t2 for small t, sin(t2)/t ~ t → 0. More rigorously, |sin(t2)/t| ≤ t2/t = t → 0 by the squeeze theorem (using |sin u| ≤ |u|).

Answer: 0

Ex. 13.2: 20

lim(x,y,z) → (0,0,0) sin√(x2 + y2 + z2)/(x2 + y2 + z2).

Put t = √(x2 + y2 + z2), so x2 + y2 + z2 = t2 and t → 0+. The limit becomes limt → 0+ sin t/t2. Since sin t ~ t, sin t/t2 ~ 1/t → +∞. Indeed sin t/t2 = (sin t/t)·(1/t) → 1·(+∞) = +∞. The function is unbounded near the origin, so no finite limit exists.

Answer: The limit does not exist (the function tends to +∞).

Ex. 13.2: 21

lim(x,y,z) → (0,0,0) e√(x2 + y2 + z2)/√(x2 + y2 + z2).

Put t = √(x2 + y2 + z2) → 0+. The limit becomes limt → 0+ et/t. The numerator tends to e0 = 1 while the denominator tends to 0 through positive values, so et/t → +∞. The function is unbounded near the origin, so the limit does not exist.

Answer: The limit does not exist (the function tends to +∞).

Ex. 13.2: 22

lim(x,y,z) → (0,0,0) tan−1(1/(x2 + y2 + z2)).

Put t = x2 + y2 + z2 → 0+ as (x, y, z) → (0, 0, 0). Then 1/t → +∞, and tan−1(1/t) → π/2, since tan−1 u → π/2 as u → +∞. The limit exists and equals π/2.

Answer: π/2

Ex. 13.2: 23

Evaluate the limit by converting to polar coordinates, as in Example 7: lim(x,y) → (0,0) (x2 + y2) ln(x2 + y2).

Put x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ, so x2 + y2 = r2 and r → 0+. The limit becomes limr → 0+ r2 ln(r2) = limr → 0+ 2r2 ln r. This is the standard limit: r2 ln r → 0 (e.g. by l'Hôpital on ln r/(1/r2)). The result is independent of θ, so the two-variable limit is 0.

Answer: 0

Ex. 13.2: 24

lim(x,y) → (0,0) y ln(x2 + y2).

In polar coordinates x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ, the expression is r sin θ · ln(r2) = 2r sin θ ln r. Now |2r sin θ ln r| ≤ 2r|ln r| (since |sin θ| ≤ 1), and 2r|ln r| → 0 as r → 0+. By the squeeze theorem the expression tends to 0, uniformly in θ, so the limit is 0.

Answer: 0

Ex. 13.2: 25

lim(x,y) → (0,0) x2y2/(x2 + y2).

In polar coordinates the expression is r4 cos2 θ sin2 θ/r2 = r2 cos2 θ sin2 θ. Since 0 ≤ cos2 θ sin2 θ ≤ 1, we have 0 ≤ |expression| ≤ r2 → 0 as r → 0+. By the squeeze theorem the limit is 0. (Equivalently, 0 ≤ x2y2/(x2 + y2) ≤ x2 + y2.)

Answer: 0

Ex. 13.2: 26

lim(x,y) → (0,0) xy/(x2 + 2y2).

In polar coordinates the expression is r2 cos θ sin θ/(r2(cos2 θ + 2 sin2 θ)) = cos θ sin θ/(cos2 θ + 2 sin2 θ), which still depends on θ — a warning that the limit may not exist. Check two paths: along the x-axis (y = 0) the function is 0, so the limit along this path is 0; along the line y = x it is x2/(x2 + 2x2) = 1/3 for x ≠ 0, so the limit along this path is 1/3. Since 0 ≠ 1/3, the limit does not exist. (Note the trap: along every parabola y = kx2 the limit is 0, yet the limit still fails to exist.)

Answer: The limit does not exist (0 along y = 0, 1/3 along y = x).

Ex. 13.2: 27

Evaluate the limit by converting to spherical coordinates (ρ, θ, φ), observing that ρ → 0+ if and only if (x, y, z) → (0, 0, 0): lim(x,y,z) → (0,0,0) xyz/(x2 + y2 + z2).

With x = ρ sin φ cos θ, y = ρ sin φ sin θ, z = ρ cos φ, the denominator is ρ2 and the numerator is ρ3 sin2 φ cos φ sin θ cos θ. The quotient is ρ·sin2 φ cos φ sin θ cos θ, and |sin2 φ cos φ sin θ cos θ| ≤ 1, so the expression is squeezed between −ρ and ρ, both tending to 0 as ρ → 0+. Hence the limit is 0.

Answer: 0

Ex. 13.2: 28

lim(x,y,z) → (0,0,0) sin x sin y/(x2 + 2y2 + 3z2).

In spherical coordinates the expression is (sin(ρ sin φ cos θ) sin(ρ sin φ sin θ))/ρ2(sin2 φ cos2 θ + 2 sin2 φ sin2 θ + 3 cos2 φ). Using sin u ~ u, this behaves like sin2 φ cos θ sin θ/(sin2 φ cos2 θ + 2 sin2 φ sin2 θ + 3 cos2 φ), which depends on the direction — so test paths directly. Along the x-axis (y = z = 0) the numerator is 0, so the limit along this path is 0. Along the line y = x, z = 0 the function is sin2 x/(3x2) → 1/3, since sin x/x → 1. Since 0 ≠ 1/3, the limit does not exist.

Answer: The limit does not exist (0 along the x-axis, 1/3 along y = x, z = 0).

Ex. 13.2: 33

The accompanying figure (Figure Ex-33) shows a portion of the graph of f(x, y) = x2y/(x4 + y2). (a) Based on the graph in the figure, does f(x, y) have a limit as (x, y) → (0, 0)? Explain your reasoning. (b) Show that f(x, y) → 0 as (x, y) → (0, 0) along any line y = mx. Does this imply that f(x, y) → 0 as (x, y) → (0, 0)? Explain. (c) Show that f(x, y) → 1/2 as (x, y) → (0, 0) along the parabola y = x2, and confirm visually that this is consistent with the graph of f(x, y). (d) Based on parts (b) and (c), does f(x, y) have a limit as (x, y) → (0, 0)? Is this consistent with your answer to part (a)?

(a) No. The graph shows a narrow ridge rising to height 1/2 along the parabola y = x2 (and symmetrically y = −x2), while the surface is flat (height 0) along the axes and most other directions. The surface does not settle to a single height near the origin, so there is no limit.

(b) Along y = mx, f(x, mx) = x2(mx)/(x4 + m2x2) = mx3/(x4 + m2x2) = mx/(x2 + m2) for x ≠ 0 (if m = 0 the function is 0). As x → 0 this tends to 0/(m2) = 0. No — this does not imply the general limit is 0: the limit must be the same along every path, and lines are only a small family of paths.

(c) Along y = x2, f(x, x2) = x2·x2/(x4 + x4) = x4/(2x4) = 1/2 for x ≠ 0, so the limit along this parabola is 1/2. This matches the graph: the ridge along y = x2 in Figure Ex-33 has height 1/2.

(d) No: the limit is 0 along every line but 1/2 along the parabola y = x2, so two paths give different values and the limit does not exist. This is consistent with (a), where the graph already suggested no single limiting height.

Answer: (a) No. (b) 0 along every line y = mx; this does not prove the limit is 0. (c) 1/2 along y = x2. (d) No limit; consistent with (a).

Ex. 13.2: 34

(a) Show that the value of x3y/(2x6 + y2) approaches 0 as (x, y) → (0, 0) along any straight line y = mx, or along any parabola y = kx2. (b) Show that lim(x,y) → (0,0) x3y/(2x6 + y2) does not exist by letting (x, y) → (0, 0) along the curve y = x3.

(a) Along y = mx: x3(mx)/(2x6 + m2x2) = mx4/(2x6 + m2x2) = mx2/(2x4 + m2) → 0/m2 = 0 as x → 0 (and it is 0 if m = 0). Along y = kx2: x3(kx2)/(2x6 + k2x4) = kx5/(2x6 + k2x4) = kx/(2x2 + k2) → 0 as x → 0.

(b) Along y = x3: x3·x3/(2x6 + x6) = x6/(3x6) = 1/3 for x ≠ 0, so the limit along this curve is 1/3 ≠ 0. Since the limit along lines and parabolas is 0 but along y = x3 it is 1/3, the general limit does not exist. (The cubic curve defeats the linear and quadratic paths.)

Answer: (a) 0 along every line and every parabola y = kx2. (b) 1/3 along y = x3, so the limit does not exist.

Ex. 13.2: 35

(a) Show that the value of xyz/(x2 + y4 + z4) approaches 0 as (x, y, z) → (0, 0, 0) along any line x = at, y = bt, z = ct. (b) Show that the limit lim(x,y,z) → (0,0,0) xyz/(x2 + y4 + z4) does not exist by letting (x, y, z) → (0, 0, 0) along the curve x = t2, y = t, z = t.

(a) Along the line, the value is (at)(bt)(ct)/(a2t2 + b4t4 + c4t4) = abct3/(a2t2 + b4t4 + c4t4) = abct/(a2 + b4t2 + c4t2) for t ≠ 0 (if a = 0 the value is 0). As t → 0 this tends to 0/a2 = 0.

(b) Along x = t2, y = t, z = t: the numerator is t2·t·t = t4 and the denominator is t4 + t4 + t4 = 3t4, so the value is 1/3 for t ≠ 0. Hence the limit along this curve is 1/3 ≠ 0, so the general limit does not exist.

Answer: (a) 0 along every line through the origin. (b) 1/3 along x = t2, y = t, z = t, so the limit does not exist.

Ex. 13.2: 36

Find lim(x,y) → (0,1) tan−1((x2 + 1)/(x2 + (y − 1)2)).

As (x, y) → (0, 1), the numerator x2 + 1 → 1, while the denominator x2 + (y − 1)2 → 0 through positive values (it is a sum of squares, zero only at (0, 1) itself). Hence the ratio tends to +∞, and tan−1 of a quantity tending to +∞ tends to π/2.

Answer: π/2

Ex. 13.2: 37

Find lim(x,y) → (0,1) tan−1((x2 − 1)/(x2 + (y − 1)2)).

As (x, y) → (0, 1), the numerator x2 − 1 → −1, while the denominator x2 + (y − 1)2 → 0 through positive values. Hence the ratio tends to −∞, and tan−1 of a quantity tending to −∞ tends to −π/2.

Answer: −π/2

Ex. 13.2: 38

Let f(x, y) = sin(x2 + y2)/(x2 + y2) if (x, y) ≠ (0, 0), and f(0, 0) = 1. Show that f is continuous at (0, 0).

Continuity at (0, 0) requires lim(x,y) → (0,0) f(x, y) = f(0, 0) = 1. Put z = x2 + y2; then z → 0+ as (x, y) → (0, 0), and the limit is limz → 0+ sin z/z = 1, the standard limit. Since the limit equals the value f(0, 0) = 1, f is continuous at (0, 0).

Answer: lim(x,y) → (0,0) f(x, y) = 1 = f(0, 0), so f is continuous at (0, 0).

Ex. 13.2: 39

A function f(x, y) is said to have a removable discontinuity at (x0, y0) if lim(x,y) → (x0,y0) f(x, y) exists but f is not continuous at (x0, y0), either because f is not defined at (x0, y0) or because f(x0, y0) differs from the value of the limit. Determine whether f(x, y) = x2/(x2 + y2) has a removable discontinuity at (0, 0).

First check whether the limit exists. Along the x-axis (y = 0) the function is x2/x2 = 1, so the limit along this path is 1. Along the y-axis (x = 0) the function is 0/y2 = 0, so the limit along this path is 0. Since 1 ≠ 0, the limit does not exist. A removable discontinuity requires the limit to exist, so f does not have a removable discontinuity at (0, 0) — the discontinuity is not removable.

Answer: No — the limit does not exist at (0, 0), so the discontinuity is not removable.

Ex. 13.2: 40

Determine whether f(x, y) = x2 + 7y2 if (x, y) ≠ (0, 0), and f(0, 0) = −4, has a removable discontinuity at (0, 0).

As (x, y) → (0, 0), x2 + 7y2 → 0 + 0 = 0 (it is continuous, and is squeezed: 0 ≤ x2 + 7y2 ≤ 7(x2 + y2) → 0). So the limit exists and equals 0, but f(0, 0) = −4 ≠ 0. Hence f is not continuous at (0, 0), but the discontinuity is removable: redefining f(0, 0) = 0 makes f continuous at the origin.

Answer: Yes — removable discontinuity; the limit is 0 but f(0, 0) = −4. Redefine f(0, 0) = 0 to remove it.

Ex. 13.2: 41

Sketch the largest region on which the function f(x, y) = y ln(1 + x) is continuous.

The logarithm is defined (and continuous) only when its argument is positive: 1 + x > 0, i.e. x > −1. The factor y is continuous everywhere. Hence f is continuous exactly on the open half-plane x > −1 (all points strictly to the right of the vertical line x = −1; the line itself is excluded).

Answer: The open half-plane x > −1.

Ex. 13.2: 42

Sketch the largest region on which the function f(x, y) = √(x − y) is continuous.

The square root is defined (and continuous) when its argument is non-negative: x − y ≥ 0, i.e. y ≤ x. Hence f is continuous on the closed half-plane on and below the line y = x (the line y = x is included).

Answer: The closed half-plane y ≤ x (including the line y = x).

Ex. 13.2: 43

Sketch the largest region on which the function f(x, y) = x2y/(25 − x2 − y2) is continuous.

A rational function is continuous wherever its denominator is non-zero. Here we need 25 − x2 − y2 ≠ 0, i.e. x2 + y2 ≠ 25. Hence f is continuous on the whole plane except for the circle of radius 5 centred at the origin.

Answer: The whole plane minus the circle x2 + y2 = 25.

Ex. 13.2: 44

Sketch the largest region on which the function f(x, y) = ln(2x − y + 1) is continuous.

We need the argument of the logarithm to be positive: 2x − y + 1 > 0, i.e. y < 2x + 1. Hence f is continuous on the open half-plane below the line y = 2x + 1 (the line itself is excluded).

Answer: The open half-plane y < 2x + 1.

Ex. 13.2: 45

Sketch the largest region on which the function f(x, y) = y/(11x2 + 3) is continuous.

The denominator 11x2 + 3 is at least 3 for all (x, y), so it is never zero. The quotient of continuous functions with a never-vanishing denominator is continuous everywhere.

Answer: The entire plane.

Ex. 13.2: 46

Sketch the largest region on which the function f(x, y) = e1−xy is continuous.

The exponential of the polynomial 1 − xy is a composition of continuous functions, defined and continuous for all (x, y).

Answer: The entire plane.

Ex. 13.2: 47

Sketch the largest region on which the function f(x, y) = sin−1(xy) is continuous.

The inverse sine is defined (and continuous) when its argument lies in [−1, 1]. We need −1 ≤ xy ≤ 1. This is the region between the two branches of the hyperbola xy = 1 and the two branches of xy = −1, including the curves themselves — i.e. all points (x, y) with |xy| ≤ 1.

Answer: The region |xy| ≤ 1 (between the hyperbolas xy = 1 and xy = −1, curves included).

Ex. 13.2: 48

Sketch the largest region on which the function f(x, y) = tan−1(y − x) is continuous.

The inverse tangent is defined and continuous for every real number, and y − x is a polynomial, so the composition is continuous everywhere.

Answer: The entire plane.

Ex. 13.2: 49

Describe the largest region on which the function f(x, y, z) = 3x2eyz cos(xyz) is continuous.

The function is built from polynomials, the exponential, and the cosine by multiplication and composition — all continuous everywhere. There is no denominator, logarithm, or root to restrict the domain.

Answer: All of 3-space, ℝ3.

Ex. 13.2: 50

Describe the largest region on which the function f(x, y, z) = ln(4 − x2 − y2 − z2) is continuous.

The logarithm requires a positive argument: 4 − x2 − y2 − z2 > 0, i.e. x2 + y2 + z2 < 4. This is the interior of the sphere of radius 2 centred at the origin.

Answer: The open ball x2 + y2 + z2 < 4 (interior of the sphere of radius 2 about the origin).

Ex. 13.2: 51

Describe the largest region on which the function f(x, y, z) = (y + 1)/(x2 + z2 − 1) is continuous.

A rational function is continuous where its denominator is non-zero: x2 + z2 − 1 ≠ 0, i.e. x2 + z2 ≠ 1. In the xz-plane this is the circle of radius 1 about the origin, and since y is unrestricted, the excluded set is the whole cylinder over that circle. Hence f is continuous everywhere in 3-space except on the cylinder x2 + z2 = 1.

Answer: All of ℝ3 except the cylinder x2 + z2 = 1 (all y).

Ex. 13.2: 52

Describe the largest region on which the function f(x, y, z) = sin√(x2 + y2 + 3z2) is continuous.

The quantity under the square root, x2 + y2 + 3z2, is a sum of squares, hence ≥ 0 for all (x, y, z), so the square root is defined everywhere; the sine of a continuous function is continuous everywhere.

Answer: All of 3-space, ℝ3.

Lecture 6 — Partial Derivatives (Anton §13.3)

A partial derivative is the slope of the landscape when you walk in exactly one direction — east, say — while staying at the same north.

You already know what a derivative is: the slope of a curve, the rate at which something changes. The trouble with a landscape is that it slopes in many directions at once — it can go steeply up to the east and gently down to the north, both at the same spot. A partial derivative is the simple, clever trick that untangles this: freeze one direction and let the other one move.

Here is the picture. Stand at a point (x₀, y₀) on the surface z = f(x, y). Now walk due east — that is, let x change while y stays exactly the same. As you walk, your height changes, and the rate at which it changes is the partial derivative with respect to x, written fx or ∂f/∂x. Geometrically, it is the slope of the curve you get when you slice the surface with the vertical plane y = y₀: that slice is an ordinary one-variable curve, and its slope is fx. Walk due north instead — x frozen, y changing — and you get fy, the slope in the y-direction. If fx is positive, the ground rises as you go east; if it is negative, it falls.

Computing them is easier than it sounds, because once you freeze a variable, it behaves like a number. To find fx, treat every y as if it were a constant — a plain number like 5 — and differentiate with respect to x using all your ordinary rules: product rule, quotient rule, chain rule. To find fy, do the opposite. Take f(x, y) = x³y². Freezing y, the derivative with respect to x is 3x²y² (the y² is just a constant multiplier). Freezing x, the derivative with respect to y is 2x³y. That is all there is to it — the new idea is the freezing, not the differentiating.

Then we go one step further: differentiate again. The second-order partials are fxx (differentiate twice in x), fyy (twice in y), and the mixed ones fxy and fyx (once in each direction, in different orders). Here is a small gift from the theory, Clairaut's theorem: if the mixed partials are continuous, then fxy = fyx — the order does not matter. But do not take it for granted without the continuity condition; the book has counterexamples where it fails.

Now, why do we need a new kind of derivative at all? In one-variable calculus, a curve has one slope at each point, and one number — the derivative — tells you everything about how fast it is changing. A hillside refuses to be described by one number. Stand on a mountainside and ask "how steep is it here?" — the question is meaningless until you say which way you are facing. Walk east and the ground may rise sharply; walk north and it may fall gently; walk north-east and you get something in between. The mountain has a different slope in every direction, so a single derivative cannot capture it. The partial derivative is the way out of this problem: instead of asking for "the" slope, we ask for the slope in one chosen direction at a time — first east, then north — and we collect the answers separately. Two directions, two numbers, and together they describe the tilt of the ground at that spot.

Here is the everyday picture to keep. Imagine a temperature map of a city: at every street corner there is a temperature. Stand at one corner and ask how fast the temperature changes as you walk east — that is one number. Walk north instead and you get a different number, because the warm part of the city might be to the north while the east is flat. A partial derivative is exactly that: the rate of change of the output when you move in one input direction and hold the other one still. And here is the reassuring part — it is not a new kind of differentiation. It is ordinary one-variable differentiation with a trick: you freeze one variable, treat it as a plain number, and differentiate with respect to the other one using every rule you already know. The new idea is the freezing, not the differentiating. The geometric picture matches: slicing the surface with the vertical plane y = y₀ (the blue plane in the diagram) cuts out an ordinary one-variable curve, and fx is simply the slope of that curve.

Now the place students most often get stuck: what "freezing" really means when the frozen variable is still sitting inside the formula. Take the term xy and differentiate it with respect to x. The beginner's instinct is to say "y is frozen, so xy is a constant, so the derivative is 0" — and that is wrong. Freezing y means y behaves like a number, say 5, and the term becomes 5x. The derivative of 5x with respect to x is 5 — which is y. So ∂/∂x of xy is y, not 0. The frozen variable is a constant multiplier, not a vanished term. The same rule explains the worked example below: in f(x, y) = xe−y + 5y, freezing y makes e−y a constant number multiplying x, so the x-derivative of xe−y is just e−y; and the term 5y contains no x at all, so it genuinely disappears. The rule of thumb: if a term contains the variable you are differentiating with respect to, it survives and the usual rules apply; if it does not contain it at all, it is a constant and differentiates to zero.

Let us do one more short example together, because it shows the chain rule working inside a freeze. Take z = sin(y² − 4x) at the point (2, 1) (Ex. 13.3-13). First freeze y and differentiate with respect to x: the chain rule gives zx = cos(y² − 4x) · (−4) = −4 cos(y² − 4x). At (2, 1) the inside is 1 − 8 = −7, and cos(−7) = cos 7 ≈ 0.754, so zx ≈ −4(0.754) ≈ −3.02. The ground falls steeply as you walk east. Now freeze x and differentiate with respect to y: zy = cos(y² − 4x) · 2y = 2y cos(y² − 4x). At (2, 1) that is 2 · 1 · cos(−7) ≈ 1.51 — the ground rises more gently as you walk north. Two directions, two slopes, one point: −3.02 east, 1.51 north. That pair of numbers is the whole content of the first derivatives at that point.

Then we go one step further and differentiate again, and the second derivatives have a meaning worth pausing on. fxx is how the east-slope itself changes as you keep walking east — it measures the curvature of the hill in the east direction, just as f″ did for a curve in one variable. fyy does the same in the north direction. The mixed partials fxy and fyx measure the twist: how the east-slope changes as you walk north, and how the north-slope changes as you walk east. On a smooth hill these two twists are the same, and Clairaut's theorem says exactly that — if the mixed partials are continuous, fxy = fyx, and the order of differentiation does not matter. Think of it as the hill having no preferred order of walking: the twist you feel is the same either way. But the continuity condition matters, and the book has counterexamples (Ex. 13.3-118) where the mixed partials exist but are not continuous, and the two twists disagree — so never quote Clairaut without checking that the function is nice enough. And when you do use it, it is a genuine labour-saver: compute whichever mixed partial is easier and use it for both.

Two traps deserve a red circle in your notes. First, the notation trap: in subscript notation, fxy means differentiate with respect to x first, then y (left to right); but in ∂-notation, ∂²f/∂y∂x means differentiate with respect to x first, then y (right to left). They mean the same thing — but if you read them the same way round, you will swap them. Second, the "freeze" mistake: when you differentiate with respect to x, a term like xy is not a constant — y is frozen, but x is still in the product, so the product rule still applies. Finally, the same freezing idea lets you differentiate implicitly: if z is defined by an equation F(x, y, z) = 0 rather than by a formula, differentiate both sides treating z as a function of x and y. And the exercises put these derivatives to work in real equations of physics — Laplace's equation zxx + zyy = 0, the heat equation, the wave equation, and the Cauchy–Riemann equations.

fx(x0, y0) = limΔx → 0 [f(x0 + Δx, y0) − f(x0, y0)] / Δx  — hold y fixed, vary x

fy(x0, y0) = limΔy → 0 [f(x0, y0 + Δy) − f(x0, y0)] / Δy  — hold x fixed, vary y

Example: f = x3y2 ⇒ fx = 3x2y2,  fy = 2x3y

Second-order partials: fxx, fyy, fxy, fyx  ·  Clairaut's theorem: if fxy and fyx are continuous, then fxy = fyx

Laplace's equation: zxx + zyy = 0  ·  Heat equation: zt = c2zxx  ·  Cauchy–Riemann: ux = vy, uy = −vx

Worked example — Ex. 13.3-12. For f(x, y) = xe−y + 5y, find fx and fy at the point (3, 0).

Step 1 — Find fx: freeze y. Treat y as a constant, so e−y is just a constant number multiplying x. The derivative of xe−y with respect to x is e−y, and the derivative of 5y (no x in it) is 0. So fx(x, y) = e−y.

Step 2 — Evaluate at (3, 0). fx(3, 0) = e0 = 1. The surface rises with slope 1 as you walk east from (3, 0).

Step 3 — Find fy: freeze x. Now x is the constant. The derivative of xe−y with respect to y is x·(−e−y) = −xe−y (chain rule on the exponent), and the derivative of 5y is 5. So fy(x, y) = −xe−y + 5.

Step 4 — Evaluate at (3, 0). fy(3, 0) = −3·e0 + 5 = −3 + 5 = 2. The surface rises with slope 2 as you walk north from (3, 0).

Answer: fx = 1, fy = 2 at (3, 0).

Watch out: when you differentiate with respect to x, y is frozen but it is still in the formula — a term like xy still needs the product rule, and in ∂-notation the derivatives are read right-to-left (∂²f/∂y∂x means x first), the opposite of the subscript order in fxy.

  • In plain words, what does fx measure, and what do you freeze to find it?
  • How do you compute fx and fy for f(x, y) = x³y², and what does each answer mean geometrically?
  • What does Clairaut's theorem say, and what condition does it need?
  • Why is ∂²f/∂y∂x the same as fxy even though the letters look reversed?

Rates along a curve / applied rates: 55. point on z = x² + 3y², y = 1, at (2, 1, 7): dz/dx; 56. same surface, x = 2: dz/dy; 57. z = 29 − x² − y², y = 3, at (4, 3, 2): dz/dx; 58. slope of tangent to intersection curves; 59. cylinder V = πr²h; 60. cone V = (π/24)d²√(4s² − d²).

Identities and tangent lines: 65. cone V = (1/3)πr²h: show ∂V/∂r = 2V/r; 66. tangent line to z = x²y at (1, 3, 3); 67–68. implicit slopes of the hyperboloid x² + y² − z² = 1 at (3, 4, ±2√6).

Second-order partials (incl. FTC with variable limits): 77. f = ∫yx et² dt; 78. f = ∫1xy et² dt; 79. f = ∫0x²y³ sin t³ dt; 80. f = ∫x+yx−y sin t³ dt; 81. z = x cos y; 82. f = 4x − 2y + 7x²y⁴; 83. f = sin(3x² + 6y²); 84. f = xe2y.
