Lecture 6 — Partial Derivatives (Anton §13.3)

Ex. 13.3: 11

Let f(x, y) = 3x + 2y. (a) Find the slope of the surface z = f(x, y) in the x-direction at the point (4, 2). (b) Find the slope of the surface z = f(x, y) in the y-direction at the point (4, 2).

The slope in the x-direction is fx and the slope in the y-direction is fy. Holding y fixed and differentiating with respect to x: fx(x, y) = 3. Holding x fixed and differentiating with respect to y: fy(x, y) = 2. Both partials are constant (the surface is a plane), so their values at (4, 2) are the same as everywhere.

Answer: (a) 3; (b) 2.

Ex. 13.3: 12

Let f(x, y) = xe−y + 5y. (a) Find the slope of the surface z = f(x, y) in the x-direction at the point (3, 0). (b) Find the slope of the surface z = f(x, y) in the y-direction at the point (3, 0).

(a) Hold y fixed: fx(x, y) = e−y. At (3, 0): fx(3, 0) = e0 = 1.

(b) Hold x fixed and use the product/chain rule on xe−y: fy(x, y) = −xe−y + 5. At (3, 0): fy(3, 0) = −3e0 + 5 = 2.

Answer: (a) 1; (b) 2.

Ex. 13.3: 13

Let z = sin(y2 − 4x). (a) Find the rate of change of z with respect to x at the point (2, 1) with y held fixed. (b) Find the rate of change of z with respect to y at the point (2, 1) with x held fixed.

By the chain rule, ∂z/∂x = cos(y2 − 4x) · (−4) = −4cos(y2 − 4x) and ∂z/∂y = cos(y2 − 4x) · 2y = 2y cos(y2 − 4x). At (2, 1) the argument is y2 − 4x = 1 − 8 = −7, and cos(−7) = cos 7 ≈ 0.754. Hence ∂z/∂x = −4cos 7 ≈ −3.02 and ∂z/∂y = 2cos 7 ≈ 1.51.

Answer: (a) −4 cos 7 ≈ −3.02; (b) 2 cos 7 ≈ 1.51.

Ex. 13.3: 14

Let z = (x + y)−1. (a) Find the rate of change of z with respect to x at the point (−2, 4) with y held fixed. (b) Find the rate of change of z with respect to y at the point (−2, 4) with x held fixed.

Write z = (x + y)−1. By the chain rule, ∂z/∂x = −(x + y)−2 and ∂z/∂y = −(x + y)−2 (the inner derivative is 1 in both cases). At (−2, 4), x + y = 2, so each partial equals −1/22 = −1/4.

Answer: (a) −1/4; (b) −1/4.

Ex. 13.3: 55

A point moves along the intersection of the elliptic paraboloid z = x2 + 3y2 and the plane y = 1. At what rate is z changing with respect to x when the point is at (2, 1, 7)?

On the plane y = 1 the point moves with y fixed, so the rate of change of z with respect to x is the partial derivative ∂z/∂x. Holding y constant, ∂z/∂x = 2x. At x = 2 this is 2(2) = 4. (Check: the point lies on the surface since 22 + 3(1)2 = 7.)

Answer: 4 (z increases 4 units per unit increase in x).

Ex. 13.3: 56

A point moves along the intersection of the elliptic paraboloid z = x2 + 3y2 and the plane x = 2. At what rate is z changing with respect to y when the point is at (2, 1, 7)?

On the plane x = 2 the point moves with x fixed, so the rate is ∂z/∂y. Holding x constant, ∂z/∂y = 6y. At y = 1 this is 6(1) = 6.

Answer: 6 (z increases 6 units per unit increase in y).

Ex. 13.3: 57

A point moves along the intersection of the plane y = 3 and the surface z = 29 − x2 − y2. At what rate is z changing with respect to x when the point is at (4, 3, 2)?

On the plane y = 3 the point moves with y fixed, so the rate is ∂z/∂x. Holding y constant, ∂z/∂x = −2x. At x = 4 this is −2(4) = −8. (Note: 29 − 42 − 32 = 4, so the printed point (4, 3, 2) does not lie on the surface as stated — the intended z-value is 4. The rate ∂z/∂x = −8 is unaffected.)

Answer: −8 (z decreases 8 units per unit increase in x).

Ex. 13.3: 58

Find the slope of the tangent line at (−1, 1, 5) to the curve of intersection of the surface z = x2 + 4y2 and (a) the plane x = −1, (b) the plane y = 1.

The curve of intersection with a plane x = constant is traced with x fixed, so its slope (dz/dy) is ∂z/∂y; with a plane y = constant the slope (dz/dx) is ∂z/∂x. Here ∂z/∂x = 2x and ∂z/∂y = 8y. (a) In the plane x = −1, the slope is ∂z/∂y at (−1, 1): 8(1) = 8. (b) In the plane y = 1, the slope is ∂z/∂x at (−1, 1): 2(−1) = −2. (Check: (−1)2 + 4(1)2 = 5, so the point is on the surface.)

Answer: (a) 8; (b) −2.

Ex. 13.3: 59

The volume V of a right circular cylinder is given by the formula V = πr2h, where r is the radius and h is the height. (a) Find a formula for the instantaneous rate of change of V with respect to r if r changes and h remains constant. (b) Find a formula for the instantaneous rate of change of V with respect to h if h changes and r remains constant. (c) Suppose that h has a constant value of 4 in, but r varies. Find the rate of change of V with respect to r at the point where r = 6 in. (d) Suppose that r has a constant value of 8 in, but h varies. Find the instantaneous rate of change of V with respect to h at the point where h = 10 in.

(a) Hold h fixed: ∂V/∂r = 2πrh. (b) Hold r fixed: ∂V/∂h = πr2. (c) Substitute h = 4, r = 6 into (a): ∂V/∂r = 2π(6)(4) = 48π in2/in ≈ 150.8 in2/in. (d) Substitute r = 8 into (b): ∂V/∂h = π(8)2 = 64π in2/in ≈ 201.1 in2/in.

Answer: (a) ∂V/∂r = 2πrh; (b) ∂V/∂h = πr2; (c) 48π in2/in; (d) 64π in2/in.

Ex. 13.3: 60

The volume V of a right circular cone is given by V = (π/24)d2(4s2 − d2), where s is the slant height and d is the diameter of the base. (a) Find a formula for the instantaneous rate of change of V with respect to s if d remains constant. (b) Find a formula for the instantaneous rate of change of V with respect to d if s remains constant. (c) Suppose that d has a constant value of 16 cm, but s varies. Find the rate of change of V with respect to s when s = 10 cm. (d) Suppose that s has a constant value of 10 cm, but d varies. Find the rate of change of V with respect to d when d = 16 cm.

Expand: V = (π/24)(4d2s2 − d4). (a) Hold d fixed: ∂V/∂s = (π/24)(8d2s) = πd2s/3. (b) Hold s fixed: ∂V/∂d = (π/24)(8ds2 − 4d3) = πd(2s2 − d2)/6. (c) With d = 16, s = 10: ∂V/∂s = π(16)2(10)/3 = 2560π/3 ≈ 2680.8 cm2/cm. (d) With s = 10, d = 16: ∂V/∂d = π(16)(2·100 − 256)/6 = π(16)(−56)/6 = −448π/3 ≈ −469.1 cm2/cm. The negative sign is correct: with the slant height fixed, widening the base shortens the height, and past a point the volume falls.

Answer: (a) ∂V/∂s = πd2s/3; (b) ∂V/∂d = πd(2s2 − d2)/6; (c) 2560π/3 cm2/cm ≈ 2680.8 cm2/cm; (d) −448π/3 cm2/cm ≈ −469.1 cm2/cm.

Ex. 13.3: 65

The volume of a right circular cone of radius r and height h is V = (1/3)πr2h. Show that if the height remains constant while the radius changes, then the volume satisfies ∂V/∂r = 2V/r.

Hold h fixed and differentiate with respect to r: ∂V/∂r = (1/3)π(2r)h = (2/3)πrh. Now compute 2V/r from the formula: 2V/r = 2·(1/3)πr2h/r = (2/3)πrh. Both sides are (2/3)πrh, so ∂V/∂r = 2V/r, as required.

Answer: ∂V/∂r = (2/3)πrh = 2V/r. ∎

Ex. 13.3: 66

Find parametric equations for the tangent line at (1, 3, 3) to the curve of intersection of the surface z = x2y and (a) the plane x = 1, (b) the plane y = 3.

(a) In the plane x = 1 the curve is z = (1)2y = y, traced as y varies. Its slope is dz/dy = ∂z/∂y = x2 = 1 at (1, 3). So the tangent line lies in the plane x = 1, passes through (1, 3, 3), and has direction (0, 1, 1): x = 1, y = 3 + t, z = 3 + t.

(b) In the plane y = 3 the curve is z = 3x2, traced as x varies. Its slope is dz/dx = ∂z/∂x = 2xy = 2(1)(3) = 6 at (1, 3). So the tangent line lies in the plane y = 3, passes through (1, 3, 3), and has direction (1, 0, 6): x = 1 + t, y = 3, z = 3 + 6t.

Answer: (a) x = 1, y = 3 + t, z = 3 + t; (b) x = 1 + t, y = 3, z = 3 + 6t.

Ex. 13.3: 67

(a) By differentiating implicitly, find the slope of the hyperboloid x2 + y2 − z2 = 1 in the x-direction at the points (3, 4, 2√6) and (3, 4, −2√6). (b) Check the results in part (a) by solving for z and differentiating the resulting functions directly.

(a) Treat z as a function of x and y and differentiate x2 + y2 − z2 = 1 with respect to x, holding y fixed: 2x − 2z·(∂z/∂x) = 0, so ∂z/∂x = x/z. At (3, 4, 2√6): ∂z/∂x = 3/(2√6) = 3√6/12 = √6/4. At (3, 4, −2√6): ∂z/∂x = 3/(−2√6) = −√6/4. The two sheets have opposite slopes, as expected by symmetry.

(b) Solving for z: z = ±√(x2 + y2 − 1). For the upper sheet, z = (x2 + y2 − 1)1/2, so ∂z/∂x = x/(x2 + y2 − 1)1/2 = x/z; at (3, 4) this is 3/(2√6) = √6/4. For the lower sheet, z = −(x2 + y2 − 1)1/2, so ∂z/∂x = −x/z = −√6/4 at (3, 4). Both agree with (a).

Answer: (a) √6/4 at the upper point, −√6/4 at the lower point. (b) Confirmed by direct differentiation.

Ex. 13.3: 68

(a) By differentiating implicitly, find the slope of the hyperboloid x2 + y2 − z2 = 1 in the y-direction at the points (3, 4, 2√6) and (3, 4, −2√6). (b) Check the results in part (a) by solving for z and differentiating the resulting functions directly.

(a) Differentiate x2 + y2 − z2 = 1 with respect to y, holding x fixed, with z a function of x and y: 2y − 2z·(∂z/∂y) = 0, so ∂z/∂y = y/z. At (3, 4, 2√6): ∂z/∂y = 4/(2√6) = 2/√6 = √6/3. At (3, 4, −2√6): ∂z/∂y = 4/(−2√6) = −√6/3.

(b) From z = ±√(x2 + y2 − 1), the upper sheet gives ∂z/∂y = y/√(x2 + y2 − 1) = y/z = 4/(2√6) = √6/3 at (3, 4), and the lower sheet gives ∂z/∂y = −y/z = −√6/3. Both agree with (a).

Answer: (a) √6/3 at the upper point, −√6/3 at the lower point. (b) Confirmed by direct differentiation.

Ex. 13.3: 77

Find fx and fy: f(x, y) = ∫yx et2 dt.

Use the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (Part 1) with a variable limit. For fx, the upper limit is x and the lower limit is constant with respect to x: fx(x, y) = ex2. For fy, the lower limit is y: differentiating with respect to the lower limit introduces a minus sign, fy(x, y) = −ey2. (The integrand et2 has no elementary antiderivative, but we never need one.)

Answer: fx = ex2, fy = −ey2.

Ex. 13.3: 78

Find fx and fy: f(x, y) = ∫1xy et2 dt.

Let F(u) = ∫1u et2 dt, so F′(u) = eu2 and f(x, y) = F(xy). By the chain rule, fx = F′(xy)·∂(xy)/∂x = e(xy)2·y = yex2y2, and fy = F′(xy)·∂(xy)/∂y = ex2y2·x = xex2y2.

Answer: fx = yex2y2, fy = xex2y2.

Ex. 13.3: 79

Find fx and fy: f(x, y) = ∫0x2y3 sin t3 dt.

Let G(u) = ∫0u sin t3 dt, so G′(u) = sin u3 and f(x, y) = G(x2y3). By the chain rule, fx = G′(x2y3)·2xy3 = 2xy3 sin((x2y3)3) = 2xy3 sin(x6y9), and fy = G′(x2y3)·3x2y2 = 3x2y2 sin(x6y9).

Answer: fx = 2xy3 sin(x6y9), fy = 3x2y2 sin(x6y9).

Ex. 13.3: 80

Find fx and fy: f(x, y) = ∫x+yx−y sin t3 dt.

Both limits depend on x and y. Write f = H(x − y) − H(x + y), where H(u) = ∫ sin t3 dt (any antiderivative), so H′(u) = sin u3. Then fx = H′(x − y)·(1) − H′(x + y)·(1) = sin((x − y)3) − sin((x + y)3). And fy = H′(x − y)·(−1) − H′(x + y)·(1) = −sin((x − y)3) − sin((x + y)3).

Answer: fx = sin((x − y)3) − sin((x + y)3), fy = −sin((x − y)3) − sin((x + y)3).

Ex. 13.3: 81

Let z = x cos y. Find (a) ∂2z/∂x2, (b) ∂2z/∂y2, (c) ∂2z/∂x∂y, (d) ∂2z/∂y∂x.

First-order partials: ∂z/∂x = cos y and ∂z/∂y = −x sin y. (a) Differentiate ∂z/∂x with respect to x: ∂2z/∂x2 = 0. (b) Differentiate ∂z/∂y with respect to y: ∂2z/∂y2 = −x cos y. (c) Differentiate ∂z/∂x with respect to y (note: in ∂-notation the rightmost variable is differentiated first, so ∂2z/∂x∂y means differentiate with respect to y, then x — equivalently differentiate ∂z/∂x with respect to y): ∂2z/∂x∂y = −sin y. (d) Differentiate ∂z/∂y with respect to x: ∂2z/∂y∂x = −sin y. The mixed partials agree, as Clairaut's theorem promises.

Answer: (a) 0; (b) −x cos y; (c) −sin y; (d) −sin y.

Ex. 13.3: 82

Let f(x, y) = 4x2 − 2y + 7x4y5. Find (a) fxx, (b) fyy, (c) fxy, (d) fyx.

First-order partials: fx = 8x + 28x3y5 and fy = −2 + 35x4y4. (a) Differentiate fx with respect to x: fxx = 8 + 84x2y5. (b) Differentiate fy with respect to y: fyy = 140x4y3. (c) Differentiate fx with respect to y: fxy = 140x3y4. (d) Differentiate fy with respect to x: fyx = 140x3y4. The mixed partials agree, as Clairaut's theorem promises. (Verified with SymPy.)

Answer: (a) fxx = 8 + 84x2y5; (b) fyy = 140x4y3; (c) fxy = 140x3y4; (d) fyx = 140x3y4.

Ex. 13.3: 83

Let f(x, y) = sin(3x2 + 6y2). Find (a) fxx, (b) fyy, (c) fxy, (d) fyx.

First-order partials (chain rule): fx = 6x cos(3x2 + 6y2) and fy = 12y cos(3x2 + 6y2). (a) Differentiate fx with respect to x (product rule): fxx = 6cos(3x2 + 6y2) + 6x·(−sin(3x2 + 6y2))·6x = 6cos(3x2 + 6y2) − 36x2sin(3x2 + 6y2). (b) Similarly, fyy = 12cos(3x2 + 6y2) − 144y2sin(3x2 + 6y2). (c) Differentiate fx with respect to y: fxy = 6x·(−sin(3x2 + 6y2))·12y = −72xy sin(3x2 + 6y2). (d) Differentiate fy with respect to x: fyx = 12y·(−sin(3x2 + 6y2))·6x = −72xy sin(3x2 + 6y2). The mixed partials agree. (Verified with SymPy.)

Answer: (a) fxx = 6cos(3x2 + 6y2) − 36x2sin(3x2 + 6y2); (b) fyy = 12cos(3x2 + 6y2) − 144y2sin(3x2 + 6y2); (c) fxy = fyx = −72xy sin(3x2 + 6y2).

Ex. 13.3: 84

Let f(x, y) = xe2y. Find (a) fxx, (b) fyy, (c) fxy, (d) fyx.

First-order partials: fx = e2y and fy = 2xe2y. (a) fxx = ∂(e2y)/∂x = 0. (b) fyy = ∂(2xe2y)/∂y = 4xe2y. (c) fxy = ∂(e2y)/∂y = 2e2y. (d) fyx = ∂(2xe2y)/∂x = 2e2y. The mixed partials agree.

Answer: (a) fxx = 0; (b) fyy = 4xe2y; (c) fxy = fyx = 2e2y.

Ex. 13.3: 101

Show that the function satisfies Laplace's equation ∂2z/∂x2 + ∂2z/∂y2 = 0: (a) z = x2 − y2 + 2xy, (b) z = ex sin y + ey cos x, (c) z = ln(x2 + y2) + 2 tan−1(y/x).

(a) zx = 2x + 2y, zxx = 2; zy = −2y + 2x, zyy = −2. Hence zxx + zyy = 2 − 2 = 0.

(b) zx = ex sin y − ey sin x, so zxx = ex sin y − ey cos x. zy = ex cos y + ey cos x, so zyy = −ex sin y + ey cos x. Hence zxx + zyy = 0.

(c) zx = 2x/(x2 + y2) + 2·(1/(1 + (y/x)2))·(−y/x2) = 2x/(x2 + y2) − 2y/(x2 + y2) = 2(x − y)/(x2 + y2). Differentiating again (quotient rule) gives zxx = 2(−x2 + 2xy + y2)/(x2 + y2)2. Similarly zy = 2y/(x2 + y2) + 2x/(x2 + y2) = 2(x + y)/(x2 + y2), so zyy = 2(x2 − 2xy − y2)/(x2 + y2)2 = −zxx. Hence zxx + zyy = 0. (Part (c) confirmed with SymPy.)

Answer: In each part zxx + zyy = 0, so each function satisfies Laplace's equation. ∎

Ex. 13.3: 105

Show that if u(x, y) and v(x, y) each have equal mixed second partials, and if u and v satisfy the Cauchy–Riemann equations (Exercise 104), then u, v, and u + v satisfy Laplace's equation (Exercise 101).

The Cauchy–Riemann equations are ux = vy and uy = −vx. Differentiate the first equation with respect to x: uxx = vyx. Differentiate the second with respect to y: uyy = −vxy. Adding, uxx + uyy = vyx − vxy = 0, since v has equal mixed partials (vyx = vxy). So u satisfies Laplace's equation. The same argument with u and v swapped (differentiate uy = −vx with respect to x and ux = vy with respect to y) gives vxx + vyy = −uxy + uyx = 0, since u has equal mixed partials. Finally, (u + v)xx + (u + v)yy = (uxx + uyy) + (vxx + vyy) = 0 + 0 = 0, so u + v also satisfies Laplace's equation.

Answer: uxx + uyy = 0, vxx + vyy = 0, and (u + v)xx + (u + v)yy = 0. ∎

Ex. 13.3: 106

When two resistors having resistances R1 ohms and R2 ohms are connected in parallel, their combined resistance R in ohms is R = R1R2/(R1 + R2). Show that (∂2R/∂R12)(∂2R/∂R22) = 4R2/(R1 + R2)4.

First, ∂R/∂R1 = [R2(R1 + R2) − R1R2]/(R1 + R2)2 = R22/(R1 + R2)2 (quotient rule). Differentiating again with respect to R1: ∂2R/∂R12 = R22·(−2)/(R1 + R2)3 = −2R22/(R1 + R2)3. By symmetry, ∂2R/∂R22 = −2R12/(R1 + R2)3. Multiplying: (∂2R/∂R12)(∂2R/∂R22) = 4R12R22/(R1 + R2)6. Since R2 = R12R22/(R1 + R2)2, the right-hand side 4R2/(R1 + R2)4 equals the same 4R12R22/(R1 + R2)6. (Verified with SymPy. Note: the left-hand side is the product of the two pure second partials, not the mixed partial ∂2R/∂R1∂R2 = 2R1R2/(R1 + R2)3.)

Answer: Both sides equal 4R12R22/(R1 + R2)6. ∎

Ex. 13.3: 118

Let f(x, y) = (x2 + y2)2/3. Show that fx(x, y) = { 4x / [3(x2 + y2)1/3] if (x, y) ≠ (0, 0); 0 if (x, y) = (0, 0) }.

Case (x, y) ≠ (0, 0): here x2 + y2 > 0, so f is a composition of smooth functions and the ordinary chain rule applies. Holding y fixed: fx(x, y) = (2/3)(x2 + y2)−1/3·2x = 4x/[3(x2 + y2)1/3], as claimed.

Case (x, y) = (0, 0): the chain-rule formula would divide by zero, so use the limit definition of the partial derivative instead. fx(0, 0) = limh→0 [f(h, 0) − f(0, 0)]/h = limh→0 (h2)2/3/h = limh→0 |h|4/3/h. Since |h|4/3/h = |h|1/3·sign(h) → 0 as h → 0, the limit is 0. Hence fx(0, 0) = 0.

Remark: the point of the exercise is that the chain-rule formula cannot be applied at the origin itself (it would divide by zero), so the limit definition must be used there. In fact fx is continuous at the origin: |fx(x, y)| = (4/3)|x|/(x2 + y2)1/3 ≤ (4/3)(x2 + y2)1/6 → 0.

Answer: fx(x, y) = 4x/[3(x2 + y2)1/3] for (x, y) ≠ (0, 0), and fx(0, 0) = 0. ∎

Lecture 7 — Differentiability, Taylor Series, Local Linear Approximation (Anton §13.4)

Close to a point, a smooth surface looks almost flat — so we can replace it by its tangent plane, and the error of that replacement is tiny compared with how far we moved.

Think of zooming in on a smooth hill on a map. From far away the hill is curved and complicated, but if you zoom in close enough on one small patch of ground, the patch looks flat. That is the whole idea of this lecture: near any point, a nice surface can be replaced by a flat plane — its tangent plane — and the replacement is very good, provided you do not wander too far.

But first, a word about the word "differentiable", because it is stricter than you might expect. A function is differentiable at a point if its change can be written as a linear part plus an error that shrinks faster than the distance you moved: Δz = fxΔx + fyΔy + ε1Δx + ε2Δy, where ε1 and ε2 go to 0 as you approach the point. In plain English: near the point, the function behaves like a flat plane, and the mistake you make by pretending it is flat is much smaller than the step you took. Here is the surprise: a function can have both partial derivatives at a point and still not be differentiable there — it can even fail to be continuous there. Having slopes in the east and north directions does not guarantee the surface is well-behaved in every direction. The practical test that saves you is this: if all the first partial derivatives exist and are continuous near the point, then the function is differentiable there. And differentiable always implies continuous — though the converse is false.

The flat replacement has a name: the local linear approximation, L(x, y) = f(x₀, y₀) + fx(x₀, y₀)(x − x₀) + fy(x₀, y₀)(y − y₀). Its graph is the tangent plane. The total differential is the same idea written differently: dz = fx dx + fy dy, and for small steps Δz ≈ dz. This is not just theory — it is the tool engineers actually use to estimate errors. Suppose you measure the sides of a rectangle and each measurement is a little bit off; how wrong can the area be? The differential tells you: the worst error in the area is roughly |fx| times the error in x, plus |fy| times the error in y. Turn that into percentages and the rule becomes beautifully simple: for an area A = xy, the maximum percentage error is the sum of the percentage errors in the sides; for a cone's volume V = (1/3)πr²h, it is twice the percentage error in r plus the percentage error in h; for a pendulum's period T = 2π√(L/g), it is half the percentage error in L plus half the percentage error in g. Always take absolute values and worst-case signs when you maximise an error — that is where marks are lost.

First, why does this lecture exist at all — why would anyone want to replace a perfectly good curved surface with a flat plane? Because curved surfaces are hard to compute with and flat planes are easy. Imagine you are a surveyor with a map of a hilly district. Over the whole district the Earth is curved and the terrain is complicated, but if you zoom in on one small village, the ground under that village looks flat, and a flat map of the village is accurate enough to build a road on. That is the whole idea: near any point, a smooth surface can be replaced by its tangent plane, and the replacement is good enough for every practical purpose — estimating values, estimating errors, doing quick calculations without a computer. The word "local" is doing the heavy lifting: the approximation is only promised near the point. Wander far away and the plane drifts off the surface, just as a flat map of a village becomes useless for a whole continent.

Now connect this to what you already know from first-year calculus, because it is the same idea with one extra direction. There, the tangent-line approximation said f(x) ≈ f(a) + f′(a)(x − a): near a point a, a curve looks like its tangent line, and the error is small. Here, the tangent line becomes a tangent plane, and the single correction term f′(a)(x − a) becomes two correction terms — one for the step east, one for the step north: L(x, y) = f(x₀, y₀) + fx(x₀, y₀)(x − x₀) + fy(x₀, y₀)(y − y₀). Nothing else changes. The partial derivatives are the slopes in the two directions, and the plane is built by starting at the height f(x₀, y₀) and walking along those two slopes. If you understand the one-variable version, you already understand this one; the only new thing is that there are two directions to walk in.

Here is the place students most often get stuck, and it is a genuine surprise, so take it slowly: having both partial derivatives does not mean the function is differentiable. That sounds wrong at first — if the surface has a slope to the east and a slope to the north, surely it must be well-behaved? But think about what the two partials actually check. fx only looks along the east–west line through the point. fy only looks along the north–south line. Together they have examined exactly two directions out of infinitely many. A surface can be perfectly smooth along those two lines and still have a crease, a ridge or a spike along a diagonal direction — like a folded sheet of paper, which is flat along the fold in two directions but has a sharp edge running across it. Differentiability is the stronger demand: the surface must look flat in every direction at once, with the error shrinking faster than the distance you moved. That is what the formula Δz = fxΔx + fyΔy + ε1Δx + ε2Δy is saying — the linear part does the work, and the leftover error terms ε1, ε2 must fade to zero as you approach the point. The practical test that saves you in exams is simple: if the first partial derivatives exist and are continuous near the point, then the function is differentiable there. And remember the chain of strength: differentiable always implies continuous, but continuous does not imply differentiable, and partials existing does not imply either.

Let us see what "error much smaller than the distance moved" actually looks like in numbers, because the phrase is vague until you measure it. Take f(x, y) = 1/√(x + y²), the point P(4, 3) and the nearby point Q(3.92, 3.01) (Ex. 13.4-33). The local linear approximation gives L(Q) ≈ 0.277, while the true value is f(Q) ≈ 0.278 — an error of about 0.001. Now measure how far we moved: the distance |PQ| is about 0.081. So the error (0.001) is only about 1% of the distance moved (0.081). That ratio is the whole point of differentiability: the mistake you make by pretending the surface is flat is a tiny fraction of the step you took. Move closer and the fraction gets smaller still. The worked example below shows the same thing in a different way: the differential df = 0.10 against the true change Δf = 0.1009, off by less than a thousandth.

The most useful payoff of all this is error estimation, and it is worth learning the pattern rather than memorising each case. The differential dz = fx dx + fy dy says: the error in the output is roughly the slope in each direction times the error in that input. Take absolute values and worst-case signs, and you get the maximum error. For an area A = xy, that gives a beautifully simple rule: the maximum percentage error in the area is the percentage error in the length plus the percentage error in the width. A rectangle measured with length wrong by up to 3% and width wrong by up to 5% can have its area wrong by up to 8% (Ex. 13.4-53) — and no more, because the errors add in the worst case. The same pattern gives 2(%r) + (%h) for a cone's volume and ½(%L) + ½(%g) for a pendulum's period (Ex. 13.4-57, max 0.30%). The two habits that lose marks here are forgetting the absolute values — errors do not cancel when you are asked for the maximum error — and using dz as if it were exactly Δz instead of an approximation to it.

Now, an honest note about the word "Taylor" in this lecture's title, because your lecture plan calls this "Taylor Series" and the book does not. Anton §13.4 contains no multivariable Taylor series. What it contains is the first-order Taylor polynomial — which is exactly the local linear approximation above. The full Taylor polynomials and series live in Chapter 9 (§9.7–9.9), and they are for functions of one variable. If your lecturer shows you a second-order, quadratic approximation for f(x, y) — the formula f ≈ f₀ + fxΔx + fyΔy + ½(fxxΔx² + 2fxyΔxΔy + fyyΔy²) — that is a natural extension of the same idea, but it is not developed in §13.4, so do not go hunting for it in this chapter, and do not quote it as if it were in the book.

So the story of this lecture is: differentiability means "locally flat, with a small error"; the tangent plane is your flat replacement; the differential turns that replacement into error estimates; and the "Taylor" in the title means the first-order approximation, nothing more, in this section.

Differentiable at (x0, y0): Δz = fxΔx + fyΔy + ε1Δx + ε2Δy, with ε1, ε2 → 0 as (Δx, Δy) → (0, 0)

Total differential: dz = fx(x0, y0) dx + fy(x0, y0) dy  ·  Approximation: Δz ≈ dz (for small Δx, Δy)

Local linear approximation: L(x, y) = f(x0, y0) + fx(x0, y0)(x − x0) + fy(x0, y0)(y − y0)

Error estimate: |Δf| ≲ |fx||Δx| + |fy||Δy|  ·  Area A = xy ⇒ max % error = % error in x + % error in y

Honest note: §13.4 has only the first-order Taylor polynomial (the linear approximation above). The full Taylor series is in Chapter 9 for one variable.

Worked example — Ex. 13.4-21. For f(x, y) = x² + 2xy − 4x, compare the differential df with the actual change Δf when moving from P(1, 2) to Q(1.01, 2.04).

Step 1 — Find the partial derivatives at P. fx = 2x + 2y − 4, so at (1, 2): fx = 2 + 4 − 4 = 2. fy = 2x, so at (1, 2): fy = 2.

Step 2 — Read off the steps. Δx = 1.01 − 1 = 0.01 and Δy = 2.04 − 2 = 0.04. These are the small steps dx and dy.

Step 3 — Compute the differential. df = fx dx + fy dy = 2(0.01) + 2(0.04) = 0.02 + 0.08 = 0.10. This is our flat-plane estimate of the change.

Step 4 — Compute the actual change. f(P) = 1 + 4 − 4 = 1. f(Q) = (1.01)² + 2(1.01)(2.04) − 4(1.01) = 1.0201 + 4.1208 − 4.04 = 1.1009. So Δf = 1.1009 − 1 = 0.1009.

Answer: df = 0.10, actual Δf = 0.1009 — the tangent-plane estimate is off by less than a thousandth. That is differentiability in action: the error is tiny compared with the step.

Watch out: "both partials exist" does NOT mean "differentiable" — a function can have both partials at a point and still not be differentiable (or even continuous) there; and dz is an approximation to Δz, not equal to it, so always compare the error with the distance moved.

  • In plain words, what does it mean for a function to be differentiable at a point — and why is it stronger than just having partial derivatives?
  • What is the local linear approximation L(x, y), and what is its graph?
  • How do you use the total differential to estimate the maximum percentage error in a computed quantity?
  • What does Anton §13.4 actually contain about Taylor series, and what does it not contain?

Ex. 13.4 — total differential vs actual change: 21. f = x² + 2xy − 4x, P(1, 2) → Q(1.01, 2.04); 22. f = x1/3y1/2, P(8, 9) → Q(7.78, 9.03); 23. f = (x + y)/(xy), P(−1, −2) → Q(−1.02, −2.04); 24. f = ln√(1 + xy), P(0, 2) → Q(−0.09, 1.98); 25. f = 2xy²z³, P(1, −1, 2) → Q(0.99, −1.02, 2.02); 26. f = xyz/(x + y + z), P(−1, −2, 4) → Q(−1.04, −1.98, 3.97).

Local linear approximation L at P, error vs distance |PQ|: 33. f = 1/√(x + y²), P(4, 3), Q(3.92, 3.01); 34. f = x0.5y0.3, P(1, 1), Q(1.05, 0.97); 35. f = x sin y, P(0, 0), Q(0.003, 0.004); 36. f = ln xy, P(1, 2), Q(1.01, 2.02); 37. f = xyz, P(1, 2, 3), Q(1.001, 2.002, 3.003); 38. f = (x + y)/(y + z), P(−1, 1, 1), Q(−0.99, 0.99, 1.01); 39. f = xeyz, P(1, −1, −1), Q(0.99, −1.01, −0.99); 40. f = ln(x + yz), P(2, 1, −1), Q(2.02, 0.97, −1.01).

Differentials for maximum (percentage) error: 53. rectangle, length error ≤ 3%, width ≤ 5% → max % error in area; 57. pendulum T = 2π√(L/g), L error ≤ 0.5%, g ≤ 0.1% → max % error in T; 60. parallel resistances 100, 200, 500 Ω, each ≤ 10% error → max % error in R.

Differentials and linearization in Multivariable Calculus

Calculus 3: Tangent Planes and Linear Approximation (Video #14) | Math with Professor V

Lecture 10: Normal: Inward and Outward, Linear approximation, Differentiability (NPTEL-style lecture)

Lecture 7 — Differentiability, Local Linear Approximation (Anton §13.4)

Anton §13.4 contains only the first-order (local linear) approximation — the tangent-plane approximation. There is no multivariable Taylor series in this section. Two tools are used throughout: the total differential df = fx dx + fy dy (+ fz dz), which approximates the change Δf for small steps, and the local linear approximation L(x, y) = f(x0, y0) + fx(x0, y0)(x − x0) + fy(x0, y0)(y − y0). All numerical answers below were checked with SymPy.

Ex. 13.4: 21

Use a total differential to approximate the change in the values of f from P to Q. Compare your estimate with the actual change in f. f(x, y) = x2 + 2xy − 4x; P(1, 2), Q(1.01, 2.04).

The steps are Δx = 1.01 − 1 = 0.01 and Δy = 2.04 − 2 = 0.04.

Partials: fx = 2x + 2y − 4 and fy = 2x. At P(1, 2): fx = 2 + 4 − 4 = 2, fy = 2.

Total differential: df = fxΔx + fyΔy = 2(0.01) + 2(0.04) = 0.02 + 0.08 = 0.10.

Actual change: f(1, 2) = 1 + 4 − 4 = 1; f(1.01, 2.04) = 1.0201 + 4.1208 − 4.04 = 1.1009, so Δf = 0.1009. The estimate 0.10 is off by only 0.0009.

Answer: df ≈ 0.10; actual Δf = 0.1009.

Ex. 13.4: 22

Use a total differential to approximate the change in the values of f from P to Q. Compare your estimate with the actual change in f. f(x, y) = x1/3y1/2; P(8, 9), Q(7.78, 9.03).

Δx = 7.78 − 8 = −0.22, Δy = 9.03 − 9 = 0.03.

Partials: fx = (1/3)x−2/3y1/2, fy = (1/2)x1/3y−1/2. At P(8, 9): fx = (1/3)(1/4)(3) = 1/4, fy = (1/2)(2)(1/3) = 1/3.

df = (1/4)(−0.22) + (1/3)(0.03) = −0.055 + 0.01 = −0.045. Since f(8, 9) = 2 × 3 = 6, the estimate is f(Q) ≈ 6 − 0.045 = 5.955.

Actual: f(7.78, 9.03) ≈ 5.9544, so Δf ≈ −0.0456 — the estimate is off by only about 0.0006.

Answer: df ≈ −0.045, so f(Q) ≈ 5.955; actual Δf ≈ −0.0456.

Ex. 13.4: 23

Use a total differential to approximate the change in the values of f from P to Q. Compare your estimate with the actual change in f. f(x, y) = (x + y)/(xy); P(−1, −2), Q(−1.02, −2.04).

Δx = −0.02, Δy = −0.04. It helps to rewrite f = 1/y + 1/x, so fx = −1/x2 and fy = −1/y2.

At P(−1, −2): fx = −1, fy = −1/4.

df = (−1)(−0.02) + (−1/4)(−0.04) = 0.02 + 0.01 = 0.03.

Actual: f(P) = (−3)/2 = −1.5; f(Q) = (−3.06)/(2.0808) ≈ −1.4706, so Δf ≈ 0.0294. The estimate 0.03 is off by only about 0.0006.

Answer: df ≈ 0.03; actual Δf ≈ 0.0294.

Ex. 13.4: 24

Use a total differential to approximate the change in the values of f from P to Q. Compare your estimate with the actual change in f. f(x, y) = ln √(1 + xy); P(0, 2), Q(−0.09, 1.98).

Δx = −0.09, Δy = −0.02. Write f = ½ ln(1 + xy), so fx = y/(2(1 + xy)) and fy = x/(2(1 + xy)).

At P(0, 2): fx = 2/2 = 1, fy = 0.

df = 1(−0.09) + 0(−0.02) = −0.09. Since f(0, 2) = ln 1 = 0, the estimate is f(Q) ≈ −0.09.

Actual: f(−0.09, 1.98) = ½ ln(1 − 0.1782) = ½ ln(0.8218) ≈ −0.0981, so Δf ≈ −0.0981. The error is about 0.008 — larger than in Ex. 21–23 because the step Δx = −0.09 is relatively big and the log curves noticeably.

Answer: df ≈ −0.09; actual Δf ≈ −0.0981.

Ex. 13.4: 25

Use a total differential to approximate the change in the values of f from P to Q. Compare your estimate with the actual change in f. f(x, y, z) = 2xy2z3; P(1, −1, 2), Q(0.99, −1.02, 2.02).

Δx = −0.01, Δy = −0.02, Δz = 0.02.

Partials: fx = 2y2z3, fy = 4xyz3, fz = 6xy2z2. At P(1, −1, 2): fx = 2(1)(8) = 16, fy = 4(1)(−1)(8) = −32, fz = 6(1)(1)(4) = 24.

df = 16(−0.01) + (−32)(−0.02) + 24(0.02) = −0.16 + 0.64 + 0.48 = 0.96. Since f(P) = 2(1)(1)(8) = 16, the estimate is f(Q) ≈ 16.96.

Actual: f(0.99, −1.02, 2.02) ≈ 16.9793, so Δf ≈ 0.9793. The estimate is off by about 0.019.

Answer: df ≈ 0.96; actual Δf ≈ 0.9793.

Ex. 13.4: 26

Use a total differential to approximate the change in the values of f from P to Q. Compare your estimate with the actual change in f. f(x, y, z) = xyz/(x + y + z); P(−1, −2, 4), Q(−1.04, −1.98, 3.97).

Δx = −0.04, Δy = 0.02, Δz = −0.03. Let S = x + y + z. By the quotient rule, fx = yz(S − x)/S2 = yz(y + z)/S2, and similarly fy = xz(x + z)/S2, fz = xy(x + y)/S2.

At P(−1, −2, 4), S = 1: fx = (−2)(4)(2) = −16, fy = (−1)(4)(3) = −12, fz = (−1)(−2)(−3) = −6.

df = (−16)(−0.04) + (−12)(0.02) + (−6)(−0.03) = 0.64 − 0.24 + 0.18 = 0.58. Since f(P) = 8/1 = 8, the estimate is f(Q) ≈ 8.58.

Actual: f(Q) ≈ 8.6053, so Δf ≈ 0.6053. The estimate is off by about 0.025.

Answer: df ≈ 0.58; actual Δf ≈ 0.6053.

Ex. 13.4: 33

(a) Find the local linear approximation L to the specified function f at the designated point P. (b) Compare the error in approximating f by L at the specified point Q with the distance between P and Q. f(x, y) = 1/√(x + y2); P(4, 3), Q(3.92, 3.01).

(a) f(4, 3) = 1/√13 ≈ 0.27735. Partials: fx = −½(x + y2)−3/2 and fy = −y(x + y2)−3/2. At P: fx = −1/(2·13√13) ≈ −0.01067, fy = −3/(13√13) ≈ −0.06400. Hence L(x, y) ≈ 0.27735 − 0.01067(x − 4) − 0.06400(y − 3).

(b) L(3.92, 3.01) ≈ 0.27735 + (−0.01067)(−0.08) + (−0.06400)(0.01) ≈ 0.27756. The actual value is f(3.92, 3.01) = 1/√12.9801 ≈ 0.27756, so the error is about 0.000001. The distance |PQ| = √(0.082 + 0.012) ≈ 0.081. The error (≈10−6) is far smaller than the distance — exactly what differentiability promises: the error shrinks faster than the distance moved.

Answer: L(x, y) ≈ 0.27735 − 0.01067(x − 4) − 0.06400(y − 3); L(Q) ≈ 0.27756, error ≈ 0.000001, |PQ| ≈ 0.081.

Ex. 13.4: 34

(a) Find the local linear approximation L to the specified function f at the designated point P. (b) Compare the error in approximating f by L at the specified point Q with the distance between P and Q. f(x, y) = x0.5y0.3; P(1, 1), Q(1.05, 0.97).

(a) f(1, 1) = 1. Partials: fx = 0.5x−0.5y0.3, fy = 0.3x0.5y−0.7. At P: fx = 0.5, fy = 0.3. Hence L(x, y) = 1 + 0.5(x − 1) + 0.3(y − 1).

(b) L(1.05, 0.97) = 1 + 0.5(0.05) + 0.3(−0.03) = 1 + 0.025 − 0.009 = 1.016. Actual: f(1.05, 0.97) ≈ 1.0154, so the error is about 0.0006. The distance |PQ| = √(0.052 + 0.032) ≈ 0.058 — the error is roughly 1% of the distance.

Answer: L(x, y) = 1 + 0.5(x − 1) + 0.3(y − 1); L(Q) = 1.016, error ≈ 0.0006, |PQ| ≈ 0.058.

Ex. 13.4: 35

(a) Find the local linear approximation L to the specified function f at the designated point P. (b) Compare the error in approximating f by L at the specified point Q with the distance between P and Q. f(x, y) = x sin y; P(0, 0), Q(0.003, 0.004).

(a) f(0, 0) = 0. Partials: fx = sin y, fy = x cos y. At P both are 0, so L(x, y) = 0 — the tangent plane at the origin is the flat plane z = 0 (the surface is horizontal there).

(b) L(Q) = 0. Actual: f(0.003, 0.004) = 0.003 sin(0.004) ≈ 0.000012, so the error is about 0.000012. The distance |PQ| = √(0.0032 + 0.0042) = 0.005. The error is only about 0.24% of the distance — small, as expected, even though the approximation itself is just zero.

Answer: L(x, y) = 0; L(Q) = 0, error ≈ 0.000012, |PQ| = 0.005.

Ex. 13.4: 36

(a) Find the local linear approximation L to the specified function f at the designated point P. (b) Compare the error in approximating f by L at the specified point Q with the distance between P and Q. f(x, y) = ln xy; P(1, 2), Q(1.01, 2.02).

(a) f(1, 2) = ln 2 ≈ 0.69315. Write f = ln x + ln y, so fx = 1/x and fy = 1/y. At P: fx = 1, fy = 1/2. Hence L(x, y) = ln 2 + (x − 1) + ½(y − 2).

(b) L(1.01, 2.02) = ln 2 + 0.01 + 0.01 ≈ 0.71315. Actual: f(1.01, 2.02) = ln(2.0402) ≈ 0.71305, so the error is about 0.0001. The distance |PQ| = √(0.012 + 0.022) ≈ 0.022 — the error is under 0.5% of the distance.

Answer: L(x, y) = ln 2 + (x − 1) + ½(y − 2); L(Q) ≈ 0.71315, error ≈ 0.0001, |PQ| ≈ 0.022.

Ex. 13.4: 37

(a) Find the local linear approximation L to the specified function f at the designated point P. (b) Compare the error in approximating f by L at the specified point Q with the distance between P and Q. f(x, y, z) = xyz; P(1, 2, 3), Q(1.001, 2.002, 3.003).

(a) f(1, 2, 3) = 6. Partials: fx = yz = 6, fy = xz = 3, fz = xy = 2 at P. Hence L(x, y, z) = 6 + 6(x − 1) + 3(y − 2) + 2(z − 3).

(b) L(Q) = 6 + 6(0.001) + 3(0.002) + 2(0.003) = 6.018. Actual: f(Q) = 1.001 × 2.002 × 3.003 ≈ 6.018018, so the error is about 0.000018. The distance |PQ| = √(0.0012 + 0.0022 + 0.0032) ≈ 0.0037 — the error is about 0.5% of the distance.

Answer: L(x, y, z) = 6 + 6(x − 1) + 3(y − 2) + 2(z − 3); L(Q) = 6.018, error ≈ 0.000018, |PQ| ≈ 0.0037.

Ex. 13.4: 38

(a) Find the local linear approximation L to the specified function f at the designated point P. (b) Compare the error in approximating f by L at the specified point Q with the distance between P and Q. f(x, y, z) = (x + y)/(y + z); P(−1, 1, 1), Q(−0.99, 0.99, 1.01).

(a) f(−1, 1, 1) = 0/2 = 0. Partials by the quotient rule: fx = 1/(y + z), fy = (z − x)/(y + z)2, fz = −(x + y)/(y + z)2. At P: fx = 1/2, fy = 2/4 = 1/2, fz = 0. Hence L(x, y, z) = ½(x + 1) + ½(y − 1).

(b) L(Q) = ½(0.01) + ½(−0.01) = 0. Actual: f(Q) = (−0.99 + 0.99)/(0.99 + 1.01) = 0/2 = 0, so the error is exactly 0 here (the two first-order changes cancel). The distance |PQ| = √(0.012 + 0.012 + 0.012) ≈ 0.0173.

Answer: L(x, y, z) = ½(x + 1) + ½(y − 1); L(Q) = 0, error = 0, |PQ| ≈ 0.0173.

Ex. 13.4: 39

(a) Find the local linear approximation L to the specified function f at the designated point P. (b) Compare the error in approximating f by L at the specified point Q with the distance between P and Q. f(x, y, z) = xeyz; P(1, −1, −1), Q(0.99, −1.01, −0.99).

(a) f(1, −1, −1) = e1 = e ≈ 2.71828. Partials: fx = eyz, fy = xzeyz, fz = xyeyz. At P (yz = 1): fx = e, fy = −e, fz = −e. Hence L(x, y, z) = e + e(x − 1) − e(y + 1) − e(z + 1).

(b) L(Q) = e + e(−0.01) − e(−0.01) − e(0.01) = e(0.99) ≈ 2.69110. Actual: f(Q) = 0.99e0.9999 ≈ 2.69083, so the error is about 0.00027. The distance |PQ| = √(0.012 + 0.012 + 0.012) ≈ 0.0173 — the error is about 1.6% of the distance.

Answer: L(x, y, z) = e[1 + (x − 1) − (y + 1) − (z + 1)]; L(Q) ≈ 2.69110, error ≈ 0.00027, |PQ| ≈ 0.0173.

Ex. 13.4: 40

(a) Find the local linear approximation L to the specified function f at the designated point P. (b) Compare the error in approximating f by L at the specified point Q with the distance between P and Q. f(x, y, z) = ln(x + yz); P(2, 1, −1), Q(2.02, 0.97, −1.01).

(a) f(2, 1, −1) = ln(2 − 1) = ln 1 = 0. Partials: fx = 1/(x + yz), fy = z/(x + yz), fz = y/(x + yz). At P (x + yz = 1): fx = 1, fy = −1, fz = 1. Hence L(x, y, z) = (x − 2) − (y − 1) + (z + 1).

(b) L(Q) = 0.02 − (−0.03) + (−0.01) = 0.04. Actual: f(Q) = ln(2.02 − 0.9797) = ln(1.0403) ≈ 0.03951, so the error is about 0.00049. The distance |PQ| = √(0.022 + 0.032 + 0.012) ≈ 0.0374 — the error is about 1.3% of the distance.

Answer: L(x, y, z) = (x − 2) − (y − 1) + (z + 1); L(Q) = 0.04, error ≈ 0.00049, |PQ| ≈ 0.0374.

Ex. 13.4: 53

The length and width of a rectangle are measured with errors of at most 3% and 5%, respectively. Use differentials to approximate the maximum percentage error in the calculated area.

Area A = xy, so dA = y dx + x dy. Divide by A = xy to get the relative error: dA/A = dx/x + dy/y.

The worst case is when both errors push the area in the same direction, so take absolute values: |dA/A| ≤ |dx/x| + |dy/y| ≤ 3% + 5% = 8%. (In general, for a product the percentage errors add.)

Answer: maximum percentage error ≈ 8%.

Ex. 13.4: 57

The period T of a simple pendulum with small oscillations is calculated from the formula T = 2π√(L/g), where L is the length of the pendulum and g is the acceleration due to gravity. Suppose that measured values of L and g have errors of at most 0.5% and 0.1%, respectively. Use differentials to approximate the maximum percentage error in the calculated value of T.

Write T = 2πL1/2g−1/2. Then dT = πL−1/2g−1/2 dL − πL1/2g−3/2 dg. Divide by T = 2πL1/2g−1/2: dT/T = ½(dL/L) − ½(dg/g).

For the maximum error take absolute values with the worst-case signs: |dT/T| ≤ ½|dL/L| + ½|dg/g| ≤ ½(0.5%) + ½(0.1%) = 0.25% + 0.05% = 0.30%. (Each square root halves the percentage error it inherits.)

Answer: maximum percentage error ≈ 0.30%.

Ex. 13.4: 60

The total resistance R of three resistances R1, R2, and R3, connected in parallel, is given by 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3. Suppose that R1, R2, and R3 are measured to be 100 ohms, 200 ohms, and 500 ohms, respectively, with a maximum error of 10% in each. Use differentials to approximate the maximum percentage error in the calculated value of R.

First find R: 1/R = 1/100 + 1/200 + 1/500 = 0.01 + 0.005 + 0.002 = 0.017, so R = 1/0.017 ≈ 58.82 ohms.

Differentiate 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3: −dR/R2 = −dR1/R12 − dR2/R22 − dR3/R32, i.e. dR/R = R(dR1/R12 + dR2/R22 + dR3/R32).

For the maximum, take absolute values and use |dRi/Ri| ≤ 10%: |dR/R| ≤ R(0.10/R1 + 0.10/R2 + 0.10/R3) = 58.82 × 0.10 × (1/100 + 1/200 + 1/500) = 58.82 × 0.10 × 0.017 = 0.10. So the maximum percentage error is 10% — the same as the error in each resistor, because R times the sum of the reciprocals is exactly 1.

Answer: maximum percentage error ≈ 10% (with R ≈ 58.82 ohms).

Lecture 8 — The Chain Rule & Euler's Theorem for Homogeneous Functions (Anton §13.5)

When one quantity depends on others, and those depend on something else again, the chain rule tells you how a small change at the far end ripples all the way through to the answer.

Imagine a relay race. The runner at the end — call her z — never touches the starting gun herself. She only receives the baton from two runners in the middle, x and y. And x and y only start running when the gun, t, goes off. If you want to know how fast z is changing, you cannot just look at z. You have to ask: how fast is x changing because of t, and how much does z care about x? Then the same for y. Add the two contributions together, and you have your answer. That is the whole chain rule. A "partial derivative", by the way, is just an ordinary rate of change while you hold everything else still — ∂z/∂x means "how fast z changes when x moves a little and y stays put".

Before you write any formula, draw the tree. Put z at the top, x and y underneath it, and t at the bottom, with lines joining them. Every line is one link in the chain. Then trace every path from the top to the bottom: each path gives you one product (a partial derivative times an ordinary derivative), and you add the products from all the paths. If your function has three middle variables — say w depends on x, y and z, and each of those depends on t — you simply get three paths and three products. The tree never lets you forget a branch, and forgetting a branch is the classic exam mistake.

The same tree works when the bottom has two variables instead of one. Suppose x and y both depend on u and v, and z depends on x and y. Then ∂z/∂u follows the two paths that end at u, and ∂z/∂v follows the two paths that end at v. Nothing new to learn — only more paths to trace, one at a time.

The chain rule also gives us a lovely shortcut for equations we cannot solve. Suppose an equation like F(x, y, z) = c secretly defines z as a function of x and y, but you cannot rearrange it to write z = … on its own. You do not need to. The chain rule tells you that ∂z/∂x = −Fx/Fz and ∂z/∂y = −Fy/Fz — you just differentiate the equation as it stands, treat z as a function of x and y while you do it, and solve for the derivative you want. The minus sign is not a typo; it is part of the answer, so keep it. This only works where Fz is not zero — if it is zero, the formula breaks down, and that itself tells you something about the surface at that point.

One more thing, and please clear up a confusion before the exam. Your lecture plan calls part of this lecture "Euler's equation", but if you search §13.5 for a heading called Euler's equation, you will not find one — it is not there. What the plan means is Euler's theorem for homogeneous functions, which Anton develops in the "Making Connections" exercises on page 999. A function is called homogeneous of degree n if scaling both inputs by a factor t scales the output by tn — in symbols, f(tx, ty) = tn f(x, y). For example, 3x² + y² is homogeneous of degree 2, because scaling x and y by t multiplies the whole thing by t². Euler's theorem says that for such a function, x·fx + y·fy = n·f. It is a beautiful check: the two partial derivatives, weighted by x and y, add up to n times the function itself. Two handy consequences the book asks you to prove are that z = f(x² − y²) always satisfies y·zx + x·zy = 0, and z = f(xy) always satisfies x·zx − y·zy = 0.

Finally, a warning from Anton himself, on page 955: the symbols ∂z and ∂x are not numbers, so you must never "cancel" them the way you cancel fractions in ordinary algebra. Cancelling ∂ symbols gives a formula that looks right and is wrong.

First, why do we need a chain rule at all — did the one-variable version not already do this job? In first-year calculus the chain rule handled y = f(g(x)): one input feeding into one function. But real quantities rarely depend on one thing. The temperature in a room depends on the heater setting and on how far the window is open, and both of those change through the day. The pressure in a tyre depends on the temperature and on the volume, and both change as you drive. Whenever the thing you care about depends on several middle variables, and those middle variables are themselves moving, a single-variable chain rule cannot even be written down — you need a rule that collects every route by which the far end can influence the answer. That is all the multivariable chain rule is: careful bookkeeping of influences, one path at a time.

Where do students actually get stuck? Two places. The first is when the bottom of the tree has two variables instead of one — x and y both depending on u and v. Then ∂z/∂u and ∂z/∂v are two separate questions, and each gets its own tree: for ∂z/∂u you trace only the paths that end at u, for ∂z/∂v only the paths that end at v. Do them one at a time and never try to answer both in one breath. The second is the minus sign in implicit differentiation. It is not a convention to memorise; it has a reason. If F(x, y, z) = c is constant, then when x increases a little, something else must give way to keep F still — so z must move in the opposite direction, and that opposition is the minus sign in ∂z/∂x = −Fx/Fz. Whenever a formula has a sign you keep forgetting, ask what it means in words, and it stops being forgettable.

A real-life check, from the exercises: Ex. 13.5-36 is the chain rule doing a job in electrical engineering. Two resistors are wired in parallel and both resistances are changing with time, so the combined resistance R changes too, and so does the voltage across them. Working through the tree gives R = 10/7 Ω, dR/dt ≈ 0.147 Ω/s, and dV/dt ≈ 0.46 V/s. Notice the structure: the answer is small not because any one rate is small, but because the two contributions partly cancel — exactly the same cancellation you saw in the worked example above, where 12 − 12 = 0.

One more piece of intuition for Euler's theorem, using the example already in this lecture. Take f(x, y) = 3x² + y². Its partial derivatives are fx = 6x and fy = 2y, so x·fx + y·fy = 6x² + 2y² = 2(3x² + y²) = 2f — exactly what Euler's theorem promises for a function of degree 2. And "degree 2" has a picture: double both inputs and the output is multiplied by 4, that is 2², just as doubling the side of a square quadruples its area. A homogeneous function is one that scales the way area, volume, or a recipe scales when you multiply everything by the same factor — and Euler's theorem says the two partial derivatives, weighted by x and y, always add up to the degree times the function itself. It is a consistency check you can run on any answer: if x·fx + y·fy does not come out to n·f, you have made an arithmetic slip somewhere.

Chain rule, one parameter: dz/dt = (∂z/∂x)(dx/dt) + (∂z/∂y)(dy/dt)

Three variables: dw/dt = (∂w/∂x)(dx/dt) + (∂w/∂y)(dy/dt) + (∂w/∂z)(dz/dt)

Chain rule, partials: ∂z/∂u = (∂z/∂x)(∂x/∂u) + (∂z/∂y)(∂y/∂u), and the same with v in place of u

Implicit differentiation: dy/dx = −(∂f/∂x)/(∂f/∂y), when f(x, y) = c and fy ≠ 0

Implicit, three variables: ∂z/∂x = −Fx/Fz and ∂z/∂y = −Fy/Fz, when F(x, y, z) = c and Fz ≠ 0

Euler's theorem (homogeneous of degree n): if f(tx, ty) = tnf(x, y), then x·fx + y·fy = n·f

Useful consequences: z = f(x² − y²) gives y·zx + x·zy = 0; z = f(xy) gives x·zx − y·zy = 0

Worked example — Ex. 13.5-13 (from the guide). Suppose f is differentiable at (4, 8) with fx = 3 and fy = −1, and x = t², y = t³. Find dz/dt at t = 2, where z = f(x, y).

Step 1 — Draw the tree in your head. z depends on x and y; x and y both depend on t. So there are two paths from z to t, and the answer will have two terms.

Step 2 — Find how fast x and y move with t. dx/dt = 2t, so at t = 2, dx/dt = 4. dy/dt = 3t², so at t = 2, dy/dt = 12.

Step 3 — Multiply along each path and add. dz/dt = fx·(dx/dt) + fy·(dy/dt) = 3·4 + (−1)·12 = 12 − 12 = 0.

Answer: dz/dt = 0 at t = 2. In words: at that instant the two contributions exactly cancel — x is pushing z up at the same rate y is pulling it down.

Watch out: never "cancel" the ∂ symbols in the chain rule as if they were fractions — ∂z/∂x times dx/dt does not collapse by cancelling ∂x, and doing so gives a false formula (Anton's Warning, p. 955). Also, never forget a branch of the tree: every intermediate variable contributes one term.

  • How do you find dz/dt when z = f(x, y) and x and y are both functions of t? Say the rule in words, then write it.
  • What is a tree diagram for, and what does each path from the top to the bottom give you?
  • If F(x, y, z) = c defines z implicitly, what are ∂z/∂x and ∂z/∂y — and when does the formula fail?
  • What does it mean for a function to be homogeneous of degree n, and what does Euler's theorem say about it?

Ex. 13.5: 7–10 — find dw/dt (w of three variables, each a function of t). Ex. 13.5: 17–30 — find ∂z/∂u, ∂z/∂v and other chain-rule derivatives. Ex. 13.5: 36 — related rates (Ohm's law, two resistors in parallel). Ex. 13.5: 45–48 — find ∂z/∂x and ∂z/∂y by implicit differentiation. Ex. 13.5: 58–60 — proofs and applications: Laplace's equation, the polar Cauchy–Riemann equations, the wave equation. Making Connections, p. 999, 1–5 — polar form of the chain rule; homogeneous functions; prove Euler's theorem and its converse.

Multivariable Chain Rule — Aggie Math Learning Center (Texas A&M)

The Multivariable Chain Rule with Tree Diagrams: Example 1

Lecture 8 — Solutions: Chain Rule (Anton §13.5)

Ex. 13.5: 7

Use the chain rule to find dw/dt if w = 5x2y3z4, x = t2, y = t3, z = t5.

By the chain rule, dw/dt = (∂w/∂x)(dx/dt) + (∂w/∂y)(dy/dt) + (∂w/∂z)(dz/dt).

∂w/∂x = 10xy3z4, ∂w/∂y = 15x2y2z4, ∂w/∂z = 20x2y3z3; and dx/dt = 2t, dy/dt = 3t2, dz/dt = 5t4.

Substituting x = t2, y = t3, z = t5: dw/dt = 10t2·t9·t20·2t + 15t4·t6·t20·3t2 + 20t4·t9·t15·5t4 = 20t32 + 45t32 + 100t32.

Answer: 165t32

Ex. 13.5: 8

Use the chain rule to find dw/dt if w = ln(3x2 − 2y + 4z3), x = t1/2, y = t2/3, z = t−2.

dw/dt = (∂w/∂x)(dx/dt) + (∂w/∂y)(dy/dt) + (∂w/∂z)(dz/dt), where ∂w/∂x = 6x/(3x2−2y+4z3), ∂w/∂y = −2/(3x2−2y+4z3), ∂w/∂z = 12z2/(3x2−2y+4z3).

With dx/dt = (1/2)t−1/2, dy/dt = (2/3)t−1/3, dz/dt = −2t−3, the numerator becomes 6x·(1/2)t−1/2 − 2·(2/3)t−1/3 + 12z2(−2t−3) = 3 − (4/3)t−1/3 − 24t−7, and the denominator is 3t − 2t2/3 + 4t−6.

Answer: dw/dt = [3 − (4/3)t−1/3 − 24t−7] / [3t − 2t2/3 + 4t−6]

Ex. 13.5: 9

Use the chain rule to find dw/dt if w = 5 cos xy − sin xz, x = 1/t, y = t, z = t3.

∂w/∂x = −5y sin xy − z cos xz, ∂w/∂y = −5x sin xy, ∂w/∂z = −x cos xz; dx/dt = −1/t2, dy/dt = 1, dz/dt = 3t2.

Note xy = 1 and xz = t2. Then dw/dt = (−5t sin 1 − t3 cos t2)(−1/t2) + (−5 sin 1 /t)(1) + (−cos t2/t)(3t2) = (5 sin 1)/t + t cos t2 − (5 sin 1)/t − 3t cos t2. The sin 1 terms cancel.

Answer: −2t cos(t2)

Ex. 13.5: 10

Use the chain rule to find dw/dt if w = 1 + x − 2yz4x, x = ln t, y = t, z = 4t.

First simplify: z4 = 256t4, so w = 1 + ln t − 512t5 ln t.

Differentiating directly, dw/dt = 1/t − 512(5t4 ln t + t4) = 1/t − 2560t4 ln t − 512t4. (The chain rule gives the same result: ∂w/∂x = 1 − 2yz4, ∂w/∂y = −2z4x, ∂w/∂z = −8yz3x, with dx/dt = 1/t, dy/dt = 1, dz/dt = 4.)

Answer: dw/dt = 1/t − 2560t4 ln t − 512t4

Ex. 13.5: 17

Find ∂z/∂u and ∂z/∂v if z = 8x2y − 2x + 3y, x = uv, y = u − v.

∂z/∂x = 16xy − 2, ∂z/∂y = 8x2 + 3. Also ∂x/∂u = v, ∂y/∂u = 1, ∂x/∂v = u, ∂y/∂v = −1.

∂z/∂u = (16xy − 2)v + (8x2 + 3)(1) = 16u2v2 − 16uv3 − 2v + 8u2v2 + 3.

∂z/∂v = (16xy − 2)u + (8x2 + 3)(−1) = 16u3v − 16u2v2 − 2u − 8u2v2 − 3.

Answer: ∂z/∂u = 24u2v2 − 16uv3 − 2v + 3; ∂z/∂v = 16u3v − 24u2v2 − 2u − 3

Ex. 13.5: 18

Find ∂z/∂u and ∂z/∂v if z = x2 − y tan x, x = u/v, y = u2v2.

∂z/∂x = 2x − y sec2x, ∂z/∂y = −tan x. Also ∂x/∂u = 1/v, ∂y/∂u = 2uv2, ∂x/∂v = −u/v2, ∂y/∂v = 2u2v.

∂z/∂u = (2x − y sec2x)(1/v) − 2uv2 tan x, ∂z/∂v = (2x − y sec2x)(−u/v2) − 2u2v tan x, with x = u/v and y = u2v2.

Answer: ∂z/∂u = (2u/v − u2v2 sec2(u/v))/v − 2uv2 tan(u/v); ∂z/∂v = −(u/v2)(2u/v − u2v2 sec2(u/v)) − 2u2v tan(u/v)

Ex. 13.5: 19

Find ∂z/∂u and ∂z/∂v if z = x/y, x = 2 cos u, y = 3 sin v.

∂z/∂x = 1/y, ∂z/∂y = −x/y2. Also ∂x/∂u = −2 sin u, ∂x/∂v = 0, ∂y/∂u = 0, ∂y/∂v = 3 cos v.

∂z/∂u = (1/y)(−2 sin u) = −2 sin u/(3 sin v).

∂z/∂v = (−x/y2)(3 cos v) = −2 cos u cos v/(3 sin2v).

Answer: ∂z/∂u = −2 sin u/(3 sin v); ∂z/∂v = −2 cos u cos v/(3 sin2v)

Ex. 13.5: 20

Find ∂z/∂u and ∂z/∂v if z = 3x − 2y, x = u + v ln u, y = u2 − v ln v.

∂z/∂x = 3, ∂z/∂y = −2. Also ∂x/∂u = 1 + v/u, ∂y/∂u = 2u, ∂x/∂v = ln u, ∂y/∂v = −ln v − 1.

∂z/∂u = 3(1 + v/u) − 2(2u) = 3 + 3v/u − 4u.

∂z/∂v = 3 ln u − 2(−ln v − 1) = 3 ln u + 2 ln v + 2.

Answer: ∂z/∂u = 3 + 3v/u − 4u; ∂z/∂v = 3 ln u + 2 ln v + 2

Ex. 13.5: 21

Find ∂z/∂u and ∂z/∂v if z = exy2, x = uv, y = 1/v.

First simplify: xy2 = uv·(1/v2) = u/v, so z = eu/v.

∂z/∂u = eu/v·(1/v), ∂z/∂v = eu/v·(−u/v2).

Answer: ∂z/∂u = eu/v/v; ∂z/∂v = −u eu/v/v2

Ex. 13.5: 22

Find ∂z/∂u and ∂z/∂v if z = cos x sin y, x = u − v, y = u2 + v2.

∂z/∂x = −sin x sin y, ∂z/∂y = cos x cos y. Also ∂x/∂u = 1, ∂y/∂u = 2u, ∂x/∂v = −1, ∂y/∂v = 2v.

∂z/∂u = −sin(u − v) sin(u2 + v2) + 2u cos(u − v) cos(u2 + v2).

∂z/∂v = sin(u − v) sin(u2 + v2) + 2v cos(u − v) cos(u2 + v2).

Answer: ∂z/∂u = 2u cos(u − v) cos(u2 + v2) − sin(u − v) sin(u2 + v2); ∂z/∂v = 2v cos(u − v) cos(u2 + v2) + sin(u − v) sin(u2 + v2)

Ex. 13.5: 23

Let T = x2y − xy3 + 2, x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ. Find ∂T/∂r and ∂T/∂θ.

Substituting, T = r3 cos2θ sin θ − r4 cos θ sin3θ + 2.

Differentiating with respect to r (θ fixed): ∂T/∂r = 3r2 cos2θ sin θ − 4r3 cos θ sin3θ = r2 sin θ cos θ (3 cos θ − 4r sin2θ).

Differentiating with respect to θ (r fixed): ∂T/∂θ = r3 cos θ (cos2θ − 2 sin2θ) − r4 sin2θ (3 cos2θ − sin2θ).

Answer: ∂T/∂r = r2 sin θ cos θ (3 cos θ − 4r sin2θ); ∂T/∂θ = r3 cos θ (cos2θ − 2 sin2θ) − r4 sin2θ (3 cos2θ − sin2θ)

Ex. 13.5: 24

Let R = e2s − t, s = 3φ, t = φ1/2. Find dR/dφ.

Substituting, R = e6φ − φ1/2. By the chain rule, dR/dφ = R·d/dφ(6φ − φ1/2) = e6φ − φ1/2(6 − 1/(2√φ)).

Answer: dR/dφ = (12√φ − 1) e6φ − √φ / (2√φ)

Ex. 13.5: 25

Let t = u/v, u = x2 − y2, v = 4xy3. Find ∂t/∂x and ∂t/∂y.

t = (x2 − y2)/(4xy3). By the quotient rule, ∂t/∂x = [2x·4xy3 − (x2 − y2)·4y3]/(4xy3)2 = (4x2y3 + 4y5)/(16x2y6).

∂t/∂y = [−2y·4xy3 − (x2 − y2)·12xy2]/(4xy3)2 = (4xy4 − 12x3y2)/(16x2y6).

Answer: ∂t/∂x = (x2 + y2)/(4x2y3); ∂t/∂y = (y2 − 3x2)/(4xy4)

Ex. 13.5: 26

Let w = rs/(r2 + s2), r = uv, s = u − 2v. Find ∂w/∂u and ∂w/∂v.

∂w/∂r = s(s2 − r2)/(r2 + s2)2 and ∂w/∂s = r(r2 − s2)/(r2 + s2)2 by the quotient rule.

∂w/∂u = (∂w/∂r)v + (∂w/∂s)(1) = (s2 − r2)(vs − r)/(r2 + s2)2. Since vs − r = v(u − 2v) − uv = −2v2, this is 2v2(r2 − s2)/(r2 + s2)2.

∂w/∂v = (∂w/∂r)u + (∂w/∂s)(−2) = (s2 − r2)(us + 2r)/(r2 + s2)2. Since us + 2r = u2, this is u2(s2 − r2)/(r2 + s2)2, with r = uv, s = u − 2v.

Answer: ∂w/∂u = 2v2(r2 − s2)/(r2 + s2)2; ∂w/∂v = u2(s2 − r2)/(r2 + s2)2, where r = uv, s = u − 2v

Ex. 13.5: 27

Let z = ln(x2 + 1), where x = r cos θ. Find ∂z/∂r and ∂z/∂θ.

z = ln(r2 cos2θ + 1). ∂z/∂r = (2r cos2θ)/(r2 cos2θ + 1) by the chain rule (derivative of ln is 1/(argument), times ∂/∂r of r2 cos2θ).

∂z/∂θ = (1/(r2 cos2θ + 1))·r2·2 cos θ(−sin θ) = −r2 sin 2θ/(r2 cos2θ + 1).

Answer: ∂z/∂r = 2r cos2θ/(1 + r2 cos2θ); ∂z/∂θ = −r2 sin 2θ/(1 + r2 cos2θ)

Ex. 13.5: 28

Let u = rs2 ln t, r = x2, s = 4y + 1, t = xy3. Find ∂u/∂x and ∂u/∂y.

u = x2(4y + 1)2 ln(xy3). ∂u/∂x = 2x(4y + 1)2 ln(xy3) + x2(4y + 1)2(1/x) = x(4y + 1)2(2 ln(xy3) + 1).

∂u/∂y = x2·2(4y + 1)·4·ln(xy3) + x2(4y + 1)2(3/y) = x2(4y + 1)[8 ln(xy3) + 3(4y + 1)/y].

Answer: ∂u/∂x = x(4y + 1)2(2 ln(xy3) + 1); ∂u/∂y = x2(4y + 1)[8 ln(xy3) + (12y + 3)/y]

Ex. 13.5: 29

Let w = 4x2 + 4y2 + z2, x = ρ sin φ cos θ, y = ρ sin φ sin θ, z = ρ cos φ. Find ∂w/∂ρ, ∂w/∂φ, and ∂w/∂θ.

Substituting, w = 4ρ2 sin2φ + ρ2 cos2φ = ρ2(3 sin2φ + 1).

∂w/∂ρ = 2ρ(3 sin2φ + 1); ∂w/∂φ = ρ2·6 sin φ cos φ = 3ρ2 sin 2φ; ∂w/∂θ = 0, since w does not depend on θ (the sphere is symmetric about the z-axis).

Answer: ∂w/∂ρ = 2ρ(3 sin2φ + 1); ∂w/∂φ = 3ρ2 sin 2φ; ∂w/∂θ = 0

Ex. 13.5: 30

Let w = 3xy2z3, y = 3x2 + 2, z = √(x − 1). Find dw/dx.

w = 3x(3x2 + 2)2(x − 1)3/2. By the product rule (three factors), dw/dx = 3(3x2 + 2)2(x − 1)3/2 + 36x2(3x2 + 2)(x − 1)3/2 + (9/2)x(3x2 + 2)2(x − 1)1/2.

Factoring √(x − 1)(3x2 + 2): dw/dx = √(x − 1)(3x2 + 2)[3(3x2 + 2)(x − 1) + 36x2(x − 1) + (9/2)x(3x2 + 2)].

Answer: dw/dx = √(x − 1)(351x5/2 − 135x4 + 162x3 − 108x2 + 30x − 12)

Ex. 13.5: 36

The voltage V across a circuit is V = IR. Two resistors R1 and R2 in parallel have combined resistance 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2. The current is 3 A and increasing at 10−2 A/s; R1 is 2 Ω and increasing at 0.4 Ω/s; R2 is 5 Ω and decreasing at 0.7 Ω/s. Estimate the rate at which the voltage is changing.

R = R1R2/(R1 + R2) = 10/7 Ω. By the chain rule, dV/dt = R·dI/dt + I·dR/dt, where dR/dt = (∂R/∂R1)(dR1/dt) + (∂R/∂R2)(dR2/dt).

∂R/∂R1 = R22/(R1 + R2)2 = 25/49 and ∂R/∂R2 = R12/(R1 + R2)2 = 4/49, so dR/dt = (25/49)(0.4) + (4/49)(−0.7) = 7.2/49 = 36/245 Ω/s.

Hence dV/dt = (10/7)(0.01) + 3(36/245) = 1/70 + 108/245 = 223/490 V/s.

Answer: dV/dt ≈ 0.46 V/s

Ex. 13.5: 45

Find ∂z/∂x and ∂z/∂y by implicit differentiation, and confirm with Theorem 13.5.4: x2 − 3yz2 + xyz − 2 = 0.

Let F(x, y, z) = x2 − 3yz2 + xyz − 2. Then Fx = 2x + yz, Fy = −3z2 + xz, Fz = −6yz + xy.

By Theorem 13.5.4, ∂z/∂x = −Fx/Fz = −(2x + yz)/(xy − 6yz) and ∂z/∂y = −Fy/Fz = (3z2 − xz)/(xy − 6yz). Differentiating the equation directly with respect to x (treating z as a function of x) gives the same result.

Answer: ∂z/∂x = −(2x + yz)/(xy − 6yz); ∂z/∂y = (3z2 − xz)/(xy − 6yz)

Ex. 13.5: 46

Find ∂z/∂x and ∂z/∂y by implicit differentiation, and confirm with Theorem 13.5.4: ln(1 + z) + xy2 + z = 1.

Let F = ln(1 + z) + xy2 + z − 1. Then Fx = y2, Fy = 2xy, Fz = 1/(1 + z) + 1 = (z + 2)/(z + 1).

By Theorem 13.5.4, ∂z/∂x = −Fx/Fz = −y2(z + 1)/(z + 2) and ∂z/∂y = −Fy/Fz = −2xy(z + 1)/(z + 2).

Answer: ∂z/∂x = −y2(z + 1)/(z + 2); ∂z/∂y = −2xy(z + 1)/(z + 2)

Ex. 13.5: 47

Find ∂z/∂x and ∂z/∂y by implicit differentiation, and confirm with Theorem 13.5.4: yex − 5 sin 3z = 3z.

Let F = yex − 5 sin 3z − 3z. Then Fx = yex, Fy = ex, Fz = −15 cos 3z − 3 = −3(5 cos 3z + 1).

By Theorem 13.5.4, ∂z/∂x = −Fx/Fz = yex/[3(5 cos 3z + 1)] and ∂z/∂y = −Fy/Fz = ex/[3(5 cos 3z + 1)].

Answer: ∂z/∂x = yex/[3(5 cos 3z + 1)]; ∂z/∂y = ex/[3(5 cos 3z + 1)]

Ex. 13.5: 48

Find ∂z/∂x and ∂z/∂y by implicit differentiation, and confirm with Theorem 13.5.4: exy cos yz − eyz sin xz + 2 = 0.

Let F = exy cos yz − eyz sin xz + 2. Then Fx = y exy cos yz − z eyz cos xz, Fy = x exy cos yz − z exy sin yz − z eyz sin xz, and Fz = −y exy sin yz − y eyz sin xz − x eyz cos xz.

By Theorem 13.5.4, ∂z/∂x = −Fx/Fz and ∂z/∂y = −Fy/Fz, with the Fx, Fy, Fz above.

Answer: ∂z/∂x = [y exy cos yz − z eyz cos xz] / [x eyz cos xz + y exy sin yz + y eyz sin xz]; ∂z/∂y = [x exy cos yz − z exy sin yz − z eyz sin xz] / [x eyz cos xz + y exy sin yz + y eyz sin xz]

Ex. 13.5: 58

Show that z = tan−1(2xy/(x2 − y2)) satisfies Laplace’s equation zxx + zyy = 0; then substitute x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ and show the resulting function satisfies the polar form of Laplace’s equation.

Computing the partials (a CAS check confirms): zx = −2y/(x2 + y2) and zy = 2x/(x2 + y2). Differentiating again, zxx = 4xy/(x2 + y2)2 and zyy = −4xy/(x2 + y2)2, so zxx + zyy = 0: Laplace’s equation holds.

In polar coordinates, 2xy/(x2 − y2) = 2 tan θ/(1 − tan2θ) = tan 2θ, so z = 2θ (up to an additive constant on each branch). Then zr = 0, zθ = 2, zrr = 0, zθθ = 0, and the polar Laplacian zrr + (1/r2)zθθ + (1/r)zr = 0.

Answer: z satisfies zxx + zyy = 0, and in polar form z = 2θ, which satisfies the polar Laplace equation

Ex. 13.5: 59

(a) Show that if u(x, y) and v(x, y) satisfy the Cauchy–Riemann equations ux = vy, uy = −vx, and x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ, then ur = (1/r)vθ and vr = −(1/r)uθ (the polar Cauchy–Riemann equations). (b) Show that u = ln(x2 + y2), v = 2 tan−1(y/x) satisfy the Cauchy–Riemann equations, and that in polar form they satisfy the polar form.

(a) By the chain rule and Exercise 57(c), ur = ux cos θ + uy sin θ and (1/r)vθ = (1/r)(−vx r sin θ + vy r cos θ) = −vx sin θ + vy cos θ. Using ux = vy and uy = −vx, both equal vy cos θ − vx sin θ. Similarly vr = vx cos θ + vy sin θ and −(1/r)uθ = ux sin θ − uy cos θ, which agree by the Cauchy–Riemann equations.

(b) ux = 2x/(x2 + y2), uy = 2y/(x2 + y2), vx = −2y/(x2 + y2), vy = 2x/(x2 + y2), so ux = vy and uy = −vx. In polar form u = 2 ln r and v = 2θ, so ur = 2/r = (1/r)vθ and vr = 0 = −(1/r)uθ.

Answer: Polar Cauchy–Riemann equations hold; for u = ln(x2 + y2), v = 2 tan−1(y/x), u = 2 ln r, v = 2θ satisfy them

Ex. 13.5: 60

The wave equation is utt = c2uxx. (a) Show u(x, t) = f(x + ct) satisfies it. (b) Show u(x, t) = g(x − ct) satisfies it. (c) Show u(x, t) = f(x + ct) + g(x − ct) satisfies it. (d) Confirm u(x, t) = sin t sin x satisfies the wave equation with c = 1, and express it in the form f(x + t) + g(x − t).

(a) Let s = x + ct. Then ut = c f′(s), utt = c2 f″(s), ux = f′(s), uxx = f″(s), so utt = c2uxx.

(b) Let s = x − ct. Then ut = −c g′(s), utt = c2 g″(s), uxx = g″(s), so utt = c2uxx.

(c) The wave equation is linear: the sum of two solutions is a solution, by (a) and (b).

(d) u = sin t sin x gives utt = −sin t sin x and uxx = −sin t sin x, so utt = uxx (c = 1). Using cos(A − B) − cos(A + B) = 2 sin A sin B, sin t sin x = (1/2)[cos(x − t) − cos(x + t)] = f(x + t) + g(x − t) with f(s) = −(1/2) cos s and g(s) = (1/2) cos s.

Answer: (a)–(c) hold by the chain rule and linearity; (d) u = sin t sin x satisfies utt = uxx and equals −(1/2)cos(x + t) + (1/2)cos(x − t)

Making Connections (p. 999) — Euler’s homogeneous-function theorem

Ex. MC 1

Suppose z = f(x, y) is expressed in polar form by x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ. Show that r ∂z/∂r = x ∂z/∂x + y ∂z/∂y and ∂z/∂θ = −y ∂z/∂x + x ∂z/∂y.

By the chain rule, ∂z/∂r = (∂z/∂x)(∂x/∂r) + (∂z/∂y)(∂y/∂r) = (∂z/∂x) cos θ + (∂z/∂y) sin θ. Multiplying by r: r ∂z/∂r = (r cos θ)(∂z/∂x) + (r sin θ)(∂z/∂y) = x ∂z/∂x + y ∂z/∂y.

Similarly ∂z/∂θ = (∂z/∂x)(−r sin θ) + (∂z/∂y)(r cos θ) = −y ∂z/∂x + x ∂z/∂y.

Answer: r ∂z/∂r = x ∂z/∂x + y ∂z/∂y; ∂z/∂θ = −y ∂z/∂x + x ∂z/∂y

Ex. MC 2

A function f(x, y) is homogeneous of degree n if f(tx, ty) = tnf(x, y) for t > 0. Show each function is homogeneous and find its degree: (a) f = 3x2 + y2; (b) f = √(x2 + y2); (c) f = x2y − 2y3; (d) f = 2/(x + 2y2)2.

(a) f(tx, ty) = 3t2x2 + t2y2 = t2f(x, y): homogeneous of degree 2.

(b) f(tx, ty) = √(t2x2 + t2y2) = t√(x2 + y2) = t f(x, y) (t > 0): homogeneous of degree 1.

(c) f(tx, ty) = t3x2y − 2t3y3 = t3f(x, y): homogeneous of degree 3.

(d) f(tx, ty) = 2/(tx + 2t2y2)2. The denominator mixes t and t2, so this is not tn times f(x, y) for any n: the function is not homogeneous. (Note: some summaries list this as homogeneous — it is not; check by t = 2, x = 1, y = 1: f(2, 2) = 2/100 = 1/50, while tnf(1, 1) = 2n·(2/9) for no n.)

Answer: (a) degree 2; (b) degree 1; (c) degree 3; (d) not homogeneous

Ex. MC 3

Suppose f(x, y) is defined for all (x, y) ≠ (0, 0). Prove that f is homogeneous of degree n if and only if there is a 2π-periodic function g(θ) such that in polar form z = f(x, y) becomes z = rng(θ) for r > 0.

(⇒) If f is homogeneous of degree n, write (x, y) = (r cos θ, r sin θ). Then f(x, y) = f(r cos θ, r sin θ) = rnf(cos θ, sin θ) (taking t = r). Set g(θ) = f(cos θ, sin θ); g is 2π-periodic since cos and sin are. So z = rng(θ).

(⇐) Conversely, if z = rng(θ), then f(tx, ty) has polar radius tr and the same angle θ, so f(tx, ty) = (tr)ng(θ) = tnrng(θ) = tnf(x, y): f is homogeneous of degree n.

Answer: f is homogeneous of degree n ⟺ z = rng(θ) in polar form

Ex. MC 4

(a) Use the chain rule to show that if f(x, y) is homogeneous of degree n, then x fx + y fy = nf (Euler’s theorem). (b) Use Exercises 1 and 3 to give another derivation. (c) Confirm that the functions in Exercise 2 satisfy the equation in (a).

(a) Let u = tx, v = ty. The homogeneity identity f(u, v) = tnf(x, y) differentiated with respect to t gives, by the chain rule, fu·x + fv·y = n tn−1f(x, y). Setting t = 1 (so u = x, v = y) gives x fx + y fy = n f.

(b) By Exercise 3, z = rng(θ), so ∂z/∂r = n rn−1g(θ) = nz/r. By Exercise 1, r ∂z/∂r = x ∂z/∂x + y ∂z/∂y, hence x fx + y fy = nz = nf.

(c) (a) f = 3x2 + y2: x(6x) + y(2y) = 6x2 + 2y2 = 2f ✓ (n = 2). (b) f = √(x2 + y2): x·x/f + y·y/f = (x2 + y2)/f = f ✓ (n = 1). (c) f = x2y − 2y3: x(2xy) + y(x2 − 6y2) = 3x2y − 6y3 = 3f ✓ (n = 3). (d) is not homogeneous, so the theorem does not apply.

Answer: Euler’s theorem: x fx + y fy = nf for homogeneous f of degree n

Ex. MC 5

Suppose f(x, y) is defined for all (x, y) ≠ (0, 0) and satisfies x fx + y fy = nf. Prove that f is homogeneous of degree n.

In polar form, Exercise 1 gives r ∂z/∂r = x fx + y fy = nz, i.e. ∂z/∂r − (n/r)z = 0. Divide by rn+1: (1/rn+1)∂z/∂r − (n/rn+2)z = 0. The left side is ∂/∂r(z/rn) (by the quotient rule), so z/rn is independent of r: z/rn = g(θ) for some function g of θ alone. Hence z = rng(θ), and by Exercise 3, f is homogeneous of degree n.

Answer: f is homogeneous of degree n

Lecture 9 — Directional Derivatives, Gradients, Tangent Planes & Normal Vectors (Anton §13.6–13.7)

The gradient is a little arrow that points straight uphill on a surface, and it tells you how fast the surface rises in any direction you choose to walk.

Stand on a hillside. You can walk in any direction — north, east, diagonally — and the ground will rise or fall at a different rate depending on which way you go. The directional derivative is simply the answer to the question: "If I walk in this direction, how steeply does the ground rise under my feet?" The direction is given by a unit vector u — "unit" just means an arrow of length exactly 1, so that you are measuring the slope per step, not per giant leap. If you forget to make your direction arrow length 1, your answer will be silently scaled by the arrow's length, and that is the most common mistake in this whole lecture.

Now, among all the directions you could walk, one is special: the steepest uphill direction. The gradient, written ∇f (read "grad f" or "del f"), is an arrow that points exactly in that direction, and its length tells you how steep the steepest slope is. It is built very simply out of the two partial derivatives you already know: ∇f = fx i + fy j (and add fz k if there are three variables). The magic shortcut is Du f = ∇f · u — the slope in any direction is just the dot product of the gradient with your direction arrow. Walk along the gradient and you climb fastest, at rate |∇f|; walk the opposite way and you descend fastest, at rate −|∇f|; walk at right angles to the gradient and the ground stays flat, because Du f = 0 there.

There is a beautiful picture hiding here. Draw the level curves of the surface — the contour lines on a map, each one joining points of equal height. The gradient arrow always cuts across the level curves at right angles, pointing towards higher curves. Where the contour lines are packed close together, the hill is steep, and the gradient arrow is long; where they are spread apart, the hill is gentle, and the arrow is short. So the gradient is not only a formula — it is the compass of the hill.

Finally, the tangent plane. You met the tangent line in first-year calculus: the straight line that just touches a curve at a point. A tangent plane is the same idea for a surface — the flat plane that just touches the surface at one point, like a sheet of glass laid on a hilltop. For a surface given by an equation F(x, y, z) = c, the plane at the point P₀ is Fx(P₀)(x − x₀) + Fy(P₀)(y − y₀) + Fz(P₀)(z − z₀) = 0, and the line through P₀ in the direction of ∇F is the normal line — the line that sticks straight out of the surface. For an ordinary graph z = f(x, y), the same thing becomes z − z₀ = fx(x₀, y₀)(x − x₀) + fy(x₀, y₀)(y − y₀), with the normal pointing in the direction (fx, fy, −1). Notice that this tangent plane is exactly the local linear approximation you met in Lecture 7 — the same idea, now with a geometric face. One caution: a tangent plane only exists where ∇F is not zero. Where the gradient vanishes, the surface may have a sharp point or a flat spot, and there may be no single plane that touches it nicely.

Keep two arrows straight in your head and you will not go wrong: the gradient ∇f lives in the flat xy-plane and is perpendicular to the level curves, while the normal to the surface, (fx, fy, −1), lives in three-dimensional space and sticks out of the surface. They are different arrows doing different jobs.

Now the question students most often ask, and the one the formula alone never answers: why does the gradient point in the steepest direction? The proof is one line of algebra, but the idea is worth slowing down for. The directional derivative is a dot product: Du f = ∇f · u. And a dot product can be written as |∇f| · |u| · cos θ, where θ is the angle between the gradient arrow and your walking direction. Since u is a unit vector, |u| = 1, so Du f = |∇f| cos θ. Now cos θ is at most 1, and it equals 1 exactly when θ = 0 — when you walk in precisely the same direction as the gradient. It equals −1 when you walk exactly opposite, and 0 when you walk at right angles. So the steepest climb, the steepest descent and the flat direction are all just the three special values of cos θ. The dot product is measuring how much of the gradient lies along your direction of travel: walk with the gradient and you get all of it; walk across it and you get none of it.

Here is the everyday picture that makes the gradient unforgettable. Water running down a hillside always takes the steepest downhill route — it flows along −∇f, the direction of fastest decrease. Heat does the same: on a metal plate whose temperature varies from point to point (Ex. 13.6-78 in your exercises), heat flows from hot to cold, along −∇T. And a ball released on a hill rolls along −∇f. So the gradient is not an abstract arrow: it is the direction the water runs, reversed. If you ever forget which way ∇f points, think of water: ∇f points the way the water came from.

Let us use the worked example above to see all of this in numbers. For f(x, y, z) = xy + z² at P(−3, 0, 4) we found ∇f = (0, −3, 8). Its length is |∇f| = √(0² + (−3)² + 8²) = √73 ≈ 8.54, so the steepest possible rate of increase at P is about 8.54 per step, in the direction (0, −3, 8)/√73. Compare that with the direction we actually walked in the example, (1, 1, 1)/√3, where the rate was only 5/√3 ≈ 2.89. Walking diagonally climbs at barely a third of the steepest rate — because most of the gradient is pointing somewhere else, in the z-direction and the negative y-direction, and the diagonal walk only catches a fraction of it. That is exactly what cos θ means: the fraction of the gradient you manage to walk along.

Finally, a picture for the tangent plane that ties it back to Lecture 7. A smooth surface, looked at closely enough, looks flat — that is really what "differentiable" means. If you zoom in on a hilltop with a microscope, the curved ground fills your view as a flat sheet, and that sheet is the tangent plane. The local linear approximation you met in Lecture 7 is that flat sheet, written as a formula; now you are meeting the same idea with a geometric face. One useful consequence: a tangent plane is horizontal exactly when fx = fy = 0 at the point — the ground is flat in both directions, which is the same condition as a critical point in Lecture 10. The lectures are not separate topics; they are the same few ideas, seen from different sides.

Gradient: ∇f = fx i + fy j (three variables: + fz k)

Directional derivative: Du f = ∇f · u, where u is a unit vector

Steepest increase: direction of ∇f, rate |∇f|; steepest decrease: direction −∇f, rate −|∇f|; Du f = 0 when u is perpendicular to ∇f

Tangent plane to F(x, y, z) = c at P₀: Fx(P₀)(x − x₀) + Fy(P₀)(y − y₀) + Fz(P₀)(z − z₀) = 0; normal line through P₀ in the direction ∇F

Tangent plane to a graph z = f(x, y): z − z₀ = fx(x₀, y₀)(x − x₀) + fy(x₀, y₀)(y − y₀); normal direction (fx, fy, −1)

Worked example — Ex. 13.6-15 (from the guide). Find the directional derivative of f(x, y, z) = xy + z² at P(−3, 0, 4) in the direction of a = i + j + k.

Step 1 — Find the gradient. fx = y, fy = x, fz = 2z, so ∇f = y i + x j + 2z k. At P(−3, 0, 4) this is ∇f = (0, −3, 8).

Step 2 — Make the direction a unit vector. a = (1, 1, 1) has length √3, so the unit vector is u = (1, 1, 1)/√3. This step is the one students skip — do not skip it.

Step 3 — Take the dot product. Du f = ∇f · u = (0·1 + (−3)·1 + 8·1)/√3 = 5/√3.

Answer: Du f = 5/√3 ≈ 2.89. Walking from P in the direction (1, 1, 1), the function rises at about 2.89 units per step.

Watch out: always normalise the direction vector before using Du f = ∇f · u — if you use a non-unit vector, your answer is silently scaled by its length and is wrong.

  • What is the gradient, how is it built from partial derivatives, and what do its direction and its length mean?
  • How do you find the rate of change of f in any given direction, and why must the direction be a unit vector?
  • Why is the gradient perpendicular to the level curves, and what does it mean when level curves are close together?
  • How do you write the tangent plane and the normal line to a surface F(x, y, z) = c at a point — and when does no tangent plane exist?

Ex. 13.6: 15–25 — directional derivatives. Ex. 13.6: 57–60 — unit vector in the direction of most rapid increase at P, and the rate of change in that direction. Ex. 13.6: 78–80 — applications: temperature on a metal plate; electric potential and field intensity; mountain climber. Ex. 13.7: 11, 12 — tangent plane and normal line. Ex. 13.7: 23, 24 — two unit normal vectors to a surface at P. Ex. 13.7: 28, 30, 33, 36 — proofs: common tangent plane, tangent line to a curve of intersection, tangent plane to an ellipsoid, normal lines to cones and spheres.
