A Tangent Line Is Easy… But What About a Tangent Plane? (MathCraft8)

Lecture 9 — Solutions: Directional Derivatives, Gradients, Tangent Planes (Anton §13.6–13.7)

Ex. 13.6: 15

Find the directional derivative of f(x, y, z) = xy + z2 at P(−3, 0, 4) in the direction of a = i + j + k.

∇f = (y, x, 2z), so ∇f(−3, 0, 4) = (0, −3, 8). The unit vector in the direction of a is u = (1, 1, 1)/√3.

Duf = ∇f · u = (0)(1/√3) + (−3)(1/√3) + (8)(1/√3) = 5/√3.

Answer: Duf = 5/√3 ≈ 2.89

Ex. 13.6: 16

Find the directional derivative of f(x, y, z) = √(y − x2 + z2) at P(−3, 1, 4) in the direction of a = 2i − 2j − k.

∇f = (−x, 1, z)/(2√(y − x2 + z2)). At P, y − x2 + z2 = 8, so ∇f(P) = (3√2/4, √2/8, √2).

The unit vector is u = (2/3, −2/3, −1/3). Duf = (3√2/4)(2/3) + (√2/8)(−2/3) + √2(−1/3) = √2/2 − √2/12 − √2/3 = √2/12.

Answer: Duf = √2/12 ≈ 0.118

Ex. 13.6: 17

Find the directional derivative of f(x, y, z) = (z − x)/(z + y) at P(1, 0, −3) in the direction of a = −6i + 3j − 2k.

fx = −1/(z + y), fy = −(z − x)/(z + y)2, fz = (y + x)/(z + y)2. At P(1, 0, −3): ∇f = (1/3, 4/9, 1/9).

|a| = √(36 + 9 + 4) = 7, so u = (−6/7, 3/7, −2/7). Duf = (1/3)(−6/7) + (4/9)(3/7) + (1/9)(−2/7) = −2/7 + 4/21 − 2/63 = −8/63.

Answer: Duf = −8/63 ≈ −0.127

Ex. 13.6: 18

Find the directional derivative of f(x, y, z) = ex+y+3z at P(−2, 2, −1) in the direction of a = 20i − 4j + 5k.

∇f = ex+y+3z(1, 1, 3). At P, x + y + 3z = −3, so ∇f(P) = e−3(1, 1, 3).

|a| = √(400 + 16 + 25) = 21, so u = (20/21, −4/21, 5/21). Duf = e−3(20 − 4 + 15)/21 = 31e−3/21.

Answer: Duf = 31e−3/21 ≈ 0.0735

Ex. 13.6: 19

Find the directional derivative of f(x, y) = xy at P(1, 4) in the direction θ = π/3.

∇f = (y, x), so ∇f(1, 4) = (4, 1). The unit vector is u = (cos π/3, sin π/3) = (1/2, √3/2).

Duf = 4(1/2) + 1(√3/2) = 2 + √3/2.

Answer: Duf = 2 + √3/2 ≈ 2.87

Ex. 13.6: 20

Find the directional derivative of f(x, y) = (x − y)/(x + y) at P(−1, −2) in the direction θ = π/2.

fx = 2y/(x + y)2, fy = −2x/(x + y)2. At P(−1, −2): fy = 2/9 (and fx = −4/9).

The unit vector is u = (cos π/2, sin π/2) = (0, 1). Duf = ∇f · u = fy = 2/9.

Answer: Duf = 2/9

Ex. 13.6: 21

Find the directional derivative of f(x, y) = tan(2x + y) at P(π/6, π/3) in the direction θ = 7π/4.

fx = 2 sec2(2x + y), fy = sec2(2x + y). At P, 2x + y = 2π/3, sec2(2π/3) = 4, so ∇f(P) = (8, 4).

u = (cos 7π/4, sin 7π/4) = (√2/2, −√2/2). Duf = (8 − 4)√2/2 = 2√2.

Answer: Duf = 2√2 ≈ 2.83

Ex. 13.6: 22

Find the directional derivative of f(x, y) = sinh x cosh y at P(0, 0) in the direction θ = π.

fx = cosh x cosh y, fy = sinh x sinh y. At (0, 0): ∇f = (1, 0).

u = (cos π, sin π) = (−1, 0). Duf = −1.

Answer: Duf = −1

Ex. 13.6: 23

Find the directional derivative of f(x, y) = x/(x + y) at P(1, 0) in the direction toward Q(−1, −1).

fx = y/(x + y)2, fy = −x/(x + y)2. At P(1, 0): ∇f = (0, −1).

The vector PQ = (−2, −1), |PQ| = √5, so u = (−2/√5, −1/√5). Duf = 0 + (−1)(−1/√5) = 1/√5 = √5/5.

Answer: Duf = √5/5 ≈ 0.447

Ex. 13.6: 24

Find the directional derivative of f(x, y) = e−x sec y at P(0, π/4) in the direction toward the origin.

fx = −e−x sec y, fy = e−x sec y tan y. At P(0, π/4): ∇f = (−√2, √2).

The direction toward the origin is (0, −π/4), whose unit vector is (0, −1). Duf = −√2.

Answer: Duf = −√2 ≈ −1.41

Ex. 13.6: 25

Find the directional derivative of f(x, y) = xy ey at P(1, 1) in the direction of the negative y-axis.

fx = y ey, fy = x ey + xy ey. At P(1, 1): ∇f = (e, 2e).

The unit vector in the negative y-direction is (0, −1). Duf = −2e.

Answer: Duf = −2e ≈ −5.44

Ex. 13.6: 57

Find the direction of most rapid increase of f(x, y, z) = x3z2 + y3z + z − 1 at (1, 1, −1), and the rate of change in that direction.

∇f = (3x2z2, 3y2z, 2x3z + y3 + 1). At (1, 1, −1): ∇f = (3, −3, 0).

The most rapid increase is in the direction of the gradient, unit vector (1/√2, −1/√2, 0), at the rate |∇f| = 3√2.

Answer: Direction (1/√2, −1/√2, 0); rate 3√2 ≈ 4.24

Ex. 13.6: 58

Find the direction of most rapid increase of f(x, y, z) = √(x − 3y + 4z) at (0, −3, 0), and the rate of change in that direction.

∇f = (1, −3, 4)/(2√(x − 3y + 4z)). At (0, −3, 0): x − 3y + 4z = 9, so ∇f = (1/6, −1/2, 2/3).

|∇f| = √(1/36 + 1/4 + 4/9) = √26/6. The direction of most rapid increase is the unit vector ∇f/|∇f| = (1/√26, −3/√26, 4/√26), at rate √26/6.

Answer: Direction (√26/26, −3√26/26, 2√26/13); rate √26/6 ≈ 0.85

Ex. 13.6: 59

Find the direction of most rapid increase of f(x, y, z) = x/z + z/y at (1, 2, −2), and the rate of change in that direction.

fx = 1/z, fy = −z/y2, fz = −x/z2 + 1/y. At (1, 2, −2): ∇f = (−1/2, 1/2, 1/4).

|∇f| = √(1/4 + 1/4 + 1/16) = 3/4. The direction of most rapid increase is ∇f/|∇f| = (−2/3, 2/3, 1/3), at rate 3/4.

Answer: Direction (−2/3, 2/3, 1/3); rate 3/4

Ex. 13.6: 60

Find the direction of most rapid increase of f(x, y, z) = tan−1(x/(y + z)) at (4, 2, 2), and the rate of change in that direction.

Let w = x/(y + z). Then fx = (1/(1 + w2))·(1/(y + z)), fy = fz = (1/(1 + w2))·(−x/(y + z)2). At (4, 2, 2): w = 1, so ∇f = (1/8, −1/8, −1/8).

|∇f| = √3/8. The direction of most rapid increase is (1/√3, −1/√3, −1/√3), at rate √3/8.

Answer: Direction (√3/3, −√3/3, −√3/3); rate √3/8 ≈ 0.217

Ex. 13.6: 78

(a) Find the directional derivative of T(x, y) = xy/(1 + x2 + y2) at (1, 1) in the direction of a = 2i − j. (b) In which direction does T decrease most rapidly at (1, 1), and what is the rate of change in that direction?

(a) Tx = y(1 − x2 + y2)/(1 + x2 + y2)2 and Ty = x(1 + x2 − y2)/(1 + x2 + y2)2. At (1, 1): ∇T = (1/9, 1/9).

The unit vector in the direction of a is (2/√5, −1/√5), so DuT = (2 − 1)/(9√5) = 1/(9√5) = √5/45.

(b) T decreases most rapidly in the direction −∇T/|∇T| = −(1/√2, 1/√2), at the rate |∇T| = √2/9.

Answer: (a) √5/45 ≈ 0.050; (b) direction −(1/√2, 1/√2), rate √2/9 ≈ 0.157

Ex. 13.6: 79

The voltage V at a point (x, y) is given by V(x, y) = e−2x cos 2y. Find the electric field E = −∇V at the point (π/4, 0).

Vx = −2e−2x cos 2y, Vy = −2e−2x sin 2y. At (π/4, 0): ∇V = (−2e−π/2, 0).

Hence E = −∇V = (2e−π/2, 0).

Answer: E = 2e−π/2 i ≈ 0.416 i

Ex. 13.6: 80

The height of a hill is z = 2000 − 0.02x2 − 0.04y2 (metres), with x, y in metres, measured from the top. A hiker is at (−20, 5). (a) In which direction is the hiker headed if she walks due west? Does she ascend or descend, and at what rate? (b) What is the rate of change of height if she heads northeast? (c) In which compass directions is her rate of change zero?

∇z = (−0.04x, −0.08y); at (−20, 5), ∇z = (0.8, −0.4) metres of height per metre travelled.

(a) Due west is u = (−1, 0): Duz = −0.8 < 0, so she descends at 0.8 m per metre.

(b) Northeast is u = (√2/2, √2/2): Duz = (0.8 − 0.4)√2/2 = √2/5 ≈ 0.28 m per metre — she ascends.

(c) Duz = 0 when u is perpendicular to ∇z = (0.8, −0.4), i.e. u = ±(1, 2)/√5. As a compass bearing this is N 26.6° E and S 26.6° W (tan−1(1/2) ≈ 26.6°).

Answer: (a) Descends at 0.8 m/m; (b) ascends at √2/5 ≈ 0.28 m/m; (c) N 26.6° E and S 26.6° W

Ex. 13.7: 11

Find an equation of the tangent plane to z = e3y sin 3x at (π/6, 0), and parametric equations of the normal line at that point.

fx = 3e3y cos 3x, fy = 3e3y sin 3x. At (π/6, 0): fx = 3 cos(π/2) = 0, fy = 3 sin(π/2) = 3, and z = e0 sin(π/2) = 1.

Tangent plane: z − 1 = 0(x − π/6) + 3(y − 0), i.e. z = 1 + 3y.

The normal line is in the direction (−fx, −fy, 1) = (0, −3, 1) through (π/6, 0, 1): x = π/6, y = −3t, z = 1 + t.

Answer: Tangent plane z = 1 + 3y; normal line x = π/6, y = −3t, z = 1 + t

Ex. 13.7: 12

Find an equation of the tangent plane to z = √x + √y at (4, 9), and parametric equations of the normal line at that point.

fx = 1/(2√x), fy = 1/(2√y). At (4, 9): fx = 1/4, fy = 1/6, and z = 2 + 3 = 5.

Tangent plane: z − 5 = (1/4)(x − 4) + (1/6)(y − 9), i.e. z = x/4 + y/6 + 5/2.

Normal line: x = 4 − t/4, y = 9 − t/6, z = 5 + t (direction (−1/4, −1/6, 1)).

Answer: Tangent plane z = x/4 + y/6 + 5/2; normal line x = 4 − t/4, y = 9 − t/6, z = 5 + t

Ex. 13.7: 23

Find a unit vector normal to the surface (z + x)/(y − 1) = z2 at the point (3, 5, 1).

Let F(x, y, z) = (z + x)/(y − 1) − z2. Then Fx = 1/(y − 1), Fy = −(z + x)/(y − 1)2, Fz = 1/(y − 1) − 2z.

At (3, 5, 1): ∇F = (1/4, −1/4, −7/4), with |∇F| = √(1 + 1 + 49)/4 = √51/4. Dividing by the length gives the unit normal ±(1, −1, −7)/√51.

Answer: ±(1, −1, −7)/√51, i.e. ±(√51/51, −√51/51, −7√51/51)

Ex. 13.7: 24

Find a unit vector normal to the surface sin xz − 4 cos yz = 4 at the point (π, π, 1).

Let F = sin xz − 4 cos yz − 4. Then Fx = z cos xz, Fy = 4z sin yz, Fz = x cos xz + 4y sin yz.

At (π, π, 1): ∇F = (−1, 0, −π), with |∇F| = √(1 + π2). The unit normal is ±(−1, 0, −π)/√(1 + π2).

Answer: ±(−1, 0, −π)/√(1 + π2)

Ex. 13.7: 28

Show that the ellipsoid 2x2 + 3y2 + z2 = 9 and the sphere x2 + y2 + z2 − 6x − 8y − 8z + 24 = 0 have the same tangent plane at (1, 1, 2).

First check (1, 1, 2) lies on both: 2 + 3 + 4 = 9 ✓ and 1 + 1 + 4 − 6 − 8 − 16 + 24 = 0 ✓.

For the ellipsoid, ∇F = (4x, 6y, 2z) = (4, 6, 4) at the point. For the sphere, ∇G = (2x − 6, 2y − 8, 2z − 8) = (−4, −6, −4) at the point — a scalar multiple of (4, 6, 4).

Since the two gradients are parallel, the two tangent planes have the same normal direction, hence the same tangent plane: 4(x − 1) + 6(y − 1) + 4(z − 2) = 0, i.e. 2x + 3y + 2z = 9.

Answer: Common tangent plane 2x + 3y + 2z = 9

Ex. 13.7: 30

Find parametric equations of the line tangent to the intersection of the cone z = √(x2 + y2) and the plane x + 2y + 2z = 20 at the point (4, 3, 5).

The tangent line is perpendicular to both surfaces’ normals, so its direction is the cross product of the gradients. For the cone, F = z − √(x2 + y2), ∇F = (−x/√(x2 + y2), −y/√(x2 + y2), 1) = (−4/5, −3/5, 1) at (4, 3, 5). For the plane, ∇G = (1, 2, 2).

Direction = ∇F × ∇G = (−16/5, 13/5, −1). Through (4, 3, 5): x = 4 − 16t/5, y = 3 + 13t/5, z = 5 − t (equivalently x = 4 − 16s, y = 3 + 13s, z = 5 − 5s).

Answer: x = 4 − 16t/5, y = 3 + 13t/5, z = 5 − t

Ex. 13.7: 33

Let f and g be differentiable functions of x and y such that z = f(x, y) and z = g(x, y) are tangent planes at a point (a, b, c). Show that fx(a, b) = gx(a, b) and fy(a, b) = gy(a, b).

Two planes tangent to the same surface at the same point are the same plane. The tangent plane to z = f(x, y) at (a, b, c) is z = c + fx(a, b)(x − a) + fy(a, b)(y − b); the tangent plane to z = g(x, y) is z = c + gx(a, b)(x − a) + gy(a, b)(y − b).

Since the two planes coincide, their coefficients must be equal: fx(a, b) = gx(a, b) and fy(a, b) = gy(a, b).

Answer: fx(a, b) = gx(a, b) and fy(a, b) = gy(a, b)

Ex. 13.7: 36

Use the result of Exercise 35 to show that the normal lines to the cone z = ±√(x2 + y2) are perpendicular to the normal lines to the sphere x2 + y2 + z2 = a2 at the points where the surfaces intersect.

Exercise 35: the normal lines to z = f(x, y) and z = g(x, y) are perpendicular at a common point if fxgx + fygy = −1. At an intersection point, x2 + y2 = z2 = a2/2.

For the upper cone z = √(x2 + y2), fx = x/z, fy = y/z. The sphere’s upper hemisphere is g = √(a2 − x2 − y2), with gx = −x/z, gy = −y/z (using z = √(a2 − x2 − y2) at the point). Then fxgx + fygy = −(x2 + y2)/z2 = −1.

The same calculation with the lower cone z = −√(x2 + y2) and the lower hemisphere gives fxgx + fygy = −1 as well. Hence the normal lines are perpendicular at every intersection point.

Answer: The normal lines are perpendicular at the intersection points

Lecture 10 — Maxima and Minima of Functions of Two Variables (Anton §13.8)

To find the highest and lowest points of a surface, first find where it is flat, then use a simple test to tell a peak from a valley from a mountain pass.

Think of the surface z = f(x, y) as a landscape. A relative maximum is the top of a hill — the highest point in its own neighbourhood, even if a taller mountain stands elsewhere. A relative minimum is the bottom of a valley. An absolute maximum is the highest point of the whole landscape you are allowed to look at, and the absolute minimum the lowest. "Relative" means local, "absolute" means global — keep those two words apart and half the confusion disappears.

Now, where can a hilltop or a valley bottom be? At the very top of a smooth hill, the ground is flat in every direction — the slope east–west is zero and the slope north–south is zero. In calculus language, that means fx = 0 and fy = 0 at the same time. A point where both partial derivatives are zero (or where one of them does not exist) is called a critical point. Every relative maximum or minimum of a smooth function must be a critical point — so finding critical points is always step one. But be careful: not every critical point is a hilltop or a valley. Some are saddle points, and a saddle is the most beautiful idea in this lecture.

Picture a mountain pass, the kind a road winds through between two peaks. If you walk along the road, the pass is the highest point of your journey; if you walk across the road, up the slopes on either side, the pass is the lowest point. So the same point is a maximum in one direction and a minimum in another — it is neither a hilltop nor a valley, it is a saddle, like the seat of a horse. The surface z = x² − y² is the classic example: it rises as you walk east and falls as you walk north.

How do you tell which kind of critical point you have found? With the Second Partials Test. Compute D = fxx·fyy − (fxy)² at the critical point. If D > 0 and fxx > 0, you are in a valley: a relative minimum. If D > 0 and fxx < 0, you are on a hilltop: a relative maximum. If D < 0, you are at a saddle point. And if D = 0, the test shrugs — it tells you nothing at all, and you must investigate the function some other way. Two famous examples show why: f = x⁴ + y⁴ and f = x⁴ − y⁴ both give D = 0 at the origin, yet the first has a minimum there and the second has a saddle. So D = 0 means "test fails", never "saddle".

For absolute maxima and minima on a closed, bounded region — a triangle, a square, a disk — there is one more step students constantly forget: the boundary. A continuous function on a closed, bounded set always attains an absolute maximum and minimum (the Extreme-Value Theorem), but the highest point is very often sitting on the edge of the region, not inside it. So the procedure is: check the critical points inside the region, then check each edge of the boundary as a one-variable problem, then compare all the values you found and pick the biggest and the smallest. The same procedure powers all the word problems — the box of maximum volume, the cheapest box, the three numbers with a fixed sum — because in every one of them you are maximising or minimising something, subject to a fixed region or a fixed total.

One last warning, because the exam loves it: in one-variable calculus, a single critical point that is a relative maximum is automatically the absolute maximum. In two variables that is false. A function can have one relative maximum and still climb higher somewhere else. Never claim "absolute" until you have checked the boundary.

Now let us slow down on the Second Partials Test, because students usually memorise D and never learn what it is checking. D = fxx·fyy − (fxy)² is a tug-of-war between bending and twisting. fxx measures how the surface bends as you walk east: positive means it curves upward like a bowl, negative means it curves downward like a dome. fyy measures the same thing walking north. If both bend the same way — both up, or both down — the surface is a bowl or a dome, and you have a valley or a hilltop. But fxy, the mixed partial, measures the twist: how the east–west slope changes as you walk north. If the twist is stronger than the bending, it wins the tug-of-war, D goes negative, and the surface is a saddle — bending up one way and down the other. So D > 0 means "bending wins, same sign both ways", D < 0 means "twisting wins", and D = 0 means the two sides exactly balance and the test cannot tell which won. That is why D = 0 is not an answer at all: it is the test admitting it is blind.

Here is a test you can run in your head at any critical point: put a marble down on it. In a valley the marble stays put; on a hilltop it rolls away in every direction; at a saddle it rolls away in some directions but stays balanced in others — exactly like a ball balanced on a horse's saddle, which is where the name comes from. And when D = 0, the marble test is the only honest method left: look at the function itself. The two famous examples in the guide show why. f = x⁴ + y⁴ and f = x⁴ − y⁴ both have every second derivative equal to zero at the origin, so D = 0 for both — yet the first is a valley (it is never negative) and the second is a saddle (it is positive along the x-axis and negative along the y-axis). The second derivatives are too weak to see fourth-power behaviour, so you have to look with your eyes instead of the formula.

A second mini-example, from the verified answers in the guide — the three-numbers problem (Ex. 13.8-37). Three positive numbers have a fixed sum of 48, and you want the largest possible product. The answer is 16, 16 and 16, with maximum product 4096. Why equal numbers? Think about it without any calculus: if two of the numbers differed, say 20 and 12, you could nudge them towards each other — 19 and 13, then 18 and 14 — and the product would grow each time, because (a + h)(b − h) is bigger than ab when a and b are unequal. You only stop improving when there is nothing left to equalise, which is when all three are the same. The calculus in §13.8 is just this argument made precise, and the answer 16 × 16 × 16 = 4096 confirms it. The same problem comes back in Lecture 13 solved with Lagrange multipliers — and the answer must come out 16, 16, 16 again. If it does not, you have made a slip, and the disagreement tells you where to look.

One more warning about a trap the exam sets every year, and it comes from Ex. 13.8-29 in the guide. In one-variable calculus, if a function has only one critical point and it is a relative maximum, then it must be the absolute maximum — there is nowhere else for a higher point to hide. In two variables that is false. A surface can have a single hilltop and still climb higher somewhere far away, because "far away" in two dimensions is a whole plane of escape routes, not just two directions. The guide's Ex. 29 is exactly such a function. So the word "absolute" is never earned by counting critical points; it is earned only by checking the boundary and comparing values, as the procedure above says.

Critical point: a point where fx = fy = 0, or where one or both partial derivatives do not exist

Second Partials Test: D = fxx·fyy − (fxy)², at a critical point

D > 0 and fxx > 0 ⇒ relative minimum; D > 0 and fxx < 0 ⇒ relative maximum

D < 0 ⇒ saddle point; D = 0 ⇒ the test gives no information

Absolute extrema on a closed, bounded region: check interior critical points, then check the boundary, then compare all values

Worked example — Ex. 13.8-11 (from the guide). Locate and classify the critical points of f(x, y) = x² + xy + y² − 3x.

Step 1 — Find the critical points. fx = 2x + y − 3 and fy = x + 2y. Set both to zero: 2x + y = 3 and x + 2y = 0. From the second equation x = −2y; putting that into the first gives −4y + y = 3, so y = −1 and x = 2. The only critical point is (2, −1).

Step 2 — Compute the second partials. fxx = 2, fyy = 2, fxy = 1. These are constants here, which makes life easy.

Step 3 — Apply the test. D = fxx·fyy − (fxy)² = 2·2 − 1² = 3. D > 0 and fxx = 2 > 0, so this is a relative minimum.

Step 4 — Find the value. f(2, −1) = 4 + (2)(−1) + 1 − 6 = −3.

Answer: relative minimum at (2, −1), with f = −3.

Watch out: D = 0 means the Second Partials Test has failed and tells you nothing — it does not mean "saddle point". And never forget the boundary when finding absolute extrema: the highest or lowest point is often sitting on the edge of the region.

  • What is a critical point, and why must a relative maximum or minimum be one — while the reverse is not true?
  • State the Second Partials Test in full: what do D > 0, D < 0 and D = 0 each tell you?
  • What is a saddle point, in plain words, and why is it a maximum in one direction and a minimum in another?
  • What are the steps for finding absolute maxima and minima on a closed, bounded region, and which step do students most often forget?

Ex. 13.8: 1–4 — by inspection / completing the square, then check with calculus. Ex. 13.8: 9–20 — locate all relative maxima, minima and saddle points. Ex. 13.8: 31–36 — absolute extrema on closed bounded sets (triangles, squares, disks). Ex. 13.8: 37–48 — optimisation applications: three numbers with a fixed sum; closest point to the origin; box of maximum volume in a sphere; suitcase of maximum volume; minimum-cost box; pricing for maximum profit; open-top box of least material; water trough of maximum cross-sectional area.

Lecture 10 — Solutions: Maxima and Minima (Anton §13.8)

Ex. 13.8: 1

Determine whether each function has a relative maximum, a relative minimum, an absolute maximum, an absolute minimum, or none of these. (a) f(x, y) = (x − 2)2 + (y + 1)2. (b) f(x, y) = 1 − x2 − y2. (c) f(x, y) = x + 2y − 5.

(a) A sum of squares, always ≥ 0, equal to 0 only at (2, −1): absolute (and relative) minimum 0 there; no maximum (f → ∞ as |(x, y)| → ∞).

(b) f ≤ 1, with f = 1 only at (0, 0): absolute (and relative) maximum 1 there; no minimum (f → −∞).

(c) A non-constant linear function is unbounded above and below along its gradient direction: no relative or absolute extrema.

Answer: (a) Absolute minimum 0 at (2, −1); (b) absolute maximum 1 at (0, 0); (c) no extrema

Ex. 13.8: 2

Determine whether each function has a relative maximum, a relative minimum, an absolute maximum, an absolute minimum, or none of these. (a) f(x, y) = 1 − (x + 1)2 − (y − 5)2. (b) f(x, y) = exy. (c) f(x, y) = x2 − y2.

(a) f ≤ 1, with f = 1 only at (−1, 5): absolute (and relative) maximum 1 there; no minimum (f → −∞).

(b) exy > 0 always, so there is no minimum (the infimum 0 is never attained) and no maximum (exy → ∞ along y = x → ∞). No critical points either: ∇f = (y exy, x exy) = (0, 0) only at (0, 0), where f = 1 is a saddle value, not an extremum.

(c) A saddle: along y = 0, f = x2 → ∞; along x = 0, f = −y2 → −∞. No extrema.

Answer: (a) Absolute maximum 1 at (−1, 5); (b) no extrema (0 < f < ∞); (c) no extrema

Ex. 13.8: 3

Use completing the square to locate and identify the relative extrema of f(x, y) = 13 − 6x + x2 + 4y + y2.

x2 − 6x = (x − 3)2 − 9 and y2 + 4y = (y + 2)2 − 4, so f(x, y) = (x − 3)2 + (y + 2)2 + 13 − 9 − 4 = (x − 3)2 + (y + 2)2.

A sum of squares: f ≥ 0, with f = 0 only at (3, −2).

Answer: Absolute and relative minimum 0 at (3, −2); no maximum

Ex. 13.8: 4

Use completing the square to locate and identify the relative extrema of f(x, y) = 1 − 2x − x2 + 4y − 2y2.

−x2 − 2x = −(x + 1)2 + 1 and −2y2 + 4y = −2(y − 1)2 + 2, so f(x, y) = 1 + 1 + 2 − (x + 1)2 − 2(y − 1)2 = 4 − (x + 1)2 − 2(y − 1)2.

f ≤ 4, with f = 4 only at (−1, 1).

Answer: Absolute and relative maximum 4 at (−1, 1); no minimum

Ex. 13.8: 9

Locate all relative extrema and saddle points of f(x, y) = y2 + xy + 3y + 2x + 3.

fx = y + 2, fy = 2y + x + 3. Setting both to zero: y = −2, then x = −2y − 3 = 1. Only critical point (1, −2).

fxx = 0, fyy = 2, fxy = 1, so D = fxxfyy − fxy2 = −1 < 0: a saddle point. f(1, −2) = 1.

Answer: Saddle point at (1, −2), f = 1; no relative extrema

Ex. 13.8: 10

Locate all relative extrema and saddle points of f(x, y) = x2 + xy − 2y − 2x + 1.

fx = 2x + y − 2, fy = x − 2. Setting both to zero: x = 2, y = 2 − 2x = −2. Only critical point (2, −2).

fxx = 2, fyy = 0, fxy = 1, so D = 2·0 − 1 = −1 < 0: a saddle point. f(2, −2) = 1.

Answer: Saddle point at (2, −2), f = 1; no relative extrema

Ex. 13.8: 11

Locate all relative extrema and saddle points of f(x, y) = x2 + xy + y2 − 3x.

fx = 2x + y − 3, fy = x + 2y. Setting both to zero: x = −2y, so 2(−2y) + y = 3 gives y = −1, x = 2. Only critical point (2, −1).

fxx = 2, fyy = 2, fxy = 1, so D = 4 − 1 = 3 > 0 and fxx > 0: a relative minimum, f(2, −1) = 4 − 2 + 1 − 6 = −3.

Answer: Relative minimum −3 at (2, −1); no other critical points

Ex. 13.8: 12

Locate all relative extrema and saddle points of f(x, y) = xy − x3 − y2.

fx = y − 3x2, fy = x − 2y. Setting both to zero: y = 3x2 and x = 2y = 6x2, so x = 0 or x = 1/6. Critical points (0, 0) and (1/6, 1/12).

fxx = −6x, fyy = −2, fxy = 1, so D = 12x − 1. At (0, 0): D = −1 < 0, saddle. At (1/6, 1/12): D = 1 > 0, fxx = −1 < 0, relative maximum, f = 1/72 − 1/216 − 1/144 = 1/432.

Answer: Saddle at (0, 0); relative maximum 1/432 at (1/6, 1/12)

Ex. 13.8: 13

Locate all relative extrema and saddle points of f(x, y) = x2 + y2 + 2/(xy).

fx = 2x − 2/(x2y), fy = 2y − 2/(xy2). Setting both to zero gives x3y = 1 and xy3 = 1, so x2 = y2; with x4 = 1 the real solutions are (1, 1) and (−1, −1) (domain x ≠ 0, y ≠ 0).

fxx = 2 + 4/(x3y), fyy = 2 + 4/(xy3), fxy = 2/(x2y2). At both points fxx = 6, fyy = 6, fxy = 2, so D = 36 − 4 = 32 > 0 and fxx > 0: relative minima, f = 4 at each.

Answer: Relative minima 4 at (1, 1) and at (−1, −1); no saddle points (real)

Ex. 13.8: 14

Locate all relative extrema and saddle points of f(x, y) = x ey.

fx = ey and fy = x ey. Since ey is never zero, fx = 0 has no solution: there are no critical points, hence no relative extrema or saddle points.

Answer: No critical points; no relative extrema or saddle points

Ex. 13.8: 15

Locate all relative extrema and saddle points of f(x, y) = x2 + y − ey.

fx = 2x, fy = 1 − ey. Setting both to zero: x = 0, y = 0. Only critical point (0, 0).

fxx = 2, fyy = −ey, fxy = 0, so D = 2(−1) − 0 = −2 < 0 at (0, 0): a saddle point, f(0, 0) = −1.

Answer: Saddle point at (0, 0), f = −1; no relative extrema

Ex. 13.8: 16

Locate all relative extrema and saddle points of f(x, y) = xy + 2/x + 4/y.

fx = y − 2/x2, fy = x − 4/y2. Setting both to zero: y = 2/x2 and x = 4/y2 = x4, so x4 − x = 0, giving the real critical point x = 1, y = 2 (x = 0 is outside the domain).

fxx = 4/x3, fyy = 8/y3, fxy = 1. At (1, 2): fxx = 4, fyy = 1, D = 4 − 1 = 3 > 0, fxx > 0: a relative minimum, f(1, 2) = 2 + 2 + 2 = 6.

Answer: Relative minimum 6 at (1, 2); no other critical points (real)

Ex. 13.8: 17

Locate all relative extrema and saddle points of f(x, y) = ex sin y.

fx = ex sin y, fy = ex cos y. For a critical point we need sin y = 0 and cos y = 0 simultaneously, which is impossible: there are no critical points, hence no relative extrema or saddle points.

Answer: No critical points; no relative extrema or saddle points

Ex. 13.8: 18

Locate all relative extrema and saddle points of f(x, y) = y sin x.

fx = y cos x, fy = sin x. Setting both to zero: sin x = 0, so x = kπ, and then y cos(kπ) = ±y = 0, so y = 0. Critical points (kπ, 0) for every integer k.

fxx = −y sin x = 0, fyy = 0, fxy = cos x = ±1 at these points, so D = 0 − 1 = −1 < 0: every (kπ, 0) is a saddle point, f = 0.

Answer: Saddle points at (kπ, 0) for every integer k, f = 0; no relative extrema

Ex. 13.8: 19

Locate all relative extrema and saddle points of f(x, y) = e−(x2 + y2 + 2x).

f = e−(x+1)2 − y2 + 1. fx = −2(x + 1)f, fy = −2yf. Setting both to zero: x = −1, y = 0 (f is never zero). Only critical point (−1, 0).

fxx = [−2 + 4(x + 1)2]f, fyy = [−2 + 4y2]f, fxy = 4(x + 1)yf. At (−1, 0): fxx = −2e, fyy = −2e, fxy = 0, so D = 4e2 > 0 and fxx < 0: a relative maximum, f(−1, 0) = e.

Answer: Relative maximum e at (−1, 0); no other critical points

Ex. 13.8: 20

Locate all relative extrema and saddle points of f(x, y) = xy + a3/x + b3/y, where a ≠ 0 and b ≠ 0.

fx = y − a3/x2, fy = x − b3/y2. Setting both to zero: y = a3/x2 and x = b3/y2 = b3x4/a6, so x3 = a6/b3, giving the real critical point (a2/b, b2/a).

fxx = 2a3/x3 = 2b3/a3, fyy = 2b3/y3 = 2a3/b3, fxy = 1, so D = 4 − 1 = 3 > 0. If a and b have the same sign, fxx > 0 and the point is a relative minimum; if they have opposite signs, fxx < 0 and it is a relative maximum. In either case f = ab + ab + ab = 3ab.

Answer: Critical point (a2/b, b2/a) with f = 3ab: a relative minimum if ab > 0, a relative maximum if ab < 0

Ex. 13.8: 31

Find the absolute maximum and absolute minimum of f(x, y) = xy − x − 3y on the triangular region with vertices (0, 0), (0, 4), (5, 0).

Interior: fx = y − 1, fy = x − 3, giving the critical point (3, 1), which lies inside the triangle; f(3, 1) = −3.

Boundary: on y = 0, f = −x ranges from 0 to −5; on x = 0, f = −3y ranges from 0 to −12; on the hypotenuse y = 4 − 4x/5, f = −(4/5)x2 + (27/5)x − 12, whose critical point x = 27/8 gives f = −231/80 ≈ −2.89, with endpoint values −12 and −5.

Comparing all candidates: the largest value is 0 and the smallest is −12.

Answer: Absolute maximum 0 at (0, 0); absolute minimum −12 at (0, 4)

Ex. 13.8: 32

Find the absolute maximum and absolute minimum of f(x, y) = xy − 2x on the triangular region with vertices (0, 0), (0, 4), (4, 0).

Interior: fx = y − 2, fy = x, giving the critical point (0, 2), which lies on the boundary x = 0; f = 0 there.

Boundary: on y = 0, f = −2x ranges from 0 to −8; on x = 0, f = 0; on the hypotenuse y = 4 − x, f = x(2 − x), whose critical point x = 1 gives f = 1, with endpoint values 0 and −8.

Comparing all candidates: the largest value is 1 and the smallest is −8.

Answer: Absolute maximum 1 at (1, 3); absolute minimum −8 at (4, 0)

Ex. 13.8: 33

Find the absolute maximum and absolute minimum of f(x, y) = x2 − 3y2 − 2x + 6y on the square region 0 ≤ x ≤ 2, 0 ≤ y ≤ 2.

Interior: fx = 2x − 2, fy = −6y + 6, giving the critical point (1, 1); f(1, 1) = 2.

Boundary: on y = 0 and on y = 2, f = x2 − 2x (min −1 at x = 1, endpoints 0); on x = 0 and on x = 2, f = −3y2 + 6y (max 3 at y = 1, endpoints 0).

Comparing all candidates: the largest value is 3 and the smallest is −1.

Answer: Absolute maximum 3 at (0, 1) and (2, 1); absolute minimum −1 at (1, 0) and (1, 2)

Ex. 13.8: 34

Find the absolute maximum and absolute minimum of f(x, y) = x ey − x2 − ey on the rectangle 0 ≤ x ≤ 2, 0 ≤ y ≤ 1.

Interior: fx = ey − 2x, fy = (x − 1)ey, giving the critical point (1, ln 2), which lies inside; f(1, ln 2) = −1.

Boundary: on y = 0, f = x − x2 − 1, max −3/4 at x = 1/2, endpoints −1, −3; on y = 1, f = xe − x2 − e, max −e + e2/4 ≈ −0.88 at x = e/2, endpoints −e, −4 + e; on x = 0, f = −ey, from −1 to −e; on x = 2, f = ey − 4, from −3 to e − 4.

Comparing all candidates: the largest value is −3/4 and the smallest is −3.

Answer: Absolute maximum −3/4 at (1/2, 0); absolute minimum −3 at (2, 0)

Ex. 13.8: 35

Find the absolute maximum and absolute minimum of f(x, y) = x2 + 2y2 − x on the disk x2 + y2 ≤ 4.

Interior: fx = 2x − 1, fy = 4y, giving the critical point (1/2, 0); f(1/2, 0) = −1/4.

Boundary x = 2 cos θ, y = 2 sin θ: f = 4 cos2θ + 8 sin2θ − 2 cos θ = 6 − 2 cos θ − 2 cos 2θ. Its derivative is 2 sin θ(4 cos θ + 1), zero when sin θ = 0 (θ = 0: f = 2; θ = π: f = 6) or cos θ = −1/4 (f = 33/4).

Comparing all candidates: the largest value is 33/4 and the smallest is −1/4.

Answer: Absolute maximum 33/4 at (−1/2, ±√15/2); absolute minimum −1/4 at (1/2, 0)

Ex. 13.8: 36

Find the absolute maximum and absolute minimum of f(x, y) = xy2 on the region x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0, x2 + y2 ≤ 1.

Interior: fx = y2, fy = 2xy, both zero only when y = 0 (on the boundary). On the axes x = 0 or y = 0, f = 0.

On the circular arc x = cos θ, y = sin θ (0 ≤ θ ≤ π/2): f = cos θ sin2θ. Its derivative sin θ(2 − 3 sin2θ) is zero for sin θ = 0 (f = 0) or sin2θ = 2/3, i.e. x = 1/√3, y = √(2/3), where f = 2/(3√3) = 2√3/9.

Comparing all candidates: the largest value is 2√3/9 and the smallest is 0.

Answer: Absolute maximum 2√3/9 at (1/√3, √(2/3)); absolute minimum 0 on the axes x = 0 or y = 0

Ex. 13.8: 37

Find three positive numbers whose sum is 48 and whose product is as large as possible.

Let the numbers be x, y, z with x + y + z = 48, and maximise P = xyz. By Lagrange multipliers (or symmetry), at the maximum ∇P = λ(1, 1, 1): yz = xz = xy = λ, so x = y = z (all positive), hence each is 16.

By AM–GM, xyz ≤ (48/3)3 = 4096, with equality when x = y = z = 16, confirming the maximum.

Answer: 16, 16, 16; maximum product 4096

Ex. 13.8: 38

Find three positive numbers whose sum is 27 and whose sum of squares is as small as possible.

Minimise S = x2 + y2 + z2 subject to x + y + z = 27. By Lagrange multipliers, 2x = 2y = 2z = λ, so x = y = z = 9.

By Cauchy–Schwarz (or QM–AM), x2 + y2 + z2 ≥ (x + y + z)2/3 = 243, with equality when x = y = z = 9, confirming the minimum.

Answer: 9, 9, 9; minimum sum of squares 243

Ex. 13.8: 39

Find the maximum value of xy2z2 subject to x + y + z = 5, where x, y, z ≥ 0.

Maximise f = xy2z2 on the compact triangle x + y + z = 5, x, y, z ≥ 0. On the boundary where any variable is 0, f = 0, so the maximum is interior. Lagrange multipliers: 1/x = 2/y = 2/z (from ∂/∂x, ∂/∂y, ∂/∂z of ln f), so y = 2x, z = 2x.

With x + y + z = 5, x + 4x = 5 gives x = 1, y = 2, z = 2, and f = 1·4·4 = 16.

Answer: Maximum 16 at (1, 2, 2)

Ex. 13.8: 40

Find the point(s) on the surface x2 − yz = 5 that are closest to the origin.

Minimise the squared distance D = x2 + y2 + z2 subject to x2 − yz = 5. Lagrange multipliers give 2x = 2λx, 2y = −λz, 2z = −λy.

If x ≠ 0 then λ = 1, so y = −z/2 and z = −y/2, forcing y = z = 0; then x2 = 5, giving (±√5, 0, 0) with D = 5. If x = 0 then yz = −5 and λ = ±2; λ = 2 gives y = −z, z2 = 5, points (0, ±√5, ∓√5) with D = 10.

The smallest distance is √5, attained at (±√5, 0, 0).

Answer: Closest points (±√5, 0, 0), distance √5

Ex. 13.8: 41

Find the volume of the largest rectangular box (with sides parallel to the coordinate planes) that can be inscribed in the ellipsoid (x/a)2 + (y/b)2 + (z/c)2 = 1, and show it is 8abc/(3√3). (In particular, for a sphere of radius a the volume is 8a3/(3√3).)

Let the box have half-sides x, y, z with x2/a2 + y2/b2 + z2/c2 = 1; its volume is V = 8xyz. Maximise ln V = ln x + ln y + ln z by Lagrange multipliers: 1/x = 2λx/a2, 1/y = 2λy/b2, 1/z = 2λz/c2, so x2/a2 = y2/b2 = z2/c2 = 1/(2λ). With the constraint, each equals 1/3.

Hence x = a/√3, y = b/√3, z = c/√3, and V = 8abc/(3√3). For a sphere a = b = c, V = 8a3/(3√3).

Answer: Maximum volume 8abc/(3√3) (box sides 2a/√3, 2b/√3, 2c/√3); for a sphere, 8a3/(3√3)

Ex. 13.8: 42

A suitcase must satisfy width + length + height ≤ 129 cm. Find the dimensions of the suitcase of maximum volume, and its volume.

Maximise V = xyz subject to x + y + z = 129, x, y, z > 0. By Lagrange multipliers (or AM–GM), x = y = z = 43 at the maximum.

By AM–GM, xyz ≤ (129/3)3 = 433 = 79,507, with equality when x = y = z = 43.

Answer: 43 cm × 43 cm × 43 cm; volume 79,507 cm3

Ex. 13.8: 43

An open box with a rectangular base is to have volume 16 ft3. The top and bottom cost 10 cents per square foot and the sides cost 5 cents per square foot. Find the dimensions that minimise the cost.

Let the base be x by y and the height z, so xyz = 16. Cost (cents) C = 20xy + 10xz + 10yz (top and bottom at 10 cents each: 2·10xy; sides at 5 cents: 2·5(xz + yz)).

By symmetry the minimum has x = y. With z = 16/x2, C = 20x2 + 320/x. Then dC/dx = 40x − 320/x2 = 0 gives x3 = 8, x = 2, so y = 2 and z = 4. The second derivative is positive, confirming a minimum; C = 240 cents.

Answer: 2 ft × 2 ft × 4 ft; minimum cost $2.40

Ex. 13.8: 44

A company sells two models of a product. The standard model sells for x dollars and the deluxe model for y dollars; the numbers sold are 500(y − x) standard and 45,000 + 500(x − 2y) deluxe. The standard model costs $40 to make and the deluxe $60. Find the prices that maximise profit.

Profit P = (x − 40)·500(y − x) + (y − 60)[45,000 + 500(x − 2y)].

∂P/∂x = 500(y − x) − 500(x − 40) + 500(y − 60) = 500(2y − 2x + 10) = 0 gives y − x = −5. ∂P/∂y = 500(x − 40) + 45,000 + 500(x − 2y) − 1000(y − 60) = 0 simplifies to 2x − 3y = −95.

Solving: x = 65, y = 75. The Hessian is negative definite (P is a concave quadratic), so this is the maximum. Profit = 25·5000 + 15·2500 = $162,500.

Answer: Standard $65, deluxe $75; maximum profit $162,500

Ex. 13.8: 45

Find the absolute maximum and absolute minimum of f(x, y) = 4x2 − 3y2 + 2xy on (a) the four sides of the unit square [0, 1] × [0, 1], (b) the two diagonals of the square, and (c) the whole square.

Interior critical point: fx = 8x + 2y, fy = −6y + 2x, both zero only at (0, 0), a saddle (D = −52); f(0, 0) = 0.

(a) Bottom y = 0: f = 4x2, 0 to 4. Top y = 1: f = 4x2 + 2x − 3, −3 to 3. Left x = 0: f = −3y2, −3 to 0. Right x = 1: f = −3y2 + 2y + 4, max 13/3 at y = 1/3, endpoints 4 and 3.

(b) Diagonal y = x: f = 3x2, 0 to 3. Diagonal y = 1 − x: f = −x2 + 8x − 3, −3 to 4 (increasing on [0, 1]).

(c) Comparing everything: the largest value is 13/3 at (1, 1/3) and the smallest is −3 at (0, 1).

Answer: (a) Sides: max 13/3 at (1, 1/3), min −3 at (0, 1); (b) diagonals: max 4 at (1, 0), min −3 at (0, 1); (c) whole square: absolute maximum 13/3 at (1, 1/3), absolute minimum −3 at (0, 1)

Ex. 13.8: 46

Show that among all parallelograms of perimeter l, the one of maximum area is a square of side l/4.

Let the sides be a and b with 2(a + b) = l, and the included angle be α. The area is A = ab sin α ≤ ab, with equality when α = π/2.

With b = l/2 − a, ab = a(l/2 − a) = (l/4)2 − (a − l/4)2 ≤ (l/4)2, with equality when a = l/4 (hence b = l/4). So A ≤ l2/16, attained by the square of side l/4.

Answer: Maximum area l2/16, attained by the square of side l/4

Ex. 13.8: 47

Find the dimensions of the open rectangular box of given volume V that has the least surface area.

Let the base be x by y and the height z, with xyz = V. The surface area (no top) is S = xy + 2xz + 2yz.

By symmetry the minimum has x = y. With z = V/x2, S = x2 + 4V/x. Then dS/dx = 2x − 4V/x2 = 0 gives x3 = 2V, so x = y = (2V)1/3 and z = V/x2 = (V/4)1/3. The second derivative is positive, confirming a minimum.

Answer: Base (2V)1/3 × (2V)1/3, height (V/4)1/3 (so the height is half the base side)

Ex. 13.8: 48

A trough is made from a 27-inch-wide sheet by bending up x inches on each side at an angle φ to the horizontal (see the figure in the book). Find x and φ that maximise the cross-sectional area, and find the maximum area.

The cross-section is a trapezoid with lower base 27 − 2x and upper base 27 − 2x + 2x cos φ, height x sin φ. Its area is A = x sin φ (27 − 2x + x cos φ).

∂A/∂x = sin φ (27 − 4x + 2x cos φ) = 0 gives 27 − 4x + 2x cos φ = 0. ∂A/∂φ = x[(27 − 2x) cos φ + x(2 cos2φ − 1)] = 0. Solving: try x = 9, cos φ = 1/2 (φ = 60°): the first equation gives 27 − 36 + 9 = 0 ✓, and the second gives 9(1/2) + 9(−1/2) = 0 ✓.

The maximum area is A = 9·(√3/2)·(27 − 18 + 9/2) = 243√3/4 ≈ 105.2 in2.

Answer: x = 9 in, φ = 60°; maximum area 243√3/4 ≈ 105 in2

These two lectures add no new mathematics — they are your chance to practise everything from Lectures 1–10 and 13–18 under exam-like conditions.

Lecture 11 (Sun 13 Sep 2026) is a problem-solving session on the first incourse syllabus, and Lecture 12 (Mon 14 Sep 2026) is the same for the second incourse syllabus. Treat them as rehearsals, not lessons: the value is in doing problems yourself, getting stuck, and finding out exactly where you get stuck.

  • Redo the assigned problems from Lectures 1–10 (first incourse) and 13–18 (second incourse) under timed conditions, without looking at the answers first.
  • For every problem you get wrong, write down which step failed — a forgotten branch of the tree, an unnormalised direction, a missed boundary — and re-read the "Watch out" note for that lecture.
  • Revisit the old recordings: Lecture 11 — https://youtu.be/0nNebT1-me8 ; Lecture 12 — https://youtu.be/7VeKoAI6rQ0

Lecture 13 — Lagrange Multipliers (Anton §13.8–13.9)

When you must maximise something but are only allowed to walk along a fixed path, the best point is where your contour map just touches that path — and at that touching point, the two gradients line up.

So far you have maximised functions freely: wander anywhere on the hill and find the top. But real problems come with rules. You want the largest product of two numbers whose sum is fixed; the closest point to the origin that lies on a given line; the biggest box that fits inside a sphere. In each case you are asked to maximise or minimise a function f(x, y) — but only at points that also satisfy a constraint, g(x, y) = c. You are no longer free to wander the whole hillside; you must stay on a path, the constraint curve. This lecture is about finding the best point on that path.

Here is the picture that makes it click. Draw two maps on the same sheet of paper. One map is the contour map of f — the level curves f = k, each labelled with its height. The other map is the constraint curve g = c, a single path winding across the paper. Now walk along the constraint path and watch the height of f as you go: it rises and falls. The highest point on your walk is the place where the path just touches one level curve and turns back — where the path and the level curve are tangent, kissing each other instead of crossing. And here is the key: at a touching point, both curves have the same tangent line, which means their perpendicular directions — their gradients — point along the same line. So ∇f and ∇g are parallel at the optimum. Parallel vectors are multiples of each other, so there is some number λ (the Greek letter lambda, called the Lagrange multiplier) with ∇f = λ∇g. That one equation, together with the constraint g(x, y) = c itself, is the whole method.

Why does it work? Think of walking along the path. As long as ∇f has any component along the path, you can walk a little further in that direction and f will keep increasing or decreasing — so you are not at the best point yet. You only stop improving when ∇f has no component along the path at all, which means ∇f is perpendicular to the path. But ∇g is also perpendicular to the constraint curve (a gradient is always perpendicular to its own level curves), so the two gradients must be parallel. The multiplier λ is just the number that stretches one gradient onto the other — you do not need to care about its value or its sign; it is a tool for finding the points, not the answer itself. Though if you are curious, λ does have a meaning: it measures how fast the optimum value changes if you loosen the constraint a little, which economists call a "shadow price".

The method, step by step: first write ∇f = λ∇g and g = c. That gives you as many equations as unknowns. Second, solve the system — and here is the exam trap: keep every algebraic case. If you factorise and get something like 2y(1 − λ) = 0, that means y = 0 or λ = 1, and both cases must be followed through; dropping one case loses candidates and loses marks. Third, evaluate f at every candidate point you found and compare — the method only finds candidates, it never tells you by itself which one is the maximum and which the minimum. Fourth, if the constraint set is closed and bounded, the Extreme-Value Theorem guarantees the maximum and minimum are among your candidates, so comparing values is enough. The method also needs ∇g ≠ 0 at the candidate — at a sharp corner of the constraint where the gradient vanishes, it can fail.

A good way to check your understanding: Exercises 25–29 redo problems from Lecture 10 — the three numbers with a fixed sum, the closest point to the origin, the biggest box in a sphere — but now with Lagrange multipliers instead of the methods of §13.8. The answers must come out the same both ways. If they do not, you have made an algebra slip somewhere, and the disagreement tells you exactly where to look.

Here is the everyday version of the problem, because the abstract statement hides how ordinary it is. A farmer has a fixed length of fence and wants the biggest field she can enclose: the area is f, the fence length is the constraint g = c. Or a hiker is walking a marked trail up a mountain — the trail is the constraint curve, the height is f — and she wants the highest point on the trail, not the summit of the mountain, which may be nowhere near the trail. In both cases the constraint is not a nuisance added to spoil the problem; it is the whole problem. Without it the answer would be trivial (an infinitely large field, the mountain summit). The constraint is what makes the question worth asking.

Now let us walk through the "why" once more, very slowly, because this is the step students recite without believing. Stand on the constraint curve at some point that is not the optimum. The gradient ∇f points uphill — and crucially, it has some component along the path you are standing on, because the path is not perpendicular to ∇f. So take one small step along the path in the direction of that component, and f increases. You have just improved your position, so you were not at the optimum. The only way this argument fails is if ∇f has no component along the path at all — if ∇f is perpendicular to the path. And ∇g is also perpendicular to the constraint curve, because a gradient is always perpendicular to its own level curves, and the constraint curve g = c is a level curve of g. Two arrows that are both perpendicular to the same line must lie along the same line — they are parallel. That is the whole proof, in words: at the optimum you cannot improve by walking, so ∇f must be perpendicular to the path, so it must be parallel to ∇g.

A second mini-example, using the worked example above, to show what λ actually does. At the candidate (√2, 1) we have ∇f = (y, x) = (1, √2) and ∇g = (8x, 16y) = (8√2, 16). The equation ∇f = λ∇g gives, from the first component, 1 = 8√2·λ, so λ = 1/(8√2) = √2/16; from the second component, √2 = 16λ, so λ = √2/16 again — the same number from both equations, which is how you know the point is genuine. Now look at the candidate (√2, −1), one of the minima: ∇f = (−1, √2) and ∇g = (8√2, −16), and the same calculation gives λ = −√2/16 from both components. The multiplier changed sign — and that is perfectly fine. λ is not the answer, it is the stretching factor that lines the two arrows up, and it is allowed to be negative, zero, or anything else. Students who try to "solve for λ" as if it were the goal of the problem have missed the point: λ is a tool for finding the points, and once you have the points you throw it away and compare f-values.

Finally, notice how this lecture connects to the one before it, because the exam loves to ask the same problem two ways. In Lecture 10 you solved the three-numbers problem by substitution: with x + y + z = 48 you wrote z = 48 − x − y and maximised a function of two variables. Here you would write the same constraint as g = x + y + z = 48 and solve ∇f = λ∇g. The answers must agree — 16, 16, 16, product 4096 — because it is the same mountain, only climbed by a different path. Substitution works when the constraint is easy to solve for one variable; Lagrange multipliers work when it is not, which is most of the time. And one practical warning for the algebra: the system is usually solved by dividing one equation by another, and dividing by something that could be zero silently throws away candidates. Factorise instead of dividing — when you see 2y(1 − λ) = 0, that is two cases, y = 0 or λ = 1, and both must be followed through to the end.

Constrained-extremum principle: at an optimum of f subject to g(x, y) = c, ∇f = λ∇g for some scalar λ, together with g(x, y) = c

Lagrangian: L = f − λ(g − c); solving ∇L = 0 gives the same system

Three variables: ∇f = λ∇g with g(x, y, z) = c

Worked example — Ex. 13.9-5 (from the guide). Find the maximum and minimum of f(x, y) = xy subject to 4x² + 8y² = 16.

Step 1 — Write ∇f = λ∇g and the constraint. ∇f = (y, x) and ∇g = (8x, 16y), so y = 8λx and x = 16λy, with 4x² + 8y² = 16, i.e. x² + 2y² = 4.

Step 2 — Solve, keeping every case. From the two equations, eliminating λ gives y = x/√2 (with the sign cases kept: x and y can be positive or negative together, or opposite in sign). Putting y = x/√2 into x² + 2y² = 4 gives x² + x² = 4, so x = ±√2 and y = ±1.

Step 3 — Evaluate f at every candidate. The four candidates are (√2, 1), (−√2, −1), (√2, −1), (−√2, 1). f = xy gives √2, √2, −√2, −√2 respectively.

Answer: maximum √2 at (√2, 1) and (−√2, −1); minimum −√2 at (√2, −1) and (−√2, 1). Notice how the method found all four points — two maxima and two minima — and only comparing values sorted them out.

Watch out: it is ∇f = λ∇g, not ∇f = ∇g — forgetting λ is the classic error. And when you solve the system, keep every algebraic case (for example, 2y(1 − λ) = 0 means y = 0 or λ = 1); dropping a case loses candidates.

  • In plain words, why must ∇f and ∇g be parallel at the best point on a constraint curve?
  • What is λ, and why do you not need to care about its value or sign to find the optimum?
  • What are the steps of the Lagrange multiplier method, and what does the method not tell you by itself?
  • When can the method fail, and why is comparing f-values at all the candidates the final step?

Ex. 13.9: 5–12 — max/min of f subject to the constraint (also find the points). Ex. 13.9: 17–29 — solve using Lagrange multipliers: closest and farthest points; points on a plane or circle closest to the origin; vector of length 5 with the largest possible sum of components; highest and lowest temperatures on a circle; and Ex. 25–29 redo §13.8 problems (three positive numbers, sum 27; points on a plane maximising xy²z²; points on x² − yz = 5 closest to the origin; max-volume box in a sphere; min-cost closed box) with Lagrange multipliers — the same answers must come out both ways.

Lecture 13 — Solutions: Lagrange Multipliers (Anton §13.9)

Ex. 13.9: 5

Find the maximum and minimum values of f(x, y) = xy subject to the constraint 4x2 + 8y2 = 16.

∇f = (y, x), ∇g = (8x, 16y) for g = 4x2 + 8y2 − 16. Lagrange: y = 8λx and x = 16λy, so y = 128λ2y, giving λ = ±1/(8√2) (y ≠ 0; if y = 0 then x = 0, contradicting the constraint).

λ = 1/(8√2): y = x/√2; the constraint gives 4x2 + 4x2 = 16, x = ±√2, points (√2, 1) and (−√2, −1), f = √2. λ = −1/(8√2): y = −x/√2, points (√2, −1) and (−√2, 1), f = −√2. The constraint curve is a compact ellipse, so these are the absolute extrema.

Answer: Maximum √2 at (√2, 1) and (−√2, −1); minimum −√2 at (√2, −1) and (−√2, 1)

Ex. 13.9: 6

Find the maximum and minimum values of f(x, y) = x2 − y2 subject to the constraint x2 + y2 = 25.

∇f = (2x, −2y), ∇g = (2x, 2y). Lagrange: 2x = 2λx and −2y = 2λy. If x ≠ 0 then λ = 1, and −2y = 2y gives y = 0, so x = ±5. If y ≠ 0 then λ = −1, and 2x = −2x gives x = 0, so y = ±5.

Candidates: (±5, 0) with f = 25, and (0, ±5) with f = −25. The constraint is a compact circle, so these are the absolute extrema.

Answer: Maximum 25 at (±5, 0); minimum −25 at (0, ±5)

Ex. 13.9: 7

Find the maximum and minimum values of f(x, y) = 4x3 + y2 subject to the constraint 2x2 + y2 = 1.

∇f = (12x2, 2y), ∇g = (4x, 2y). Lagrange: 12x2 = 4λx and 2y = 2λy. From the second equation, y = 0 or λ = 1.

If y = 0, the constraint gives x = ±1/√2 = ±√2/2, with f = ±√2. If λ = 1, then 12x2 = 4x gives x = 0 or x = 1/3: x = 0 gives y = ±1, f = 1; x = 1/3 gives y = ±√7/3, f = 4/27 + 7/9 = 25/27.

Comparing values √2, −√2, 1, 25/27: the largest is √2 and the smallest is −√2.

Answer: Maximum √2 at (√2/2, 0); minimum −√2 at (−√2/2, 0)

Ex. 13.9: 8

Find the maximum and minimum values of f(x, y) = x − 3y − 1 subject to the constraint x2 + 3y2 = 16.

∇f = (1, −3), ∇g = (2x, 6y). Lagrange: 1 = 2λx and −3 = 6λy, so x = 1/(2λ), y = −1/(2λ). The constraint gives 1/(4λ2) + 3/(4λ2) = 1/λ2 = 16, so λ = ±1/4.

λ = 1/4 gives (2, −2), f = 2 + 6 − 1 = 7. λ = −1/4 gives (−2, 2), f = −2 − 6 − 1 = −9. The constraint is a compact ellipse, so these are the absolute extrema.

Answer: Maximum 7 at (2, −2); minimum −9 at (−2, 2)

Ex. 13.9: 9

Find the maximum and minimum values of f(x, y, z) = 2x + y − 2z subject to the constraint x2 + y2 + z2 = 4.

∇f = (2, 1, −2), ∇g = (2x, 2y, 2z). Lagrange: (2, 1, −2) = λ(2x, 2y, 2z), so (x, y, z) = (1/λ, 1/(2λ), −1/λ).

The constraint gives 1/λ2 + 1/(4λ2) + 1/λ2 = 9/(4λ2) = 4, so λ = ±3/4. λ = 3/4 gives (4/3, 2/3, −4/3), f = 6; λ = −3/4 gives (−4/3, −2/3, 4/3), f = −6. (Equivalently, the extrema of a linear function on a sphere of radius 2 are ±2|∇f| = ±6, at ±2∇f/|∇f|.)

Answer: Maximum 6 at (4/3, 2/3, −4/3); minimum −6 at (−4/3, −2/3, 4/3)

Ex. 13.9: 10

Find the maximum and minimum values of f(x, y, z) = 3x + 6y + 2z subject to the constraint 2x2 + 4y2 + z2 = 70.

∇f = (3, 6, 2), ∇g = (4x, 8y, 2z). Lagrange: 3 = 4λx, 6 = 8λy, 2 = 2λz, so x = 3/(4λ), y = 3/(4λ), z = 1/λ.

The constraint gives 2·9/(16λ2) + 4·9/(16λ2) + 1/λ2 = 35/(8λ2) = 70, so λ2 = 1/16, λ = ±1/4. λ = 1/4 gives (3, 3, 4), f = 9 + 18 + 8 = 35; λ = −1/4 gives (−3, −3, −4), f = −35.

Answer: Maximum 35 at (3, 3, 4); minimum −35 at (−3, −3, −4)

Ex. 13.9: 11

Find the maximum and minimum values of f(x, y, z) = xyz subject to the constraint x2 + y2 + z2 = 1.

∇f = (yz, xz, xy), ∇g = (2x, 2y, 2z). Lagrange: yz = 2λx, xz = 2λy, xy = 2λz. If any coordinate is 0, then f = 0 (and the other two equations force two of x, y, z to be 0, e.g. (±1, 0, 0)).

Otherwise, multiplying the three equations by x, y, z respectively gives xyz = 2λx2 = 2λy2 = 2λz2, so x2 = y2 = z2 = 1/3, i.e. each coordinate is ±1/√3, with f = ±1/(3√3).

The maximum 1/(3√3) occurs where xyz > 0: (1/√3, 1/√3, 1/√3) and the three points with exactly two negative coordinates. The minimum −1/(3√3) occurs at the other four diagonal points.

Answer: Maximum 1/(3√3) at (1/√3, 1/√3, 1/√3), (1/√3, −1/√3, −1/√3), (−1/√3, 1/√3, −1/√3), (−1/√3, −1/√3, 1/√3); minimum −1/(3√3) at the other four points (±1/√3, ±1/√3, ±1/√3)

Ex. 13.9: 12

Find the maximum and minimum values of f(x, y, z) = x4 + y4 + z4 subject to the constraint x2 + y2 + z2 = 1.

∇f = (4x3, 4y3, 4z3), ∇g = (2x, 2y, 2z). Lagrange: 4x3 = 2λx, i.e. x(2x2 − λ) = 0, and similarly for y and z. So each coordinate is either 0 or has square λ/2.

Case one coordinate ±1, the others 0: f = 1 (six points). Case two coordinates ±1/√2, one 0: f = 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2 (twelve points). Case three coordinates ±1/√3: f = 3·(1/9) = 1/3 (eight points).

Comparing: the largest value is 1 and the smallest is 1/3.

Answer: Maximum 1 at (±1, 0, 0), (0, ±1, 0), (0, 0, ±1); minimum 1/3 at (±1/√3, ±1/√3, ±1/√3)

Ex. 13.9: 17

Find the point on the line 2x − 4y = 3 that is closest to the origin.

Minimise the squared distance D = x2 + y2 subject to 2x − 4y = 3. Lagrange: 2x = 2λ and 2y = −4λ, so x = λ, y = −2λ.

The constraint gives 2λ + 8λ = 10λ = 3, so λ = 3/10, x = 3/10, y = −3/5. The distance is √(9/100 + 36/100) = √0.45 = 3/√20 ≈ 0.67.

Answer: Closest point (3/10, −3/5), distance √0.45 ≈ 0.67

Ex. 13.9: 18

Find the point on the line y = 2x + 3 that is closest to the point (4, 2).

Minimise the squared distance D = (x − 4)2 + (y − 2)2 with y = 2x + 3, i.e. D = (x − 4)2 + (2x + 1)2. Then dD/dx = 2(x − 4) + 4(2x + 1) = 10x − 4 = 0 gives x = 2/5, y = 19/5.

The distance is √[(−18/5)2 + (9/5)2] = √(405/25) = 9/√5 ≈ 4.02. (Geometrically, this is the foot of the perpendicular from (4, 2) to the line, since the line has slope 2 and the perpendicular has slope −1/2.)

Answer: Closest point (2/5, 19/5), distance 9/√5 ≈ 4.02

Ex. 13.9: 19

Find the point on the plane x + 2y + z = 1 that is closest to the origin.

Minimise D = x2 + y2 + z2 subject to x + 2y + z = 1. Lagrange: 2x = λ, 2y = 2λ, 2z = λ, so (x, y, z) = (λ/2, λ, λ/2).

The constraint gives λ/2 + 2λ + λ/2 = 3λ = 1, so λ = 1/3 and the point is (1/6, 1/3, 1/6). The distance is 1/√6 ≈ 0.41. (This is the foot of the perpendicular from the origin along the normal (1, 2, 1).)

Answer: Closest point (1/6, 1/3, 1/6), distance 1/√6 ≈ 0.41

Ex. 13.9: 20

Find the point on the plane 4x + 3y + z = 2 that is closest to the point (1, −1, 1).

Check first whether the point lies on the plane: 4(1) + 3(−1) + 1 = 4 − 3 + 1 = 2. It does.

Since the point is already on the plane, it is itself the closest point on the plane, at distance 0. (Formally, Lagrange multipliers give the foot of the perpendicular along the normal (4, 3, 1), and here the perpendicular foot is the point itself.)

Answer: The point (1, −1, 1) itself — it already lies on the plane, so the distance is 0

Ex. 13.9: 21

Find the points on the circle x2 + y2 = 45 that are closest to and farthest from the point (1, 2).

Minimise/maximise the squared distance D = (x − 1)2 + (y − 2)2 subject to x2 + y2 = 45. Lagrange: 2(x − 1) = 2λx and 2(y − 2) = 2λy, so (x, y) is a scalar multiple of (1, 2): the extrema lie on the line through the origin and (1, 2).

Writing (x, y) = k(1, 2), the constraint gives 5k2 = 45, k = ±3. The point (3, 6) is closest, at distance √(4 + 16) = 2√5; the point (−3, −6) is farthest, at distance √(16 + 64) = 4√5.

Answer: Closest (3, 6), distance 2√5 ≈ 4.47; farthest (−3, −6), distance 4√5 ≈ 8.94

Ex. 13.9: 22

Find the point(s) on the surface xy − z2 = 1 that are closest to the origin.

Minimise D = x2 + y2 + z2 subject to xy − z2 = 1. Lagrange: 2x = λy, 2y = λx, 2z = −2λz.

From 2z = −2λz, either z = 0 or λ = −1. If λ = −1, then 2x = −y and 2y = −x, forcing x = y = 0, which cannot satisfy xy − z2 = 1. So z = 0, xy = 1, and 2x = λy, 2y = λx give x2 = y2; with xy = 1, x = y = 1 or x = y = −1.

The closest points are (1, 1, 0) and (−1, −1, 0), each at distance √2.

Answer: Closest points (1, 1, 0) and (−1, −1, 0), distance √2

Ex. 13.9: 23

A vector of length 5 is given. Find the vector whose sum of components is as large as possible.

Maximise f = x + y + z subject to x2 + y2 + z2 = 25. Lagrange: (1, 1, 1) = 2λ(x, y, z), so x = y = z.

The constraint gives 3x2 = 25, x = 5/√3 (positive for the maximum). The vector is (5/√3, 5/√3, 5/√3) and the maximum sum is 5√3.

Answer: Vector (5/√3, 5/√3, 5/√3); maximum sum 5√3 ≈ 8.66

Ex. 13.9: 24

Find the maximum and minimum values of the temperature T(x, y) = 4x2 − 4xy + y2 on the circle x2 + y2 = 25.

Note T = (2x − y)2 ≥ 0. On the circle, the maximum of |2x − y| is achieved in the direction of (2, −1): by Cauchy–Schwarz, |2x − y| ≤ √(4 + 1)·√(x2 + y2) = 5√5, so T ≤ 125.

The maximum 125 occurs at (2√5, −√5) and (−2√5, √5). The minimum 0 occurs where 2x − y = 0, i.e. y = 2x on the circle: (√5, 2√5) and (−√5, −2√5).

Answer: Maximum 125 at (2√5, −√5) and (−2√5, √5); minimum 0 at (√5, 2√5) and (−√5, −2√5)

Ex. 13.9: 25

Find three positive numbers whose sum is 27 and whose sum of squares is as small as possible. (Same problem as Exercise 13.8: 38, solved here with Lagrange multipliers.)

Minimise S = x2 + y2 + z2 subject to x + y + z = 27. Lagrange: 2x = 2y = 2z = λ, so x = y = z = 9.

The minimum sum of squares is 3·81 = 243. (Compare Exercise 13.8: 38.)

Answer: 9, 9, 9; minimum sum of squares 243

Ex. 13.9: 26

Find the maximum value of xy2z2 subject to x + y + z = 5, where x, y, z ≥ 0. (Same problem as Exercise 13.8: 39, solved here with Lagrange multipliers.)

Maximise f = xy2z2 on the compact triangle x + y + z = 5, x, y, z ≥ 0. Where f > 0, maximise ln f = ln x + 2 ln y + 2 ln z: Lagrange gives 1/x = 2/y = 2/z = λ, so y = 2x, z = 2x.

With x + y + z = 5, x = 1, y = 2, z = 2, and f = 1·4·4 = 16. On the boundary where any variable is 0, f = 0, so 16 is the maximum. (Compare Exercise 13.8: 39.)

Answer: Maximum 16 at (1, 2, 2)

Ex. 13.9: 27

Find the point(s) on the surface x2 − yz = 5 that are closest to the origin. (Same problem as Exercise 13.8: 40, solved here with Lagrange multipliers.)

Minimise D = x2 + y2 + z2 subject to x2 − yz = 5. Lagrange: 2x = 2λx, 2y = −λz, 2z = −λy.

If x ≠ 0 then λ = 1, so y = −z/2 and z = −y/2, forcing y = z = 0; then x2 = 5, giving (±√5, 0, 0) with D = 5. If x = 0 then yz = −5 and λ = ±2; λ = 2 gives the points (0, ±√5, ∓√5) with D = 10, and λ = −2 gives nothing.

The closest points are (±√5, 0, 0), at distance √5. (Compare Exercise 13.8: 40.)

Answer: Closest points (±√5, 0, 0), distance √5

Ex. 13.9: 28

Find the volume of the largest rectangular box (with sides parallel to the coordinate planes) that can be inscribed in the ellipsoid (x/a)2 + (y/b)2 + (z/c)2 = 1. (Same problem as Exercise 13.8: 41, solved here with Lagrange multipliers.)

Let the box have half-sides x, y, z with x2/a2 + y2/b2 + z2/c2 = 1; its volume is V = 8xyz. Maximise ln V = ln x + ln y + ln z: Lagrange gives 1/x = 2λx/a2, 1/y = 2λy/b2, 1/z = 2λz/c2, so x2/a2 = y2/b2 = z2/c2 = 1/(2λ).

With the constraint, each term equals 1/3, so x = a/√3, y = b/√3, z = c/√3, and V = 8abc/(3√3). For a sphere of radius a, V = 8a3/(3√3). (Compare Exercise 13.8: 41.)

Answer: Maximum volume 8abc/(3√3); for a sphere, 8a3/(3√3)

Ex. 13.9: 29

An open box with a rectangular base is to have volume 16 ft3. The top and bottom cost 10 cents per square foot and the sides cost 5 cents per square foot. Find the dimensions that minimise the cost. (Same problem as Exercise 13.8: 43, solved here with Lagrange multipliers.)

Let the base be x by y and the height z, so xyz = 16. Cost (cents) C = 20xy + 10xz + 10yz.

Lagrange: 20y + 10z = λyz, 20x + 10z = λxz, 10x + 10y = λxy. Dividing the first two equations by yz and xz respectively and subtracting gives 20/x = 20/y, so x = y. Then by symmetry the third equation is consistent, and z = 16/x2; minimising C = 20x2 + 320/x gives dC/dx = 40x − 320/x2 = 0, x = 2, so y = 2 and z = 4.

The minimum cost is 240 cents = $2.40. (Compare Exercise 13.8: 43.)

Answer: 2 ft × 2 ft × 4 ft; minimum cost $2.40

Lecture 14 — Double Integrals in Cartesian Coordinates (Anton §14.1–14.2)

A double integral adds up the volume under a surface over a flat region, one thin column at a time.

Imagine you have a flat piece of land — call it the region R — and above it sits a bumpy surface, like a hill, whose height at each point is f(x, y). The double integral ∬R f(x, y) dA is simply the volume of the solid trapped between the land and the hill. That is the whole idea; everything else in this lecture is just a clever way of computing that volume.

How do we compute it? We chop the region into tiny rectangles, and over each tiny rectangle we stand a thin column whose height is the value of f there. The volume of one column is (height) × (base area), and we add up all the columns. When the rectangles get smaller and smaller, the sum settles down to the exact volume. That limit of sums is the double integral. The little symbol dA just means "a tiny piece of area".

Now, adding up columns one by one would take forever, so we do it in two sweeps instead — this is an iterated integral. First we add up a whole row of columns in one direction (say, in the y-direction), which gives us the volume of a thin slice; then we add up all the slices in the other direction. Fubini's theorem is the reassuring promise that, when f is continuous (no jumps or tears), the order does not matter: sweeping y first and then x gives the same answer as sweeping x first and then y, at least over a rectangle.

Over a rectangle, life is easy: the limits are plain numbers, like x from 0 to 3 and y from 0 to 2. But most regions are not rectangles. A Type I region is one you can describe by saying "x runs from a to b, and for each x, y runs from a bottom curve g1(x) up to a top curve g2(x)". A Type II region is the mirror image: "y runs from c to d, and for each y, x runs from a left curve h1(y) to a right curve h2(y)". Many regions are both types — you get to choose whichever description is simpler. The golden rule: the outer limits must always be plain numbers, never functions.

Two special uses you must know. First, if you set f = 1, every column has height 1, so the "volume" is just the area of the region. Second, sometimes the integral as written is impossible — you cannot integrate sin(y³) with respect to y, or ex³ with respect to x, because those have no elementary antiderivative. The trick is to reverse the order of integration: sketch the region from the given limits, describe it the other way round (Type I becomes Type II), and suddenly the impossible integral becomes easy. In an exam, when you see sin(y³), e−y², ex³ or cos(x²) as the integrand, reversing the order is almost certainly the intended move.

Finally, the average value of f over R is just the total volume divided by the area of the base: fave = (1 / A(R)) ∬R f dA. Think of it as flattening the hill into a flat roof of the same volume — the height of that flat roof is the average value.

Why do we need this at all? A single integral ∫ f(x) dx adds up height × tiny width along a line, and gives an area. But a hill is not a line — it has a height at every point of a whole patch of ground. One variable is not enough to walk over a patch; you need two sweeps, one across and one along. The double integral is simply the single integral done twice: first you add up a strip, then you add up the strips. If you can picture a single integral as "area under a curve", picture a double integral as "volume under a surface" — same idea, one more direction.

An everyday picture: imagine a field of wheat. At each spot (x, y) the wheat stands f(x, y) tall, and you want the total harvest. You cannot measure every stalk; instead you chop the field into tiny squares, and for each square you take (height of the wheat there) × (area of the square) — that is one little bundle of wheat. Add up all the bundles and you have the harvest. The double integral is that sum, with the squares made smaller and smaller until the answer stops changing. The "tiny square" is dA, and the whole point of the symbol dA is that it is a piece of area, not a length. When you see ∬ f dA, read it as "add up f × (tiny area) over the whole region".

Where students get stuck: reading the limits. An iterated integral is read from the outside in, and the rule that saves you is this: the outer limits are always plain numbers, because the outer variable runs over the whole extent of the region; the inner limits may be functions, because the inner variable runs only as far as the region goes at that particular outer value. So when you look at ∫04 ∫√x2 ... dy dx, read it as a sentence: "x runs from 0 to 4; and for each x, y runs from the curve y = √x up to the line y = 2." If you ever write an outer integral whose limits still contain x or y, stop — you have the region backwards. And if the top curve of your region changes halfway across — say the top is y = x for a while and then y = 2 — then no single pair of limits can describe it, and you must split the region into two integrals (that is the trap in Ex. 14.1-34). Sketching the region first is not a luxury; it is the step that makes the limits obvious.

How to choose the order. Look at the integrand first, then at the region. If the integrand is something like sin(y³) or ex³ that you cannot integrate in one direction, that direction must go second — reverse the order, as in the worked example below. If the integrand is friendly either way, look at the region: choose the description (Type I or Type II) whose boundary curves are simpler. Many regions are both types, and the two setups are both correct; one is just less painful.

Mini-example — read a region back out of its limits. Look at the reversed integral in the worked example below: ∫02 ∫0y² sin(y³) dx dy. Read it as a sentence. The outer limits are the plain numbers 0 and 2, so y runs from 0 to 2. The inner limits are 0 and y², so for each y, x runs from 0 to y² — that is, from the y-axis to the curve x = y². So the region is bounded by x = 0, y = 2 and x = y², exactly the region in the problem. Every iterated integral can be read this way, and reading it is the skill that lets you reverse the order: once you can say the region in words, you can say it the other way round.

One more idea that the exercises use: the volume between two surfaces. If a solid is trapped between a lower surface z = g(x, y) and an upper surface z = f(x, y) over the same region R, its volume is ∬R [f(x, y) − g(x, y)] dA — at each point you take the height of the gap between the surfaces, and add up gap × tiny area. It is the same column picture, with the column starting at the lower surface instead of at the ground.

∬R f(x, y) dA = ∫ab ∫cd f(x, y) dy dx = ∫cd ∫ab f(x, y) dx dy  (Fubini, over a rectangle [a, b] × [c, d])

Type I: ∬R f dA = ∫ab ∫g1(x)g2(x) f(x, y) dy dx

Type II: ∬R f dA = ∫cd ∫h1(y)h2(y) f(x, y) dx dy

Area of R = ∬R 1 dA

Volume under z = f(x, y) over R = ∬R f(x, y) dA  (f ≥ 0)

Average value: fave = (1 / A(R)) ∬R f(x, y) dA

Worked example — Ex. 14.2-25 (verified answer: (1 − cos 8) / 3).

Problem: Evaluate ∬R sin(y³) dA, where R is bounded by y = √x, y = 2 and x = 0.

Step 1 — Try the given order and notice the trap. The region is naturally described as Type I: x from 0 to 4, and for each x, y from √x to 2. That would give ∫04 ∫√x2 sin(y³) dy dx — but sin(y³) has no elementary antiderivative with respect to y, so the inner integral cannot be done. This is the signal to reverse the order.

Step 2 — Sketch the region and re-describe it as Type II. The curves y = √x (that is, x = y²), y = 2 and x = 0 enclose a region with corners at (0, 0), (0, 2) and (4, 2). Reading it sideways: y runs from 0 to 2, and for each y, x runs from 0 to y².

Step 3 — Write the reversed integral. ∬R sin(y³) dA = ∫02 ∫0y² sin(y³) dx dy. Now the inner integral is easy, because sin(y³) does not depend on x at all: ∫0y² sin(y³) dx = y² sin(y³).

Step 4 — Finish with a substitution. We need ∫02 y² sin(y³) dy. Let u = y³, so du = 3y² dy, and the limits become u = 0 to u = 8. The integral is (1/3) ∫08 sin u du = (1/3)[−cos u]08 = (1/3)(1 − cos 8).

Answer: (1 − cos 8) / 3. The whole trick was one sentence: when the integrand cannot be integrated in the given order, reverse the order first.

Watch out: the outer limits of an iterated integral must be plain numbers — if your outer integral still has x or y in its limits, you have written the region the wrong way round.

  • What does a double integral measure when f ≥ 0, in one sentence?
  • What is the difference between a Type I region and a Type II region?
  • Why would you reverse the order of integration, and which integrands are the giveaway?
  • How do you find the average value of a function over a region?

Ex. 14.1 — Iterated integrals over rectangles / basic evaluation: 11, 12, 15, 16. Volume under a surface / volume of a solid: 30, 31, 32, 33, 34. Average value: 36, 37. (Note: Ex. 14.1-11 has no clean closed-form answer — work it numerically.)

Ex. 14.2 — Setting up limits, Type I vs Type II: 3, 4, 9–12, 15–18, 24, 26. Area between curves: 29–32. Volumes: 37–44. Reversing the order of integration: 25, 47–56. Average value: 61, 62.

MULTIPLE INTEGRALS

Fubini's Theorem, Multivariable Calculus Unit 4 Lecture 2

Reversing the Order of Integration | Double Integrals | Math with Professor V

Solutions — Exercise Sets 14.1 and 14.2 (Anton, 10th edition)

Double integrals over rectangles (14.1) and over general regions (14.2). All answers were checked with SymPy and against the book's answers appendix (odd-numbered exercises). Where the text extraction garbled a symbol, the reading adopted is noted in the solution.

Ex. 14.1: 11

Evaluate the iterated integral ∫0ln 2 ∫01 xy ey−x dy dx.

Integrate with respect to y first. For fixed x, ∫01 xy ey−x dy = x e−x ∫01 y ey dy. Since ∫ y ey dy = (y − 1)ey, the y-integral from 0 to 1 is [(y−1)ey]01 = 0 − (−1) = 1, so the inner integral is x e−x.

Now ∫0ln 2 x e−x dx = [−(x + 1)e−x]0ln 2 = 1 − (ln 2 + 1)·(1/2) = (1 − ln 2)/2.

Note on the statement: the text extraction renders the exponent as "yx"; the minus sign is confirmed by the book's answers appendix, which gives (1 − ln 2)/2. (Reading the exponent as yx instead gives ≈ 0.166, with no closed form.)

Answer: (1 − ln 2)/2 ≈ 0.153

Ex. 14.1: 12

Evaluate the iterated integral ∫34 ∫12 1/(x + y)2 dy dx.

Inner integral: ∫12 (x + y)−2 dy = [−1/(x + y)]12 = 1/(x + 1) − 1/(x + 2).

Outer integral: ∫34 [1/(x + 1) − 1/(x + 2)] dx = [ln(x + 1) − ln(x + 2)]34 = ln(5/6) − ln(4/5) = ln(25/24).

Answer: ln(25/24) ≈ 0.041

Ex. 14.1: 15

Evaluate ∬R x√(1 − x2) dA, where R = {(x, y) : 0 ≤ x ≤ 1, 2 ≤ y ≤ 3}.

The integrand is a product of a function of x alone and a function of y alone (namely 1), so the double integral factors: ∬R x√(1 − x2) dA = (∫01 x√(1 − x2) dx)(∫23 dy). The y-integral is 1. For the x-integral, put u = 1 − x2: ∫01 x√(1 − x2) dx = [−(1 − x2)3/2/3]01 = 1/3.

Answer: 1/3

Ex. 14.1: 16

Evaluate ∬R (x sin y − y sin x) dA, where R = {(x, y) : 0 ≤ x ≤ π/2, 0 ≤ y ≤ π/3}.

Split the integral and factor each term. ∬R x sin y dA = (∫0π/2 x dx)(∫0π/3 sin y dy) = (π2/8)(1 − cos(π/3)) = (π2/8)(1/2) = π2/16. And ∬R y sin x dA = (∫0π/2 sin x dx)(∫0π/3 y dy) = (1)(π2/18) = π2/18. Subtracting: π2/16 − π2/18 = π2(9 − 8)/144 = π2/144.

Answer: π2/144 ≈ 0.0685

Ex. 14.1: 30

Use a double integral to find the volume under the surface z = 3x3 + 3x2y and over the rectangle R = {(x, y) : 1 ≤ x ≤ 3, 0 ≤ y ≤ 2}.

Volume = ∫13 ∫02 (3x3 + 3x2y) dy dx. Inner: ∫02 (3x3 + 3x2y) dy = 6x3 + 6x2. Outer: ∫13 (6x3 + 6x2) dx = [3x4/2 + 2x3]13 = (243/2 + 54) − (3/2 + 2) = 172.

Answer: 172

Ex. 14.1: 31

Use a double integral to find the volume of the solid enclosed by the surface z = x2 and the planes x = 0, x = 2, y = 3, y = 0, and z = 0.

The solid sits over the rectangle 0 ≤ x ≤ 2, 0 ≤ y ≤ 3 in the xy-plane, with height z = x2. Volume = ∫02 ∫03 x2 dy dx = ∫02 3x2 dx = [x3]02 = 8.

Answer: 8

Ex. 14.1: 32

Use a double integral to find the volume in the first octant bounded by the coordinate planes, the plane y = 4, and the plane x/3 + z/5 = 1.

From x/3 + z/5 = 1, the top surface is z = 5(1 − x/3), over the rectangle 0 ≤ x ≤ 3, 0 ≤ y ≤ 4 in the xy-plane. Volume = ∫04 ∫03 5(1 − x/3) dx dy = 4 · 5 · [x − x2/6]03 = 20 · (3 − 3/2) = 30.

Answer: 30

Ex. 14.1: 33

Evaluate the integral by choosing a convenient order of integration: ∬R x cos(xy) cos2(πx) dA, where R = [0, 1/2] × [0, π].

Integrating with respect to x first is hopeless (the x-integral of x cos(xy)cos2(πx) is messy), so integrate with respect to y first. Inner: ∫0π x cos(xy) dy = [sin(xy)]0π = sin(πx). Outer: ∫01/2 sin(πx) cos2(πx) dx. Put u = cos(πx), du = −π sin(πx) dx: the integral becomes (1/π)∫01 u2 du = 1/(3π).

Answer: 1/(3π) ≈ 0.106

Ex. 14.1: 34

(a) Sketch the solid in the first octant that is enclosed by the planes x = 0, z = 0, x = 5, z − y = 0, and z = −2y + 6. (b) Find the volume of the solid by breaking it into two parts.

(a) The solid is a prism running from x = 0 to x = 5 with the same triangular cross-section in every plane x = constant. In the yz-plane the cross-section is bounded below by z = 0, on one side by the line z = y and on the other by the line z = −2y + 6. The two sloping lines meet where y = −2y + 6, i.e. y = 2, z = 2; the line z = −2y + 6 meets z = 0 at y = 3. So the cross-section is the triangle with vertices (y, z) = (0, 0), (2, 2), (3, 0).

(b) The top of the cross-section changes at y = 2, so split there. For 0 ≤ y ≤ 2 the height is z = y; for 2 ≤ y ≤ 3 the height is z = −2y + 6. Volume = ∫05 [∫02 y dy + ∫23 (−2y + 6) dy] dx = 5 · ([y2/2]02 + [−y2 + 6y]23) = 5 · (2 + 1) = 15.

Answer: 15

Ex. 14.1: 36

Find the average value of f(x, y) = x + 7y over the rectangle [0, 3] × [0, 6].

The area is A(R) = 3 · 6 = 18. ∬R (x + 7y) dA = ∫03 ∫06 (x + 7y) dy dx = ∫03 (6x + 126) dx = 27 + 378 = 405. Hence fave = 405/18 = 45/2.

Answer: 45/2 = 22.5

Ex. 14.1: 37

Find the average value of f(x, y) = y sin(xy) over the rectangle [0, 1] × [0, π/2].

The area is A(R) = π/2. Integrate with respect to x first (integrating y sin(xy) with respect to y first would need integration by parts and leaves a messy x-integral): ∫01 y sin(xy) dx = [−cos(xy)]01 = 1 − cos y. Then ∫0π/2 (1 − cos y) dy = π/2 − 1. Hence fave = (π/2 − 1)/(π/2) = 1 − 2/π.

Answer: 1 − 2/π ≈ 0.363

Evaluate the iterated integral ∫1/41 ∫x2x (1/y) dy dx.

Inner: ∫x2x (1/y) dy = ln x − ln x2 = −ln x. Outer: ∫1/41 (−ln x) dx = [x − x ln x]1/41 = 1 − (1/4 + (ln 4)/4) = 3/4 − (ln 2)/2 ≈ 0.403.

Ex. 14.2: 11

The top edge is y = 3, the bottom edge is y = 1. The left edge joins (1, 3) to (2, 1): slope −2, equation y = −2x + 5. The right edge joins (4, 1) to (5, 3): slope 2, equation y = 2x − 7.

(a) In the order dy dx the top and bottom curves change, so three integrals are needed: for 1 ≤ x ≤ 2, y runs from −2x + 5 to 3; for 2 ≤ x ≤ 4, y runs from 1 to 3; for 4 ≤ x ≤ 5, y runs from 2x − 7 to 3.

(b) In the order dx dy a single integral suffices: y runs from 1 to 3, and for each y, x runs from the left edge x = (5 − y)/2 to the right edge x = (y + 7)/2.

Answer: (a) ∫12 ∫−2x+53 f dy dx + ∫24 ∫13 f dy dx + ∫45 ∫2x−73 f dy dx; (b) ∫13 ∫(5−y)/2(y+7)/2 f dx dy

(b) As a Type II region, y runs from 2 to 8 and x runs from the curve x = 16/y (for 2 ≤ y ≤ 4) or the line x = y (for 4 ≤ y ≤ 8) to x = 8: ∫24 ∫16/y8 x2 dx dy + ∫48 ∫y8 x2 dx dy, which also evaluates to 576.

Ex. 14.2: 26

Use double integration to find the volume of the solid shown in Figure Ex-37: the solid in the first octant bounded by the coordinate planes and the plane 3x + 2y + 4z = 12.

The plane meets the axes at (4, 0, 0), (0, 6, 0) and (0, 0, 3), so the solid is the tetrahedron with those intercepts. The top surface is z = (12 − 3x − 2y)/4, over the triangular region in the xy-plane bounded by x = 0, y = 0 and 3x + 2y = 12, i.e. 0 ≤ x ≤ 4, 0 ≤ y ≤ 6 − 3x/2. Volume = ∫04 ∫06−3x/2 (3 − 3x/4 − y/2) dy dx. The inner integral is (3 − 3x/4)(6 − 3x/2) − (6 − 3x/2)2/4 = 9(4 − x)2/16, so the volume is ∫04 9(4 − x)2/16 dx = (9/16)·(64/3) = 12. (Check: volume of a tetrahedron = (1/6)·4·6·3 = 12.)

Answer: 12
