Answer: (9 ln 3)/2 − 2 ≈ 2.944

Ex. 14.2: 61

Find the average value of 1/(1 + x2) over the triangular region with vertices (0, 0), (1, 1), and (0, 1).

The triangle has area A(R) = 1/2. As a Type II region it is 0 ≤ y ≤ 1, 0 ≤ x ≤ y. ∬R 1/(1 + x2) dA = ∫01 ∫0y dx/(1 + x2) dy = ∫01 arctan y dy. Since ∫ arctan y dy = y arctan y − (1/2)ln(1 + y2), the integral is π/4 − (ln 2)/2. Dividing by the area 1/2 gives fave = π/2 − ln 2.

Answer: π/2 − ln 2 ≈ 0.878

Ex. 14.2: 62

Find the average value of f(x, y) = x2 − xy over the region enclosed by y = x and y = 3x − x2.

The curves meet where x = 3x − x2, i.e. x = 0 and x = 2. First the area: A(R) = ∫02 [(3x − x2) − x] dx = ∫02 (2x − x2) dx = 4 − 8/3 = 4/3. Next the integral: ∬R (x2 − xy) dA = ∫02 ∫x3x−x2 (x2 − xy) dy dx = ∫02 [x2y − xy2/2]x3x−x2 dx = ∫02 (−2x3 + 2x4 − x5/2) dx = −8/15. Hence fave = (−8/15)/(4/3) = −2/5. (The negative sign is correct: on this region y ≥ x, so x2 − xy = x(x − y) ≤ 0.)

Answer: −2/5 = −0.4

Lecture 15 — Double Integrals in Polar Coordinates (Anton §14.3)

When the region is round, describe each point by how far out it is and which direction it points, and remember that a wedge of paper gets wider the further out you go.

In the last lecture we chopped regions into little rectangles. That works beautifully for squares and triangles — but what if the region is a circle, a cardioid (a heart-shaped curve), or a rose with petals? Chopping a circle into rectangles is like trying to tile a round table with square tiles: you can do it, but the edges are a mess. Polar coordinates are the right tool for round things.

Instead of saying "go x across and y up", polar coordinates say: "stand at the origin, turn to face an angle θ (theta, measured from the positive x-axis), and walk out a distance r". Every point in the plane is then just a pair (r, θ). The conversions are x = r cos θ and y = r sin θ, and the useful combination x² + y² is simply r² — the square of the distance from the origin. So whenever you see x² + y², √(x² + y²) or e−(x²+y²) in the integrand, or a region bounded by circles, polar coordinates are calling your name.

Now here is the one idea you must never forget. In Cartesian coordinates, a tiny piece of area is a rectangle, dA = dx dy, and every tiny rectangle has the same area wherever it sits. In polar coordinates, a tiny piece is a wedge — a little slice of pie between two nearby angles and two nearby radii. And a wedge is wider the further out it is: a slice of pie near the centre is a thin sliver, but the same angular slice near the crust is a fat piece. That is why the polar area element is dA = r dr dθ, with an extra r in front. The r is the Jacobian of the polar transformation — a fancy word that just means "how much the little piece stretches". Forget that r, and every answer will be wrong.

How do you set up a polar integral? First, read the region: what are the θ-limits (which directions does the region cover?) and, for each direction, what are the r-limits (where do you enter the region and where do you leave it?). A full circle is θ from 0 to 2π; a first-quadrant sector is θ from 0 to π/2. Then replace x and y in the integrand, tack on the extra r, and integrate: ∬R f dA = ∬S f(r cos θ, r sin θ) r dr dθ. The inner integral is usually in r, the outer in θ.

Two things need care. First, area in polar form: setting f = 1 gives A = ∬ dA = ½∫ r² dθ for a region bounded by a single polar curve — that is how you get the area of a cardioid or a rose. But watch the θ-range for roses and lemniscates: a petal is traced over a limited interval, and r = sin 2θ traces only two of its four petals over 0 ≤ θ ≤ π — you need the full 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π for all four, and going further than that traces the same petals twice. Second, offset circles: the circle (x − 1)² + y² = 1 is not centred at the origin, and in polar form it becomes r = 2 cos θ, so r does not start at 0 for every θ. Always find where r starts and ends for the direction you are looking in.

Finally, a practical exam skill: converting a Cartesian iterated integral to polar. Before you touch anything, read the region from the limits. If you see ∫01 ∫0√(1−x²), that inner limit y = √(1 − x²) is the top half of the unit circle, and x from 0 to 1 keeps you in the first quadrant — so the region is the quarter-disk, and in polar it is simply 0 ≤ r ≤ 1, 0 ≤ θ ≤ π/2. Describe the region first, convert second.

Why polar at all? Cartesian coordinates are a street grid: "go 3 blocks east, 2 blocks north". That is perfect for a rectangular city. But a dartboard is not a city: the natural way to describe a point on a dartboard is "how far from the bullseye, and in which direction" — that is r and θ. Polar coordinates are the dartboard description, and they are the right language whenever the region or the integrand is round. The lighthouse version of the same idea: a lighthouse does not say "the ship is 3 miles east and 4 miles north"; it says "the ship is 5 miles away at a bearing of 53°". Whenever you see a circle, a sector, a cardioid or a rose, or an integrand built out of x² + y², reach for polar coordinates first.

Why the extra r — slowly. Cut a pizza into 8 slices. The slice near the centre is a thin sliver; the same slice near the crust is wide. Now cut each slice into little pieces by drawing circles at r = 1, 2, 3. The little piece at radius r has one side dr (along the slice) and one side r dθ (along the arc — and an arc of angle dθ at radius r really is r dθ long, because a full circle of radius r has circumference 2πr). So the little piece is a tiny rectangle of sides dr and r dθ, and its area is r dr dθ. That is all the extra r is: the wedge gets wider as you go out. You can also see it from the Jacobian determinant. With x = r cos θ and y = r sin θ, the partial derivatives are ∂x/∂r = cos θ, ∂x/∂θ = −r sin θ, ∂y/∂r = sin θ, ∂y/∂θ = r cos θ, and the determinant is (cos θ)(r cos θ) − (−r sin θ)(sin θ) = r cos² θ + r sin² θ = r. The determinant is the stretch factor, and it comes out to exactly r — the same r you see in the pizza picture. Two completely different-looking arguments, one answer.

Where students get stuck: the θ-range. The r-limits are usually easy (0 to the curve, or between two curves). The θ-limits are where marks are lost, because a polar curve can retrace itself. Take the rose r = sin 2θ. Over 0 ≤ θ ≤ π it traces only two of its four petals; you need the full 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π to trace all four. (The guide is explicit about this: r = sin 2θ traces only two of the four petals over 0 ≤ θ ≤ π, and the full rose needs 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π.) The rule is: never assume the θ-range — ask "as θ runs, when does the curve come back to where it started?" For a cardioid r = 1 − cos θ, one full turn 0 to 2π traces it once. For a rose, check how many petals appear and whether you have traced each one exactly once; tracing a petal twice doubles its area in your answer.

Mini-example — the quarter-disk, two ways. The guide points out that ∫01 ∫0√(1−x²) ... dy dx describes the quarter-disk: x runs 0 to 1, and for each x, y runs 0 up to the top half of the unit circle. In polar coordinates that region is simply 0 ≤ r ≤ 1 and 0 ≤ θ ≤ π/2. Its area by the polar area formula is A = ½∫0π/2 1² dθ = ½ × (π/2) = π/4 — and you can check it instantly, because a quarter of the unit disk has area (π × 1²)/4 = π/4. The two agree, and the polar version was one line. That is the payoff: describe the region in the language it is written in, and the integral becomes easy.

x = r cos θ,   y = r sin θ,   x² + y² = r²

dA = r dr dθ  (the extra r is the polar Jacobian)

∬R f(x, y) dA = ∬S f(r cos θ, r sin θ) r dr dθ

Area of a region bounded by r = r(θ): A = ½ ∫αβ r² dθ

Volume under z = f over a polar region = ∬ f(r cos θ, r sin θ) r dr dθ

Worked example — Ex. 14.3-7 (verified answer: 3π/2).

Problem: Find the area of the cardioid r = 1 − cos θ.

Step 1 — Choose the area formula. For a region bounded by a single polar curve, A = ½ ∫ r² dθ, with θ running over the range that traces the curve once. The cardioid is traced once as θ goes from 0 to 2π.

Step 2 — Substitute and expand. A = ½ ∫02π (1 − cos θ)² dθ = ½ ∫02π (1 − 2 cos θ + cos² θ) dθ. The cos² term looks awkward, so use cos² θ = (1 + cos 2θ)/2: the integrand becomes 1 − 2 cos θ + ½ + (½) cos 2θ = (3/2) − 2 cos θ + (½) cos 2θ.

Step 3 — Integrate term by term. Over a full period 0 to 2π, the integrals of cos θ and cos 2θ are both zero — a full wave has equal area above and below. Only the constant (3/2) survives: ∫02π (3/2) dθ = 3π.

Step 4 — Remember the ½ in front. A = ½ × 3π = 3π/2.

Answer: 3π/2. The moral: in polar area problems, expand, use the half-angle identity, and let the cosine terms vanish over a full period.

Watch out: dropping the extra r in dA = r dr dθ is the single most common error in this chapter — a polar wedge is not a rectangle, and its area grows with r.

  • Why is the polar area element r dr dθ and not just dr dθ?
  • When should you switch a double integral to polar coordinates?
  • Over what θ-range is the rose r = sin 2θ traced once, and why does 0 to π only give two of its four petals?
  • How do you read the region out of a Cartesian iterated integral before converting it?

Double Integrals in Polar Coordinates: Where the Extra r Comes From (short)

Solutions — Exercise Set 14.3 (Anton, 10th edition)

Double integrals in polar coordinates. All answers were checked with SymPy and against the book's answers appendix (odd-numbered exercises). Notes on the text extraction: in Ex. 25 the extraction reads "x + y = 4" — the two superscript 2s were displaced to the end of the line, and the book's answer (π/8) ln 5 only follows from x2 + y2 = 4, so that is the boundary used; in Ex. 30 the extraction garbles the outer limit as 1/√2, but the integral is over the quarter-disk, so the outer limit is 1; in Ex. 31 one transcription gives √(a2 + x2) but the book text and its answer give √(a2 − x2); in Ex. 33 the extraction drops the square-root sign in the integrand, which is 1/√(1 + x2 + y2). Ex. 13 as printed has only two conditions (no "above z = 0"), so the solid is the whole sphere outside the cylinder.

Ex. 14.3: 7

Use a double integral in polar coordinates to find the area of the region enclosed by the cardioid r = 1 − cos θ.

The cardioid is traced once as θ runs from 0 to 2π. Its area is A = ∬R dA = ½∫02π r2 dθ = ½∫02π (1 − cos θ)2 dθ.

Expand: (1 − cos θ)2 = 1 − 2 cos θ + cos2 θ. Over a full period ∫02π cos θ dθ = 0 and ∫02π cos2 θ dθ = π, so A = ½(2π − 0 + π) = 3π/2.

Answer: 3π/2 ≈ 4.71

Ex. 14.3: 8

Use a double integral in polar coordinates to find the area of the region enclosed by the rose r = sin 2θ.

The rose r = sin 2θ has four petals. It is traced once only as θ runs from 0 to 2π (over 0 ≤ θ ≤ π only two of the four petals are traced: for π/2 ≤ θ ≤ π the radius is negative, so those points land in the fourth quadrant, and the petals in the second and third quadrants come from π ≤ θ ≤ 2π).

Hence A = ½∫02π sin2 2θ dθ. Since sin2 2θ has average value ½ over the interval, ∫02π sin2 2θ dθ = π, so A = π/2. (Equivalently, one petal has area ½∫0π/2 sin2 2θ dθ = π/8, and there are four of them.)

Answer: π/2 ≈ 1.57

Ex. 14.3: 9

Use a double integral in polar coordinates to find the area of the region in the first quadrant bounded by r = 1 and r = sin 2θ, with π/4 ≤ θ ≤ π/2.

For π/4 ≤ θ ≤ π/2 the petal r = sin 2θ lies inside the circle r = 1: at θ = π/4 both are 1, and as θ increases the petal shrinks to 0 at θ = π/2 while the circle stays at 1. So the region is the crescent between the two curves, with r running from sin 2θ out to 1.

A = ∫π/4π/2 ∫sin 2θ1 r dr dθ = ½∫π/4π/2 (1 − sin2 2θ) dθ = ½∫π/4π/2 cos2 2θ dθ. Since ∫ cos2 2θ dθ = θ/2 + sin 4θ/8, this is ½[(π/4 + 0) − (π/8 + 0)] = π/16.

Answer: π/16 ≈ 0.196

Ex. 14.3: 10

Use a double integral in polar coordinates to find the area of the region inside the circle x2 + y2 = 4 and to the right of the line x = 1.

The region is the circular segment of the radius-2 disk cut off by the vertical line x = 1. The line meets the circle where 1 + y2 = 4, i.e. at the points (1, ±√3), where the polar angle is θ = ±π/3. In polar coordinates the line x = 1 is r = sec θ, so for −π/3 ≤ θ ≤ π/3, r runs from sec θ out to 2.

A = ∫−π/3π/3 ∫sec θ2 r dr dθ = ½∫−π/3π/3 (4 − sec2 θ) dθ = [2θ − ½ tan θ]−π/3π/3 = (2π/3 − √3/2) − (−2π/3 + √3/2) = 4π/3 − √3.

Answer: 4π/3 − √3 ≈ 2.46

Ex. 14.3: 17

Find the volume of the solid described in Exercise 13: inside of x2 + y2 + z2 = 9, outside of x2 + y2 = 1.

The solid is the part of the ball of radius 3 outside the cylinder of radius 1. There is no "above z = 0" condition, so for each (x, y) with 1 ≤ r ≤ 3 the solid extends from the lower hemisphere z = −√(9 − r2) to the upper hemisphere z = +√(9 − r2); its height is 2√(9 − r2). In polar coordinates, with 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π,

V = ∫02π ∫13 2√(9 − r2) r dr dθ. Put u = 9 − r2: ∫13 2r√(9 − r2) dr = ∫08 √u du = (2/3)·83/2 = 32√2/3. Hence V = 2π · 32√2/3 = 64π√2/3.

Answer: 64π√2/3 ≈ 94.78

Ex. 14.3: 18

Find the volume of the solid described in Exercise 14: below z = √(x2 + y2), inside of x2 + y2 = 2y, above z = 0.

The top is the cone z = r and the base is the disk x2 + y2 = 2y, i.e. r = 2 sin θ, which is traced for 0 ≤ θ ≤ π. So

V = ∫0π ∫02 sin θ r · r dr dθ = ∫0π (8/3) sin3 θ dθ. Since ∫0π sin3 θ dθ = 4/3, V = (8/3)(4/3) = 32/9.

Answer: 32/9 ≈ 3.56

Ex. 14.3: 19

Find the volume of the solid described in Exercise 15: below z = 1 − x2 − y2, inside of x2 + y2 − x = 0, above z = 0.

The top is the paraboloid z = 1 − r2 and the base is the disk x2 + y2 = x, i.e. r = cos θ, traced for −π/2 ≤ θ ≤ π/2. So

V = ∫−π/2π/2 ∫0cos θ (1 − r2) r dr dθ = ∫−π/2π/2 (cos2 θ/2 − cos4 θ/4) dθ. Using ∫−π/2π/2 cos2 θ dθ = π/2 and ∫−π/2π/2 cos4 θ dθ = 3π/8, V = (1/2)(π/2) − (1/4)(3π/8) = π/4 − 3π/32 = 5π/32.

Answer: 5π/32 ≈ 0.491

Ex. 14.3: 20

Find the volume of the solid described in Exercise 16: below z = (x2 + y2)−1/2, outside of x2 + y2 = 1, inside of x2 + y2 = 9, above z = 0.

The top is z = 1/r and the base is the annulus 1 ≤ r ≤ 3, 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π. The r in the polar area element cancels the 1/r in the height:

V = ∫02π ∫13 (1/r) · r dr dθ = ∫02π ∫13 1 dr dθ = 2π · 2 = 4π.

Answer: 4π ≈ 12.57

Ex. 14.3: 23

Use polar coordinates to evaluate ∬R sin(x2 + y2) dA, where R is the region enclosed by the circle x2 + y2 = 9.

R is the disk r ≤ 3. With x2 + y2 = r2 and dA = r dr dθ,

∬R sin(x2 + y2) dA = ∫02π ∫03 sin(r2) r dr dθ. Put u = r2: ∫03 r sin(r2) dr = ½(1 − cos 9). Hence the integral is 2π · ½(1 − cos 9) = π(1 − cos 9), where cos 9 is cos of 9 radians.

Answer: π(1 − cos 9) ≈ 6.00

Ex. 14.3: 24

Use polar coordinates to evaluate ∬R √(9 − x2 − y2) dA, where R is the region in the first quadrant within the circle x2 + y2 = 9.

R is the quarter-disk 0 ≤ r ≤ 3, 0 ≤ θ ≤ π/2. The integrand is √(9 − r2), so

∬R √(9 − x2 − y2) dA = ∫0π/2 ∫03 √(9 − r2) r dr dθ. Put u = 9 − r2: ∫03 r√(9 − r2) dr = [−(9 − r2)3/2/3]03 = 27/3 = 9. Hence the integral is (π/2) · 9 = 9π/2.

Answer: 9π/2 ≈ 14.14

Ex. 14.3: 25

Use polar coordinates to evaluate ∬R 1/(1 + x2 + y2) dA, where R is the sector in the first quadrant bounded by y = 0, y = x, and x2 + y2 = 4.

R is the sector of the disk of radius 2 cut by the rays θ = 0 (the line y = 0) and θ = π/4 (the line y = x): 0 ≤ θ ≤ π/4, 0 ≤ r ≤ 2.

∬R 1/(1 + x2 + y2) dA = ∫0π/4 ∫02 r/(1 + r2) dr dθ. The inner integral is [½ ln(1 + r2)]02 = ½ ln 5, independent of θ, so the integral is (π/4)(½ ln 5) = (π/8) ln 5.

Answer: (π/8) ln 5 ≈ 0.632

Ex. 14.3: 26

Use polar coordinates to evaluate ∬R 2y dA, where R is the region in the first quadrant bounded above by the circle (x − 1)2 + y2 = 1 and below by the line y = x.

The circle (x − 1)2 + y2 = 1 is x2 + y2 = 2x, i.e. r = 2 cos θ. It meets the line y = x (θ = π/4) at (1, 1), and both pass through the origin, so in the first quadrant R is 0 ≤ θ ≤ π/4, 0 ≤ r ≤ 2 cos θ.

∬R 2y dA = ∫0π/4 ∫02 cos θ (2r sin θ) r dr dθ = ∫0π/4 (16/3) sin θ cos3 θ dθ. Put u = cos θ: ∫0π/4 sin θ cos3 θ dθ = [−cos4 θ/4]0π/4 = (1 − 1/4)/4 = 3/16. Hence the integral is (16/3)(3/16) = 1.

Answer: 1

Ex. 14.3: 27

Evaluate the iterated integral ∫01 ∫0√(1 − x2) (x2 + y2) dy dx by converting to polar coordinates.

The limits describe the quarter-disk x2 + y2 ≤ 1 in the first quadrant: 0 ≤ θ ≤ π/2, 0 ≤ r ≤ 1. The integrand is r2, and dA = r dr dθ, so

∫01 ∫0√(1 − x2) (x2 + y2) dy dx = ∫0π/2 ∫01 r3 dr dθ = (π/2)(1/4) = π/8.

Answer: π/8 ≈ 0.393

Ex. 14.3: 28

Evaluate the iterated integral ∫−22 ∫−√(4 − y2)√(4 − y2) e−(x2 + y2) dx dy by converting to polar coordinates.

For each y between −2 and 2, x runs across the full width of the circle x2 + y2 = 4, so the region is the whole disk of radius 2: 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π, 0 ≤ r ≤ 2.

∫−22 ∫−√(4 − y2)√(4 − y2) e−(x2 + y2) dx dy = ∫02π ∫02 e−r2 r dr dθ. Put u = r2: ∫02 r e−r2 dr = ½(1 − e−4). Hence the integral is 2π · ½(1 − e−4) = π(1 − e−4).

Answer: π(1 − e−4) ≈ 3.08

Ex. 14.3: 29

Evaluate the iterated integral ∫02 ∫0√(2x − x2) √(x2 + y2) dy dx by converting to polar coordinates.

The upper limit y = √(2x − x2) is the upper semicircle of (x − 1)2 + y2 = 1, i.e. r = 2 cos θ, with y ≥ 0, so 0 ≤ θ ≤ π/2 and 0 ≤ r ≤ 2 cos θ. The integrand is r, so

∫02 ∫0√(2x − x2) √(x2 + y2) dy dx = ∫0π/2 ∫02 cos θ r · r dr dθ = ∫0π/2 (8/3) cos3 θ dθ. Since ∫0π/2 cos3 θ dθ = 2/3, the integral is (8/3)(2/3) = 16/9.

Answer: 16/9 ≈ 1.78

Ex. 14.3: 30

Evaluate the iterated integral ∫01 ∫0√(1 − y2) cos(x2 + y2) dx dy by converting to polar coordinates.

The limits describe the quarter-disk x2 + y2 ≤ 1 in the first quadrant: 0 ≤ θ ≤ π/2, 0 ≤ r ≤ 1. The integrand becomes cos(r2), so

∫01 ∫0√(1 − y2) cos(x2 + y2) dx dy = ∫0π/2 ∫01 cos(r2) r dr dθ. Put u = r2: ∫01 r cos(r2) dr = ½ sin 1. Hence the integral is (π/2)(½ sin 1) = (π/4) sin 1.

Answer: (π/4) sin 1 ≈ 0.661

Ex. 14.3: 31

Evaluate the iterated integral ∫0a ∫0√(a2 − x2) dy dx / (1 + x2 + y2)3/2 (a > 0) by converting to polar coordinates.

The limits describe the quarter-disk of radius a in the first quadrant: 0 ≤ θ ≤ π/2, 0 ≤ r ≤ a. The integrand becomes 1/(1 + r2)3/2, so

∫0a ∫0√(a2 − x2) dy dx / (1 + x2 + y2)3/2 = ∫0π/2 ∫0a r/(1 + r2)3/2 dr dθ. The inner integral is [−1/√(1 + r2)]0a = 1 − 1/√(1 + a2). Hence the integral is (π/2)(1 − 1/√(1 + a2)).

Answer: (π/2)(1 − 1/√(1 + a2))

Ex. 14.3: 32

Evaluate the iterated integral ∫01 ∫y√y √(x2 + y2) dx dy by converting to polar coordinates.

The region is 0 ≤ y ≤ 1 with x between the line x = y and the curve x = √y, i.e. y = x2. In polar coordinates y = x2 becomes r sin θ = r2 cos2 θ, i.e. r = tan θ sec θ, and the line x = y is θ = π/4. A ray at angle 0 ≤ θ ≤ π/4 enters the region at the origin and leaves it on the curve y = x2, so 0 ≤ r ≤ tan θ sec θ.

∫01 ∫y√y √(x2 + y2) dx dy = ∫0π/4 ∫0tan θ sec θ r2 dr dθ = (1/3)∫0π/4 tan3 θ sec3 θ dθ. Put u = sec θ (du = sec θ tan θ dθ): the integral becomes (1/3)∫1√2 (u4 − u2) du = (1/3)[u5/5 − u3/3]1√2 = (1/3)(2√2/15 + 2/15) = 2(√2 + 1)/45.

Answer: 2(√2 + 1)/45 ≈ 0.107

Ex. 14.3: 33

Evaluate the iterated integral ∫0√2 ∫y√(4 − y2) dx dy / √(1 + x2 + y2) by converting to polar coordinates.

The limits describe the part of the disk of radius 2 with x ≥ y (that is, θ ≤ π/4) and y ≤ √2: it is the sector 0 ≤ θ ≤ π/4, 0 ≤ r ≤ 2. The integrand is 1/√(1 + r2), so

∫0√2 ∫y√(4 − y2) dx dy / √(1 + x2 + y2) = ∫0π/4 ∫02 r/√(1 + r2) dr dθ. The inner integral is [√(1 + r2)]02 = √5 − 1. Hence the integral is (π/4)(√5 − 1).

Answer: (π/4)(√5 − 1) ≈ 0.971

Ex. 14.3: 34

Evaluate the iterated integral ∫−40 ∫−√(16 − x2)√(16 − x2) 3x dy dx by converting to polar coordinates.

The limits describe the left half of the disk of radius 4 (x ≤ 0): π/2 ≤ θ ≤ 3π/2, 0 ≤ r ≤ 4. The integrand is 3x = 3r cos θ, so

∫−40 ∫−√(16 − x2)√(16 − x2) 3x dy dx = ∫π/23π/2 ∫04 (3r cos θ) r dr dθ = (∫04 3r2 dr)(∫π/23π/2 cos θ dθ) = 64 · [sin θ]π/23π/2 = 64 · (−1 − 1) = −128. The answer is negative because x < 0 throughout the region — this is a signed integral, not a volume.

Answer: −128

Ex. 14.3: 35

True–False. Determine whether the statement is true or false. Explain your answer. The disk of radius 2 that is centered at the origin is a polar rectangle.

True. A polar rectangle is a simple polar region bounded by circular arcs and rays, i.e. a region of the form r1 ≤ r ≤ r2, θ1 ≤ θ ≤ θ2. The disk of radius 2 centered at the origin is exactly the region 0 ≤ r ≤ 2, 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π, which is of that form (the inner "arc" r = 0 is the origin). So the disk is a polar rectangle.

Answer: True

Ex. 14.3: 36

True–False. Determine whether the statement is true or false. Explain your answer. If f is continuous and nonnegative on a simple polar region R, then the volume of the solid enclosed between R and the surface z = f(r, θ) is expressed as ∬R f(r, θ) r dA.

False. The volume is V = ∬R f(r, θ) dA, and in polar coordinates the area element dA is already r dr dθ, so V = ∫∫ f(r, θ) r dr dθ. The statement as printed has an extra factor of r: ∬R f(r, θ) r dA would evaluate to ∫∫ f(r, θ) r2 dr dθ, which is wrong. (For example, with f = 1 over the unit disk the correct volume is π, while the printed formula gives 2π/3.) The r belongs in the conversion of dA, not in front of it.

Answer: False

Ex. 14.3: 44

Use polar coordinates to find the volume of the solid that is above the xy-plane, inside the cylinder x2 + y2 − ay = 0, and inside the ellipsoid x2/a2 + y2/a2 + z2/c2 = 1.

The cylinder x2 + y2 = ay is r = a sin θ, a circle of diameter a in the upper half-plane, traced for 0 ≤ θ ≤ π. Inside the ellipsoid the top is z = c√(1 − r2/a2), and the solid sits above z = 0, so

V = ∫0π ∫0a sin θ c√(1 − r2/a2) r dr dθ. The inner integral is (a2c/3)(1 − |cos θ|3): substituting u = 1 − r2/a2 gives −(a2c/3)(1 − r2/a2)3/2 evaluated at r = a sin θ, and (1 − sin2 θ)3/2 = |cos θ|3 — the absolute value matters, because cos θ is negative for θ > π/2.

Hence V = (a2c/3)∫0π (1 − |cos θ|3) dθ. Splitting at π/2: ∫0π/2 (1 − cos3 θ) dθ = π/2 − 2/3 and ∫π/2π (1 + cos3 θ) dθ = π/2 − 2/3, so V = (a2c/3)(π − 4/3) = πa2c/3 − 4a2c/9.

Answer: (a2c/3)(π − 4/3) = πa2c/3 − 4a2c/9

Ex. 14.3: 45

Find the area of the region enclosed by the lemniscate r2 = 2a2 cos 2θ.

The lemniscate has two lobes, one to the right and one to the left of the origin, along the x-axis. The right lobe is traced for −π/4 ≤ θ ≤ π/4, where cos 2θ ≥ 0. Its area is ½∫−π/4π/4 r2 dθ = ½∫−π/4π/4 2a2 cos 2θ dθ = a2[½ sin 2θ]−π/4π/4 = a2 · (1/2)(1 − (−1)) = a2. The left lobe has the same area by symmetry, so the total enclosed area is 2a2.

Answer: 2a2

Ex. 14.3: 46

Find the area in the first quadrant that is inside the circle r = 4 sin θ and outside the lemniscate r2 = 8 cos 2θ.

In the first quadrant the circle r = 4 sin θ is the circle x2 + (y − 2)2 = 4, and the lemniscate r2 = 8 cos 2θ exists only for 0 ≤ θ ≤ π/4. The two curves meet where 16 sin2 θ = 8 cos 2θ, i.e. 16 sin2 θ = 8(1 − 2 sin2 θ), so sin2 θ = 1/4 and θ = π/6. For 0 ≤ θ < π/6 the circle lies inside the lemniscate, so there is no region there; for π/6 ≤ θ ≤ π/4 the region runs from the lemniscate out to the circle; for π/4 ≤ θ ≤ π/2 the lemniscate is gone and the region runs from the origin out to the circle.

A = ½∫π/6π/4 (16 sin2 θ − 8 cos 2θ) dθ + ½∫π/4π/2 16 sin2 θ dθ. The first integral is ∫π/6π/4 (4 − 8 cos 2θ) dθ = [4θ − 4 sin 2θ]π/6π/4 = π/3 − 4 + 2√3. The second is ∫π/4π/2 (4 − 4 cos 2θ) dθ = [4θ − 2 sin 2θ]π/4π/2 = π + 2. Adding: A = 4π/3 + 2√3 − 2.

Answer: 4π/3 + 2√3 − 2 ≈ 5.65

Lecture 16 — Triple Integrals in Cartesian Coordinates (Anton §14.5)

A triple integral adds up the contents of a solid, one tiny box at a time — and setting it up is just a matter of describing the solid correctly.

Last lecture we added up columns over a flat region to get a volume. Now we go one dimension further: we have a solid — a real three-dimensional lump, like a wedge of cheese or a tetrahedron — and we want to add up something spread through it. If the "something" is just the number 1, the triple integral gives the volume of the solid. If it is a density (mass per unit volume), the integral gives the total mass. If it is anything else, it gives the total amount of that thing. The symbol is ∭G f(x, y, z) dV, where dV is a tiny box of volume, and G is the solid.

The picture to hold in your head is stacking boxes. Chop the solid into tiny boxes, each with volume dV = dx dy dz. In each box, the value of f is almost constant, so the box contributes about f × dV. Add up all the boxes and let them shrink, and you have the triple integral. That is the definition — and just as before, we never actually add up boxes one by one; we do it in three sweeps, one variable at a time. That is an iterated integral in three variables.

Setting up the limits is the whole skill of this lecture, and there is a reliable method. First, look at the solid from above and find its shadow on the xy-plane — that is, the flat region D you get by squashing the solid straight down. Then, for each point (x, y) in the shadow, ask: where does a vertical line enter the solid (the lower surface z = z1(x, y)) and where does it leave (the upper surface z = z2(x, y))? The integral is then ∭G f dV = ∬D ∫z1z2 f dz dA: integrate in z first (up the vertical line), then do the double integral over the shadow exactly as you learned in Lecture 14.

That method uses z as the innermost variable, but you are free to choose any variable innermost — and there are six possible orders: dx dy dz, dx dz dy, dy dx dz, dy dz dx, dz dx dy, dz dy dx. The choice is yours, and the clever choice is the one that makes the shadow and the limits simplest. Exercises 39–40 ask you to rewrite a given iterated integral in a different order, which is really a test of whether you can read the solid back out of the limits: the outermost variable's limits are always plain numbers, the middle variable's limits depend only on the outermost, and the innermost may depend on both. That pattern — constants outside, functions inside — is your best friend when reordering.

Two practical warnings. First, when a solid is bounded by a plane and a paraboloid or cylinder, you need their intersection curve to find the shadow: the shadow is the region where the two surfaces meet, projected down. Second, in the first octant all three variables are ≥ 0, which sounds trivial but is the easiest thing to forget — it trims the shadow to a triangle or a quarter-disk instead of the whole shape. And never integrate over the whole box that contains the solid when the solid is only part of it (Exercises 11–12 are built around exactly that mistake).

One more useful idea: the average value of f over the solid is fave = (1 / V(G)) ∭G f dV — the total amount divided by the volume, just as the average value over a flat region was the volume divided by the area.

Why a third integral? A single integral adds up along a line; a double integral adds up over a patch of ground. But a loaf of bread is not a patch — it has depth, and the dough is not the same all the way through: suppose the bottom of the loaf is denser than the top. To find the total mass you need to add up (density at each crumb) × (volume of each crumb) over the whole loaf. That is the triple integral. The double integral gave you the volume under a surface; the triple integral gives you the total amount of anything spread through a solid — mass if the integrand is density, volume if the integrand is 1, and the average value if you divide by the volume. Each new integral is the same idea — chop into tiny pieces, multiply, add — with one more direction to chop in.

The shadow method, slowly. The hard part is never the integrating; it is describing the solid. Here is the reliable way. Stand above the solid and look straight down: the flat shape you see is the shadow D on the xy-plane. Now pick one point (x, y) in the shadow and drop a vertical line through it. The line enters the solid at the lower surface z = z1(x, y) and leaves at the upper surface z = z2(x, y). So for that one vertical line, the contribution is ∫z1z2 f dz — you have added up a single column. Then do that for every point of the shadow, which is exactly a double integral over D. That is why the setup is ∭ f dV = ∬D ∫z1z2 f dz dA. And here is the rule that keeps the shadow right: you always project onto the plane perpendicular to the innermost variable. If z is innermost, the shadow is on the xy-plane; if x is innermost, the shadow is on the yz-plane. Project onto the wrong plane and the limits will be nonsense.

Where students get stuck: finding the shadow. The shadow is almost never given to you — you have to find it from where the surfaces meet. If the solid is bounded below by a paraboloid and above by a plane, set them equal: the curve where they intersect, dropped straight down, is the boundary of the shadow. In the first octant, remember that x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0 and z ≥ 0 are themselves boundaries: they cut the shadow down to a triangle or a quarter-disk, and forgetting them is the easiest way to integrate over a solid twice as big as the real one. And never integrate over the whole box that contains the solid (the trap in Ex. 14.5-11 and 12): the box is not the solid.

Choosing among the six orders. There are six because there are 3! = 6 ways to order three variables. You are free to pick any of them, so pick the one that makes life easy: the order whose shadow is the simplest shape, and whose innermost integral you can actually do. If the solid is tall in z and its shadow on the xy-plane is a nice triangle, put z innermost. If the shadow on the xy-plane is horrible but the shadow on the xz-plane is a rectangle, put y innermost instead. Exercises 39–40 test exactly this: you are given an iterated integral and must rewrite it in another order, which means reading the solid back out of the limits first — the outermost limits are constants, the middle limits depend only on the outermost variable, and the innermost may depend on both.

Mini-example — read the solid back out of its limits. Take the integral from the worked example below: ∫04 ∫02 − x/2 ∫03 − 3x/4 − 3y/2 dz dy dx. Read it from the outside in. The outer limits are the plain numbers 0 and 4, so x runs 0 to 4. The middle limits are 0 and 2 − x/2, so for each x, y runs 0 to 2 − x/2 — that is the triangular shadow with corners (0, 0), (4, 0) and (0, 2). The inner limits are 0 and 3 − (3/4)x − (3/2)y, so for each (x, y), z runs from 0 up to the plane 3x + 6y + 4z = 12. So the solid is the tetrahedron in the first octant under that plane — and its volume is (1/6) × 4 × 2 × 3 = 4, which matches the integral. Reading limits this way is the whole skill of Exercises 39–40.

∭G f(x, y, z) dV = ∬D ∫z1(x,y)z2(x,y) f(x, y, z) dz dA  (D = shadow of G on the xy-plane)

Volume of G = ∭G 1 dV

Mass of G (density δ) = ∭G δ(x, y, z) dV

Average value: fave = (1 / V(G)) ∭G f(x, y, z) dV

Six orders: dx dy dz, dx dz dy, dy dx dz, dy dz dx, dz dx dy, dz dy dx

Volume of a tetrahedron with intercepts a, b, c = (1/6)abc

Worked example — Ex. 14.5-15 (verified answer: 4).

Problem: Find the volume of the solid in the first octant bounded by the coordinate planes and the plane 3x + 6y + 4z = 12.

Step 1 — Find the intercepts. Set two variables to zero at a time: y = z = 0 gives x = 4; x = z = 0 gives y = 2; x = y = 0 gives z = 3. The solid is a tetrahedron with intercepts 4, 2 and 3.

Step 2 — Find the shadow. Squash the solid onto the xy-plane: put z = 0 in the plane equation to get 3x + 6y = 12, or y = 2 − x/2. The shadow D is the triangle with corners (0, 0), (4, 0) and (0, 2).

Step 3 — Set up the triple integral. For each (x, y) in the shadow, z runs from 0 up to the plane, z = 3 − (3/4)x − (3/2)y. With f = 1 (we want volume): V = ∫04 ∫02 − x/2 ∫03 − 3x/4 − 3y/2 dz dy dx.

Step 4 — Integrate in z, then in y. The inner integral is just the height, 3 − (3/4)x − (3/2)y. Integrating that in y from 0 to 2 − x/2 gives (3 − (3/4)x)(2 − x/2) − (3/4)(2 − x/2)². A cleaner way to see it: for fixed x, the y-integral of the height is the area of a triangle of base (2 − x/2) and height (3 − (3/4)x), which is ½(2 − x/2)(3 − (3/4)x) = (3/4)(2 − x/2)².

Step 5 — Integrate in x. V = ∫04 (3/4)(2 − x/2)² dx. Let u = 2 − x/2, du = −(1/2)dx; the integral becomes (3/2) ∫02 u² du = (3/2)(8/3) = 4.

Answer: 4. Check it the quick way: a tetrahedron with intercepts 4, 2, 3 has volume (1/6) × 4 × 2 × 3 = 4. The two methods agree — and in an exam, that quick check is worth doing.

Watch out: project onto the plane perpendicular to the innermost variable — if you integrate in z first, the shadow must be on the xy-plane, and the z-limits are the lower and upper surfaces, not numbers.

  • What does a triple integral give when the integrand is 1? When it is a density?
  • Describe the shadow method for setting up a triple integral, in your own words.
  • Why are there six possible orders of integration, and how do you read a solid back out of a set of limits?
  • What is the volume of a tetrahedron with intercepts a, b and c?

Lecture 16 — Solutions: Ex. 14.5: 9, 10, 11, 12, 15, 16, 17, 18, 33, 34, 39, 40

Statements are copied from Anton, Calculus, 10th edition, Exercise Set 14.5 (pp. 1046–1047). In Ex. 39–40 the limits are stacked in the book and the plain-text extraction garbles them; the statements below were checked against the printed page. Answers were verified with SymPy.

Ex. 14.5: 9

Evaluate the triple integral ∭G xy sin yz dV, where G is the rectangular box defined by the inequalities 0 ≤ x ≤ π, 0 ≤ y ≤ 1, 0 ≤ z ≤ π/6.

On a box the integral separates into an iterated integral with constant limits:

∫0π ∫01 ∫0π/6 xy sin yz dz dy dx.

Integrate in z first. For fixed y, ∫0π/6 sin yz dz = [−cos yz / y]0π/6 = (1 − cos(πy/6)) / y, so after multiplying by xy the integrand becomes x(1 − cos(πy/6)).

Integrate in y: ∫01 (1 − cos(πy/6)) dy = [y − (6/π) sin(πy/6)]01 = 1 − 3/π.

Finally ∫0π x(1 − 3/π) dx = (1 − 3/π) · π2/2 = π(π − 3)/2.

Answer: π(π − 3)/2.

Ex. 14.5: 10

Evaluate the triple integral ∭G y dV, where G is the solid enclosed by the plane z = y, the xy-plane, and the parabolic cylinder y = 1 − x2.

The cylinder y = 1 − x2 meets the xy-plane (z = 0, hence y = 0 on the plane z = y) at x = ±1, so the shadow of G on the xy-plane is 0 ≤ y ≤ 1 − x2, −1 ≤ x ≤ 1. For each (x, y) in the shadow, z runs from 0 (the xy-plane) up to z = y.

∫−11 ∫01−x2 ∫0y y dz dy dx = ∫−11 ∫01−x2 y2 dy dx = ∫−11 (1 − x2)3/3 dx.

The integrand is even, so this is (2/3)∫01 (1 − 3x2 + 3x4 − x6) dx = (2/3)(1 − 1 + 3/5 − 1/7) = (2/3)(16/35) = 32/105.

Answer: 32/105.

Ex. 14.5: 11

Evaluate the triple integral ∭G xyz dV, where G is the solid in the first octant that is bounded by the parabolic cylinder z = 2 − x2 and the planes z = 0, y = x, and y = 0.

In the first octant x, y, z ≥ 0. The cylinder meets z = 0 at x = √2, and y runs from 0 to the plane y = x. So 0 ≤ x ≤ √2, 0 ≤ y ≤ x, 0 ≤ z ≤ 2 − x2.

∫0√2 ∫0x ∫02−x2 xyz dz dy dx. The z-integral gives (2 − x2)2/2 and the y-integral gives x2/2, leaving ∫0√2 x3(2 − x2)2/4 dx.

Put u = x2 (du = 2x dx): this becomes (1/8)∫02 u(2 − u)2 du = (1/8)∫02 (4u − 4u2 + u3) du = (1/8)(8 − 32/3 + 4) = (1/8)(4/3) = 1/6.

Answer: 1/6.

Ex. 14.5: 12

Evaluate the triple integral ∭G cos(z/y) dV, where G is the solid defined by the inequalities π/6 ≤ y ≤ π/2, y ≤ x ≤ π/2, 0 ≤ z ≤ xy.

Integrate in z first, since cos(z/y) has an easy z-antiderivative: ∫0xy cos(z/y) dz = y sin(z/y) evaluated from 0 to xy, which is y sin x.

Next integrate in x: ∫yπ/2 y sin x dx = y[−cos x]yπ/2 = y cos y.

Finally ∫π/6π/2 y cos y dy = [y sin y + cos y]π/6π/2 = (π/2 + 0) − (π/12 + √3/2) = 5π/12 − √3/2.

Answer: 5π/12 − √3/2.

Ex. 14.5: 15

Use a triple integral to find the volume of the solid in the first octant bounded by the coordinate planes and the plane 3x + 6y + 4z = 12.

The plane meets the axes at (4, 0, 0), (0, 2, 0) and (0, 0, 3), so the solid is the tetrahedron with those intercepts. Solving for z gives z = (12 − 3x − 6y)/4; the shadow on the xy-plane is the triangle 0 ≤ x ≤ 4, 0 ≤ y ≤ (12 − 3x)/6.

V = ∫04 ∫0(12−3x)/6 (12 − 3x − 6y)/4 dy dx. The inner integral is [(12 − 3x)y − 3y2]/4 from 0 to (12 − 3x)/6, which simplifies to (12 − 3x)2/48.

Hence V = (1/48)∫04 (12 − 3x)2 dx = (1/48) · 192 = 4.

Answer: 4 (cubic units).

Ex. 14.5: 16

Use a triple integral to find the volume of the solid bounded by the surface z = y and the planes x + y = 1, x = 0, and z = 0.

The solid sits over the triangle in the xy-plane bounded by x = 0, y = 0 (from z = y meeting z = 0) and x + y = 1: 0 ≤ x ≤ 1, 0 ≤ y ≤ 1 − x. For each (x, y) there, z runs from 0 up to the surface z = y.

V = ∫01 ∫01−x ∫0y dz dy dx = ∫01 ∫01−x y dy dx = ∫01 (1 − x)2/2 dx = [−(1 − x)3/6]01 = 1/6.

Answer: 1/6 (cubic units).

Ex. 14.5: 17

Use a triple integral to find the volume of the solid bounded by the surface y = x2 and the planes y + z = 4 and z = 0.

The parabolic cylinder y = x2 meets the plane y + z = 4 at z = 4 − x2; z = 0 gives y = 4, so x runs from −2 to 2. For fixed x, y runs from x2 to 4 and z from 0 to 4 − y.

V = ∫−22 ∫x24 ∫04−y dz dy dx = ∫−22 ∫x24 (4 − y) dy dx = ∫−22 (4 − x2)2/2 dx.

By symmetry this is ∫02 (4 − x2)2 dx = ∫02 (16 − 8x2 + x4) dx = 32 − 64/3 + 32/5 = 256/15.

Answer: 256/15 (cubic units).

Ex. 14.5: 18

Use a triple integral to find the volume of the wedge in the first octant that is cut from the solid cylinder y2 + z2 ≤ 1 by the planes y = x and x = 0.

In the first octant the cylinder y2 + z2 ≤ 1 gives 0 ≤ z ≤ √(1 − y2) with 0 ≤ y ≤ 1. The plane y = x cuts the wedge so that, for fixed x, y runs from 0 to x, and x runs from 0 to 1.

V = ∫01 ∫0x √(1 − y2) dy dx. Reversing the order in the xy-plane (the triangle 0 ≤ y ≤ x ≤ 1 becomes 0 ≤ y ≤ 1, y ≤ x ≤ 1) gives V = ∫01 (1 − y)√(1 − y2) dy.

Split it: ∫01 √(1 − y2) dy is the area of a quarter unit circle, π/4; and ∫01 y√(1 − y2) dy = [−(1 − y2)3/2/3]01 = 1/3. So V = π/4 − 1/3.

Answer: π/4 − 1/3 (cubic units).

Ex. 14.5: 33

Find the average value of f(x, y, z) = x + y + z over the tetrahedron shown in Figure Ex-33.

Figure Ex-33 shows the tetrahedron in the first octant with vertices (1, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0) and (0, 0, 1), i.e. the solid bounded by the coordinate planes and the plane x + y + z = 1. Its volume is V = (1/6)(1)(1)(1) = 1/6.

By symmetry ∭G x dV = ∭G y dV = ∭G z dV. Computing one: ∭G x dV = ∫01 ∫01−x ∫01−x−y x dz dy dx = ∫01 ∫01−x x(1 − x − y) dy dx = ∫01 x(1 − x)2/2 dx = 1/24.

So ∭G (x + y + z) dV = 3 · (1/24) = 1/8, and the average value is fave = (1/V)∭G f dV = (1/8)/(1/6) = 3/4.

Answer: 3/4.

Ex. 14.5: 34

Find the average value of f(x, y, z) = xyz over the spherical region x2 + y2 + z2 ≤ 1.

The region is the unit ball, symmetric about each coordinate plane, and its volume is V = 4π/3. The integrand xyz is an odd function of x: replacing x by −x changes the sign of xyz, while the ball is unchanged.

Hence the integral over the half-ball x > 0 exactly cancels the integral over the half-ball x < 0, so ∭G xyz dV = 0. (The same argument works with y or z in place of x.)

Therefore fave = (1/V) · 0 = 0.

Answer: 0.

Ex. 14.5: 39

Express each integral as an equivalent integral in which the z-integration is performed first, the y-integration second, and the x-integration last.
(a) ∫05 ∫02 ∫0√(4−y2) f(x, y, z) dx dy dz    (b) ∫09 ∫03−√x ∫0z f(x, y, z) dy dz dx    (c) ∫04 ∫y8−y ∫0√(4−y) f(x, y, z) dx dz dy

(a) The limits say 0 ≤ z ≤ 5, 0 ≤ y ≤ 2, 0 ≤ x ≤ √(4 − y2), i.e. x2 + y2 ≤ 4 with x, y ≥ 0 (a quarter-disk of radius 2 in the xy-plane), extruded in z from 0 to 5. Reading the same solid with z innermost: x runs 0 to 2, and for fixed x, y runs 0 to √(4 − x2), while z still runs 0 to 5. So the integral is ∫02 ∫0√(4−x2) ∫05 f(x, y, z) dz dy dx.

(b) The limits say 0 ≤ x ≤ 9, 0 ≤ z ≤ 3 − √x, 0 ≤ y ≤ z. For fixed x, y is bounded by the largest z can take, so 0 ≤ y ≤ 3 − √x; and for fixed x and y, z runs from the plane z = y up to z = 3 − √x. So the integral is ∫09 ∫03−√x ∫y3−√x f(x, y, z) dz dy dx.

(c) The limits say 0 ≤ y ≤ 4, y ≤ z ≤ 8 − y, 0 ≤ x ≤ √(4 − y). For fixed x, y runs 0 to 4 − x2 (from x = √(4 − y)); for fixed x and y, z still runs from y to 8 − y. So the integral is ∫02 ∫04−x2 ∫y8−y f(x, y, z) dz dy dx.

Answer: (a) ∫02 ∫0√(4−x2) ∫05 f dz dy dx; (b) ∫09 ∫03−√x ∫y3−√x f dz dy dx; (c) ∫02 ∫04−x2 ∫y8−y f dz dy dx.

Ex. 14.5: 40

Express each integral as an equivalent integral in which the z-integration is performed first, the y-integration second, and the x-integration last.
(a) ∫03 ∫0√(9−z2) ∫0√(9−y2−z2) f(x, y, z) dx dy dz    (b) ∫04 ∫02 ∫0x/2 f(x, y, z) dy dz dx    (c) ∫04 ∫04−y ∫0√z f(x, y, z) dx dz dy

(a) The limits say x2 + y2 + z2 ≤ 9 with x, y, z ≥ 0: the part of the ball of radius 3 in the first octant. Reading it with z innermost: x runs 0 to 3, for fixed x, y runs 0 to √(9 − x2), and for fixed x and y, z runs 0 to √(9 − x2 − y2). So the integral is ∫03 ∫0√(9−x2) ∫0√(9−x2−y2) f(x, y, z) dz dy dx.

(b) The limits say 0 ≤ x ≤ 4, 0 ≤ z ≤ 2, 0 ≤ y ≤ x/2: a solid whose z-range does not depend on x or y. With z innermost, x still runs 0 to 4, y runs 0 to x/2, and z runs 0 to 2. So the integral is ∫04 ∫0x/2 ∫02 f(x, y, z) dz dy dx.

(c) The limits say 0 ≤ y ≤ 4, 0 ≤ z ≤ 4 − y, 0 ≤ x ≤ √z, i.e. x2 ≤ z ≤ 4 − y with x, y ≥ 0. For fixed x, z ranges from x2 to 4, so y runs 0 to 4 − x2; and for fixed x and y, z runs from x2 up to 4 − y. So the integral is ∫02 ∫04−x2 ∫x24−y f(x, y, z) dz dy dx.

Answer: (a) ∫03 ∫0√(9−x2) ∫0√(9−x2−y2) f dz dy dx; (b) ∫04 ∫0x/2 ∫02 f dz dy dx; (c) ∫02 ∫04−x2 ∫x24−y f dz dy dx.

Lecture 17 — Change of Variables in Multiple Integrals (Anton §14.7)

When a region or an integrand is ugly in x and y, rename the coordinates so the region becomes a rectangle and the integrand becomes simple — and multiply by the Jacobian, which measures how much the renaming stretches area.

Remember u-substitution from first-year calculus? You had an ugly integral in x, you set u equal to something inside it, and suddenly the integral became easy — but you had to remember the little correction factor, dx = g′(u) du. This lecture is the same idea, grown up into two and three dimensions. We rename the coordinates, the integral becomes easy, and the correction factor is called the Jacobian.

Here is the picture. Imagine you have a map drawn on a rubber sheet, and you stretch the sheet. A small square of paper on the original sheet becomes a slanted little parallelogram on the stretched sheet — bigger or smaller, depending on how hard you pulled. The Jacobian is exactly that stretch factor: it tells you how much a tiny patch of area (or volume) grows or shrinks under the transformation. If the Jacobian is 2, every little patch doubles in area; if it is ½, every patch halves. That is why the change-of-variables formula has the Jacobian multiplied in: ∬R f(x, y) dA = ∬S f(g(u, v), h(u, v)) · |∂(x, y)/∂(u, v)| du dv. The absolute value is there because area is never negative — the stretch factor is a size, not a direction.

What is the Jacobian, concretely? For a transformation x = g(u, v), y = h(u, v), it is a 2×2 determinant: ∂(x, y)/∂(u, v) = (∂x/∂u)(∂y/∂v) − (∂x/∂v)(∂y/∂u). For three variables it is the analogous 3×3 determinant. You do not need to memorise the formula as a magic spell — just remember it is the determinant of all the partial derivatives, the same "cross-multiplied" pattern you already know from 2×2 determinants.

There are two reasons to change variables. The first is to fix a complicated region: an ellipse becomes a circle (or even the unit disk) if you set x = 3u, y = 4v; a slanted rectangle bounded by the lines x − 2y = 1, 4 and 2x + y = 1, 3 becomes an ordinary axis-aligned rectangle if you set u = x − 2y, v = 2x + y (Exercise 21). The second is to fix a complicated integrand: if the integrand contains (x − y)ex²−y², set u = x + y and v = x − y and the exponent becomes simply uv (Exercise 22). The golden rule for choosing u and v: read them off the boundary curves or the integrand — whatever expressions keep repeating are your new variables.

How do you actually do it, step by step? First choose u and v. Then solve for x and y in terms of u and v (you will need the integrand in the new variables). Then compute the Jacobian — and here is a handy shortcut: it is often easier to compute ∂(u, v)/∂(x, y) first (the derivatives you can read off directly) and then use the reciprocal relation ∂(x, y)/∂(u, v) = 1 / ∂(u, v)/∂(x, y). Finally, read the new limits off the transformed boundary curves: each boundary curve in x and y becomes a constant value of u or v, and those constants are your limits.

One more thing, and it is important: you have already met Jacobians twice without knowing the name. The extra r in polar coordinates is the Jacobian ∂(x, y)/∂(r, θ) = r, and in the next lecture you will meet r again in cylindrical coordinates and ρ² sin φ in spherical coordinates. The Jacobian unifies all of them — polar, cylindrical and spherical are just special changes of variables.

Two honest corrections about the book and the plan. First, the lecture plan lists this lecture's exercise set as "Ex. 13.9" — that is a typo. Section 13.9 is Lagrange multipliers, which was Lecture 13. The problems listed (15, 16, 21–38, 44–46) are really Ex. 14.7, and the problem numbers match Ex. 14.7 exactly, so correct the sheet to Ex. 14.7. Second, in the book as printed, Ex. 14.7-15 states "∂(x, y)/∂(r, θ) = r²". That statement is false — the polar Jacobian is r, not r². It is a True–False item, and the correct answer is False. Do not memorise r²; memorise r.

Why rename the coordinates? You already did this in one variable: u-substitution. Faced with ∫ x√(x² + 1) dx, you set u = x² + 1, the integral became easy, and you multiplied by the correction factor du = 2x dx. Change of variables is that same move, grown up: when a region is a tilted, slanted shape, or an integrand is built out of the same awkward expressions over and over, you rename the coordinates so the problem becomes easy — and the correction factor is the Jacobian. An everyday version: a farmer's field is a tilted rectangle, and measuring it north–south and east–west gives messy numbers; but if you measure along the field's own sides, the field is just "30 by 20". The field did not change — the ruler did. That is what u and v are: a ruler laid along the problem instead of across it.

The Jacobian, slowly — and why it is a determinant. Take a tiny rectangle in the uv-plane, with sides Δu and Δv. Under the transformation it becomes a tiny parallelogram in the xy-plane. The sides of that parallelogram are the vectors (∂x/∂u, ∂y/∂u)Δu and (∂x/∂v, ∂y/∂v)Δv, and the area of a parallelogram is the absolute value of the determinant of its side vectors — that determinant is exactly ∂(x, y)/∂(u, v). So the Jacobian is not a magic formula to memorise; it is the area of the little parallelogram, divided by the area of the little rectangle. That is why the formula multiplies the integrand by |J|: without it you would be measuring area with the wrong ruler, and your answer would be off by the stretch factor. And the absolute value is there because area is a size — a stretch of −2 and a stretch of 2 both double the area.

The unification you should notice. You have already met Jacobians twice without the name. In Lecture 15 the extra r in dA = r dr dθ is the Jacobian ∂(x, y)/∂(r, θ). Check it: x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ, so ∂x/∂r = cos θ, ∂x/∂θ = −r sin θ, ∂y/∂r = sin θ, ∂y/∂θ = r cos θ, and the determinant is (cos θ)(r cos θ) − (−r sin θ)(sin θ) = r(cos² θ + sin² θ) = r. In the next lecture you will meet r again in cylindrical coordinates and ρ² sin φ in spherical coordinates. Polar, cylindrical and spherical are not three separate tricks — they are three special changes of variables, and the Jacobian is the one idea behind all of them.

Where students get stuck. Three traps, and they account for nearly every lost mark. First, forgetting the absolute value bars on the Jacobian — a negative determinant is fine as a determinant, but area is never negative. Second, using the Jacobian in the wrong direction: the formula needs ∂(x, y)/∂(u, v), the derivatives of the old variables with respect to the new ones. It is often easier to compute ∂(u, v)/∂(x, y) first, because u and v are usually given as simple expressions in x and y — but then you must take the reciprocal, ∂(x, y)/∂(u, v) = 1 / ∂(u, v)/∂(x, y), or your answer comes out upside down. Third, transforming only half the problem: if you change the integrand but keep the old region (or change the region but keep the old integrand), the integral is neither the old one nor the new one — it is nonsense. Transform everything: integrand, region, and area element.

Mini-example — the setup for Ex. 14.7-21. The region is bounded by the lines x − 2y = 1, x − 2y = 4, 2x + y = 1 and 2x + y = 3 — a slanted rectangle. Read u and v off the boundary curves, exactly as the guide advises: set u = x − 2y and v = 2x + y. Then the four boundary lines become u = 1, u = 4, v = 1 and v = 3, so in the uv-plane the region is the ordinary axis-aligned rectangle 1 ≤ u ≤ 4, 1 ≤ v ≤ 3. Now the Jacobian, via the shortcut: ∂(u, v)/∂(x, y) = (∂u/∂x)(∂v/∂y) − (∂u/∂y)(∂v/∂x) = (1)(1) − (−2)(2) = 5, so by the reciprocal relation ∂(x, y)/∂(u, v) = 1/5 — every little patch shrinks to a fifth of its size. The integral over the slanted region is now an integral over a plain rectangle with the factor 1/5 in front, and the guide's verified answer for this exercise is (3/2) ln 3. Notice what made it work: the new variables were not chosen at random — they were the expressions already written on the boundary.

Jacobian (2 variables): ∂(x, y)/∂(u, v) = (∂x/∂u)(∂y/∂v) − (∂x/∂v)(∂y/∂u)

Change of variables: ∬R f(x, y) dA = ∬S f(g(u, v), h(u, v)) · |∂(x, y)/∂(u, v)| du dv

Reciprocal relation: ∂(x, y)/∂(u, v) = 1 / ∂(u, v)/∂(x, y)

Polar Jacobian: ∂(x, y)/∂(r, θ) = r  (NOT r² — Ex. 14.7-15 as printed is FALSE)

Cylindrical Jacobian: r  ·  Spherical Jacobian: ρ² sin φ

Worked example — Ex. 14.7-25 (verified answer: 96π).

Problem: Evaluate ∬R √(16x² + 9y²) dA over the ellipse x²/9 + y²/16 = 1.

Step 1 — Choose the transformation from the region. The ellipse has denominators 9 and 16, so set x = 3u and y = 4v. Then x²/9 + y²/16 becomes u² + v², and the ellipse becomes the unit disk u² + v² ≤ 1. That is the whole point: an awkward region becomes a friendly one.

Step 2 — Compute the Jacobian. ∂(x, y)/∂(u, v) = (∂x/∂u)(∂y/∂v) − (∂x/∂v)(∂y/∂u) = (3)(4) − (0)(0) = 12. So dA = 12 du dv — every patch is stretched twelvefold.

Step 3 — Transform the integrand. 16x² + 9y² = 16(9u²) + 9(16v²) = 144(u² + v²), so √(16x² + 9y²) = 12√(u² + v²). The integral is now ∬unit disk 12√(u² + v²) · 12 du dv = 144 ∬ √(u² + v²) du dv.

Step 4 — Finish in polar coordinates. On the unit disk, √(u² + v²) = r and du dv = r dr dθ, so the integral is 144 ∫02π ∫01 r · r dr dθ = 144 · 2π · [r³/3]01 = 144 · 2π · (1/3) = 96π.

Answer: 96π. Notice how three ideas chained together: change of variables to fix the region, the Jacobian to fix the area, and polar coordinates to finish the job.

Watch out: the Jacobian in the formula is ∂(x, y)/∂(u, v), not ∂(u, v)/∂(x, y) — they are reciprocals of each other, and using the wrong one flips your answer upside down. And never forget the absolute value bars.

  • What is the Jacobian, in plain words — what does it measure?
  • What are the two reasons to change variables, and how do you choose u and v in each case?
  • Why is the polar Jacobian r, and why is the printed statement ∂(x, y)/∂(r, θ) = r² false?
  • What is the correct exercise set for this lecture, and why is the plan's "Ex. 13.9" wrong?

Ex. 14.7 — Compute Jacobians: 1–12. True–False on Jacobian facts: 13–16 (including 15, the false r² statement). Sketch the image of a set under a transformation: 17–20. Evaluate double integrals by a given/own transformation: 21–28, 35–38. Triple integrals by transformation: 29, 30. Find the transformation mapping region R to region S: 31–34. Harder transformations: 44–46.

CHANGE OF VARIABLES IN MULTIPLE INTEGRAL

Change of Variables & The Jacobian | Multi-variable Integration

Change of Variables and the Jacobian

Change of Variables Explained Visually | Why the Jacobian Appears in Integrals

Lecture 17 — Change of Variables in Multiple Integrals (Anton §14.7)

Note on the source: the lecture plan lists this set as "Ex. 13.9" — that is a typo; the correct set is Ex. 14.7 (Anton, pp. 1069–1070). In the text extraction the superscript in Ex. 15 prints as "r2"; it is r2. Answers were checked with SymPy.

Ex. 14.7: 15

True–False. The Jacobian of the transformation x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ is ∂(x, y)/∂(r, θ) = r2. Explain your answer.

Compute the Jacobian determinant directly: ∂x/∂r = cos θ, ∂x/∂θ = −r sin θ, ∂y/∂r = sin θ, ∂y/∂θ = r cos θ. Hence ∂(x, y)/∂(r, θ) = (cos θ)(r cos θ) − (−r sin θ)(sin θ) = r cos2 θ + r sin2 θ = r. This is r, not r2, so the statement as printed is false. (The polar area element is dA = r dr dθ.)

Answer: False — the polar Jacobian is r, not r2.

Ex. 14.7: 16

True–False. The Jacobian of the transformation x = ρ sin φ cos θ, y = ρ sin φ sin θ, z = ρ cos φ is ∂(x, y, z)/∂(ρ, φ, θ) = ρ2 sin φ. Explain your answer.

Form the 3 × 3 determinant of partial derivatives. The rows are (sin φ cos θ, ρ cos φ cos θ, −ρ sin φ sin θ), (sin φ sin θ, ρ cos φ sin θ, ρ sin φ cos θ) and (cos φ, −ρ sin φ, 0). Expanding the determinant (for instance along the third row) gives ρ2 sin φ (cos2 θ + sin2 θ) = ρ2 sin φ, which is exactly the stated value. This is the familiar spherical volume element dV = ρ2 sin φ dρ dφ dθ.

Answer: True — the spherical Jacobian is ρ2 sin φ.

Ex. 14.7: 21

Use the transformation u = x − 2y, v = 2x + y to find ∬R (x − 2y)/(2x + y) dA, where R is the rectangular region enclosed by the lines x − 2y = 1, x − 2y = 4, 2x + y = 1, 2x + y = 3.

The boundary lines are exactly u = 1, u = 4, v = 1, v = 3, so in the uv-plane the region is the rectangle S: 1 ≤ u ≤ 4, 1 ≤ v ≤ 3. The Jacobian ∂(u, v)/∂(x, y) = (1)(1) − (−2)(2) = 5, so by the reciprocal relation ∂(x, y)/∂(u, v) = 1/5. The integrand becomes u/v. Hence ∬R (x − 2y)/(2x + y) dA = ∫13 ∫14 (u/v)(1/5) du dv = (1/5)(∫14 u du)(∫13 dv/v) = (1/5)(15/2)(ln 3) = (3/2) ln 3.

Answer: (3/2) ln 3.

Ex. 14.7: 22

Use the transformation u = x + y, v = x − y to find ∬R (x − y)ex2 − y2 dA over the rectangular region R enclosed by the lines x + y = 0, x + y = 1, x − y = 1, x − y = 4.

The region becomes the rectangle S: 0 ≤ u ≤ 1, 1 ≤ v ≤ 4. Solving, x = (u + v)/2 and y = (u − v)/2, so ∂(x, y)/∂(u, v) = (1/2)(−1/2) − (1/2)(1/2) = −1/2, and |∂(x, y)/∂(u, v)| = 1/2. Also x2 − y2 = (x − y)(x + y) = uv, and x − y = v, so the integral is (1/2)∫01∫14 v euv dv du. Integrating with respect to u first is easier: ∫01 v euv du = ev − 1. Hence the integral is (1/2)∫14 (ev − 1) dv = (1/2)[ev − v]14 = (1/2)(e4 − 4 − e + 1) = (e4 − e − 3)/2.

Answer: (e4 − e − 3)/2.

Ex. 14.7: 23

Use the transformation u = ½(x + y), v = ½(x − y) to find ∬R sin ½(x + y) cos ½(x − y) dA over the triangular region R with vertices (0, 0), (2, 0), (1, 1).

Solving, x = u + v and y = u − v, so ∂(x, y)/∂(u, v) = (1)(−1) − (1)(1) = −2, and |∂(x, y)/∂(u, v)| = 2. The vertices map as (0, 0) → (0, 0), (2, 0) → (1, 1), (1, 1) → (1, 0), so S is the triangle 0 ≤ u ≤ 1, 0 ≤ v ≤ u. The integrand is sin u cos v, so the integral is 2∫01∫0u sin u cos v dv du = 2∫01 sin u · sin u du = 2∫01 sin2 u du = 2[u/2 − sin 2u/4]01 = 1 − (sin 2)/2.

Answer: 1 − (sin 2)/2 ≈ 0.545.

Ex. 14.7: 24

Use the transformation u = y/x, v = xy to find ∬R xy3 dA over the region R in the first quadrant enclosed by y = x, y = 3x, xy = 1, xy = 4.

The boundary curves are u = 1, u = 3, v = 1, v = 4, so S is the rectangle 1 ≤ u ≤ 3, 1 ≤ v ≤ 4. Compute ∂(u, v)/∂(x, y): ∂u/∂x = −y/x2, ∂u/∂y = 1/x, ∂v/∂x = y, ∂v/∂y = x, so the determinant is (−y/x2)(x) − (1/x)(y) = −2y/x = −2u. Hence |∂(x, y)/∂(u, v)| = 1/(2u). Also y2 = (y/x)(xy) = uv, so xy3 = (xy)y2 = v · uv = uv2. The integral is ∫13∫14 uv2 · (1/(2u)) dv du = (1/2)(∫13 du)(∫14 v2 dv) = (1/2)(2)(63/3) = 21.

Answer: 21.

Ex. 14.7: 25

∬R √(16x2 + 9y2) dA, where R is the region enclosed by the ellipse (x2/9) + (y2/16) = 1. (Transform the elliptical region into a circular region and evaluate in polar coordinates.)

Put x = 3u, y = 4v, so that the ellipse becomes the unit disk u2 + v2 ≤ 1 and |∂(x, y)/∂(u, v)| = 12. The integrand becomes √(16 · 9u2 + 9 · 16v2) = 12√(u2 + v2) = 12r in polar coordinates. Hence the integral is ∫02π∫01 12r · 12 · r dr dθ = 144 · 2π · (1/3) = 96π.

Answer: 96π.

Ex. 14.7: 26

∬R e−(x2 + 4y2) dA, where R is the region enclosed by the ellipse (x2/4) + y2 = 1. (Transform the elliptical region into a circular region and evaluate in polar coordinates.)

Put x = 2u, y = v, so the ellipse becomes the unit disk u2 + v2 ≤ 1 and |∂(x, y)/∂(u, v)| = 2. The exponent becomes x2 + 4y2 = 4u2 + 4v2 = 4r2 in polar coordinates. Hence the integral is ∫02π∫01 e−4r2 · 2 · r dr dθ = 4π · ∫01 r e−4r2 dr. With w = 4r2, the inner integral is (1/8)(1 − e−4), so the result is 4π(1 − e−4)/8 = (π/2)(1 − e−4).

Answer: (π/2)(1 − e−4).

Ex. 14.7: 27

∬R sin(4x2 + 9y2) dA, where R is the region in the first quadrant enclosed by the ellipse 4x2 + 9y2 = 1 and the coordinate axes. (Transform the elliptical region into a circular region and evaluate in polar coordinates.)

Put x = u/2, y = v/3, so 4x2 + 9y2 = u2 + v2 and |∂(x, y)/∂(u, v)| = 1/6. The first quadrant gives the quarter-disk 0 ≤ r ≤ 1, 0 ≤ θ ≤ π/2. Hence the integral is ∫0π/2∫01 sin(r2) · (1/6) · r dr dθ = (π/2)(1/6)∫01 r sin(r2) dr. With w = r2, the inner integral is (1 − cos 1)/2, so the result is (π/12)(1 − cos 1)/2 = π(1 − cos 1)/24.

Answer: π(1 − cos 1)/24.

Ex. 14.7: 28

Show that the area of the ellipse x2/a2 + y2/b2 = 1 is πab.

Put x = au, y = bv (a, b > 0). This maps the unit disk u2 + v2 ≤ 1 onto the ellipse, with |∂(x, y)/∂(u, v)| = ab. The area is ∬R dA = ∬u2 + v2 ≤ 1 ab du dv = ab · (area of the unit disk) = ab · π(1)2 = πab.

Answer: πab.

Ex. 14.7: 29

∭G x2 dV, where G is the region enclosed by the ellipsoid 9x2 + 4y2 + z2 = 36. (Transform the ellipsoidal region into a spherical region and evaluate in spherical coordinates.)

Write the ellipsoid as x2/4 + y2/9 + z2/36 = 1, so a = 2, b = 3, c = 6. Put x = 2u, y = 3v, z = 6w; then |∂(x, y, z)/∂(u, v, w)| = 2 · 3 · 6 = 36 and G becomes the unit ball u2 + v2 + w2 ≤ 1. The integral is 36∭unit ball (2u)2 dV = 144∭unit ball u2 dV. By symmetry ∭u2 dV = ∭v2 dV = ∭w2 dV = (1/3)∭(u2 + v2 + w2) dV = (1/3)∫01 ρ2 · 4πρ2 dρ = 4π/15. Hence the integral is 144 · 4π/15 = 192π/5.

Answer: 192π/5.

Ex. 14.7: 30

∭G (y2 + z2) dV, where G is the region enclosed by the ellipsoid x2/a2 + y2/b2 + z2/c2 = 1 (a, b, c positive constants). (Transform the ellipsoidal region into a spherical region and evaluate in spherical coordinates.)

Put x = au, y = bv, z = cw; then |∂(x, y, z)/∂(u, v, w)| = abc and G becomes the unit ball. The integral is abc∭unit ball (b2v2 + c2w2) dV = abc(b2∭v2 dV + c2∭w2 dV). As in Ex. 29, each of ∭v2 dV and ∭w2 dV over the unit ball equals 4π/15, so the result is abc(b2 + c2) · 4π/15 = (4π/15)abc(b2 + c2).

Answer: (4π/15)abc(b2 + c2).

Ex. 14.7: 31

Find a transformation u = f(x, y), v = g(x, y) that when applied to the region R in the xy-plane has as its image the region S in the uv-plane. R is the upper half-annulus 1 ≤ √(x2 + y2) ≤ 2, y ≥ 0 (bounded by the semicircles of radius 1 and 2 above the x-axis); S is the rectangle 0 ≤ u ≤ π, 1 ≤ v ≤ 2. (Figure, Anton p. 1069, Ex. 31.)

R is described in polar coordinates by 1 ≤ r ≤ 2 and 0 ≤ θ ≤ π, while S is a rectangle in the (θ, r) variables. Take u = θ and v = r, i.e. u = tan−1(y/x) (with θ taken in [0, π] for the upper half-plane) and v = √(x2 + y2). Then r = 1 maps to v = 1, r = 2 maps to v = 2, θ = 0 maps to u = 0 and θ = π maps to u = π, so R maps onto S. (The answer is not unique; any equivalent choice of the angle, e.g. u = cos−1(x/√(x2 + y2)), works.)

Answer: u = tan−1(y/x), v = √(x2 + y2).

Ex. 14.7: 32

Find a transformation u = f(x, y), v = g(x, y) that when applied to the region R in the xy-plane has as its image the region S in the uv-plane. R is the right half-annulus 1 ≤ √(x2 + y2) ≤ 3, x ≥ 0 (bounded by the semicircles of radius 1 and 3 to the right of the y-axis); S is the rectangle 1 ≤ u ≤ 3, 0 ≤ v ≤ 1. (Figure, Anton p. 1069, Ex. 32.)

In polar coordinates R is 1 ≤ r ≤ 3 and −π/2 ≤ θ ≤ π/2. Take u = r = √(x2 + y2), which runs from 1 to 3, and rescale the angle to run from 0 to 1: v = (θ + π/2)/π = 1/2 + θ/π, i.e. v = 1/2 + (1/π)tan−1(y/x). Then θ = −π/2 gives v = 0 and θ = π/2 gives v = 1, so R maps onto the rectangle 1 ≤ u ≤ 3, 0 ≤ v ≤ 1. (The answer is not unique.)

Answer: u = √(x2 + y2), v = 1/2 + (1/π)tan−1(y/x).

Ex. 14.7: 33

Find a transformation u = f(x, y), v = g(x, y) that when applied to the region R in the xy-plane has as its image the region S in the uv-plane. R is the parallelogram with vertices (0, 0), (2, 3), (5, 4), (3, 1); S is the unit square 0 ≤ u ≤ 1, 0 ≤ v ≤ 1. (Figure, Anton p. 1069, Ex. 33.)

The sides of R lie on the lines 3x − 2y = 0 and 3x − 2y = 7 (through (0, 0), (2, 3) and through (3, 1), (5, 4)) and on the lines 3y − x = 0 and 3y − x = 7 (through (0, 0), (3, 1) and through (2, 3), (5, 4)). Dividing by 7 normalises each pair to the range [0, 1], so set u = (3x − 2y)/7 and v = (3y − x)/7. Check the vertices: (0, 0) → (0, 0), (2, 3) → (0, 1), (5, 4) → (1, 1), (3, 1) → (1, 0), so R maps onto the unit square. (The answer is not unique; swapping u and v also works.)

Answer: u = (3x − 2y)/7, v = (3y − x)/7.

Ex. 14.7: 34

Find a transformation u = f(x, y), v = g(x, y) that when applied to the region R in the xy-plane has as its image the region S in the uv-plane. R is the parallelogram with vertices (−3, 0), (0, 3), (4, 3), (1, 0); S is the square 0 ≤ u ≤ 3, 0 ≤ v ≤ 3. (Figure, Anton p. 1069, Ex. 34.)

The top and bottom of R are y = 3 and y = 0, so take v = y, which runs from 0 to 3. The slanted sides lie on y = x + 3 and y = x − 1, i.e. x − y = −3 and x − y = 1, so x − y runs over an interval of length 4; rescaling by 3/4 and shifting gives u = (3/4)(x − y + 3), which runs from 0 to 3. Check the vertices: (−3, 0) → (0, 0), (0, 3) → (0, 3), (4, 3) → (3, 3), (1, 0) → (3, 0), so R maps onto the 3 × 3 square. (The answer is not unique.)

Answer: u = 3(x − y + 3)/4, v = y.

Ex. 14.7: 35

Evaluate ∬R (y − 4x)/(y + 4x) dA, where R is the region enclosed by the lines y = 4x, y = 4x + 2, y = 2 − 4x, y = 5 − 4x, by making an appropriate change of variables.

The boundary lines suggest u = y − 4x and v = y + 4x: then u = 0, u = 2, v = 2, v = 5, so S is the rectangle 0 ≤ u ≤ 2, 2 ≤ v ≤ 5. Now ∂(u, v)/∂(x, y) = (−4)(1) − (1)(4) = −8, so |∂(x, y)/∂(u, v)| = 1/8. The integrand is u/v, so the integral is (1/8)∫25∫02 (u/v) du dv = (1/8)(∫02 u du)(∫25 dv/v) = (1/8)(2)(ln(5/2)) = (1/4) ln(5/2).

Answer: (1/4) ln(5/2).

Ex. 14.7: 36

Evaluate ∬R (x2 − y2) dA, where R is the rectangular region enclosed by the lines y = −x, y = 1 − x, y = x, y = x + 2, by making an appropriate change of variables.

Write x2 − y2 = (x − y)(x + y) and set u = x + y, v = x − y. The boundary lines become u = 0, u = 1, v = 0, v = −2, so S is the rectangle 0 ≤ u ≤ 1, −2 ≤ v ≤ 0. Solving, x = (u + v)/2, y = (u − v)/2, so |∂(x, y)/∂(u, v)| = 1/2. The integral is (1/2)∫01∫−20 uv dv du = (1/2)(∫01 u du)(∫−20 v dv) = (1/2)(1/2)(−2) = −1/2. (The answer is negative because x2 − y2 < 0 on most of R, where |y| > |x|.)

Answer: −1/2.

Ex. 14.7: 37

Evaluate ∬R sin(x − y)/cos(x + y) dA, where R is the triangular region enclosed by the lines y = 0, y = x, x + y = π/4, by making an appropriate change of variables.

Set u = x + y, v = x − y. Then x = (u + v)/2, y = (u − v)/2, so |∂(x, y)/∂(u, v)| = 1/2. The boundary lines become v = u (from y = 0), v = 0 (from y = x) and u = π/4, so S is the triangle 0 ≤ u ≤ π/4, 0 ≤ v ≤ u. The integrand is sin v/cos u, so the integral is (1/2)∫0π/4 (1/cos u)∫0u sin v dv du = (1/2)∫0π/4 (1 − cos u)/cos u du = (1/2)∫0π/4 (sec u − 1) du = (1/2)[ln|sec u + tan u| − u]0π/4 = (1/2)(ln(√2 + 1) − π/4).

Answer: (1/2)(ln(√2 + 1) − π/4).

Ex. 14.7: 38

Evaluate ∬R e(y − x)/(y + x) dA, where R is the region in the first quadrant enclosed by the trapezoid with vertices (0, 1), (1, 0), (0, 4), (4, 0), by making an appropriate change of variables.

The slanted sides are x + y = 1 and x + y = 4, and the other sides are the axes x = 0 and y = 0. Set u = x + y, v = y − x, so (y − x)/(y + x) = v/u. Then x = (u − v)/2, y = (u + v)/2, so |∂(x, y)/∂(u, v)| = 1/2. For fixed u, the axes give −u ≤ v ≤ u (from x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0), and 1 ≤ u ≤ 4. Hence the integral is (1/2)∫14∫−uu ev/u dv du = (1/2)∫14 u[ev/u]−uu du = (1/2)∫14 u(e − e−1) du = (1/2)(e − 1/e)(15/2) = (15/4)(e − 1/e) = (15/2) sinh 1.

Answer: (15/4)(e − 1/e) = (15/2) sinh 1.

Ex. 14.7: 44

Use the transformation u = xy, v = xy4 to find ∬R sin(xy) dA, where R is the region enclosed by the curves xy = π, xy = 2π, xy4 = 1, xy4 = 2. (Use ∂(x, y)/∂(u, v) = 1 / (∂(u, v)/∂(x, y)) to avoid solving for x and y.)

The region becomes the rectangle S: π ≤ u ≤ 2π, 1 ≤ v ≤ 2. Compute ∂(u, v)/∂(x, y) = (y)(4xy3) − (x)(y4) = 4xy4 − xy4 = 3xy4 = 3v. By the reciprocal relation, |∂(x, y)/∂(u, v)| = 1/(3v). The integrand is sin u, so the integral is ∫π2π∫12 sin u · (1/(3v)) dv du = (1/3)(∫π2π sin u du)(∫12 dv/v) = (1/3)(−2)(ln 2) = −(2/3) ln 2. (The answer is negative because sin(xy) < 0 throughout R, since π < xy < 2π there.)

Answer: −(2/3) ln 2.

Ex. 14.7: 45

Use the transformation u = x2 − y2, v = x2 + y2 to find ∬R xy dA, where R is the region in the first quadrant that is enclosed by the hyperbolas x2 − y2 = 1, x2 − y2 = 4 and the circles x2 + y2 = 9, x2 + y2 = 16. (Use ∂(x, y)/∂(u, v) = 1 / (∂(u, v)/∂(x, y)) to avoid solving for x and y.)

The region becomes the rectangle S: 1 ≤ u ≤ 4, 9 ≤ v ≤ 16. Compute ∂(u, v)/∂(x, y) = (2x)(2y) − (−2y)(2x) = 8xy. By the reciprocal relation, |∂(x, y)/∂(u, v)| = 1/(8xy). The integrand xy therefore cancels exactly: xy · 1/(8xy) = 1/8. Hence the integral is (1/8) · (area of S) = (1/8)(4 − 1)(16 − 9) = (1/8)(3)(7) = 21/8.

Answer: 21/8.

Ex. 14.7: 46

Use the transformation u = xy, v = x2 − y2 to find ∬R (x4 − y4)exy dA, where R is the region in the first quadrant enclosed by the hyperbolas xy = 1, xy = 3, x2 − y2 = 3, x2 − y2 = 4. (Use ∂(x, y)/∂(u, v) = 1 / (∂(u, v)/∂(x, y)) to avoid solving for x and y.)

The region becomes the rectangle S: 1 ≤ u ≤ 3, 3 ≤ v ≤ 4. Compute ∂(u, v)/∂(x, y) = (y)(−2y) − (x)(2x) = −2(x2 + y2). Now (x2 + y2)2 = (x2 − y2)2 + 4x2y2 = v2 + 4u2, so x2 + y2 = √(v2 + 4u2) (positive in the first quadrant), and |∂(x, y)/∂(u, v)| = 1/(2√(v2 + 4u2)). Also x4 − y4 = (x2 − y2)(x2 + y2) = v√(v2 + 4u2), so the transformed integrand is v√(v2 + 4u2) · eu · 1/(2√(v2 + 4u2)) = (v/2)eu — the square roots cancel. Hence the integral is (1/2)(∫13 eu du)(∫34 v dv) = (1/2)(e3 − e)(7/2) = (7/4)(e3 − e) = (7e/4)(e2 − 1).

Answer: (7/4)(e3 − e).

Lecture 18 — Triple Integrals in Cylindrical and Spherical Coordinates (Anton §14.6)

Cylindrical coordinates are polar coordinates with height added; spherical coordinates aim at a point with a distance and two angles — pick whichever system matches the shape of your solid.

You already know polar coordinates from Lecture 15: a point in the plane is (r, θ) — how far out, and in which direction. Cylindrical coordinates are the laziest possible extension of that idea into three dimensions: keep r and θ exactly as they are, and just add z, the height, unchanged. So x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ, z = z. That is it. Nothing about the height changes, and the volume element is dV = r dz dr dθ — the same extra r from polar coordinates, because the horizontal slice is still a polar wedge.

When do you use cylindrical coordinates? When the solid has an axis of symmetry — a cylinder, a cone, a paraboloid — or when the integrand contains x² + y². Think of it this way: if the solid looks the same when you spin it around the z-axis, cylindrical coordinates will make the limits simple. The coordinate surfaces tell the story: r = constant is a cylinder, θ = constant is a half-plane through the z-axis, and z = constant is a horizontal plane. If your solid's boundaries are made of those surfaces, you are in the right system.

Spherical coordinates are a different way of aiming at a point, and they are the right choice when the solid involves spheres or cones with their vertex at the origin, or when the integrand contains x² + y² + z². Here you need three numbers: ρ (rho), the straight-line distance from the origin to the point; φ (phi), the angle down from the positive z-axis; and θ, the usual angle around the z-axis. The conversions are x = ρ sin φ cos θ, y = ρ sin φ sin θ, z = ρ cos φ, and the volume element is dV = ρ² sin φ dρ dφ dθ — the ρ² sin φ is the spherical Jacobian, the stretch factor of this change of variables.

The angle φ is the one students get wrong most often, so let me say it slowly: φ is measured from the positive z-axis, not from the xy-plane. φ = 0 points straight up along the +z-axis; φ = π/2 is the xy-plane itself; φ = π points straight down. A cone with its vertex at the origin is simply φ = constant — a beautiful, simple boundary in spherical coordinates, and a nightmare in Cartesian ones. And a sphere centred at the origin is just ρ = constant. That is the whole game: choose the system whose coordinate surfaces match your solid's boundaries. Sphere → ρ = a. Cone → φ = constant. Cylinder → r = a. Plane → z = constant.

One warning about notation: Anton uses ρ, θ, φ, but some books and videos swap θ and φ, or use different letters entirely. When you watch a video or read another source, always check which angle is measured from the z-axis before copying any formula. In this course, φ is always the angle from the z-axis.

Finally, a comparison that ties the chapter together: Exercise 27 asks for the volume of a sphere of radius a in both cylindrical and spherical coordinates, and Exercise 28 evaluates ∭ xyz dV over the first-octant part of the sphere x² + y² + z² = 4 in all three systems — rectangular, cylindrical and spherical. Both answers must come out the same (the sphere's volume is 4πa³/3), and doing the same problem three ways is the best possible revision: it forces you to see that the coordinate system is a choice, not a property of the solid.

Why two new systems? Cartesian coordinates are a street grid, and a street grid is wonderful until you need to describe a ball. Try describing a beach ball in street-grid language: "the set of points with x² + y² + z² ≤ 9" — correct, but the limits it gives you are a mess of square roots. Spherical coordinates describe the same ball as "ρ ≤ 3", one line. The point of a coordinate system is not to be "true" — it is to be convenient. Cylindrical and spherical coordinates are two more rulers, each built for a different shape, and the whole skill of this lecture is choosing the right ruler. The analogy to keep: describing a point in a room. Cartesian says "3 metres from the south wall, 2 from the west wall, 1 up from the floor". Spherical says "stand in the corner, aim at the point: it is 4 metres away, 60° down from the ceiling, and 30° around from the south wall". Same point, different description — and if the thing you care about is a sphere centred on that corner, the second description is far better.

Why ρ² sin φ — slowly. In cylindrical coordinates the extra r is the same polar wedge you already know: each horizontal slice is a polar wedge, so dV = r dz dr dθ. In spherical coordinates, picture a tiny box at the point (ρ, φ, θ). Its three sides are: a short step outward, of length dρ; a short step in the φ direction, which sweeps an arc of radius ρ, so its length is ρ dφ; and a short step in the θ direction, which sweeps an arc around the z-axis — but the circle it sweeps has radius ρ sin φ, the point's distance from the z-axis, so its length is ρ sin φ dθ. Multiply the three sides: dV = (dρ)(ρ dφ)(ρ sin φ dθ) = ρ² sin φ dρ dφ dθ. Every factor has a picture behind it, and the sin φ is there because the θ-circle shrinks as you approach the poles — at the north pole (φ = 0) the θ-circle has radius zero, so a step in θ moves you nowhere, and the volume element correctly collapses to zero.

How to choose: a decision tree. Look at the solid's boundaries and at the integrand, and ask three questions. First, is the solid a sphere, a ball, or a cone with its vertex at the origin — or does the integrand contain x² + y² + z²? If yes, spherical. Second, is the solid a cylinder, a paraboloid or a cone with an axis of symmetry, or does the integrand contain x² + y²? If yes, cylindrical. Third, is the solid a box, a tetrahedron or a wedge with flat faces? Then stay in Cartesian — no coordinate system beats a flat face. The coordinate surfaces are the cheat sheet: a sphere centred at the origin is ρ = a, a cone with vertex at the origin is φ = constant, a cylinder is r = a, a plane is z = constant. Match the solid's boundaries to the list, and the system picks itself.

Where students get stuck: φ, and the θ-range. The single most common error is measuring φ from the xy-plane, like a latitude on a globe. It is the opposite: φ is measured from the positive z-axis, like the angle of a searchlight beam pointing down from the ceiling. φ = 0 is straight up, φ = π/2 is the xy-plane, φ = π is straight down. So the upper half of a ball is 0 ≤ φ ≤ π/2, not 0 ≤ φ ≤ π — and the cone that is the upper half of an ice-cream cone is φ = π/4, a single constant. The second trap is the θ-range: a solid that is not a full revolution — say, only the first-octant part of a sphere — has θ running only 0 to π/2, and forgetting that integrates over four times as much solid as you have. And a note on notation, because it will bite you in videos: Anton uses ρ, θ, φ with φ from the z-axis, but some books swap θ and φ. Always check which angle is measured from the z-axis before copying a formula.

Mini-example — the volume of a sphere, in spherical coordinates (Ex. 14.6-27). The guide's verified answer is 4πa³/3, and spherical coordinates make it a three-line computation. The ball of radius a is 0 ≤ ρ ≤ a, 0 ≤ φ ≤ π, 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π, and with f = 1 the volume is V = ∫02π ∫0π ∫0a ρ² sin φ dρ dφ dθ. The three integrals separate: ∫0a ρ² dρ = a³/3, ∫0π sin φ dφ = 2, and ∫02π dθ = 2π. Multiply them: (a³/3) × 2 × 2π = 4πa³/3. The guide notes that the same answer comes out in cylindrical coordinates too — and doing it both ways is the best revision there is, because it proves the volume belongs to the ball, not to the coordinate system you chose.

Cylindrical: x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ, z = z

Cylindrical volume element: dV = r dz dr dθ

Spherical: x = ρ sin φ cos θ, y = ρ sin φ sin θ, z = ρ cos φ

Spherical volume element: dV = ρ² sin φ dρ dφ dθ

Sphere (origin): ρ = a  ·  Cone (vertex at origin): φ = constant  ·  Cylinder: r = a

Volume of a sphere of radius a = 4πa³ / 3

Worked example — Ex. 14.6-9 (verified answer: 81π/2).

Problem: Find the volume of the solid between the paraboloid z = x² + y² and the plane z = 9.

Step 1 — Choose the system. The solid is a paraboloid capped by a horizontal plane — it is symmetric about the z-axis, and the integrand for volume is just 1, so cylindrical coordinates are the natural choice.

Step 2 — Find where the surfaces meet. The paraboloid and the plane meet where x² + y² = 9, a circle of radius 3. In cylindrical coordinates that is r = 3, so the shadow on the xy-plane is the disk 0 ≤ r ≤ 3, and θ runs the full circle, 0 to 2π.

Step 3 — Set up the integral. For each (r, θ), z runs from the paraboloid (z = r²) up to the plane (z = 9). With dV = r dz dr dθ: V = ∫02π ∫03 ∫r²9 r dz dr dθ.

Step 4 — Integrate in z, then in r. The inner integral is (9 − r²) · r = 9r − r³. Integrating in r: ∫03 (9r − r³) dr = [ (9/2)r² − r⁴/4 ]03 = 81/2 − 81/4 = 81/4.

Step 5 — Integrate in θ. The θ-integral just multiplies by 2π: V = 2π × (81/4) = 81π/2.

Answer: 81π/2. The pattern to remember: find the intersection curve first (it gives the r-limit), then z runs from the lower surface to the upper one.

Watch out: φ is measured from the positive z-axis, not from the xy-plane — φ = π/2 is the xy-plane, and forgetting the sin φ in dV = ρ² sin φ dρ dφ dθ is the spherical version of dropping the r.

  • How are cylindrical coordinates built out of polar coordinates, and what is dV in each system?
  • What do ρ, φ and θ each measure in spherical coordinates, and from where is φ measured?
  • How do you decide whether to use cylindrical or spherical coordinates for a given solid?
  • Why is a cone with vertex at the origin so simple in spherical coordinates?

Ex. 14.6 — Volume via cylindrical coordinates: 9, 11, 12. Volume via spherical coordinates: 10, 13–16, 29. Convert / evaluate given iterated integrals: 17–20. Compare coordinate systems: 27, 28.
