Lecture 18 — Solutions: Ex. 14.6: 9–20, 27–29

Anton, Calculus, 10th edition, §14.6 (Triple Integrals in Cylindrical and Spherical Coordinates). All answers were checked with SymPy. Note on the book text: the text extraction drops the radical sign in the cone z = √(x2 + y2) in Ex. 10 and Ex. 16, and in the upper limit √(1 − x2 − y2) in Ex. 18; the statements below use the correct (radical) forms, which are the standard Anton problems.

Ex. 14.6: 9

Use cylindrical coordinates to find the volume of the solid enclosed by the paraboloid z = x2 + y2 and the plane z = 9.

The paraboloid meets the plane where x2 + y2 = 9, so in cylindrical coordinates the solid is 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π, 0 ≤ r ≤ 3, r2 ≤ z ≤ 9. Its volume is

V = ∫02π ∫03 ∫r29 r dz dr dθ = 2π ∫03 (9 − r2)r dr = 2π [ (9r2)/2 − r4/4 ]03 = 2π (81/2 − 81/4) = 81π/2.

Answer: 81π/2.

Ex. 14.6: 10

Use cylindrical coordinates to find the volume of the solid that is bounded above by the sphere x2 + y2 + z2 = 1 and below by the cone z = √(x2 + y2).

In cylindrical coordinates the sphere is z = √(1 − r2) and the cone is z = r. They meet where r = √(1 − r2), i.e. r = 1/√2. Hence the solid is 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π, 0 ≤ r ≤ 1/√2, r ≤ z ≤ √(1 − r2), so

V = ∫02π ∫01/√2 (√(1 − r2) − r) r dr dθ = 2π [ −(1 − r2)3/2/3 − r3/3 ]01/√2 = 2π (1/3 − √2/6) = π(2 − √2)/3.

(In spherical coordinates this is the cone φ = π/4 inside the sphere ρ = 1: V = 2π·(1/3)(1 − cos π/4), the same result.)

Answer: π(2 − √2)/3.

Ex. 14.6: 11

Use cylindrical coordinates to find the volume of the solid that is inside the surface r2 + z2 = 20 but not above the surface z = r2.

The solid lies inside the sphere of radius √20, with z ≤ r2 (and z ≥ −√(20 − r2), the bottom of the sphere). The paraboloid and the sphere meet where r2 = √(20 − r2), i.e. r4 + r2 − 20 = 0, so r = 2 (and z = 4). For 0 ≤ r ≤ 2 the top is the paraboloid z = r2; for 2 ≤ r ≤ √20 the paraboloid is above the sphere, so the top is the sphere z = √(20 − r2). Hence

V = 2π ∫02 (r2 + √(20 − r2)) r dr + 2π ∫2√20 2√(20 − r2) r dr.

With u = 20 − r2, ∫ r√(20 − r2) dr = −(20 − r2)3/2/3, and ∫02 r3 dr = 4. Evaluating: the first integral is 4 + (20√20 − 163/2)/3 = 4 + (40√5 − 64)/3, the second is 2·163/2/3 = 128/3. Adding and multiplying by 2π gives V = 8π(19 + 10√5)/3 ≈ 346.5.

Answer: 8π(19 + 10√5)/3.

Ex. 14.6: 12

Use cylindrical coordinates to find the volume of the solid enclosed between the cone z = (hr)/a and the plane z = h.

The cone has its vertex at the origin and meets the plane z = h where r = a. At height z the cross-section is a disc of radius r = az/h, so by discs

V = ∫0h π(az/h)2 dz = (πa2/h2) · h3/3 = πa2h/3,

the familiar volume of a cone of base radius a and height h. In cylindrical coordinates this is ∫02π ∫0a ∫hr/ah r dz dr dθ, which gives the same result.

Answer: πa2h/3.

Ex. 14.6: 13

Use spherical coordinates to find the volume of the solid bounded above by the sphere ρ = 4 and below by the cone φ = π/3.

The solid is the spherical cap 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π, 0 ≤ φ ≤ π/3, 0 ≤ ρ ≤ 4. With dV = ρ2 sin φ dρ dφ dθ,

V = ∫02π ∫0π/3 ∫04 ρ2 sin φ dρ dφ dθ = 2π · (64/3) · (1 − cos π/3) = 2π · (64/3) · (1/2) = 64π/3.

Answer: 64π/3.

Ex. 14.6: 14

Use spherical coordinates to find the volume of the solid within the cone φ = π/4 and between the spheres ρ = 1 and ρ = 2.

The solid is 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π, 0 ≤ φ ≤ π/4, 1 ≤ ρ ≤ 2. Hence

V = ∫02π ∫0π/4 ∫12 ρ2 sin φ dρ dφ dθ = 2π · (8 − 1)/3 · (1 − cos π/4) = (14π/3)(1 − √2/2) = 7π(2 − √2)/3.

Answer: 7π(2 − √2)/3.

Ex. 14.6: 15

Use spherical coordinates to find the volume of the solid enclosed by the sphere x2 + y2 + z2 = 4a2 and the planes z = 0 and z = a.

The solid is the slab 0 ≤ z ≤ a of the sphere of radius 2a. In spherical coordinates z = ρ cos φ, so the plane z = a is ρ = a sec φ, which meets the sphere ρ = 2a where cos φ = 1/2, i.e. φ = π/3. For 0 ≤ φ ≤ π/3 the plane is the outer limit (ρ ≤ a sec φ); for π/3 ≤ φ ≤ π/2 the sphere is the outer limit (ρ ≤ 2a). Thus

V = 2π ∫0π/3 ∫0a sec φ ρ2 sin φ dρ dφ + 2π ∫π/3π/2 ∫02a ρ2 sin φ dρ dφ

= (2πa3/3) ∫0π/3 sec2 φ tan φ dφ + (16πa3/3)(1/2) = (2πa3/3)·(3/2) + (8πa3/3) = 11πa3/3.

(Check by discs: V = ∫0a π(4a2 − z2) dz = π(4a3 − a3/3) = 11πa3/3.)

Answer: 11πa3/3.

Ex. 14.6: 16

Use spherical coordinates to find the volume of the solid within the sphere x2 + y2 + z2 = 9, outside the cone z = √(x2 + y2), and above the xy-plane.

The cone z = √(x2 + y2) is φ = π/4, the sphere is ρ = 3, and "above the xy-plane" is φ ≤ π/2. "Outside the cone" means φ ≥ π/4. So the solid is 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π, π/4 ≤ φ ≤ π/2, 0 ≤ ρ ≤ 3, and

V = ∫02π ∫π/4π/2 ∫03 ρ2 sin φ dρ dφ dθ = 2π · 9 · (cos π/4 − cos π/2) = 18π · (√2/2) = 9√2 π.

Answer: 9√2 π.

Ex. 14.6: 17

Use cylindrical or spherical coordinates to evaluate the integral ∫0a ∫0√(a2 − x2) ∫0a2 − x2 − y2 x2 dz dy dx (a > 0).

The region is the first-quadrant part (x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0) under the paraboloid z = a2 − r2, above z = 0. In cylindrical coordinates x = r cos θ, 0 ≤ θ ≤ π/2, 0 ≤ r ≤ a, 0 ≤ z ≤ a2 − r2, and dV = r dz dr dθ:

I = ∫0π/2 ∫0a ∫0a2 − r2 (r cos θ)2 r dz dr dθ = ∫0π/2 cos2 θ dθ · ∫0a (a2r3 − r5) dr

= (π/4) · (a6/4 − a6/6) = (π/4)(a6/12) = πa6/48.

Answer: πa6/48.

Ex. 14.6: 18

Use cylindrical or spherical coordinates to evaluate the integral ∫−11 ∫0√(1 − x2) ∫0√(1 − x2 − y2) e−(x2 + y2 + z2)3/2 dz dy dx.

The region is the half-ball x2 + y2 + z2 ≤ 1 with y ≥ 0, z ≥ 0. In spherical coordinates the integrand is e−ρ3 (since (x2 + y2 + z2)3/2 = ρ3) and dV = ρ2 sin φ dρ dφ dθ, with 0 ≤ ρ ≤ 1, 0 ≤ φ ≤ π/2, and 0 ≤ θ ≤ π (the half y ≥ 0):

I = ∫0π ∫0π/2 ∫01 e−ρ3 ρ2 sin φ dρ dφ dθ = π · 1 · ∫01 ρ2 e−ρ3 dρ.

With u = ρ3, du = 3ρ2 dρ, the last integral is (1/3)∫01 e−u du = (1 − e−1)/3. (A numerical check in cylindrical coordinates gives 0.66196, matching π(1 − e−1)/3.)

Answer: π(1 − e−1)/3.

Ex. 14.6: 19

Use cylindrical or spherical coordinates to evaluate the integral ∫02 ∫0√(4 − y2) ∫√(x2 + y2)√(8 − x2 − y2) z2 dz dx dy.

The region is the first-quadrant (x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0) part between the cone z = r (φ = π/4) and the sphere of radius √8 = 2√2. In spherical coordinates z = ρ cos φ, dV = ρ2 sin φ dρ dφ dθ, with 0 ≤ θ ≤ π/2, 0 ≤ φ ≤ π/4, 0 ≤ ρ ≤ 2√2:

I = ∫0π/2 ∫0π/4 ∫02√2 (ρ cos φ)2 ρ2 sin φ dρ dφ dθ = (π/2) · ∫0π/4 cos2 φ sin φ dφ · ∫02√2 ρ4 dρ.

∫0π/4 cos2 φ sin φ dφ = (1 − (√2/2)3)/3 = (4 − √2)/12, and ∫02√2 ρ4 dρ = (2√2)5/5 = 128√2/5. Hence I = (π/2)·((4 − √2)/12)·(128√2/5) = 32π(2√2 − 1)/15.

Answer: 32π(2√2 − 1)/15.

Ex. 14.6: 20

Use cylindrical or spherical coordinates to evaluate the integral ∫−33 ∫−√(9 − y2)√(9 − y2) ∫−√(9 − x2 − y2)√(9 − x2 − y2) (x2 + y2 + z2) dz dx dy.

The region is the whole ball of radius 3, and the integrand is ρ2. In spherical coordinates, with dV = ρ2 sin φ dρ dφ dθ:

I = ∫02π ∫0π ∫03 ρ2 · ρ2 sin φ dρ dφ dθ = 2π · 2 · (35/5) = 972π/5.

Answer: 972π/5.

Ex. 14.6: 27

Find the volume enclosed by x2 + y2 + z2 = a2 using (a) cylindrical coordinates (b) spherical coordinates.

(a) Cylindrical: the sphere is −√(a2 − r2) ≤ z ≤ √(a2 − r2), 0 ≤ r ≤ a, 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π. So V = ∫02π ∫0a 2√(a2 − r2) r dr dθ = 2π · [ −(2/3)(a2 − r2)3/2 ]0a = 2π · (2a3/3) = 4πa3/3.

(b) Spherical: 0 ≤ ρ ≤ a, 0 ≤ φ ≤ π, 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π. So V = ∫02π ∫0π ∫0a ρ2 sin φ dρ dφ dθ = 2π · 2 · (a3/3) = 4πa3/3, the same as in (a), as it must be.

Answer: 4πa3/3 (both methods).

Ex. 14.6: 28

Let G be the solid in the first octant bounded by the sphere x2 + y2 + z2 = 4 and the coordinate planes. Evaluate ∭G xyz dV (a) using rectangular coordinates (b) using cylindrical coordinates (c) using spherical coordinates.

(a) Rectangular: I = ∫02 ∫0√(4 − x2) ∫0√(4 − x2 − y2) xyz dz dy dx. The z-integral gives xy(4 − x2 − y2)/2. Then ∫0√(4 − x2) xy(4 − x2 − y2)/2 dy = x(4 − x2)2/8, and ∫02 x(4 − x2)2/8 dx = 4/3.

(b) Cylindrical: xyz = r2 cos θ sin θ · z and dV = r dz dr dθ, with 0 ≤ θ ≤ π/2, 0 ≤ r ≤ 2, 0 ≤ z ≤ √(4 − r2). The z-integral gives (4 − r2)/2, so I = ∫0π/2 cos θ sin θ dθ · ∫02 r3(4 − r2)/2 dr = (1/2) · (8/3) = 4/3.

(c) Spherical: xyz = ρ3 sin2 φ cos φ sin θ cos θ and dV = ρ2 sin φ dρ dφ dθ, with 0 ≤ ρ ≤ 2, 0 ≤ φ ≤ π/2, 0 ≤ θ ≤ π/2. The integral separates: I = ∫02 ρ5 dρ · ∫0π/2 sin3 φ cos φ dφ · ∫0π/2 sin θ cos θ dθ = (32/3) · (1/4) · (1/2) = 4/3.

All three systems agree, as they must.

Answer: 4/3 (rectangular, cylindrical, and spherical).

Ex. 14.6: 29

Find the volume of the solid in the first octant bounded by the sphere ρ = 2, the coordinate planes, and the cones φ = π/6 and φ = π/3.

The first octant gives 0 ≤ θ ≤ π/2; the two cones bound φ between π/6 and π/3; the sphere gives 0 ≤ ρ ≤ 2. Hence

V = ∫0π/2 ∫π/6π/3 ∫02 ρ2 sin φ dρ dφ dθ = (π/2) · (8/3) · (cos π/6 − cos π/3) = (4π/3)(√3/2 − 1/2) = 2π(√3 − 1)/3.

Answer: 2π(√3 − 1)/3.

Lecture 19 — Vector Fields, Line Integrals & Conservative Fields (Anton §15.1–15.3)

A vector field puts a little arrow at every point of space, a line integral adds up how much of that arrow pushes you along a path, and a conservative field is one where only your starting and finishing heights matter — never the road you took.

Imagine you are looking at a weather map. At every town on the map there is a little arrow showing which way the wind blows there, and how strongly. That is all a vector field is: a rule that attaches one arrow — one vector — to every point. We write it as F(x, y) = f(x, y)i + g(x, y)j in the plane, or with a third component h(x, y, z)k in space. The wind is the classic example; gravity is another (every point in space has a pull towards the Earth), and so is the electric field around a charge.

Now suppose you walk along a path C through that wind. Sometimes the wind is at your back and helps you, sometimes it is in your face and fights you, sometimes it blows sideways and does nothing at all. A line integral is simply the total of all that helping and fighting, added up along the whole walk. In symbols, the work done is W = ∫C F · dr. The dot product is the key: only the part of the wind that points along your path counts. Wind blowing across your path contributes nothing, however strong it is. There is also a simpler kind of line integral, ∫C f ds, which adds up a number (like the mass of a wire, if f is its density) along a curve — here ds is just a tiny piece of arc length, and walking the path backwards changes nothing.

Two new measuring tools come with vector fields. Divergence (div F) is a single number at each point that says whether the field is spreading out from that point, like water flowing out of a tap, or flowing in, like water down a drain. Curl (curl F) is a vector that says whether the field is spinning around that point, like water swirling around a plughole — and which way it spins. Divergence is a number, curl is an arrow: do not mix them up.

The most important idea of this lecture is the conservative field. Think of walking on a hill. The work gravity does on you depends only on how high you start and how high you finish — walk straight up, or take the long winding path, and gravity does exactly the same work. A field like that is called conservative, and it can always be written as the gradient of some height function, called its potential φ: F = ∇φ. Then the Fundamental Theorem of Line Integrals says ∫C F · dr = φ(end) − φ(start). You never need to integrate along the path at all — just read off the two heights. And round any closed loop the answer is zero, because you end where you started.

How do you test whether a field is conservative? In the plane, check whether ∂f/∂y = ∂g/∂x — that is, differentiate the i-component with respect to y and the j-component with respect to x, and see if they match. In space, check whether curl F = 0. But be careful: the test is only a guarantee when the region has no holes in it (mathematicians say "simply connected"). A field can pass the test and still fail to be conservative if its domain has a hole at the origin — the field F = y/(x² + y²) i − x/(x² + y²) j is the famous example. The potential, when it exists, is never unique: you can always add a constant K, and it cancels in φ(end) − φ(start).

Before going further, stop and ask why this lecture exists at all. In first-year calculus every integral was over an interval on the x-axis: ∫ab f(x) dx. But the quantities that matter in the real world do not live on the x-axis. The work done pushing a boat through a current, the mass of a bent wire, the charge sitting on a curved filament — all of these live along a curve in space. The line integral is the tool that lets you add things up along a curve instead of along a straight line. It is the same idea as the ordinary integral — chop something into tiny pieces, add the pieces up, take the limit — only now the "something" is a path.

So what is a line integral actually adding up? Chop the path C into tiny steps. On one tiny step, the field F pushes with some strength in some direction, and you move a tiny distance Δr along the path. The work of that one step is roughly F · Δr, and the line integral is the sum of all those little works. The dot product is doing real work here: it throws away the part of the push that is sideways to your motion. Imagine pushing a shopping trolley forward while someone shoves it sideways — the sideways shove does not help it move forward at all, however hard it is. That is why only the tangential part of F contributes, and why the formula can be written ∫C F · T ds, with T the unit tangent to the path. The other kind of line integral, ∫C f ds, adds up a plain number instead — if f is the density of a wire, the integral is its mass, and for f ≥ 0 it is also the area of the vertical "curtain" standing above the curve under the surface z = f(x, y).

This is also where students most often trip: the two kinds of line integral behave differently when you walk the path backwards. The mass of a wire does not care which end you start from, so ∫−C f ds = +∫C f ds. But work does care — walk the same hill backwards and gravity does exactly the opposite work — so ∫−C F · dr = −∫C F · dr, and the same sign flip happens for ∫ f dx, ∫ f dy and ∫ f dz. If a sign ever looks wrong in your answer, check the direction of travel first. The other classic slip is in the parametrisation step: ∫C f ds = ∫ab f(x(t), y(t)) ‖r′(t)‖ dt, and that ‖r′(t)‖ factor — the speed at which you travel the parametrisation — is easy to forget and fatal to leave out.

Now the deep idea: why does path-independence mean the field is a gradient? It is the same pattern as the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus you already know, ∫ab f′(x) dx = F(b) − F(a): the integral of a derivative only sees the endpoints. Here the "derivative" is the gradient, and the theorem says the same thing one dimension up. And the test ∂f/∂y = ∂g/∂x has a physical meaning too: it says the field has no local spin anywhere — the curl is zero, there are no whirlpools for a path to gain extra circulation from, so no route can beat any other route. That is also why a hole in the region breaks the guarantee: a path can loop round the hole and trap circulation that no local test can see, which is exactly what happens with the field F = y/(x² + y²) i − x/(x² + y²) j on the plane with the origin removed.

Mini-example — using the potential from the worked example above. Take the same field F = 3y² i + 6xy j, whose potential is φ = 3xy² + C. What is ∫C F · dr from (0, 0) to (1, 2) — along any path at all? By the Fundamental Theorem of Line Integrals it is just φ(1, 2) − φ(0, 0) = 3(1)(2)² − 0 = 12. No parametrisation, no dot product, no integral to compute — and the +C cancels, as it always does. Whenever you spot a conservative field, this is the shortcut the examiner expects you to take.

F(x, y) = f(x, y)i + g(x, y)j — a vector field: one vector at every point.

div F = ∂f/∂x + ∂g/∂y + ∂h/∂z — divergence: a number; spreading out (+) or flowing in (−).

curl F = (∂h/∂y − ∂g/∂z)i + (∂f/∂z − ∂h/∂x)j + (∂g/∂x − ∂f/∂y)k — curl: a vector; how much the field spins.

∫C f ds = ∫ab f(x(t), y(t)) ‖r′(t)‖ dt — line integral with respect to arc length (orientation does not matter).

∫C F · dr = ∫C f dx + g dy + h dz = ∫ab F(r(t)) · r′(t) dt — line integral of a vector field; work W = ∫C F · dr.

If F = ∇φ, then ∫C F · dr = φ(end) − φ(start) — Fundamental Theorem of Line Integrals.

Conservative test (plane): ∂f/∂y = ∂g/∂x (and the region has no holes). In space: curl F = 0.

∇²φ = div(∇φ) = φxx + φyy + φzz — the Laplacian; ∇²φ = 0 is Laplace's equation.

Worked example — Ex. 15.3-2 (verified answer from the guide). Is F = 3y² i + 6xy j conservative? If so, find a potential φ.

Step 1 — Read off the components. Here f = 3y² (the i-component) and g = 6xy (the j-component).

Step 2 — Apply the test. Differentiate f with respect to y: ∂f/∂y = 6y. Differentiate g with respect to x: ∂g/∂x = 6y. They match, so the test passes — and the whole plane has no holes, so the field is conservative.

Step 3 — Find the potential. We need φ with φx = 3y² and φy = 6xy. Integrating φx = 3y² with respect to x gives φ = 3xy² + (a function of y only). Differentiating that with respect to y gives 6xy, which already matches φy = 6xy, so the extra function of y is just a constant.

Answer: F is conservative, with potential φ = 3xy² + C.

Watch out: ∫ f ds does not change sign when you walk the path backwards, but ∫ f dx, ∫ f dy and ∫ F · dr all do — and in the conservative test, differentiate the i-component with respect to y and the j-component with respect to x; swapping them round is the classic slip.

  • What is a vector field, in one sentence, and what do divergence and curl each measure?
  • Why does only the tangential part of F contribute to ∫C F · dr, and what happens to the integral if you reverse the path?
  • What does it mean for a field to be conservative, and how do you evaluate its line integral without integrating along the path?
  • When does the test ∂f/∂y = ∂g/∂x fail to guarantee a field is conservative?

Ex. 15.1 (15–28): confirm φ is a potential (15, 16); find div F and curl F (17–22); find ∇·(F×G) (23, 24); find ∇·(∇×F) (25, 26); find ∇×(∇×F) (27, 28).

Ex. 15.2 (7–10, 13, 19–30, 33–56): ∫C F·dr along a line segment (7–10); same integral, four different paths (13); line integral w.r.t. s (19–22); ∫C f dx + g dy along a given curve (23–30); figure-based integrals (33–36); ∫C F·dr (37–40); mass of a thin wire (41–44); work (45–50); surface area via line integral (51, 52); applications / harder (53–56). Note: Ex. 15.2-33/34, 35/36, 49/50 depend on figures in the book.

Ex. 15.3 (1–18): determine if conservative; find φ if so (1–6); evaluate by two paths (7); show path-independence and evaluate directly and by the Fundamental Theorem (8–14); confirm conservative and find work P→Q (15–18).

Exercise Set 15.1

Ex. 15.1: 15(a)

Confirm that φ(x, y) = tan−1(xy) is a potential function for F(x, y) = y/(1 + x2y2) i + x/(1 + x2y2) j on some region, and state the region.

∂φ/∂x = y/(1 + (xy)2) and ∂φ/∂y = x/(1 + (xy)2) by the chain rule, since d/du tan−1u = 1/(1 + u2). Hence ∇φ = y/(1 + x2y2) i + x/(1 + x2y2) j = F.

Answer: Confirmed; φ is defined for all (x, y), so the region is the whole xy-plane.

Ex. 15.1: 15(b)

Confirm that φ(x, y, z) = x2 − 3y2 + 4z2 is a potential function for F(x, y, z) = 2x i − 6y j + 8z k on some region, and state the region.

∇φ = (2x, −6y, 8z) = F, by direct differentiation.

Answer: Confirmed; the region is all of 3-space.

Ex. 15.1: 16(a)

Confirm that φ(x, y) = 2y2 + 3x2y − xy3 is a potential function for F(x, y) = (6xy − y3) i + (4y + 3x2 − 3xy2) j on some region, and state the region.

∂φ/∂x = 6xy − y3 and ∂φ/∂y = 4y + 3x2 − 3xy2, which are exactly the components of F.

Answer: Confirmed; the region is the whole xy-plane.

Ex. 15.1: 16(b)

Confirm that φ(x, y, z) = x sin z + y sin x + z sin y is a potential function for F(x, y, z) = (sin z + y cos x) i + (sin x + z cos y) j + (sin y + x cos z) k on some region, and state the region.

∂φ/∂x = sin z + y cos x, ∂φ/∂y = sin x + z cos y, ∂φ/∂z = x cos z + sin y, which are the components of F.

Answer: Confirmed; the region is all of 3-space.

Ex. 15.1: 17

Find div F and curl F for F(x, y, z) = x2 i − 2 j + yz k.

div F = ∂(x2)/∂x + ∂(−2)/∂y + ∂(yz)/∂z = 2x + 0 + y. curl F = (∂(yz)/∂y − ∂(−2)/∂z, ∂(x2)/∂z − ∂(yz)/∂x, ∂(−2)/∂x − ∂(x2)/∂y) = (z, 0, 0).

Answer: div F = 2x + y; curl F = z i.

Ex. 15.1: 18

Find div F and curl F for F(x, y, z) = xz3 i + 2y4x2 j + 5z2y k.

div F = z3 + 8x2y3 + 10yz. curl F = (∂(5z2y)/∂y − 0, ∂(xz3)/∂z − 0, ∂(2y4x2)/∂x − 0) = (5z2, 3xz2, 4xy4).

Answer: div F = z3 + 8x2y3 + 10yz; curl F = 5z2 i + 3xz2 j + 4xy4 k.

Ex. 15.1: 19

Find div F and curl F for F(x, y, z) = 7y3z2 i − 8x2z5 j − 3xy4 k.

div F = 0 + 0 + 0 = 0. curl F: i-component ∂(−3xy4)/∂y − ∂(−8x2z5)/∂z = −12xy3 + 40x2z4; j-component ∂(7y3z2)/∂z − ∂(−3xy4)/∂x = 14y3z + 3y4; k-component ∂(−8x2z5)/∂x − ∂(7y3z2)/∂y = −16xz5 − 21y2z2.

Answer: div F = 0; curl F = (40x2z4 − 12xy3) i + (14y3z + 3y4) j − (16xz5 + 21y2z2) k.

Ex. 15.1: 20

Find div F and curl F for F(x, y, z) = exy i − cos y j + sin2z k.

div F = yexy + sin y + 2 sin z cos z = yexy + sin y + sin 2z. curl F: only the k-component is nonzero, ∂(−cos y)/∂x − ∂(exy)/∂y = −xexy.

Answer: div F = yexy + sin y + sin 2z; curl F = −xexy k.

Ex. 15.1: 21

Find div F and curl F for F(x, y, z) = (1/(x2 + y2 + z2))(x i + y j + z k).

Write r2 = x2 + y2 + z2. Then ∂/∂x (x/r2) = 1/r2 − 2x2/r4, and similarly for y, z. Adding: div F = 3/r2 − 2(x2 + y2 + z2)/r4 = 1/r2. The curl vanishes by symmetry (each component is a difference of equal terms, e.g. ∂(z/r2)/∂y − ∂(y/r2)/∂z = −2yz/r4 + 2yz/r4 = 0).

Answer: div F = 1/(x2 + y2 + z2); curl F = 0 (for (x, y, z) ≠ (0, 0, 0)).

Ex. 15.1: 22

Find div F and curl F for F(x, y, z) = ln x i + exyz j + tan−1(z/x) k.

div F = 1/x + xz exyz + (1/(1 + (z/x)2))·(1/x) = 1/x + xz exyz + x/(x2 + z2). curl F: i-component 0 − xy exyz; j-component 0 − (1/(1 + (z/x)2))·(−z/x2) = z/(x2 + z2); k-component yz exyz − 0.

Answer: div F = 1/x + xz exyz + x/(x2 + z2); curl F = −xy exyz i + z/(x2 + z2) j + yz exyz k.

Ex. 15.1: 23

Find ∇ · (F × G) for F(x, y, z) = 2x i + j + 4y k and G(x, y, z) = x i + y j − z k.

F × G = |i j k; 2x 1 4y; x y −z| = (−z − 4y2) i + (2xz + 4xy) j + (2xy − x) k. Then ∇ · (F × G) = ∂(−z − 4y2)/∂x + ∂(2xz + 4xy)/∂y + ∂(2xy − x)/∂z = 0 + 4x + 0.

Answer: ∇ · (F × G) = 4x.

Ex. 15.1: 24

Find ∇ · (F × G) for F(x, y, z) = yz i + xz j + xy k and G(x, y, z) = xy j + xyz k.

F × G = |i j k; yz xz xy; 0 xy xyz| = (x2yz2 − x2y2) i − xy2z2 j + xy2z k. Then ∇ · (F × G) = (2xyz2 − 2xy2) − 2xyz2 + xy2 = −xy2.

Answer: ∇ · (F × G) = −xy2.

Ex. 15.1: 25

Find ∇ · (∇ × F) for F(x, y, z) = sin x i + cos(x − y) j + z k.

For any twice-differentiable field, div(curl F) = 0 identically (the mixed partials cancel in pairs). Directly: ∇ × F = (0, 0, sin(x − y)), whose divergence is 0.

Answer: ∇ · (∇ × F) = 0.

Ex. 15.1: 26

Find ∇ · (∇ × F) for F(x, y, z) = exz i + 3xey j − eyz k.

Again div(curl F) = 0 by the identity div(∇ × F) = 0. (Directly, ∇ × F = (−yeyz, −zexz, 3ey), and its divergence is −yzeyz + yzeyz + 0 = 0.)

Answer: ∇ · (∇ × F) = 0.

Ex. 15.1: 27

Find ∇ × (∇ × F) for F(x, y, z) = xy j + xyz k.

∇ × F = (∂(xyz)/∂y − 0, 0 − ∂(xyz)/∂x, ∂(xy)/∂x − 0) = xz i − yz j + y k. Then ∇ × (∇ × F) = (∂(y)/∂y − ∂(−yz)/∂z, ∂(y)/∂x − ∂(xz)/∂z, ∂(−yz)/∂x − ∂(xz)/∂y) = (1 + y) i + x j.

Answer: ∇ × (∇ × F) = (1 + y) i + x j.

Ex. 15.1: 28

∇ × F = (∂(xy)/∂y − ∂(−3yz)/∂z, ∂(y2x)/∂z − ∂(xy)/∂x, ∂(−3yz)/∂x − ∂(y2x)/∂y) = (x + 3y) i − y j − 2xy k. Then ∇ × (∇ × F) = (∂(−2xy)/∂y − 0, ∂(−2xy)/∂x − 0 with sign, ∂(−y)/∂x − ∂(x + 3y)/∂y) = −2x i + 2y j − 3 k.

Answer: ∇ × (∇ × F) = −2x i + 2y j − 3 k.

Parametrize x = t2, y = t3, t from −1 to 1. Then (y − x) dx + x2y dy = (t3 − t2)(2t) dt + t4·t3·3t2 dt = (2t4 − 2t3 + 3t9) dt. Integrating from −1 to 1, the odd powers vanish and ∫−11 2t4 dt = 4/5.

Answer: 4/5.

Evaluate ∫C y dx − x dy along the curve C shown in Figure Ex-33: (a) the triangle with vertices (0, 0), (1, 0), (0, 1) traversed (0, 1) → (0, 0) → (1, 0) → (0, 1); (b) the square with vertices (0, 0), (1, 0), (1, 1), (0, 1) traversed counterclockwise.

Ex. 15.2: 34

Evaluate ∫C y dx − x dy along the curve C shown in Figure Ex-34: (a) the triangle with vertices (0, 0), (2, 0), (1, 1) traversed (0, 0) → (1, 1) → (2, 0) → (0, 0); (b) the semicircle from (−5, 0) to (5, 0) through (0, 5), then back along the x-axis.

Evaluate ∫C x2z dx − yx2 dy + 3 dz along the curve C shown in Figure Ex-35: the path in the unit cube from (0, 0, 0) along the x-axis to (1, 0, 0), then along the y-direction to (1, 1, 0), then vertically up to (1, 1, 1).

Find the mass of a thin wire shaped in the form of the circular arc y = √(9 − x2) (0 ≤ x ≤ 3) if the density function is δ(x, y) = x√y.

dx = dt, dy = −dt/t2. F · dr = (t2 + 1) dt + (1/t − t2)(−1/t2) dt = (t2 + 2 − t−3) dt. Work = ∫13 (t2 + 2 − t−3) dt = [t3/3 + 2t + 1/(2t2)]13 = 110/9.

Segment 1 (y = 3, dy = 0): ∫06 dx/(x2 + 9) = (1/3)tan−12. Segment 2 (x = 6, dx = 0): ∫30 4 dy/(36 + y2) = −(2/3)tan−1(1/2). Total (1/3)tan−12 − (2/3)tan−1(1/2) = π/6 − tan−1(1/2) ≈ 0.0600.

Use a line integral to find the area of the surface that extends upward from the parabola y = x2 (0 ≤ x ≤ 2) in the xy-plane to the plane z = 3x.

As illustrated in Figure Ex-53, a sinusoidal cut is made in the top of a cylindrical tin can. The base is modeled by x = cos t, y = sin t, z = 0 (0 ≤ t ≤ 2π), and the height of the cut is z = 2 + 0.5 sin 3t. (a) Use a geometric argument to find the lateral surface area of the cut can. (b) Write down a line integral for the surface area. (c) Use the line integral to calculate the surface area.

On the circle, x dy − y dx = a2 dt (with x = a cos t, y = a sin t), and x2 + y2 = a2, so the integrand is 1 dt. The curve −C is the clockwise traversal, t from 2π to 0, so the integral is ∫2π0 dt = −2π.

Ex. 15.2: 55

Suppose that a particle moves through the force field F(x, y) = xy i + (x − y) j from the point (0, 0) to the point (1, 0) along the curve x = t, y = λt(1 − t). For what value of λ will the work done by the force field be 1?

Work = ∫01 [xy + (x − y)λ(1 − 2t)] dt = ∫01 [λt2(1 − t) + λt(1 − 2t) − λ2t(1 − t)(1 − 2t)] dt = λ(1/12) + λ(−1/6) − λ2·0 = −λ/12. Setting −λ/12 = 1 gives λ = −12.

Answer: λ = −12.

Ex. 15.2: 56

A farmer weighing 150 lb carries a sack of grain weighing 20 lb up a circular helical staircase around a silo of radius 25 ft. As the farmer climbs, grain leaks from the sack at a rate of 1 lb per 10 ft of ascent. How much work is performed by the farmer in climbing through a vertical distance of 60 ft in exactly four revolutions? [Hint: Find a vector field that represents the force exerted by the farmer in lifting his own weight plus the weight of the sack upward at each point along his path.]

After ascending z ft, the sack weighs 20 − z/10 lb, so the total weight being lifted is 170 − z/10 lb. The force is F = (170 − z/10) k, and the work is ∫060 (170 − z/10) dz = 170·60 − 602/20 = 10,200 − 180 = 10,020 ft·lb. (The radius and the four revolutions do not affect the work, since the force is vertical and only the vertical displacement matters.)

Answer: 10,020 ft·lb.

Exercise Set 15.3

Ex. 15.3: 1

Determine whether F(x, y) = x i + y j is a conservative vector field. If so, find a potential function for it.

∂(x)/∂y = 0 = ∂(y)/∂x, so F is conservative on the whole plane. Integrating φx = x gives φ = x2/2 + h(y); then φy = h′(y) = y gives h = y2/2.

Answer: Conservative; φ(x, y) = x2/2 + y2/2 + K.

Ex. 15.3: 2

Determine whether F(x, y) = 3y2 i + 6xy j is a conservative vector field. If so, find a potential function for it.

∂(3y2)/∂y = 6y = ∂(6xy)/∂x, so F is conservative. Integrating φx = 3y2 gives φ = 3xy2 + h(y); then φy = 6xy + h′(y) = 6xy, so h is constant.

Answer: Conservative; φ(x, y) = 3xy2 + C.

Ex. 15.3: 3

Determine whether F(x, y) = x2y i + 5xy2 j is a conservative vector field. If so, find a potential function for it.

∂(x2y)/∂y = x2, but ∂(5xy2)/∂x = 5y2. These are not equal, so the cross-partial test fails.

Answer: Not conservative.

Ex. 15.3: 4

Determine whether F(x, y) = ex cos y i − ex sin y j is a conservative vector field. If so, find a potential function for it.

∂(ex cos y)/∂y = −ex sin y = ∂(−ex sin y)/∂x, so F is conservative. Integrating φx = ex cos y gives φ = ex cos y + h(y); then φy = −ex sin y + h′(y) = −ex sin y, so h is constant.

Answer: Conservative; φ(x, y) = ex cos y + C.

Ex. 15.3: 5

Determine whether F(x, y) = (cos y + y cos x) i + (sin x − x sin y) j is a conservative vector field. If so, find a potential function for it.

∂(cos y + y cos x)/∂y = −sin y + cos x = ∂(sin x − x sin y)/∂x, so F is conservative. Integrating φx = cos y + y cos x gives φ = x cos y + y sin x + h(y); then φy = −x sin y + sin x + h′(y) = sin x − x sin y, so h is constant.

Answer: Conservative; φ(x, y) = x cos y + y sin x + K.

Ex. 15.3: 6

Determine whether F(x, y) = x ln y i + y ln x j is a conservative vector field. If so, find a potential function for it.

∂(x ln y)/∂y = x/y, but ∂(y ln x)/∂x = y/x. These are equal only on the line y = x, not on any open region, so the cross-partial test fails.

Answer: Not conservative.

Ex. 15.3: 7

Evaluate ∫C 2xy3 dx + (1 + 3x2y2) dy over the curve C, and compare your answer with the result of Example 5. (a) C is the line segment from (1, 4) to (3, 1). (b) C consists of the line segment from (1, 4) to (1, 1), followed by the line segment from (1, 1) to (3, 1).

The field is conservative: ∂(2xy3)/∂y = 6xy2 = ∂(1 + 3x2y2)/∂x, with potential φ = x2y3 + y (check: φx = 2xy3, φy = 3x2y2 + 1). Hence the integral depends only on the endpoints: φ(3, 1) − φ(1, 4) = (9 + 1) − (64 + 4) = −58, for both (a) and (b). This agrees with Example 5.

Answer: (a) −58; (b) −58.

Ex. 15.3: 8

(a) Show that the line integral ∫C y sin x dx − cos x dy is independent of the path. (b) Evaluate the integral in part (a) along the line segment from (0, 1) to (π, −1). (c) Evaluate ∫(0,1)(π,−1) y sin x dx − cos x dy using Theorem 15.3.1, and confirm that the value is the same as that obtained in part (b).

(a) ∂(y sin x)/∂y = sin x = ∂(−cos x)/∂x, so the field is conservative with potential φ = −y cos x (φx = y sin x, φy = −cos x); hence the integral is path-independent. (b) Along the segment x = πt, y = 1 − 2t: ∫01 [(1 − 2t) sin πt · π + cos πt · 2] dt = 0 (the two terms cancel: the first integrates to −2 and the second to 2). (c) By Theorem 15.3.1, the integral is φ(π, −1) − φ(0, 1) = −(−1)cos π − (−1·cos 0) = −1 − (−1) = 0, confirming (b).

Answer: (a) Conservative, φ = −y cos x; (b) 0; (c) 0.

Ex. 15.3: 9

Show that the integral ∫(1,2)(4,0) 3y dx + 3x dy is independent of the path, and use Theorem 15.3.1 to find its value.

∂(3y)/∂y = 3 = ∂(3x)/∂x, so the field is conservative with potential φ = 3xy. By Theorem 15.3.1 the value is φ(4, 0) − φ(1, 2) = 0 − 6 = −6.

Answer: −6.

Ex. 15.3: 10

Show that the integral ∫(0,0)(1,π/2) ex sin y dx + ex cos y dy is independent of the path, and use Theorem 15.3.1 to find its value.

∂(ex sin y)/∂y = ex cos y = ∂(ex cos y)/∂x, so the field is conservative with potential φ = ex sin y. The value is φ(1, π/2) − φ(0, 0) = e·1 − 0 = e.

Answer: e.

Ex. 15.3: 11

Show that the integral ∫(0,0)(3,2) 2xey dx + x2ey dy is independent of the path, and use Theorem 15.3.1 to find its value.

∂(2xey)/∂y = 2xey = ∂(x2ey)/∂x, so the field is conservative with potential φ = x2ey. The value is φ(3, 2) − φ(0, 0) = 9e2 − 0 = 9e2.

Answer: 9e2.

Ex. 15.3: 12

Show that the integral ∫(−1,2)(0,1) (3x − y + 1) dx − (x + 4y + 2) dy is independent of the path, and use Theorem 15.3.1 to find its value.

∂(3x − y + 1)/∂y = −1 = ∂(−x − 4y − 2)/∂x, so the field is conservative. Integrating φx = 3x − y + 1 gives φ = 3x2/2 − xy + x + h(y); φy = −x + h′(y) = −x − 4y − 2 gives h = −2y2 − 2y. So φ = 3x2/2 − xy + x − 2y2 − 2y, and the value is φ(0, 1) − φ(−1, 2) = (−4) − (−19/2) = 11/2.

Answer: 11/2.

Ex. 15.3: 13

Show that the integral ∫(2,−2)(−1,0) 2xy3 dx + 3y2x2 dy is independent of the path, and use Theorem 15.3.1 to find its value.

∂(2xy3)/∂y = 6xy2 = ∂(3y2x2)/∂x, so the field is conservative with potential φ = x2y3. The value is φ(−1, 0) − φ(2, −2) = 0 − (4·(−8)) = 32.

Answer: 32.

Ex. 15.3: 14

Show that the integral ∫(1,1)(3,3) (ex ln y − ey/x) dx + (ex/y − ey ln x) dy, where x and y are positive, is independent of the path, and use Theorem 15.3.1 to find its value.

∂(ex ln y − ey/x)/∂y = ex/y − ey/x = ∂(ex/y − ey ln x)/∂x, so the field is conservative on x > 0, y > 0, with potential φ = ex ln y − ey ln x. The value is φ(3, 3) − φ(1, 1) = (e3 ln 3 − e3 ln 3) − 0 = 0.

Answer: 0.

Ex. 15.3: 15

Confirm that the force field F(x, y) = xy2 i + x2y j is conservative in some open connected region containing P(1, 1) and Q(0, 0), and then find the work done by the force field on a particle moving along an arbitrary smooth curve in the region from P to Q.

∂(xy2)/∂y = 2xy = ∂(x2y)/∂x, so F is conservative on the whole plane, with potential φ = x2y2/2. Work = φ(Q) − φ(P) = 0 − 1/2 = −1/2.

Answer: W = −1/2.

Ex. 15.3: 16

Confirm that the force field F(x, y) = 2xy3 i + 3x2y2 j is conservative in some open connected region containing P(−3, 0) and Q(4, 1), and then find the work done by the force field on a particle moving along an arbitrary smooth curve in the region from P to Q.

∂(2xy3)/∂y = 6xy2 = ∂(3x2y2)/∂x, so F is conservative on the whole plane, with potential φ = x2y3. Work = φ(4, 1) − φ(−3, 0) = 16 − 0 = 16.

Answer: W = 16.

Ex. 15.3: 17

Confirm that the force field F(x, y) = yexy i + xexy j is conservative in some open connected region containing P(−1, 1) and Q(2, 0), and then find the work done by the force field on a particle moving along an arbitrary smooth curve in the region from P to Q.

∂(yexy)/∂y = exy + xyexy = ∂(xexy)/∂x, so F is conservative on the whole plane, with potential φ = exy. Work = φ(2, 0) − φ(−1, 1) = 1 − e−1.

Answer: W = 1 − e−1.

Ex. 15.3: 18

Confirm that the force field F(x, y) = e−y cos x i − e−y sin x j is conservative in some open connected region containing P(π/2, 1) and Q(−π/2, 0), and then find the work done by the force field on a particle moving along an arbitrary smooth curve in the region from P to Q.

∂(e−y cos x)/∂y = −e−y cos x = ∂(−e−y sin x)/∂x, so F is conservative on the whole plane, with potential φ = e−y sin x. Work = φ(−π/2, 0) − φ(π/2, 1) = sin(−π/2) − e−1 sin(π/2) = −1 − e−1.

Answer: W = −1 − e−1.

Lecture 20 — Green's Theorem (Anton §15.4)

Instead of walking all the way round the fence of a field and adding up the wind's push at every step, Green's Theorem lets you count the total spin inside the field — one double integral over the region instead of a long line integral round its edge.

Last lecture you learned to walk along a curve and add up the push of a vector field — the line integral ∮C P dx + Q dy round a closed curve C. Now imagine that curve is the fence round a field, and the walk is long and awkward. Green's Theorem gives you a shortcut: instead of walking the fence, you can stand inside the field and add up the tiny bits of spin at every point inside it. The total spin inside equals the total circulation round the fence. That is the whole theorem in one picture.

What is "spin" here? For a field F = P i + Q j, the spin at a point is the number ∂Q/∂x − ∂P/∂y. Think of it as the curl of the field, flattened into two dimensions: it measures how much the field is swirling anticlockwise around that point, like a tiny whirlpool. If the field swirls anticlockwise everywhere, the total circulation round the fence is positive; if it swirls clockwise, it is negative. The theorem says: ∮C P dx + Q dy = ∬R (∂Q/∂x − ∂P/∂y) dA, where R is the region enclosed by C.

There are conditions, and the exam loves to test them. First, C must be a closed curve — a fence with no gaps. Green's Theorem says nothing about an open path. Second, C must be travelled counterclockwise, so that the region R is always on your left as you walk. Walk it clockwise and the answer flips sign — that is the single most common lost mark in this lecture. Third, the region R must be simply connected (no holes), and P and Q must have continuous first partial derivatives there. If the region has a hole, the inner boundary must be walked clockwise — the hole's fence goes the other way round.

Here is how to use it in an exam, in three steps. Step 1: read off P and Q from the line integral — P is the thing multiplying dx, Q is the thing multiplying dy. Step 2: compute ∂Q/∂x − ∂P/∂y, and simplify it first before you do anything else. Very often it collapses to something simple — a constant, or even zero. Step 3: set up the double integral over R, and use symmetry. If the integrand is an odd function over a symmetric region, its integral is zero and you are done in seconds.

Two spin-offs are worth knowing. First, the area of a region can be found from a line integral: A = ∮ x dy = −∮ y dx = ½∮(−y dx + x dy). This is the mathematics behind the planimeter, a little instrument that measures the area of a shape just by tracing round its edge. Second, the work done by a force field round a closed loop is the double integral of the spin — so if the spin is zero everywhere, the work round any closed loop is zero, which is exactly what it means for the field to be conservative. Green's Theorem is the bridge between Lecture 19 and everything that follows.

One last piece of exam wisdom, straight from the verified answers: problems 1, 2, 3, 5, 12 and 13 of Exercise 15.4 all have answer zero. If you get a non-zero answer for one of those, do not re-check your double integral — re-check your partial derivatives, because that is where the mistake almost certainly is. And problems 6, 7 and 11 are "integrand is constant" problems in disguise: once you simplify ∂Q/∂x − ∂P/∂y to a constant, the double integral is just that constant times the area of the region.

It helps to see why anyone would want this theorem. Parametrising a closed curve and integrating round it is usually the hardest part of a line-integral problem — the parametrisation is awkward, the dot product is messy, and the integral is long. Green's Theorem is a trade: instead of measuring something on the boundary, you measure something inside, where the region is often a simple disk, rectangle or triangle and the integral is easy. Here is the picture to hold in your head. Imagine a pond with water swirling in it. You want the total circulation round the edge of the pond. You could walk all the way round the bank measuring the flow at every step — or you could add up the spin of every little whirlpool inside the pond. Both give the same number, because every whirlpool's spin contributes to the flow past its neighbours, and the interior contributions cancel in pairs, leaving only the flow round the outer edge. That cancellation is the same idea you will meet again in Lecture 22, in three dimensions.

So what is the theorem really saying? It says that circulation — a boundary quantity — is the same thing as total spin — an interior quantity. The number ∂Q/∂x − ∂P/∂y is the spin at a single point: positive where the field turns anticlockwise, negative where it turns clockwise, zero where it does not turn at all. If the field is conservative, the spin is zero everywhere (that is just the test ∂f/∂y = ∂g/∂x again, rearranged), and the theorem tells you the circulation round every closed loop is zero — which is exactly what conservative means. Green's Theorem is the bridge that connects Lecture 19 to everything after it. There is also a second version of the theorem, the normal form, where the boundary integral measures the flow across the curve instead of along it, and the interior integral is the divergence instead of the spin — that version is the two-dimensional ancestor of the Divergence Theorem in Lecture 22.

Here is where students get stuck, and it is almost never the double integral. First, the conditions: the curve must be closed, travelled counterclockwise, and the region must have no holes. A hole changes the rules — the inner boundary has to be walked clockwise, so that the region stays on your left everywhere. Second, reading P and Q: P is whatever multiplies dx, Q is whatever multiplies dy, and swapping them is a silent error that no later step will catch. Third, forgetting to simplify ∂Q/∂x − ∂P/∂y before setting up the double integral. The simplification is the whole point of the exercise — if the spin collapses to a constant, the double integral is just that constant times the area, and if it collapses to zero, you are done.

Mini-example — Ex. 15.4-6 (verified answer from the guide). Evaluate ∮ y tan²x dx + tan x dy, where C is the circle x² + (y + 1)² = 1, travelled counterclockwise. Read off P = y tan²x and Q = tan x. Then ∂Q/∂x = sec²x and ∂P/∂y = tan²x, so the spin is ∂Q/∂x − ∂P/∂y = sec²x − tan²x = 1 — the trigonometric identity does all the work. By Green's Theorem the line integral equals ∬R 1 dA over the disk, which is just the area of the unit disk: π. A problem that looks terrifying from the boundary becomes one line from the inside. That is the pattern to recognise: whenever the spin simplifies to a constant, the answer is that constant times the area — and Ex. 15.4-7 works the same way, with spin 1 + 1 = 2 over a disk of radius 2, giving 8π.

∮C P dx + Q dy = ∬R (∂Q/∂x − ∂P/∂y) dA — Green's Theorem (C simple, closed, piecewise-smooth, counterclockwise; R simply connected).

Area: A = ∮C x dy = −∮C y dx = ½ ∮C (−y dx + x dy) — the planimeter formulas.

Work: W = ∮C F · dr = ∬R (∂Q/∂x − ∂P/∂y) dA for F = P i + Q j.

Method: (1) read off P, Q; (2) compute and simplify ∂Q/∂x − ∂P/∂y first; (3) set up the double integral, use symmetry.

Worked example — Ex. 15.4-4 (verified answer from the guide). Evaluate ∮ (x² − y²) dx + x dy, where C is the circle x² + y² = 9, travelled counterclockwise.

Step 1 — Read off P and Q. P = x² − y² (the thing multiplying dx) and Q = x (the thing multiplying dy).

Step 2 — Compute the spin and simplify first. ∂Q/∂x = 1, and ∂P/∂y = −2y, so ∂Q/∂x − ∂P/∂y = 1 − (−2y) = 1 + 2y.

Step 3 — Set up the double integral over the disk. By Green's Theorem the line integral equals ∬R (1 + 2y) dA over the disk of radius 3.

Step 4 — Split it and use symmetry. ∬R 1 dA is just the area of the disk, π·3² = 9π. And ∬R 2y dA = 0, because 2y is an odd function of y and the disk is symmetric top-to-bottom — every positive bit cancels a negative bit.

Answer: 9π.

Watch out: Green's Theorem needs a closed curve travelled counterclockwise — walk it clockwise and the sign flips, and it does not apply to an open path at all.

  • In one sentence, what does Green's Theorem let you replace, and what do you replace it with?
  • What is the "spin" ∂Q/∂x − ∂P/∂y, and why should you simplify it before setting up the double integral?
  • What happens to the answer if C is travelled clockwise instead of counterclockwise?
  • How can you find the area of a region using only a line integral round its boundary?

Ex. 15.4 (1–13): evaluate by Green's Theorem, then check directly (1–2): 1. ∮ y² dx + x² dy, unit square, CCW; 2. ∮ y dx + x dy, unit circle, CCW. Use Green's Theorem, C CCW (3–13): 3. ∮ 3xy dx + 2xy dy, rectangle x∈[−2,4], y∈[1,2]; 4. ∮ (x²−y²) dx + x dy, circle x²+y²=9; 5. ∮ x cos y dx − y sin x dy, square [0,π/2]²; 6. ∮ y tan²x dx + tan x dy, circle x²+(y+1)²=1; 7. ∮ (x²−y) dx + x dy, circle x²+y²=4; 8. ∮ (ex+y²) dx + (ey+x²) dy, between y = x² and y = x; 9. ∮ ln(1+y) dx − xy/(1+y) dy, triangle (0,0),(2,0),(0,4); 10. ∮ x²y dx − y²x dy, first quadrant inside x²+y²=16 (polar); 11. ∮ tan−1y dx − xy²/(1+y²) dy, unit square; 12. ∮ cos x sin y dx + sin x cos y dy, triangle (0,0),(3,3),(0,3); 13. ∮ x²y dx + (y+xy²) dy, between y = x² and x = y².

Pattern to remember: problems 1, 2, 3, 5, 12, 13 are all 0 — a non-zero answer there means recheck the partials, not the double integral; problems 6, 7, 11 are "integrand is constant" problems, i.e. area problems in disguise.

Lecture 20 — Green's Theorem (§15.4)

Green's Theorem (for C counterclockwise): ∮C P dx + Q dy = ∬R (∂Q/∂x − ∂P/∂y) dA.

Exercise Set 15.4

Ex. 15.4: 1

Evaluate the line integral ∮C y2 dx + x2 dy using Green's Theorem and check by evaluating it directly, where C is the square with vertices (0, 0), (1, 0), (1, 1), (0, 1), oriented counterclockwise.

∂Q/∂x − ∂P/∂y = 2x − 2y. By Green's Theorem the integral is ∬[0,1]² (2x − 2y) dA = 0, since ∫01∫01 2x dx dy = 1 and ∫01∫01 2y dx dy = 1. Direct check: the bottom and top edges contribute ∫01 x2 dx = 1/3 and ∫10 x2 dx = −1/3; the left and right edges contribute ∫01 y2 dy = 1/3 and ∫10 y2 dy = −1/3; total 0.

Answer: 0.

Ex. 15.4: 2

Evaluate the line integral ∮C y dx + x dy using Green's Theorem and check by evaluating it directly, where C is the unit circle oriented counterclockwise.

∂Q/∂x − ∂P/∂y = 1 − 1 = 0, so by Green's Theorem the integral is ∬R 0 dA = 0. Direct check: with x = cos t, y = sin t, the integrand is (sin t)(−sin t) + (cos t)(cos t) = cos 2t, whose integral over [0, 2π] is 0.

Answer: 0.

Ex. 15.4: 3

Evaluate ∮C 3xy dx + 2xy dy, where C is the rectangle bounded by x = −2, x = 4, y = 1, and y = 2, oriented counterclockwise.

∂Q/∂x − ∂P/∂y = 2y − 3x. ∬R (2y − 3x) dA = ∫12∫−24 (2y − 3x) dx dy = ∫12 (12y − 18) dy = [6y2 − 18y]12 = (−12) − (−12) = 0.

Answer: 0.

Ex. 15.4: 4

Evaluate ∮C (x2 − y2) dx + x dy, where C is the circle x2 + y2 = 9, oriented counterclockwise.

∂Q/∂x − ∂P/∂y = 1 + 2y. ∬R (1 + 2y) dA = (area of R)·1 + 2∬R y dA = 9π + 0 (the y-integral vanishes by symmetry about the x-axis).

Answer: 9π.

Ex. 15.4: 5

Evaluate ∮C x cos y dx − y sin x dy, where C is the square with vertices (0, 0), (π/2, 0), (π/2, π/2), and (0, π/2), oriented counterclockwise.

∂Q/∂x − ∂P/∂y = −y cos x + x sin y. ∬R (−y cos x + x sin y) dA = −(∫0π/2 cos x dx)(∫0π/2 y dy) + (∫0π/2 x dx)(∫0π/2 sin y dy) = −(1)(π2/8) + (π2/8)(1) = 0.

Answer: 0.

Ex. 15.4: 6

Evaluate ∮C y tan2x dx + tan x dy, where C is the circle x2 + (y + 1)2 = 1, oriented counterclockwise.

∂Q/∂x − ∂P/∂y = sec2x − tan2x = 1. Hence the integral is ∬R 1 dA = area of the disk = π.

Answer: π.

Ex. 15.4: 7

Evaluate ∮C (x2 − y) dx + x dy, where C is the circle x2 + y2 = 4, oriented counterclockwise.

∂Q/∂x − ∂P/∂y = 1 + 1 = 2. Hence the integral is ∬R 2 dA = 2·(area) = 2·4π = 8π.

Answer: 8π.

Ex. 15.4: 8

Evaluate ∮C (ex + y2) dx + (ey + x2) dy, where C is the boundary of the region between y = x2 and y = x, oriented counterclockwise.

∂Q/∂x − ∂P/∂y = 2x − 2y. The region is 0 ≤ x ≤ 1, x2 ≤ y ≤ x. ∬R (2x − 2y) dA = ∫01 [2xy − y2]x²x dx = ∫01 (x2 − 2x3 + x4) dx = 1/3 − 1/2 + 1/5 = 1/30.

Answer: 1/30.

Ex. 15.4: 9

Evaluate ∮C ln(1 + y) dx − (xy/(1 + y)) dy, where C is the triangle with vertices (0, 0), (2, 0), and (0, 4), oriented counterclockwise.

∂Q/∂x − ∂P/∂y = −y/(1 + y) − 1/(1 + y) = −1. Hence the integral is ∬R (−1) dA = −(area of the triangle) = −(1/2·2·4) = −4.

Answer: −4.

Ex. 15.4: 10

Evaluate ∮C x2y dx − y2x dy, where C is the boundary of the region in the first quadrant, enclosed between the coordinate axes and the circle x2 + y2 = 16, oriented counterclockwise.

∂Q/∂x − ∂P/∂y = −y2 − x2 = −(x2 + y2). In polar coordinates the integral is ∬R −r2 dA = −∫0π/2∫04 r3 dr dθ = −(π/2)(64) = −32π.

Answer: −32π.

Ex. 15.4: 11

Evaluate ∮C tan−1y dx − (y2x/(1 + y2)) dy, where C is the square with vertices (0, 0), (1, 0), (1, 1), and (0, 1), oriented counterclockwise.

∂Q/∂x − ∂P/∂y = −y2/(1 + y2) − 1/(1 + y2) = −1. Hence the integral is ∬[0,1]² (−1) dA = −1.

Answer: −1.

Ex. 15.4: 12

Evaluate ∮C cos x sin y dx + sin x cos y dy, where C is the triangle with vertices (0, 0), (3, 3), and (0, 3), oriented counterclockwise.

∂Q/∂x − ∂P/∂y = cos x cos y − cos x cos y = 0. Hence the integral is ∬R 0 dA = 0. (Indeed the field is conservative, with potential sin x sin y.)

Answer: 0.

Ex. 15.4: 13

Evaluate ∮C x2y dx + (y + xy2) dy, where C is the boundary of the region enclosed by y = x2 and x = y2, oriented counterclockwise.

∂Q/∂x − ∂P/∂y = y2 − x2. The region is 0 ≤ x ≤ 1, x2 ≤ y ≤ √x. ∬R (y2 − x2) dA = ∫01 [y3/3 − x2y]x²√x dx = ∫01 (x3/2/3 − x5/2 − x6/3 + x4) dx = 2/15 − 2/7 − 1/21 + 1/5 = 0.

Answer: 0.

Lecture 21 — Surface Area, Surface Integrals & Flux (Anton §14.4, §15.5–15.6)

A line integral adds things up along a curve; this lecture does the same thing on a surface — its area, the total of some quantity spread over it, and the amount of fluid flowing through it.

Everything in this lecture is a lift from one dimension to two. In Lecture 19 you added things up along a curve. Now the curve becomes a surface — a curved sheet in space, like a bowl, a sphere, or a bent piece of tin — and you add things up over the whole sheet. There are three questions you can ask about a surface, and this lecture answers all three: how big is it (surface area), how much of something is spread over it (surface integral), and how much fluid flows through it (flux).

Start with area. A flat sheet is easy, but a curved sheet is tilted, and tilted things have more area than their shadow on the floor. For a surface given as a graph z = f(x, y) over a region R in the xy-plane, the area is S = ∬R √[(∂z/∂x)² + (∂z/∂y)² + 1] dA. That square root is the "tilt factor": it measures how steep the surface is at each point, and it is always at least 1, so the area is always bigger than the area of the flat shadow R. The classic example is the paraboloid z = x² + y² below z = 1, whose area is π(5√5 − 1)/6 — you work it in polar coordinates, because the shadow is the unit disk.

But not every surface is a graph — a sphere is not, because it has a top and a bottom over the same point. So we describe surfaces parametrically: r(u, v) = x(u, v)i + y(u, v)j + z(u, v)k, where two parameters u and v sweep out the sheet the way latitude and longitude sweep out the Earth. The two little tangent arrows ru and rv span a tiny parallelogram on the surface, and its area is |ru × rv| — the cross product gives both the size of the patch and, in its direction, the normal to the surface. The unit normal is n = (ru × rv)/|ru × rv|. A surface is smooth wherever ru × rv ≠ 0; at the poles of a sphere the parametrisation fails, which is allowed as long as it only fails on the boundary.

Once you can measure area, a surface integral is the natural next step: ∬σ f dS adds up a quantity f spread over the surface σ. If f is 1, you get the area back. If f is a density, you get the mass of a curved lamina. The recipe is always the same: put the surface into parametric form (or graph form), and replace dS by |ru × rv| dA — or by √[gx² + gy² + 1] dA for a graph z = g(x, y). The most common exam mistake in the whole lecture is writing dS = dA and forgetting that factor. And symmetry can save you a whole page of work: on the unit sphere, ∬ x² dS = ∬ y² dS = ∬ z² dS, and since x² + y² + z² = 1 there, each one is a third of the sphere's area, 4π/3 — no integration needed.

Finally, flux. Imagine the surface is a fishing net held in a river, and F is the velocity of the water. Flux is the net volume of water crossing the net per unit time: Φ = ∬σ F · n dS. The dot product with the normal n is everything: only the part of the flow that goes through the net counts. Water sliding along the net contributes nothing. That is why the parametric formula is Φ = ∬R F · (ru × rv) dA — notice the vector cross product, not its magnitude: the direction of ru × rv carries the orientation, and swapping u and v flips the sign. For a closed surface, outward is positive by convention. For a graph z = g(x, y) oriented upward, Φ = ∬R F · ⟨−zx, −zy, 1⟩ dA; oriented downward, negate it. Flux is a single number, not a vector — and zero net flux does not mean the field is everywhere tangent to the surface; it only means as much flows in as flows out.

The best drill problem in this lecture is §15.6 Ex. 11: the flux of F = x i + y j + 2z k across the paraboloid z = 1 − x² − y² above the xy-plane, oriented up. It uses the graph-flux formula, polar coordinates, and the integrand collapses to the constant 2 — which is exactly the kind of collapse the examiners love. Work it below, then try the rest of the practice list.

Step back and ask why this lecture exists. Double integrals (Lectures 14–18) answer one kind of question: how much volume sits under a surface, or how much of something is spread over a flat region. But a surface is a thing in its own right — a curved sheet in space, like a bowl, a sail, or a piece of tin bent into shape — and you can ask three different questions about the sheet itself: how big is it, how much stuff is spread over it, and how much fluid passes through it. This lecture answers all three, and all three are the same idea you have already met, lifted one dimension higher: a line integral adds things up along a curve, a surface integral adds things up over a surface. The recipe never changes — chop the object into tiny pieces, measure the piece, add them up.

The first question, area, has one idea that catches everyone out: a tilted patch has more area than its flat shadow. Think of a roof and the floor plan of the house beneath it. The floor plan is the shadow; the roof itself is bigger, and the steeper the roof, the bigger the difference. The tilt factor √[(∂z/∂x)² + (∂z/∂y)² + 1] is exactly that ratio — how much bigger the real patch is than its shadow — and it is always at least 1, because a surface can never be smaller than its own shadow. For a flat surface the partial derivatives are zero, the factor is 1, and the area is just the area of the shadow, as it should be.

The second idea that needs slow thinking is the parametrisation. A graph z = f(x, y) only works when the surface has one height over each point of the floor — a sphere fails, because it has a top and a bottom over the same point. So instead you describe the surface with two parameters, u and v, the way latitude and longitude describe the Earth: as u and v vary, the point r(u, v) sweeps out the sheet. The two little arrows ru and rv are tangent to the surface, and their cross product does two jobs at once — its length |ru × rv| is the area of the tiny patch, and its direction is the normal to the surface. One calculation, both answers. Note the honest limitation the book admits: the sphere's parametrisation fails at the poles (φ = 0 and φ = π), where all the longitude lines meet — exactly like the North Pole on a map. That is allowed as long as it only fails on the boundary of the parameter region.

Flux deserves its own slow paragraph, because it is the idea students misunderstand most. Flux is a net quantity: water can cross the net in both directions, and flux counts what goes through one way minus what comes back the other way. So zero net flux does not mean nothing is flowing — it means as much flows in as flows out, like a room with the same number of people entering and leaving. And flux needs the surface to have two distinct sides, so that "through, this way" means something — a Möbius strip, which has only one side, is excluded from the theory for exactly this reason. Finally, notice the difference between the two surface integrals: ∬ f dS adds up a number spread over the surface (a density, giving a mass), while ∬ F · n dS adds up a flow through it. Confusing the two is a common exam error — the first takes the magnitude |ru × rv|, the second must keep the vector ru × rv, because the direction carries the orientation.

Mini-example 1 — surface area, Ex. 14.4-2 (verified answer from the guide). Find the area of the portion of the plane 2x + 2y + z = 8 in the first octant. The plane is a graph, z = 8 − 2x − 2y, so ∂z/∂x = −2 and ∂z/∂y = −2, and the tilt factor is √[1 + 4 + 4] = 3 — the plane is tilted enough that every patch is three times its shadow. The shadow R is the triangle in the xy-plane with intercepts (4, 0) and (0, 4), whose area is 8. So the surface area is S = 3 × 8 = 24. A constant tilt factor means you never integrate at all — you just multiply.

Mini-example 2 — symmetry, Ex. 15.5-1 (verified answer from the guide). Evaluate ∬σ x² dS over the unit sphere. Integrating x² over a sphere directly is horrible. But the sphere is perfectly symmetric: x, y and z play identical roles, so ∬ x² dS = ∬ y² dS = ∬ z² dS. Add all three together and you get ∬ (x² + y² + z²) dS — and on the unit sphere x² + y² + z² = 1, so that sum is just ∬ 1 dS, the area of the sphere, 4π. Each of the three equal integrals is therefore a third of it: 4π/3. No integration needed. The same trick — odd powers integrate to zero, even powers split equally — is what the guide's symmetry shortcuts (Ex. 15–18) are built on, and it is worth reaching for before you ever set up an integral.

Graph z = f(x, y) over R: S = ∬R √[(∂z/∂x)² + (∂z/∂y)² + 1] dA — surface area; the square root is the tilt factor.

Parametric surface r(u, v): S = ∬R |ru × rv| dA; unit normal n = (ru × rv)/|ru × rv|.

Surface integral: ∬σ f dS = ∬R f(x(u, v), …) |ru × rv| dA; for a graph z = g(x, y): ∬σ f dS = ∬R f(x, y, g(x, y)) √[gx² + gy² + 1] dA.

Flux: Φ = ∬σ F · n dS = ∬R F · (ru × rv) dA — note the vector cross product, not its magnitude.

Graph, oriented up: Φ = ∬R F · ⟨−zx, −zy, 1⟩ dA; oriented down, negate. Also Φ = ∬R F · ∇G dA.

Sphere: r = a sin φ cos θ i + a sin φ sin θ j + a cos φ k; outward normal n = r/a.

Worked example — Ex. 15.6-11 (verified answer from the guide; the guide calls it the single best drill problem for this lecture). Find the flux of F = x i + y j + 2z k across the portion of the paraboloid z = 1 − x² − y² above the xy-plane, with upward normals.

Step 1 — Write the surface as G = 0 and find ∇G. Put G = z − 1 + x² + y², so ∇G = ⟨2x, 2y, 1⟩. This points upward (its z-component is +1), which matches the required orientation.

Step 2 — Form the dot product F · ∇G. F · ∇G = x(2x) + y(2y) + 2z(1) = 2x² + 2y² + 2z.

Step 3 — Use the surface equation to simplify. On the surface, z = 1 − x² − y², so 2x² + 2y² + 2z = 2x² + 2y² + 2(1 − x² − y²) = 2. The integrand collapses to the constant 2 — this is the collapse the examiners love.

Step 4 — Integrate over the shadow R. The shadow is the unit disk x² + y² ≤ 1 (where z = 0), whose area is π. So Φ = ∬R 2 dA = 2π.

Answer: 2π.

Watch out: writing dS = dA and forgetting the tilt factor √[1 + zx² + zy²] (or |ru × rv|) is the most common exam mistake in this lecture — and in flux, use the vector ru × rv, never its magnitude, because the direction carries the orientation.

  • Why is the area of a curved surface always bigger than the area of its flat shadow, and what factor corrects for it?
  • What is a parametric surface, and how do ru and rv give you both the area of a patch and the normal to the surface?
  • What is the difference between a surface integral ∬ f dS and a flux integral ∬ F · n dS — and what does each one measure?
  • What happens to the flux if you reverse the orientation of the surface, and why must you not take the magnitude of ru × rv in the flux formula?

Ex. 14.4 (1–10) — surface area as a double integral: 1. portion of cylinder y² + z² = 9 above R = {(x,y): 0 ≤ x ≤ 2, −3 ≤ y ≤ 3}; 2. portion of plane 2x + 2y + z = 8 in the first octant; 3. portion of cone z² = 4x² + 4y² above the first-quadrant region bounded by y = x and y = x²; 4. portion of z = 2x + y² above the triangle (0,0),(0,1),(1,1); 5. portion of cone z = √(x²+y²) inside cylinder x² + y² = 2x; 6. portion of paraboloid z = 1 − x² − y² above the xy-plane; 7. portion of z = xy above the first-quadrant sector bounded by y = x/√3, y = 0, circle x² + y² = 9; 8. portion of paraboloid 2z = x² + y² inside cylinder x² + y² = 8; 9. portion of sphere x² + y² + z² = 16 between planes z = 1 and z = 2; 10. portion of sphere x² + y² + z² = 8 inside cone z = √(x²+y²).

Ex. 15.5 (1–8, 13, 14, 35–38) — surface integrals: evaluate ∬σ f dS (1–8); improper integrals, by a limit and by reparametrisation (13, 14); ∬σ f dS over a given r(u,v) (35–38).

Ex. 15.6 (9–22) — flux: flux across a graph / plane / cone / paraboloid (9–16); flux across a given r(u,v), positive orientation (17–20); closed surfaces — cube and capped paraboloid (21, 22).
